This guide takes you from "I have never heard of Test Data Management" to "I can sit in front of three real tools and use them". It is written for the 60-day programme whose syllabus you will find mapped chapter by chapter further down this page. This first chapter is a map. What Test Data Management (TDM) is, in one paragraph, and where the rest of the guide goes deeper. What the three tools are (Informatica TDM, GenRocket, Delphix) and why a programme would teach three. How each chapter is built, what the coloured boxes mean, and how to use search and the theme toggle. A study plan that ties syllabus days 43 to 60 to chapters. ( the why-TDM chapter ) Production The live system real customers use, holding real data. Also called "prod". ( the why-TDM chapter ) Non-production environment Any copy of the application that is not live: development, QA, UAT, staging. Testing happens here. ( the why-TDM chapter ) Masking Replacing real sensitive values (a real name, a real ID number) with realistic but fake ones. ( the masking concepts chapter ) Subsetting Taking a small, consistent slice of a big database instead of all of it. ( the discovery and subsetting concepts chapter ) Synthetic data Data created by a program from rules, not copied from real people. ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
h: 1.2 What TDM is, in one paragraph
x: 1.2 What TDM is, in one paragraph Test Data Management is the discipline of getting the right data to the people who test software, at the right time, without exposing anyone's private information. Testers need data that looks and behaves like real data. The easy way to get it is to copy the live database, but that copy contains real people's names, phone numbers and ID numbers, it is huge, and it goes stale. So TDM teams find the sensitive values ( discovery ), cut the data down to a usable size ( subsetting ), replace sensitive values with fake ones ( masking ), create brand-new data from rules where no real data fits ( generation ), and deliver fresh copies on request ( provisioning ). the why-TDM chapter explains each of these properly, starting from why testing needs data at all. The Informatica documentation frames the same idea from the tool side: an organisation creates a smaller copy of production data, masks the sensitive data, finds the sensitive columns, and can create test data that never contained sensitive values (Informatica TDM 10.5.10 User Guide, p.21).

h: 1.3.1 Why three tools and not one?
x: 1.3.1 Why three tools and not one? The syllabus does not explain this, so here is an honest answer in two parts. The programme's choice. Which tools are taught is decided by the programme and the organisation behind it. If you want the business reason, ask your trainer. What you gain from seeing three. From reading the three documentation sets, each product puts its weight in a different place. Informatica presents discovery, subset, masking and generation together in one client. GenRocket is built around generating data from scratch. Delphix is built around masking plus fast delivery of copies. Seeing the same ideas in three products teaches you the idea, not a menu. A TDM engineer who knows what masking is can pick up a fourth tool quickly. The second part is my reading of the documentation, not a statement from any vendor. Why this matters Beginners often learn "click here, then here" for one tool and are lost when the project uses another. This guide teaches the concept first (Part I), then shows each tool as one way to carry out that concept. When two tools do the same job you will see the same concept page referenced from both.

Why Test Data Management exists Every tool in this guide exists to solve one problem: software has to be tested, testing needs data, and the obvious source of data (the live system) is the one place you must not copy carelessly. This section builds that argument from zero. By the end you will understand why a whole discipline, Test Data Management, grew up around what looks like a small chore. It is the first chapter of the programme syllabus (Day 43: "Importance of test data in testing, COTS product overview, partnership, Cog IPs, TDM architecture"). The architecture of each tool comes later; here we deal with the importance of test data and the product landscape. Read the start-here chapter first if you have not yet met ShopSphere, the fictional company used throughout. What you will learn What software testing is, and why it cannot happen without data. What dev, QA, UAT, staging and production environments are, in plain words. The "copy production" shortcut and the eight things that go wrong with it. What TDM is, its goals, and its six capabilities: discover, subset, mask, generate, provision, govern. Who does what in a TDM effort, and how it plays out in real ShopSphere scenarios. Benefits, trade-offs, and the usual stages of TDM maturity. What "COTS" means, and what the programme's three tools are. x: 1.5 Words to know first Software testing Checking, before real users rely on it, that a program does what it should and does not break when something unexpected happens. Test case One specific check: "do this, with this data, and expect that result". Example: place an order for a customer with no previous orders and expect a confirmation. Test data The data a test case needs: the customers, products and orders that exist before the test starts, and the values typed in during it. Environment A complete running copy of the application with its own servers and its own database. Different environments serve different purposes. Production (prod) The live environment used by real customers. It holds real data. Non-production Every environment that is not production: dev, QA, UAT, staging and so on. Sensitive data Information that would harm a person or the company if leaked: names with ID numbers, health records, card numbers. The sensitive data and regulations chapter covers it fully. Refresh Replacing the data in a test environment with a newer copy. Edge case An unusual but possible input, such as an empty name, a very long address or a date on 29 February. COTS Commercial off-the-shelf: software you buy ready-made from a vendor and configure, instead of building it yourself. TDM Test Data Management, the subject of this guide.

h: 1.6 What software testing is, and why it needs data
x: 1.6 What software testing is, and why it needs data

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.6.1 Testing in brief Imagine ShopSphere's developers have just changed how discounts are calculated. Before the change reaches real shoppers, someone has to check it. They log into a copy of the app, place an order, and look at the total. If the discount is wrong, they report a bug. That checking is software testing . Testing is not a single activity. Teams run many kinds: a developer checks one function, a QA engineer clicks through a whole purchase, a performance tester sends thousands of orders at once, a business user confirms the app does what the business asked. They all share one need.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
h: 1.6.2 An application without data does nothing
x: 1.6.2 An application without data does nothing An online shop with an empty database has no customers to log in, no products to buy, no orders to total. A test that says "check the discount for a returning customer" needs a returning customer to exist. So before the test starts, the environment must already contain: customers with the right attributes (a returning customer, a new one, one with an expired card); products with prices; earlier orders for those customers, linked correctly to them. That pre-loaded information is test data. It is as essential to a test as the code under test. Why this matters Bad test data produces two kinds of waste. Tests that should pass fail because the data is wrong (a false alarm that costs a developer an afternoon). Or tests pass when they should fail because the data never contained the tricky case (a bug reaches customers). Good data is not a luxury; it decides whether the test result can be trusted.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.6.3 What makes test data "good"? Testers usually want data that is: Quality Meaning ShopSphere example Realistic Looks and behaves like real data, so the app reacts as it would in production. Phone numbers have 10 digits; emails contain "@"; order totals match their line items. Consistent Related records agree with each other. Every order points to a customer that exists. Complete enough Covers the cases the tests need, including odd ones. A customer with zero orders; an order with 100 items; a customer born on 29 February. Right-sized Big enough to be meaningful, small enough to load and refresh quickly. Thousands of customers for functional tests, millions only for performance tests. Safe Cannot hurt anyone if it leaks. No real names with real ID numbers. Available There when the tester needs it, not three weeks later. A fresh dataset the morning a release starts testing. Repeatable Can be put back to a known state so a test gives the same result twice. Re-running yesterday's test on yesterday's data. Notice that these seven qualities pull against each other. "Realistic" and "safe" fight: the most realistic data is real data, which is the least safe. "Complete" and "right-sized" fight too. TDM is the work of balancing them deliberately instead of by accident.

x: 1.7 Test environments in plain words An environment is a full copy of the application with its own servers and its own database. Teams run several, each with a job. Names vary between companies, but the pattern is common. Environment Who uses it What it is for Typical data Dev (development) Developers Building and debugging new code. Breaks often, and that is fine. Small, often hand-made; developers need to reset it freely. QA / Test QA engineers, automation Systematic testing of features and bugs. Broad and varied; needs edge cases. UAT (user acceptance testing) Business users The business confirms the app does what they asked. Must look believable to business people. Staging / pre-prod Release team, performance testers A rehearsal as close to production as possible. Large volumes; production-like shape. Production Real customers The live business. Real, sensitive, valuable. Security is usually weaker outside production The Informatica User Guide points out that organisations typically keep strict controls on production systems, while data security in non-production systems is often not as strong (User Guide 10.5.10, p.21). That gap is exactly where leaks happen, and why the rest of this section matters.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.7.1 Who needs data, and when? In ShopSphere, a single sprint can ask for data in several ways at once: A developer fixing a rounding bug needs one customer with a specific order total. A QA engineer testing refunds needs hundreds of orders in different states (paid, shipped, returned). A performance tester needs millions of orders to see whether the site slows down. A business analyst in UAT needs data that "looks like our real customers" so they can judge whether a screen makes sense. An automation engineer needs the same data every night so the automated tests are repeatable. Five people, five different requirements. If nobody manages this, each one solves it alone, usually in the least safe way. That is the next section.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
h: 1.7.2 Types of testing and the data each one wants
x: 1.7.2 Types of testing and the data each one wants The word "testing" covers several activities. They need different data, which is why one dataset rarely suits everyone. Kind of testing What it checks Data it wants Unit testing One small piece of code, by the developer. A handful of hand-made values, often created inside the test and thrown away. Integration testing Whether separate parts (web app, database, payment service) work together. Consistent data across all the systems involved, so the same customer exists everywhere. System / functional testing Whole features from the user's point of view. A broad mix of customers, products and order states. Regression testing That old features still work after a change. The same data every run, so results can be compared. Performance / load testing Speed and stability under heavy use. Very large volumes with realistic shape. User acceptance testing Whether the business accepts it. Believable data that business users recognise as "like ours". Security testing Whether the app resists attacks. Data that includes hostile input such as unusual characters; it must not include real people's data.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.8 The naive approach: copy production The quickest way to get realistic, consistent data is to take a backup of the production database and restore it into the test environment. It is what many teams do first, because it works on day one and needs no special tool. This is the production copy approach. It feels right: the data is as real as data can be, and every relationship between tables is already correct. The problems appear later, and they are serious. Here are eight, each shown with ShopSphere. SHOPSPHERE_PROD 4 TB, real people full backup restore Dev: 4 TB copy QA: 4 TB copy UAT: 4 TB copy real names and IDs in every copy days to restore each copy stale the day after the copy rare cases may not exist Original diagram: what "just copy production" produces. The 4 TB size is an invented illustration for ShopSphere, not a measurement.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.8.1 Problem 1: privacy and security leaks Production holds real names, phone numbers, ID numbers and dates of birth. A full copy puts all of that into environments where far more people have access: every developer, every tester, contractors, sometimes outside vendors. Non-production systems usually have weaker access controls, weaker monitoring and more people logged in. ShopSphere example. The row for customer 1001 (Asha Menon, her email, her phone, her SSN) is now in the dev database, in the QA database, in the UAT database, in a test engineer's laptop dump, and in a screenshot attached to a bug report. Any one of those is a breach waiting to happen. It is also often a legal problem. Laws and standards such as GDPR, HIPAA and PCI restrict how personal data can be used. The Delphix introduction names exactly these three (HIPAA, PCI and GDPR) as mandates organisations must stay compliant with, and notes that growing pressure from regulators and consumers makes protecting sensitive data across the enterprise essential ( Introduction to Delphix Masking ). the sensitive data and regulations chapter explains the regulations.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.8.2 Problem 2: huge size Production databases grow for years. A full copy needs the same disk space as production, multiplied by the number of environments. Storage costs add up, and so does the time to move and back up the copies. ShopSphere example. If production is 4 TB (invented for illustration), five test environments need 20 TB, and most of the content is orders from five years ago that no current test will ever read.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.8.3 Problem 3: slow refreshes Copying terabytes takes hours or days. Teams therefore refresh rarely, queue for the operations team, and sometimes freeze the data for weeks to avoid doing it again. ShopSphere example. QA breaks the data while testing refunds. Restoring it takes two days. Everyone waits, or carries on with broken data and gets false test results.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.8.4 Problem 4: stale data A copy is a snapshot of one moment. The day after, production has moved on. New products, new account types and new features may be missing from the copy, so tests of the newest code run against data that does not contain it. ShopSphere example. A "gift card" payment type launched last week. The copy taken last month has no orders that use it, so the gift-card tests find nothing to test.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.8.5 Problem 5: missing edge cases Real data contains the cases that happened. It does not contain the cases that have not happened yet, or have happened too rarely to be in your copy. Tests need values at the boundary: the largest allowed order, an empty field, a name with an apostrophe, a negative quantity that the app must reject. ShopSphere example. Nobody in production has a 300-character last name, so no test checks that the screen handles one. The first customer who does crashes the checkout page. This is where synthetic data comes in. GenRocket's help site defines synthetic test data as data manufactured by an algorithm rather than collected from real-world events, and says companies can maximise test coverage by using it to test all permutations and combinations ( Why Synthetic Test Data? ).

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
h: 1.8.6 Problem 6: broken relationships when people shrink or edit it
x: 1.8.6 Problem 6: broken relationships when people shrink or edit it Realising the copy is too big, someone tries to cut it down by hand: "delete orders older than 2023". But orders are linked to customers and order items are linked to orders. Delete in the wrong order or the wrong rows and you leave order items pointing to orders that no longer exist, or orders for customers who have been removed. The application then crashes or gives nonsense, for reasons unrelated to the code being tested. ShopSphere example. A script deletes customers who have not logged in since 2022. It forgets their rows in ORDERS . Now there are orders with a customer_id that matches nobody. The "my orders" page fails for the wrong reason. The same breakage happens if someone replaces names with random text by hand and uses different replacements in different tables: the customer is "Asha" in one table and "Priya" in another. The data basics chapter explains the keys that tie tables together and why every TDM operation must respect them. The Informatica documentation describes the goal directly: a data subset keeps primary and foreign key relationships so that the data stays referentially intact (User Guide 10.5.10, p.23).

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.8.7 Problem 7: cost The costs are not only disk space. Add the time of people who run restores, the delay while testers wait, the licence and infrastructure cost of big environments, and the risk cost of a breach or regulator fine. None of it appears as a line "test data" on a budget, which is partly why the problem lingers.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
h: 1.8.8 Problem 8: no repeatability and no control
x: 1.8.8 Problem 8: no repeatability and no control If every team makes its own copy at its own time, nobody knows which data version a bug was found on. Tests that passed Monday fail Tuesday because the data under them changed. Nobody can say who has a copy of what. # Problem Symptom you would see TDM capability that addresses it 1 Privacy leaks Real names and IDs in dev databases Discover and mask 2 Huge size Disk full; slow restores Subset (or virtual copies) 3 Slow refreshes Waiting days for new data Provision and refresh 4 Stale data New features have no test data Refresh; generate 5 Missing edge cases Bugs only appear in production Generate 6 Broken relationships Orders with no customer Subset and mask while keeping keys 7 Cost Big storage and waiting bills All of the above, plus governance 8 No repeatability or control "It passed on my copy" Govern: catalogue, versions, access "But we only use it internally" is not a defence A breach through a test environment is still a breach of the people whose data it is. Internal staff, contractors and vendors can all misuse or lose data, and many regulations make no exception for non-production systems. The sensitive data and regulations chapter goes through this carefully. Worked example: one bug report, three failures A ShopSphere tester finds that the "order history" screen shows an empty page for customer 1002 in the QA environment. She files a bug. The developer cannot reproduce it on his machine because his data is different. After a day of investigation they discover that the QA database was a partial manual copy in which customer 1002's orders were not copied. The bug is not in the code at all. That one incident shows three problems from the list: broken relationships (problem 6), no control (8) and slow refresh (3: fixing it means a new copy). It also cost a day of two people's time. Multiply by a team and a year and the cost of unmanaged test data becomes visible.

h: 1.9 So what is Test Data Management?
x: 1.9 So what is Test Data Management? Test Data Management (TDM) is the set of processes, roles and tools that plan, create, protect, deliver and retire the data used in non-production environments. In simpler words: it is how you make sure the right testers get the right safe data at the right time, without copying production carelessly. Some people use "TDM" for the software and some for the practice. In this guide "TDM" is the practice, and "a TDM tool" is software that supports it.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.9.1 Goals of TDM Protect people. No real sensitive data in non-production. Fit the test. Data that is realistic, consistent and covers the cases the tests need. Right size. Smaller than production where possible, large only where tests need it. Be fast. Data on request, refreshed in minutes or hours, not weeks. Be repeatable and traceable. Known data versions, known owners, known copies. Lower cost. Less storage, less waiting, less rework, lower breach risk.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.10 The six capabilities of TDM TDM splits into six capabilities. A project may use all six or only a few. The first four change the data; the last two deliver and control it. 1 Discover find where the sensitive data is "ssn" column in CUSTOMERS 2 Subset take a small, consistent slice 5,000 customers and their orders 3 Mask replace real values with fake ones Asha Menon becomes a made-up name 4 Generate create new data from rules a 300-character last name 5 Provision deliver and refresh on request new QA data by Monday 6 Govern who, what, when, audit, policy who got which dataset? Typical order for protecting real data: 1 discover, then 2 subset, then 3 mask, then 5 deliver. Generation (4) is an alternative or an addition: use it when no real data fits, or when real data may not be used at all. wraps around all the others Original diagram: the six capabilities of TDM, each with a ShopSphere example. This is a teaching model, not a product architecture.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.10.1 1. Discover You cannot protect what you cannot find. Discovery means scanning a database or a set of files to locate sensitive data: which columns hold names, ID numbers, phone numbers. Large databases can have thousands of columns, and sensitive values hide in odd places such as a "notes" column. Discovery also finds the relationships between tables, which later steps need. Why it matters: if discovery misses a column, that column goes into test unmasked. ShopSphere: discovery flags ssn , phone , email , date_of_birth and tax_id in CUSTOMERS . The discovery and subsetting concepts chapter teaches this in depth.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.10.2 2. Subset Subsetting builds a smaller database from a big one: for example "only customers from the last two years, and everything linked to them". Done properly, every order in the subset still has its customer and its items. Smaller means cheaper, faster to load and easier to refresh. ShopSphere: pick 5,000 customers and bring their orders and items along, leaving the other millions of rows behind. The discovery and subsetting concepts chapter covers it; the Informatica data subset chapter shows it in Informatica.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.10.3 3. Mask Masking replaces sensitive values with realistic but fake ones. The application still works because the fake values look right (a fake phone has ten digits), but nobody can learn about a real person from them. Good masking is consistent: the same real value always becomes the same fake value, so relationships between tables survive. The Delphix documentation describes masking as replacing confidential information such as social security numbers, patient records and card numbers with fictitious yet realistic data, and contrasts it with encryption: masking is irreversible, while encryption can be bypassed through schemes to obtain user credentials ( Introduction to Delphix Masking ). ShopSphere: Asha Menon, 9876543210, 123-45-6789 becomes, say, a made-up name, a made-up ten-digit number and a made-up SSN pattern. The masking concepts chapter teaches the techniques. Before and after: what masked data looks like The first table is the real (fake-for-this-guide) data; the second shows what a masked copy might look like. The masked values are invented for illustration and do not come from any tool's output. CUSTOMERS before masking (ShopSphere fake rows) customer_id first_name last_name phone ssn 1001 Asha Menon 9876543210 123-45-6789 1002 Ravi Kumar 9123456780 234-56-7890 CUSTOMERS after masking (illustrative) customer_id first_name last_name phone ssn 1001 Lakshmi Pillai 9404418273 581-20-3347 1002 Arjun Das 9051627384 672-31-4458 Notice what changed and what did not. Names, phones and SSNs are different, but they keep their shape: ten-digit phones, SSNs in the nnn-nn-nnnn pattern. The customer_id stayed the same, so every order that points to customer 1001 still finds its customer. If the same real SSN appeared in another table, it would have to receive the same fake value there too. That consistency requirement is the heart of the masking concepts chapter .

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.10.4 4. Generate Generation creates data from rules instead of copying real data. You describe what you need ("fifty customers, each with a first name, a last name, a phone number") and a tool produces it. Use it when real data does not exist yet (a new feature), when you need edge cases, when you need very large volumes, or when real data cannot be used at all. Informatica's documentation gives the second reason almost word for word: use data generation when you need test data but do not want to use production data, for example when test teams handle sensitive data and have no access to production (User Guide 10.5.10, p.23). ShopSphere: generate a customer whose name is 300 characters long. The classification and generation concepts chapter covers the idea; Part III is GenRocket, a tool built around it.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.10.5 5. Provision and refresh Provisioning means delivering a ready dataset into an environment: loading it into the QA database, or placing a file where a test tool expects it. Refreshing means doing it again later to get new or reset data. Speed and repeatability matter most here. Both Informatica and Delphix address this in their own way. Informatica describes a test data warehouse that stores multiple versions of test data and can restore a version to put an environment back into a particular state (User Guide 10.5.10, p.23). Delphix describes virtual copies that are readable and writable, can be created or removed in minutes, and take a fraction of the storage of physical copies; in its example ten virtual copies fit in the space of one physical copy ( Introduction to Delphix Masking ).

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.10.6 6. Govern Governance is the rules and records around the other five: who may request what, which data is approved for which environment, which masking rules are in force, an audit trail of who received which dataset. It is the least glamorous capability and the first one auditors ask about. Delphix says the platform lets operators audit, monitor and report against access and usage, and generates reports and email notifications confirming sensitive data has been masked. Informatica's administrator manages roles and privileges that decide what each TDM user can do (User Guide 10.5.10, p.23). Official screenshot: Delphix's own platform diagram. Sources (applications, files, databases, on-premises or cloud) enter through "Connect", then pass through Virtualize (sync, compress, provision), Secure (compliance, policy, masking) and Manage (distribute, audit and report), and leave through APIs as "data pods" for developers, QA, analysts and data scientists. It is a vendor view of capabilities 3, 5 and 6 above. Source page ↗ Why the six are separate ideas Beginners often use "masking" to mean everything. It is only one of six. A team that masks but never subsets still has a huge, slow copy. A team that subsets but never discovers may mask the wrong columns. Learn the six as separate tools in a toolbox, then pick the ones a project needs.

h: 1.12 Putting numbers on the cost of copying
x: 1.12 Putting numbers on the cost of copying Lab: price the cost of "just copy it" (thinking lab, invented numbers) Goal: see in numbers why unmanaged test data is expensive. All figures below are invented for practice; replace them with your own project's. Storage. Production is 4 TB and ShopSphere has five non-production environments, each holding a full copy. Compute the total storage for the copies. An answer in TB. Waiting. A restore takes 2 days. QA needs one restore per fortnight and the team of 6 testers is idle half of the restore time. Compute idle tester-days per year. An answer in tester-days. Subset effect. A subset keeps 5 percent of the data. Recompute step 1. A much smaller number. Show a worked answer 1. 5 environments x 4 TB = 20 TB. 2. About 26 fortnights a year. Each restore idles 6 testers for half of 2 days = 1 day each, so 6 tester-days per restore, 26 x 6 = 156 tester-days per year. 3. 5 percent of 4 TB is 0.2 TB, so 5 x 0.2 = 1 TB, one twentieth of the 20 TB. A smaller copy also restores faster, which shrinks the idle time in step 2 as well. The numbers are made up, but the shape is real: costs multiply by the number of copies and the frequency of refreshes. Do not quote them as ShopSphere facts.

x: 1.13 Roles in a TDM effort TDM is a team activity. Titles vary by company, and one person may wear several hats, but the responsibilities are consistent. Role What they do in TDM ShopSphere example QA engineer / tester Defines what data the tests need and consumes it. Reports when data is wrong. "I need 200 orders in a 'returned' state." Developer Needs small, resettable data to debug and build features. "I need one customer with an order total of exactly 0.01." TDM engineer Builds and runs the process: discovers sensitive data, designs subsets, configures masking and generation, schedules refreshes, fixes failures. This is your target role. Sets up the masking job that turns SHOPSPHERE_PROD into safe QA data every week. Data steward / data owner Knows what each data item means, which is sensitive, how it may be used; approves rules. Confirms that tax_id is sensitive and must be masked. Compliance / privacy officer Ensures practice meets laws and internal policy; reviews evidence. Asks: "Prove no real SSN exists in UAT." Database administrator (DBA) Gives access to source and target databases, helps with performance and storage. Creates the account the TDM tool uses to read production. Tool administrator Installs, upgrades and manages the TDM product and its users. Sets which users may run masking jobs. Release / environment manager Plans which environment gets which data and when. x: 1.14 Real-world scenarios at ShopSphere Three short stories, each choosing a different mix of the six capabilities. Scenario 1: weekly QA refresh Situation. QA tests every Monday and needs realistic data, but production holds real customers. Approach. Each Friday night a job reads production, picks the last 12 months of customers and their orders ( subset ), replaces names, emails, phones, SSNs and dates of birth with fake but consistent values ( mask ), and loads the result into QA ( provision ). Discovery was done once, and its results are re-checked when the schema changes. Outcome. QA gets fresh, safe, small data every Monday without anyone touching production data by hand. Scenario 2: a new loyalty-points feature Situation. ShopSphere adds loyalty points. No production data has points yet. Approach. Nothing to copy, so the team generates 10,000 customers with random point balances, including zero, the maximum and a negative balance that the app must reject. Outcome. The feature is tested before launch, including the edge cases, with no personal data involved. Scenario 3: performance test before the holiday sale Situation. The company expects ten times normal traffic and needs 50 million orders in the performance environment. Approach. Real production does not have that many. The TDM engineer generates the volume, and masks a real sample so that distributions (how many items per order, typical prices) match the real shape. Outcome. The load test runs at realistic scale, safely. Lab: choose the capabilities (thinking lab, no tool needed) Goal: practise mapping a testing problem to the six capabilities. For each situation, write down which of discover, subset, mask, generate, provision and govern you would use, and in what order. The UAT team complains the database is too slow to refresh and takes 6 TB. Think about size and speed. A developer wants to test what happens when a customer's email is blank. Think about whether such a record exists in production. ShopSphere acquires another retailer whose database has unfamiliar columns and nobody knows what is sensitive. Think about what must come first. Show a worked answer 1. Subset first (cut the size). Mask what remains, then provision. If a virtual-copy product is available, that also speeds provisioning (Delphix describes this; the Delphix overview and terminology chapter ). 2. Generate. A blank email is probably rare or absent in real data and may be rejected by production's own form, so create it on purpose. 3. Discover first. Until you know which columns hold sensitive data you cannot decide what to mask or subset. Then mask, then provision, and govern by recording the decisions.

x: 1.15 Benefits and trade-offs Benefits Lower privacy and compliance risk. Faster test cycles because data is ready. Smaller storage and infrastructure cost. Better test coverage through generated edge cases. Repeatable tests on known data. Fewer false bug reports from bad data. Trade-offs and costs Set-up effort: discovery, rules and approvals take time up front. Licence and infrastructure cost for commercial tools. Masked data is never exactly real data; some production-only bugs may not reproduce. Generated data is only as good as its rules; it can miss real-world quirks you did not think of. New skills and a new process for the team to learn. Ongoing upkeep as the schema and the regulations change. Masked and generated data compared Masking starts from real data and hides the identifying parts, so it keeps real-world shape and messiness. Generation starts from rules, so it is safe by construction and covers cases you design, but only the cases you thought of. Many teams use both: masked data for realism, generated data for edge cases and volume. the classification and generation concepts chapter compares them in detail.

h: 1.16 TDM maturity: from ad hoc to self-service
x: 1.16 TDM maturity: from ad hoc to self-service Organisations do not jump straight to full TDM. A common way to describe the journey is a ladder of stages. This is a teaching model, not an official standard; names and numbers of levels vary between authors. Stage How data is obtained Typical pain 1. Ad hoc Each team copies production or types data by hand, whenever it can. Privacy risk, inconsistent data, long waits. 2. Scripted Someone writes scripts to subset or mask. Works, but depends on a few people. Scripts break when the schema changes; knowledge sits in heads. 3. Managed A TDM team uses a tool with defined rules: discovery, masking, subsetting, scheduled refreshes, approvals. Requests still go through the team, which becomes a bottleneck. 4. Self-service and automated Testers request or refresh data themselves through a portal or API, often inside the build pipeline; governance is automatic. Needs investment and discipline to keep rules current. The product documentation points toward the top of the ladder. Informatica mentions a self-service portal for users who use test data warehouse data but do not create it (User Guide 10.5.10, p.22). Delphix describes a self-service service where testers can refresh, rewind, bookmark and share copies. Both are vendor views of what later stages look like, not proof of how any particular organisation works. Why maturity matters to you When you join a project, find out which stage it is in. A stage 1 team needs convincing and a small pilot. A stage 3 team needs a good TDM engineer to keep the machine running. The final syllabus days on "end-to-end plan development" and "assessment on a particular LOB" (line of business) are about exactly this: understanding where a client is and what to do next ( the planning real engagements chapter ).

You assemble and support it yourself; coverage varies. COTS products Many capabilities in one supported product; connectors to many databases; auditing and role-based access; vendor support. Licence cost; training; you follow the vendor's way of working; version upgrades. The comparison is general; real products vary, so evaluate with a proof of concept (a small trial on your own data). x: 1.18 Common mistakes and gotchas "We mask it, so it is safe" Masking only protects the columns you masked. If discovery missed a column, or a free-text "notes" field contains names, sensitive data survives. Discovery and verification matter as much as the masking itself. Treating TDM as a one-off project Production changes every day: new columns, new data, new rules. A TDM set-up that is never maintained goes stale just like a copied database. Using one technique for everything Masking is not always right. If no real data exists for the case, or real data cannot be used at all, generate. If the problem is only size or speed, subset or virtualise. Ignoring relationships Any change to the data (subset, mask, generate) must keep related tables consistent. The data basics chapter explains how; skipping it leads to the "orders with no customer" bug. Believing tool names are the concepts "Plan", "rule set", "scenario" and "domain" mean different things in different products. Learn the concept, then learn each tool's word for it.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.19 Recap Recap Testing needs data; good test data is realistic, consistent, complete, right-sized, safe, available and repeatable. Copying production gives real data but causes privacy leaks, huge size, slow refreshes, stale data, missing edge cases, broken relationships, cost and loss of control. TDM is the set of processes, roles and tools that deliver safe, right-sized, realistic test data on demand. Its six capabilities are discover, subset, mask, generate, provision and govern; most projects use several. Roles include testers, developers, the TDM engineer, data steward, compliance officer, DBA and administrators. Maturity runs from ad hoc, through scripted and managed, to self-service and automated. COTS means commercial off-the-shelf; the programme uses Informatica TDM, GenRocket and Delphix. Ask the trainer about "partnership" and "Cog IPs". Data basics every TDM beginner needs Everything a TDM tool does is done to data: it finds data, cuts it down, hides parts of it, makes more of it, and moves it. To follow any of that you need a small, firm vocabulary about how data is organised. This section gives it to you from zero. You will not become a database administrator, but you will be able to read a table, spot a key, tell a CSV from a fixed-width file and run a basic SQL query. These ideas return constantly. Subsetting, masking and generation all have one rule in common: keep the relationships between records intact . You cannot follow that rule if you do not know what a relationship is. This section is also the preparation for the primary-key work in the Delphix part of the syllabus (Day 51) and the file-masking work (Day 53). What you will learn The difference between data and information, and what a database, table, row and column are. Data types, and what a schema and metadata are. Primary keys, foreign keys, parent and child tables, one-to-many relationships and referential integrity. Why keys matter so much to subsetting, masking and generation, and what logical keys are. Flat files (text, .dat, CSV, delimited, fixed-width), headers, footers, records and encodings, with sample files. XML and JSON at a glance. Basic SQL: SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, INSERT, UPDATE and COUNT, with runnable ShopSphere examples. Why data volume matters, and a hands-on exercise on finding keys in files. What this section is based on The data concepts and SQL are general knowledge, marked ; the SQL examples were run against the ShopSphere sample data in SQLite to check the results shown. Tool-specific statements come from three places. The Informatica TDM 10.5.10 User Guide (PDF, February 2026) is cited by page, for logical keys and key profiles. The Delphix Continuous Compliance 2026.5 help pages Managing file formats , Managing rule sets and Managing record types and header/footer records are used for how that product treats file formats and keys. Those statements are marked .

x: 1.20 Words to know first Data Raw facts, such as "1001", "Asha" and "560001", before anyone says what they mean. Information Data with meaning: "customer 1001 is Asha, living in postal area 560001". Database An organised store of data that a program can search and change reliably. Table A grid of data about one kind of thing, like one sheet in a spreadsheet. Row / record One item in a table: one customer, one order. Column / field One attribute of every row: first name, phone, order date. Primary key (PK) A column (or columns) whose value is unique for every row and identifies it. Foreign key (FK) A column whose values point to the primary key of another table. Referential integrity The rule that every foreign key value must match an existing primary key value. Schema / metadata The description of the data (table names, columns, types, keys) as opposed to the data itself. Flat file A plain file holding records as lines of text, with no built-in database engine behind it. SQL The language used to ask a relational database questions and to change it.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.21 Data and information Look at this: 1001 | Asha | Menon | 560001 . On its own it is just data: four values. You can guess it is a person, but you are guessing. Add labels ( customer_id, first_name, last_name, zip_code ) and a table name ( CUSTOMERS ) and it becomes information: customer 1001 is Asha Menon in postal area 560001. That distinction matters for TDM because tools often see only data and have to work out the meaning. Discovery (see the discovery and subsetting concepts chapter ) is largely the job of recovering meaning: "this column, called col_17 , contains phone numbers". Column names, data types and descriptions are the clues.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.22.1 The spreadsheet analogy If you have used a spreadsheet you already know the idea. A table is one sheet: columns across the top with names, rows below, one item per row. A database is the whole workbook, with several sheets (tables) that belong together. Here is the ShopSphere CUSTOMERS table: CUSTOMERS (fake sample rows, first five columns) customer_id first_name last_name email phone 1001 Asha Menon asha.menon@example.com 9876543210 1002 Ravi Kumar ravi.k@example.com 9123456780 1003 Meera Nair meera.n@example.com 9988776655 Each row (also called a record ) is one customer. Each column (also called a field or attribute) is one fact about every customer. Each cell is one value: the phone number of customer 1002. Unlike a spreadsheet sheet, a database table enforces each column's declared type, can be linked to other tables by keys, can hold millions of rows, and is queried with SQL (later in this section). ShopSphere uses a relational database (Oracle, SQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL and DB2 are examples): tables relate through keys.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.22.2 Data types Each column has a data type that says what kind of value it holds. The type controls what is allowed, how much space it takes and how it can be used (you can add numbers but not names). Type family Typical names ShopSphere example Why a TDM person cares Whole numbers INTEGER, INT, NUMBER customer_id , quantity Generated or masked values must still be whole numbers. Decimal numbers DECIMAL(10,2), NUMERIC unit_price , total_amount Precision matters: 10,2 means up to 10 digits, 2 after the point. Text VARCHAR(50), CHAR(10) first_name , email A masked name must fit the length limit. Dates and times DATE, TIMESTAMP date_of_birth , order_date A masked date of birth must still be a real date. True/false BOOLEAN, BIT (none in ShopSphere) Only two values exist. Binary / large objects BLOB, CLOB, images (none in ShopSphere) Special handling; many masking techniques do not apply. Notice something about the ShopSphere sample data: phone , ssn and zip_code look like numbers, but they are stored as text . You never add two phone numbers, and a leading zero would be lost if they were numbers. That choice affects how you mask them: a text column can hold dashes (123-45-6789); a numeric column cannot. Why this matters A TDM operation must produce values the column accepts. A masked or generated name longer than the column's limit makes the load fail. A fake date such as 31 February is rejected. Many job failures in the tool chapters come down to "the new value did not fit the column's type or length".

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.22.3 Schema and metadata Metadata means "data about data". For a database it is the list of tables, their columns, each column's name and type, which columns are keys, and which tables relate to which. The collection of all that is the schema . Here is part of the ShopSphere schema written as a simple description (not the data): CUSTOMERS customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY first_name VARCHAR(50) last_name VARCHAR(50) email VARCHAR(100) phone VARCHAR(15) ssn VARCHAR(11) date_of_birth DATE zip_code VARCHAR(10) tax_id VARCHAR(20) The metadata tells a tool a lot without reading a single row. A column called ssn of type VARCHAR(11) is a strong hint (11 characters fits 123-45-6789). TDM tools therefore read metadata first, then sample the actual data. The Informatica guide describes a TDM repository that stores the metadata you import into Test Data Manager from a source database (User Guide 10.5.10, p.26). The Delphix introduction describes two profiling methods, one scanning column names (metadata) and one scanning the data itself ( Introduction to Delphix Masking ).

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.23 Keys and relationships A single table is easy. Real applications split data across many tables and connect them. Keys are the connectors. This section is the most important in the whole chapter.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
h: 1.23.1 Why data is split into several tables
x: 1.23.1 Why data is split into several tables Imagine ShopSphere stored everything in one big sheet: one row per ordered item, with the customer's name, phone and address repeated on every row. Customer Asha has two orders with three items in total, so her phone number would be typed three times. If she changes her phone number you must update every copy, and if you miss one the data disagrees with itself. The fix is to store each fact once, in the table where it belongs, and refer to it from elsewhere. Customer facts live in CUSTOMERS . An order stores only the customer's ID , not the name and phone. To get the name, you look the ID up. The ID is a key.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.23.2 Primary key A primary key is a column (or a small group of columns) whose value is unique in every row and is never empty (null). It is the row's identity, like a library card number or a passport number. CUSTOMERS.customer_id : 1001, 1002, 1003. No two customers share an ID. ORDERS.order_id , ORDER_ITEMS.item_id and PRODUCTS.product_code are the primary keys of their tables. A database enforces this: it refuses to insert a second customer with ID 1001. Why not use the name as the key? Two customers can share a name; names change; spellings vary. A key must be stable and unique. That is why tables carry an artificial ID such as customer_id . (Keys made up of real-world data, like an email address, are called natural keys ; made-up IDs are surrogate keys . Both appear in the real world.) A key can have more than one column. Suppose a table ORDER_ITEM_NOTES allowed one note per item per language; then (item_id, language) together would be unique, though neither alone is. That is a composite key .

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.23.3 Foreign key A foreign key is a column in one table whose values must match the primary key of another table. It is the link. ORDERS.customer_id is a foreign key to CUSTOMERS.customer_id : it says which customer placed the order. ORDER_ITEMS.order_id is a foreign key to ORDERS.order_id : it says which order this line belongs to. ORDER_ITEMS.product_code is a foreign key to PRODUCTS.product_code : it says which product was bought. The foreign key column is allowed to repeat. Customer 1001 can appear in many order rows, because Asha can place many orders. The primary key side cannot repeat.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.23.4 Parent and child tables, one-to-many The table that holds the primary key is the parent ; the table with the foreign key pointing at it is the child . One customer (parent) can have many orders (children), and one order can have many items. That shape is called one-to-many . CUSTOMERS PK customer_id first_name, last_name email, phone, ssn date_of_birth, zip_code, tax_id ORDERS PK order_id FK customer_id order_date total_amount ORDER_ITEMS PK item_id FK order_id FK product_code quantity unit_price PRODUCTS PK product_code product_name, price 1 : many 1 : many 1 : many Arrows run from parent (PK) to child (FK). The parent must exist before the child. Delete a parent and its children are orphaned. PK = primary key, FK = foreign key Original diagram: ShopSphere's four tables and the keys that connect them. Compare with the table definitions in the start-here chapter .
