ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.23.6 Referential integrity Referential integrity is the rule that every foreign key value must match a primary key value that exists. Every order must belong to a customer who exists; every item to an order that exists. A child row whose parent is missing is called an orphan . Suppose someone deletes customer 1001 but leaves orders 5001 and 5002. Those orders now point to nobody. The "my orders" page crashes. When the database has the foreign key declared, it refuses such a delete, and it refuses to insert an order for a customer ID that does not exist. (When I tried this in SQLite with foreign key enforcement switched on, both attempts were rejected with a foreign key constraint error.) Why keys matter so much to TDM Every TDM operation reshapes data. Each one can break referential integrity if done carelessly. Operation How it can break keys What it must do instead Subsetting Pick 100 customers but leave out their orders (missing children), or pick orders but leave out their customers (orphans). Follow the keys: choose a starting table, then bring along every related row in the other tables. Masking Mask customer_id in CUSTOMERS to a new value but leave ORDERS.customer_id unchanged, or mask them differently. Orders no longer match customers. Apply the same masking to the parent key and every child foreign key so the values still match, or leave keys alone. Generation Generate 1,000 orders with customer IDs that no generated customer has. Generate parents first and give each child a valid parent ID. Provisioning Load child tables before parent tables so foreign key checks fail. Load parents first; delete children first. Each tool has its own way to say this. The Informatica documentation says a data subset retains primary and foreign key relations so that the data stays referentially intact (User Guide 10.5.10, p.23). The Delphix introduction says it scans metadata and data to identify and preserve primary/foreign key relationships so that data is masked the same way across tables and databases ( Introduction to Delphix Masking ).

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
h: 1.23.7 Logical keys: keys the database does not know about
x: 1.23.7 Logical keys: keys the database does not know about Everything above assumed the keys are declared in the database. In real life they often are not. Older systems, performance-minded designs and imported data frequently have tables with no declared primary or foreign keys at all, even though the application treats certain columns as keys. The relationships exist in the developers' heads and in the code, not in the schema. TDM tools cannot follow a relationship they do not know about. So they let you (or their profilers) describe the relationships separately. Keys defined this way are called logical keys in this guide: the tool is told "treat this column as the key" without any change to the real database. Tool What its documentation says Informatica Primary-key and foreign-key profiles can discover potential relationships (p.21). The foreign key profile adds the discovered logical constraints to the TDM repository but does not apply them in the source tables; the subset workflow uses them to produce referentially intact data (p.86). You can also add a logical primary key to a table (p.109) and a logical foreign key choosing a column from a parent table (p.110). In its worked example the database contains no primary or foreign keys, so the developer creates logical ones (p.34). For data sets it advises creating logical keys in transactional tables that have no primary keys (p.239). Delphix In a rule set, a logical key is a unique, non-null value identifying a row. If a table has no primary key defined and you use in-place masking, you must name an existing column or columns as the logical key. It does not change the target database; it only informs Delphix. Without one, an identity column may be created, which requires permission to modify the schema or the job may fail. The rule set "Checklist" validates that every table has a primary key, an indexed identity column or a logical key ( Managing rule sets ). The idea is the same in both: a key you declare to the tool, which the database may know nothing about . Chapters on Informatica subsetting and Delphix rule sets and keys show the screens. Logical keys are only as good as your understanding If you declare a column as a key but it is not actually unique, masking or subsetting will misbehave. A logical key must be unique and never null for every row, exactly like a real primary key. You prove it by checking the data (for example by counting rows and counting distinct values), not by assuming.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.24 Flat files Not all test data lives in databases. Banks, insurers and retailers exchange huge amounts of data as files : one system writes a file overnight, another reads it in the morning. The syllabus includes masking "files (txt, dat)" (Day 53), so you need to read them comfortably. A flat file is a file holding records as lines of text. "Flat" means there is no table engine, no keys, no data types: it is just text in a layout that both sides agree on. All the structure lives in the agreement, not in the file.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.24.1 .txt, .dat, .csv: what the extension tells you (little) A file extension is only a label. .txt says "text", .csv says "comma-separated values", .dat says "data". None of them tells you how the records are laid out. A .dat file can be comma-separated, pipe-separated, fixed-width or something else; a .txt file can hold any of those too. You find the layout from the file specification (a document from the team that produces the file), or by opening the file and looking. Why this matters A tool that masks files has to be told the layout, because the file itself does not say. The Delphix documentation puts it directly: unlike databases, files typically have no built-in metadata describing the format of their fields, so you must provide that information ( Managing file formats ).

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.24.2 Records, fields, headers and footers A record is one line (one customer, one order), ending with an end-of-record marker, usually a line break. A field is one value within the record. A header is a record at the top that is not data: often the column names, or a label with a date. A footer (or trailer) is a record at the end, often a count or a total so the reader can check nothing was lost.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.24.3 Delimited files In a delimited file a special character, the delimiter , separates the fields. The most famous is the comma, giving the CSV (comma-separated values) format. Pipes (|), tabs and semicolons are also common, especially when data itself contains commas. Here is a ShopSphere customer file in CSV with a header row. All values are fake: customer_id,first_name,last_name,email,phone 1001,Asha,Menon,asha.menon@example.com,9876543210 1002,Ravi,Kumar,ravi.k@example.com,9123456780 1003,Meera,Nair,meera.n@example.com,9988776655 And an orders file, .dat extension, pipe-delimited, with a header record (H), data records (D) and a footer record (T) that carries the record count: H|ORDERS|20260215 D|5001|1001|2026-01-15|1098.00 D|5002|1001|2026-02-03|1499.00 D|5003|1002|2026-02-10|598.00 T|3 Reading it: the first field of each line says what kind of record it is. This is a file with several record types in one file, a layout common in business exchanges. The footer says "3 data records", so a reader can detect a truncated file. What if the data contains the delimiter? If a last name were "O'Neil, Jr." in a comma file the comma would split it into two fields. The usual answer is an enclosure (also called a qualifier or quote character), commonly the double quote: 1004,Liam,"O'Neil, Jr.",liam@example.com,9000000001 . Then a literal quote inside the field needs an escape , often by doubling it. The Delphix rule-set page documents settings for exactly this: an enclosure escaping strategy for delimited files, with a default of "Double enclosure" (the escape character is the same as the enclosure), and an option to use a custom single character ( Managing rule sets ).

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.24.4 Fixed-width files In a fixed-width file there is no delimiter. Each field occupies an exact range of character positions, padded with spaces. The layout is defined by position: Layout specification for customers.txt (fixed-width) Field Start Length Positions customer_id 1 4 1-4 first_name 5 10 5-14 last_name 15 10 15-24 phone 25 10 25-34 The data, with a ruler line on top so you can count columns (the ruler is not part of the file): 1234567890123456789012345678901234 1001Asha Menon 9876543210 1002Ravi Kumar 9123456780 1003Meera Nair 9988776655 Every record is exactly 34 characters long. "Asha" is followed by six spaces so that the last name starts at position 15. Without the layout table you could not tell where "Asha" ends and "Menon" begins. Delimited Fields found by a separator character. Field length can vary. Needs rules for delimiters inside values. Easy to open in a spreadsheet. Fixed-width Fields found by position. Every field has a set length; short values are padded. No delimiter issues, but a masked value must not exceed the field width. Needs the layout specification to read at all. Fixed-width and masking If you mask a name in a fixed-width file and the new name is longer than the field, it either overflows into the next field (corrupting the record) or is cut off. Masked values must fit the field. More detail for Delphix is in the Delphix file masking chapter .

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.24.5 Line endings The end of a record is marked by invisible characters that differ by platform. Windows traditionally uses two characters (carriage return then line feed, often written CR+LF); Linux uses one (line feed, LF). If a tool assumes the wrong one, records are read wrongly or every line gets an odd extra character. Delphix asks you to choose the end-of-record, Windows/DOS (CR+LF) or Linux (LF), when you assign a file format, and to enter the delimiter for a delimited file ( Managing file formats ). It also supports using a control character as the delimiter or end of record, entered in a particular format ( Managing rule sets ).

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
h: 1.24.6 Records of different shapes in one file
x: 1.24.6 Records of different shapes in one file The orders file above mixed header, data and footer lines. Other files mix different kinds of data record. The Delphix documentation gives an example where some records carry an account number and a postal address while others carry an account number and an email address, told apart by the first field ("address" or "email"). It calls the differentiating field a record type qualifier, supports up to three qualifiers, and says a record gets exactly one record type. It also says that header and footer records can be configured so unmodified copies go into the masked output, and that these features apply only to delimited and fixed-width formats ( Managing record types and header/footer records ). The point for you: a file is rarely "just rows". Before touching it, list the record types it contains. Masking a header line as if it were a customer would corrupt it.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.24.7 Encodings: how text becomes bytes Computers store characters as numbers; an encoding is the agreed table. Two matter to you: ASCII : an old, small table with 128 characters: English letters, digits, punctuation. One byte per character. UTF-8 : a modern encoding that can represent essentially every writing system, including Tamil, Hindi, Chinese and emoji. It is ASCII-compatible: plain English text looks identical, but other characters take two, three or four bytes. This causes two classic problems. Garbled text. A file written in one encoding and read as another turns "Müller" into something like "MÃ¼ller". The data is not lost; it was read with the wrong table. Fixed-width surprises. If a layout counts bytes but a name has an accented letter, "Müller" is 7 bytes in UTF-8 though it is 6 characters. The field after it shifts by one. Always ask whether widths are in bytes or characters. The Delphix page on control characters says the control-character value supports the UTF-8 character set ( Managing rule sets ); I did not find an encoding-selection setting described in the pages I read for this section, so check your version for how it handles encodings.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
h: 1.24.8 XML and JSON at a glance
x: 1.24.8 XML and JSON at a glance Some files are not line-and-column shaped at all; they are nested . Two formats dominate. XML wraps values in named tags (for example <firstName>Asha</firstName> ); JSON uses braces, names and values: { "customerId": 1001, "firstName": "Asha", "orders": [ { "orderId": 5001, "total": 1098.00 }, { "orderId": 5002, "total": 1499.00 } ] } In both formats the orders are inside the customer. The parent-child relationship is shown by nesting instead of by a foreign key. For TDM, the thing to remember is that sensitive values (here the name) hide inside the structure, and a tool must know the path to them. The Delphix rule-set page lists source types of Database, Fixed Width, Delimited, JSON, XML and DataSet, and the rule-set creation dialog offers Database, Semi-Structured, Flat Files and Copybook ( Managing rule sets ). A copybook describes mainframe record layouts; this guide only mentions it so that you recognise the word.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
h: 1.24.9 How the Delphix documentation treats file formats and keys
x: 1.24.9 How the Delphix documentation treats file formats and keys A short orientation, so that later Delphix chapters feel familiar. All statements below are from the pages linked; details come later in the Delphix rule sets and keys chapter and the Delphix file masking chapter . Formats are defined separately from files. You add them under Settings, in a Data Formats area with a tab for File formats and one for Mainframe ( Managing file formats ). A format is shared. Changing a file format's inventory affects every data file that uses that format. This applies to Fixed-Width, Delimited, Mainframe, JSON and XML formats. Rule sets group the tables or files a job will work on, and a rule set can be of type database, flat file, semi-structured or copybook ( Managing rule sets ). Keys appear in the rule set. A database table's rule-set row shows a logical key column, and a table without a primary key needs one for in-place masking (see the logical keys section above). A filter is a WHERE clause that limits the rows from a table, which is how a rule set does a simple subset. You will see WHERE in the SQL section next.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.25 Basic SQL you will see SQL (Structured Query Language, often said "sequel") is the language for asking a relational database questions and changing its data. You will meet it in TDM tools in small doses: a WHERE filter for a subset, a custom query for a table, a check of results. You need to read it, not master it. All statements below were run against the ShopSphere tables and sample rows from this section, and the results shown are what they returned. To try them yourself, use any relational database you can access; for a free practice option, SQLite works on a laptop. The create-table statements are in the lab at the end of this section. Details such as date handling differ slightly between databases.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.25.1 SELECT: read data SELECT chooses columns; FROM names the table. SELECT first_name, last_name, zip_code FROM customers; Result first_name last_name zip_code Asha Menon 560001 Ravi Kumar 600017 Meera Nair 682001 SELECT * means "all columns". Handy for a quick look, but on a big table it returns everything, which can be slow and can display sensitive columns you did not need.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.25.2 WHERE: choose rows WHERE keeps only the rows that satisfy a condition. SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1001; Result: Asha's two orders order_id customer_id order_date total_amount 5001 1001 2026-01-15 1098.00 5002 1001 2026-02-03 1499.00 Text values go in quotes; numbers do not. Because zip_code is text in our table, WHERE zip_code = '600017' returns Ravi Kumar. You can combine conditions with AND and OR , and compare with < , > , LIKE and others. Why this matters A WHERE clause is the simplest subset there is: "only customers in postal area 600017". Both the Informatica and Delphix documentation use filters like this to limit rows. Delphix describes a rule-set filter as a WHERE clause, and says to prefix the column with the table name, for example customer.cust_id < 1000 ( Managing rule sets ). Note that a WHERE on one table does not by itself bring along the related rows of other tables; keys do that, which is why subsetting is more than a filter.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.25.3 JOIN: combine tables through keys A join follows a foreign key. Here, each order is matched to its customer by customer_id : SELECT c.first_name, o.order_id, o.total_amount FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id; Result first_name order_id total_amount Asha 5001 1098.00 Asha 5002 1499.00 Ravi 5003 598.00 c and o are short nicknames (aliases) for the tables. The ON line states the key match. Meera does not appear: she has no orders, and a plain JOIN keeps only matches. A LEFT JOIN keeps every customer and shows empty (null) where there is no order: SELECT c.first_name, o.order_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id; This returns Asha 5001, Asha 5002, Ravi 5003 and Meera with no order id. You can chain joins to walk the whole chain customer, order, item, product: SELECT c.last_name, p.product_name, i.quantity FROM order_items i JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = i.order_id JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN products p ON p.product_code = i.product_code ORDER BY i.item_id; The result has four rows: Menon with Wireless Mouse (1), Menon with USB-C Cable (1), Menon with Laptop Stand (1) and Kumar with USB-C Cable (2). A subsetting tool does something like this walk in reverse: start from the customers you chose and follow the keys out to every related row.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.25.4 COUNT: how many? SELECT COUNT(*) AS customer_count FROM customers; Returns 3. With GROUP BY you can count per group: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id; Returns 1001 with 2 orders and 1002 with 1 order. TDM people use COUNT constantly: how many rows before and after a subset? Does the masked table have as many rows as the source? Does the number of distinct values in a candidate key equal the number of rows? ( COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) counts the unique values.)

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.25.5 INSERT and UPDATE: change data INSERT INTO customers (...) VALUES (...) adds a row (the lab below has full examples); the column list and value list must line up. If you inserted an order with customer_id 9999 when no such customer exists, a database that enforces the foreign key rejects it. UPDATE customers SET zip_code = '560002' WHERE customer_id = 1001; After the UPDATE, a SELECT for customer 1001 returns zip_code 560002. Never write UPDATE without a WHERE unless you really mean to change every row: the statement above, without its last line, would give all three customers the same postal code. Masking is, at its core, a very large controlled UPDATE: replace the value in a sensitive column in every row (with a consistent rule). Delphix's in-place masking updates the source table; a copy-style approach writes to a different target. The tool generates the SQL for you, but understanding that it is an UPDATE explains why a table with no key is a problem: the tool needs a way to say "this exact row". Delphix's documentation says the custom SQL for a table must include the primary key column(s) and the columns to be masked ( Managing rule sets ). Lab: run the ShopSphere queries (database needed, any relational database) Goal: create the four tables, load the fake rows and reproduce this section's results. Create the tables in the order parents first, children second. A child table with a foreign key can only be created once its parent exists (in most databases), and rows must be inserted in the same order. CREATE TABLE customers ( customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, first_name VARCHAR(50), last_name VARCHAR(50), email VARCHAR(100), phone VARCHAR(15), ssn VARCHAR(11), date_of_birth DATE, zip_code VARCHAR(10), tax_id VARCHAR(20)); CREATE TABLE products ( product_code VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY, product_name VARCHAR(100), price DECIMAL(10,2)); CREATE TABLE orders ( order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL, order_date DATE, total_amount DECIMAL(10,2), FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers (customer_id)); CREATE TABLE order_items ( item_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_id INTEGER NOT NULL, product_code VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL, quantity INTEGER, unit_price DECIMAL(10,2), FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders (order_id), FOREIGN KEY (product_code) REFERENCES products (product_code)); Four tables created with no errors. Insert the rows. Use the sample rows shown earlier in this section. Customers and products first, then orders, then items. INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1001,'Asha','Menon','asha.menon@example.com','9876543210','123-45-6789','1990-04-12','560001','TAX-A1001'); INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1002,'Ravi','Kumar','ravi.k@example.com','9123456780','234-56-7890','1985-11-02','600017','TAX-R1002'); INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1003,'Meera','Nair','meera.n@example.com','9988776655','345-67-8901','1999-07-23','682001','TAX-M1003'); INSERT INTO products VALUES ('P100','Wireless Mouse',799.00); INSERT INTO products VALUES ('P200','USB-C Cable',299.00); INSERT INTO products VALUES ('P300','Laptop Stand',1499.00); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (5001,1001,'2026-01-15',1098.00); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (5002,1001,'2026-02-03',1499.00); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (5003,1002,'2026-02-10',598.00); INSERT INTO order_items VALUES (9001,5001,'P100',1,799.00); INSERT INTO order_items VALUES (9002,5001,'P200',1,299.00); INSERT INTO order_items VALUES (9003,5002,'P300',1,1499.00); INSERT INTO order_items VALUES (9004,5003,'P200',2,299.00); Three customer rows, three products, three orders and four items. (The tax_id values are invented placeholders for this guide.) Run the orphan check. This query lists orders whose customer does not exist. In a healthy database it returns no rows. It is the check you will run after every subset and mask to prove integrity. SELECT o.order_id FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL; No rows returned. Write two queries of your own. (a) How many order items does each order have? (b) Which customers have no orders? Show a worked answer (a) SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS item_count FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id; returns 5001 with 2, 5002 with 1, 5003 with 1. (b) SELECT c.first_name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL; returns Meera. This is the same "LEFT JOIN then look for nulls" trick as the orphan check, aimed the other way.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
h: 1.26 Data volumes and why size matters
x: 1.26 Data volumes and why size matters ShopSphere's sample tables hold ten rows between them. The real database holds millions of customers and tens of millions of orders. Size changes everything about TDM. Sizes run from KB (a short text file) through MB (a CSV of tens of thousands of customers) and GB (a small production database) to TB (a large enterprise database). Why size matters to a TDM engineer: Time. Masking updates every row of every sensitive column. Ten times the rows is roughly ten times the work unless you add parallelism. Delphix profile jobs have a setting for the number of parallel streams, for example two streams to run two tables of a rule set at once ( Delphix masking terminology ). Storage. Every environment that holds a full copy multiplies the cost. See the why-TDM chapter . Memory and file limits. A file of many gigabytes cannot be opened in a spreadsheet; you work on it with tools or by sampling. Test fitness. Performance tests need volume; functional tests do not. Matching size to purpose is part of the job. Row count versus width. A table with a hundred million narrow rows and a table with a million rows of large documents behave very differently. Ask for both numbers. Always ask for counts first Before any TDM job, ask for the row count of each table. It tells you whether a subset is needed, how long a job should take, and gives you a number to verify afterwards (row counts before and after should reconcile with what you expect).

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
h: 1.27 Hands-on: which keys exist in the ShopSphere files?
x: 1.27 Hands-on: which keys exist in the ShopSphere files? This exercise rehearses the real situation from the logical keys section: data arrives as files, no database has declared any keys, and you must work out the relationships. It needs no tool, only reasoning. It matches the Day 51 topic "primary key basics and discovery". ShopSphere's partner system sends three files. None of them states any key. customers.csv customer_id,first_name,last_name,email 1001,Asha,Menon,asha.menon@example.com 1002,Ravi,Kumar,ravi.k@example.com 1003,Meera,Nair,meera.n@example.com 1004,Asha,Menon,asha.m2@example.com orders.dat (pipe-delimited, no header) 5001|1001|2026-01-15|1098.00 5002|1001|2026-02-03|1499.00 5003|1002|2026-02-10|598.00 5004|1004|2026-02-11|299.00 order_items.txt (fixed width: item_id 1-4, order_id 5-8, product 9-12, qty 13-15) 90015001P100 1 90025001P200 1 90035002P300 1 90045003P200 2 90055004P200 1 Splitting the first item line by position gives item_id 9001, order_id 5001, product P100 and qty 1 (padded with two spaces to fill its field). Without the layout line above the file, the run of digits at the start would be meaningless. The layout specification is part of the data. Lab: find the keys (thinking lab, no tool needed) Goal: decide the primary key of each file, the foreign keys between them, and any problems. For each file, name a candidate primary key. A candidate must be unique and never empty in every row. Test it by looking for repeats. Find the foreign keys. Which column in one file should match the primary key of another? Write each as child.column to parent.column . Check integrity. For each foreign key, list the values and check each one exists in the parent. Note any orphans. Spot a trap. Customers 1001 and 1004 look similar. Is that a key problem? Decide how you would tell a tool. The files have no declared keys. What would you tell a TDM tool to treat as logical keys? Show a worked answer 1. Primary keys. customers.csv : customer_id (1001 to 1004, all distinct). Not the name: Asha Menon appears twice. Not the email as a choice either; it is unique in this sample but emails can change, so it is a weaker key. orders.dat : the first field, the order id (5001 to 5004, all distinct). order_items.txt : item_id (9001 to 9005, all distinct). 2. Foreign keys. orders field 2 (customer id) refers to customers.customer_id . order_items.order_id refers to the order id in orders.dat . A product column also exists; it would point to a products file or table, which the partner did not send here. 3. Integrity. Order customers are 1001, 1001, 1002, 1004: all exist. Item orders are 5001, 5001, 5002, 5003, 5004: all exist. No orphans. Note that customer 1003 has no orders (legal). 4. The trap. Customers 1001 and 1004 share a first and last name but have different emails and IDs. They may be two people or one person registered twice. The keys are fine (the IDs are distinct); this is a data quality question, not a key problem. It matters for masking: a consistent masking rule that works on the name alone would give both the same fake name, which may or may not be what you want. Ask the data steward. 5. Telling the tool. Declare customer_id, order id and item_id as the logical primary keys of their files, and declare the two foreign key relationships as logical foreign keys, so that a subset starting from a customer follows its orders and items. In Informatica that is the logical constraints from the Discover > Tables view; in Delphix it is the logical key on the table, and file relationships are handled by the formats and the masking design. Details are in the tool chapters.

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.28 Common mistakes and gotchas Treating a column as unique because the sample looks unique Three rows with distinct emails do not prove emails are unique across three million rows. Test with counts of all rows against counts of distinct values. Assuming the database enforces the keys Many databases, especially older ones and data warehouses, have no declared foreign keys. Relationships exist only by convention. That is why profiling for keys and logical keys exist. Masking keys inconsistently If a key is masked in one table and not in its child tables (or masked differently), relationships break. Mask keys the same way everywhere, or leave them alone. Uploading real data to define a format A layout needs only structure. Delphix says not to upload production data, sample records or PII when defining file formats ( Managing file formats ).

ct: Welcome: why TDM exists and the data basics you need
x: 1.29 Recap Recap A database holds tables; a table has rows (records) and columns (fields) with data types. Metadata and schema describe the data without containing it. A primary key uniquely identifies a row; a foreign key in a child table points at a parent's primary key; together they give one-to-many relationships. Referential integrity means every foreign key matches an existing parent. Subsetting, masking and generation must all preserve it. Logical keys are keys declared to the tool when the database does not declare them. Informatica and Delphix both support them. Flat files have no built-in schema: know the layout (delimited or fixed-width), header and footer records, record types, line endings and encoding. XML and JSON nest children inside parents instead of using foreign keys. SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, COUNT, INSERT and UPDATE cover most of the SQL you will read. The orphan check (LEFT JOIN where the parent is null) is a TDM staple. Size drives time, cost and test fitness: ask for row counts first.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
h: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: Sensitive data, privacy laws and policies In the why-TDM chapter you saw why teams cannot simply copy production into testing. The main reason is simple: production is full of real people's private details. In the data basics chapter you learned what tables, columns and keys are. This section joins the two ideas. Before any tool can protect data, someone has to say what "sensitive" means, which laws care about it, and how a tool can recognise it among thousands of columns. This is the vocabulary layer of TDM. Every later chapter (discovery, subsetting, masking, and all three tools) uses the words defined here: PII, PHI, PCI, policy, rule, data domain, classification. If those words are fuzzy, the tools will feel like a maze of unexplained menus. If they are clear, the tools will feel like different dialects of the same language.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.1 Words to know first Sensitive data Any data that could hurt a person or a company if it leaked or was misused: identity details, health records, payment details, passwords, trade secrets. "Sensitive" is a business and legal judgement, not just a technical one. PII (Personally Identifiable Information) Data that identifies a person, alone or combined with other data. Examples: name, email, phone number, a government ID number, a home address. PHI (Protected Health Information) Health-related data that can be tied to a person: diagnoses, treatments, medical record numbers, insurance member IDs. Informatica describes its PHI pack as aimed at the healthcare and pharmaceutical industries (User Guide 10.5.10, p.79). PCI (Payment Card Industry) data Payment card details such as the card number and expiry date. Informatica describes its PCI pack as aimed at banking and finance (User Guide 10.5.10, p.80). Identifier A piece of data that points to one person. A direct identifier does it on its own (an SSN). An indirect identifier (also called a quasi-identifier) only does it when combined with others (zip code plus birth date). Re-identification Working out who a "nameless" record belongs to by combining it with other information. Data classification Sorting data into sensitivity levels (for example public, internal, confidential, restricted) so each level gets the right protection. Data domain A named kind of data, such as "Social Security number" or "First name", described by how the data looks and what its column is usually called. Both Informatica and Delphix use this word, with slightly different meanings. Rule In Informatica, the logic that changes a value: a masking rule uses a masking technique (such as substitution) with chosen settings. Rules are covered in the masking concepts chapter . Policy In TDM, a named bundle that says which kinds of data are sensitive and how to protect each kind. Section 2.8 shows the exact Informatica structure. Data steward The person who knows a data set's meaning and quality and answers questions such as "what is in this column and who may see it?". Compliance officer The person responsible for making sure the organisation follows laws and internal rules about data.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.2 What is sensitive data? Start with the ShopSphere database from the data basics chapter . Here are three real-looking (but fictional) rows from CUSTOMERS : ShopSphere CUSTOMERS, first three rows (all fake) customer_id first_name last_name email phone ssn date_of_birth zip_code 1001 Asha Menon asha.menon@example.com 9876543210 123-45-6789 1990-04-12 560001 1002 Ravi Kumar ravi.k@example.com 9123456780 234-56-7890 1985-11-02 600017 1003 Meera Nair meera.n@example.com 9988776655 345-67-8901 1999-07-23 682001 Ask one question of each column: if this leaked, could someone be harmed or could ShopSphere be in trouble? customer_id is just a number the system made up. On its own it harms nobody. But it links to orders, so it still needs careful handling (more in the masking concepts chapter ). first_name and last_name tell you who the person is. email and phone let a stranger contact, spam, phish or impersonate the person. ssn (a government ID number) is the classic example: with a name and a birth date it is enough to open credit in someone's name. date_of_birth is used by banks and call centres to "prove" who you are. zip_code looks harmless. Section 2.4 shows why it is not. Why it matters in testing Production data is protected by firewalls, access reviews and monitoring. A test database usually has none of that. Many people can log in, copies get passed around, and some environments live with outside vendors or in the cloud. If a real SSN sits in a test table, it carries production's legal weight into a place with a fraction of production's security. That mismatch is the whole reason this section exists. Delphix's own introduction makes the same point from the tool side: organisations face data breaches and pressure from regulators, and encryption helps protect data on disks and in transit but is, in their words, ill-suited for protecting non-production environments used for development, testing and reporting. Their answer is to replace confidential values with fictitious but realistic ones. (Delphix "Introduction to Delphix Masking", source page ↗ ). A quick test you can apply at work Look at a column and ask three questions: (1) Does it identify a person? (2) Would a regulator or customer be upset if it leaked? (3) Would a tester still be able to do their job if it held a believable fake value instead? If the answers are yes, yes, yes, the column is a masking candidate. Question 3 matters: if the column cannot be faked without breaking the test, you have found a design problem to solve, not a reason to leave real data in place.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
h: 2.3 The three families: PII, PHI and PCI
x: 2.3 The three families: PII, PHI and PCI People in TDM talk in three abbreviations. They overlap, and a single column can belong to more than one family, but each one points at a different law or standard and a different industry.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.3.1 PII: personally identifiable information PII is data that identifies a person. The definition differs a little between countries and laws, but the everyday list is stable: Names, email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses. Government-issued numbers: SSN (US), passport number, driver's licence number, national ID. India's Aadhaar and PAN are comparable examples. Date of birth, age, gender, place of birth. Online identifiers such as IP addresses. ShopSphere's CUSTOMERS table is almost pure PII: first_name , last_name , email , phone , ssn , date_of_birth , zip_code and tax_id . Informatica ships a ready-made PII policy pack . It lists 26 data domains, each paired with a default masking rule (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.78 to 79). Reading the list is a quick way to see what a vendor treats as PII: Data domains in the Informatica PII policy pack (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.78-79), grouped by us for readability Group (our label) Data domains in the pack Names First Name, Last Name, Full Name Contact Email Address, Phone, Full Address UPPER, Street Name, State, ZIP, Country Government and travel IDs Social Security Number, Passport, Drivers License Number, UK National Identifier, Vehicle Registration Number Personal facts Birth Date, Birth Place, Age, Gender Money and work Credit Card, Salary, Job Position, Organization Name Other IP Address, School Name, Grades Notice that the pack includes things you might not call "identity", such as Salary and Grades. A vendor's list is a starting point. Your organisation decides what else counts.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.3.2 PHI: protected health information PHI is health data that can be linked to a person. The health data alone ("type 2 diabetes") is not what makes it PHI. The link to an identifiable individual does. A list of diagnoses with no names or IDs and no way to trace back is a different thing from a patient record. ShopSphere is a retailer, so it has no medical records. To make the idea concrete, imagine a hypothetical ShopSphere feature, "ShopSphere Pharmacy", with a table PRESCRIPTIONS(rx_id, customer_id, diagnosis_code, drug_name, insurer_member_id) . Then: Illustrative only: a hypothetical ShopSphere PRESCRIPTIONS table (not part of the shared schema) rx_id customer_id diagnosis_code drug_name insurer_member_id 9001 1001 E11.9 Metformin HP-5501-882 9002 1003 J45.909 Salbutamol inhaler HP-5501-913 Here diagnosis_code and drug_name are health facts, insurer_member_id is an identifier, and customer_id links them to Asha or Meera. Together they are PHI. The same pack idea exists in Informatica: the PHI policy pack lists 17 domains, among them Medical Record Number, Health Plan Beneficiary Number, Device Identifier Serial Number, Certificate License Number, Account Number, Birth Date, Email Address, IP Address, Web URL, Social Security Number and ZIP (User Guide 10.5.10, p.79). Look closely at what the pack contains The PHI pack is mostly identifiers that appear in healthcare data: names, record numbers, plan numbers, dates, ZIP. It does not try to list every diagnosis. That tells you how privacy rules think: what makes a health record dangerous is that it can be traced to a person, so removing or masking the identifiers does most of the protective work. Delphix organises its detection logic into profile sets . Besides the recommended ASDD Standard set, it ships legacy sets named "Financial - Legacy" and "HIPAA - Legacy" (Delphix "Out of the box profiling settings"). Delphix's standard set also has domains with explicitly medical names, such as MEDICAL_CODES, MEDICAL_DRUG and BLOOD_TYPE, and a domain called HIPAA_DATE (Delphix "ASDD standard profile set" listing). The words "HIPAA Date" hint at a rule HIPAA has about dates, which section 2.5 explains.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.3.3 PCI: payment card data PCI refers to the Payment Card Industry. The PCI DSS (Data Security Standard) is a rulebook created by the card brands for anyone who stores, processes or sends card data. It is not a government law. It is a contractual standard: merchants who ignore it can lose the right to take card payments, and can be fined by their payment partners. In TDM talk, "PCI data" means card number, card expiry date, security code, cardholder name. ShopSphere's shared schema has no card column, but any real online shop would have one (or would store a token from a payment provider). If it did, it would look like 4539 1596 8210 2773 . This is the number Informatica's own documentation uses as a masking example (User Guide 10.5.10, p.158). The Informatica PCI policy pack is short: Account Number, Birth Date, Credit Card, Expiration Date, First Name and Last Name (User Guide 10.5.10, p.80). Do not copy these numbers from the docs into your own tests A card number from a documentation page may look fake and still be a real, working card by coincidence. When you need card numbers for testing, use numbers designed for testing (payment providers publish "test card numbers") or let a generator or masking tool make numbers that pass the format check but belong to no account.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
h: 2.4 Direct and indirect identifiers: why "just remove the names" fails
x: 2.4 Direct and indirect identifiers: why "just remove the names" fails A common beginner idea is: "We will delete the name column and then the data is anonymous." It is not, and understanding why is the most important privacy idea in this section.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.4.1 Two kinds of identifier Direct identifiers Point to one person by themselves. Full name (mostly) SSN, passport number Email address, phone number Card number Removing or replacing these is the obvious first step. Indirect identifiers (quasi-identifiers) Harmless alone, identifying in combination. Zip or postal code Date of birth Gender Job title, employer Rare product or rare diagnosis Easy to forget, which is why they cause leaks. Research on public records, most famously by the computer scientist Latanya Sweeney, has found that a large share of people in the United States can be singled out from just three facts: zip code, full date of birth and gender. The exact percentage depends on the data set and the year, so do not quote a number from this guide. Remember the shape of the result: three boring columns, one unique person.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.4.2 A worked example with ShopSphere Imagine a careless tester shares an "anonymised" extract with a contractor. Names, emails, phones and SSNs were deleted. What remains: "Anonymised" extract: direct identifiers removed, indirect ones kept customer_id date_of_birth zip_code total_spent 1001 1990-04-12 560001 41,250 1002 1985-11-02 600017 9,800 1003 1999-07-23 682001 27,430 Now suppose the contractor also has an outside list: a public club membership page, a leaked mailing list, a social media profile that mentions "born 12 April 1990" and a city. Matching the outside list against the extract on birth date plus zip code finds exactly one row. The contractor now knows that Asha spent 41,250 at ShopSphere. No name was ever in the extract. Take the extract. Birth date and zip code are in it. Take any outside list that has the same two facts plus a name. The linking columns do not have to be sensitive on their own. Result: the outside list's "Asha Menon" matches one row of the extract. Read everything else in the matched row. Everything in the row now belongs to a named person. What this means for masking Protecting a data set means looking at combinations . It is why the PII and PHI packs both include Birth Date, ZIP and State, not only names and ID numbers. It is also why masking techniques that move a date a little or blur a number (see the masking concepts chapter ) exist: they weaken the combination while keeping the data useful for testing. Free text is the other hiding place Informatica's data domain page notes that a Social Security number might sit in an SSN column, in a column called SOCIAL_SECURITY in another table, and also inside a COMMENTS column (User Guide 10.5.10, p.73). A support agent typing "customer 123-45-6789 called about refund" into a notes field has just put an SSN where no column name will ever warn you. Delphix's Free Text Redaction algorithm exists for exactly this problem ( the masking concepts chapter explains it).

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
h: 2.5 Privacy laws and standards in plain words
x: 2.5 Privacy laws and standards in plain words This is not legal advice Everything in this section is a plain-language orientation , written so you can follow a meeting and ask good questions. Laws change, have exceptions, and apply differently depending on where your company and your customers are. Treat every statement here as "roughly true, check with legal". The tool documentation does not teach law, so none of this comes from the tool sources, except where marked. Why should a tester care about laws? Because when a court or regulator looks at a data leak, they do not ask "was it production or test?". They ask "was personal data properly protected?". A copy in a test database is still personal data.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.5.1 GDPR in plain words The GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) is a European Union law that has applied since May 2018. What it protects: "personal data", meaning any information about an identifiable person. That is broader than a name and number: online identifiers and location data can count. Who it applies to: organisations that handle the personal data of people in the EU, even if the organisation sits outside Europe. A ShopSphere selling to customers in Germany would likely be in scope wherever its servers are. Ideas behind it: there must be a lawful reason to use the data (consent is one such reason); use it only for the purpose it was collected for; collect and keep no more than needed ("data minimisation"); keep it secure; let people see and delete their data. Fines at a high level: the most serious breaches can lead to fines of up to 20 million euros or 4 percent of worldwide yearly turnover, whichever is higher. Lesser breaches have a lower ceiling. The consequence for test data. Two GDPR ideas hit TDM directly. First, purpose : a customer who gave details so ShopSphere could deliver an order did not necessarily agree to have them copied into a test lab. Second, minimisation and security : copying a whole production database to a loosely guarded test server is hard to justify when a small, masked copy would do. The law also treats truly anonymous data (nobody can be identified any more) as outside its scope, which is one reason masking and subsetting are popular. Whether a particular masked data set counts as anonymous is a question for your compliance officer.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.5.2 HIPAA in plain words HIPAA is a United States law from 1996 that, through its Privacy and Security Rules, protects health information. What it protects: PHI, health information that identifies a person (section 2.3). Who it applies to: "covered entities" (health plans, healthcare providers, healthcare clearinghouses) and their "business associates", meaning vendors who handle PHI for them. A software company testing a hospital's billing system is typically a business associate. Minimum necessary: people and systems should receive only the least PHI they need for their job. Testers rarely need the real thing. De-identification: HIPAA describes two accepted ways to de-identify health data so it is no longer treated as PHI. One removes a defined list of 18 kinds of identifiers (names, detailed locations, most date elements except the year, phone numbers, record numbers and so on). The other has a qualified expert certify that the risk of identifying anyone is very small. This may be why Delphix has a domain called HIPAA_DATE, and why dates and ZIP codes feature so heavily in PHI discussions. Penalties at a high level: civil penalties in tiers depending on how careless the organisation was, and criminal penalties for knowing misuse. Both tools mention these regimes only briefly. Delphix's introduction lists HIPAA, PCI and GDPR as examples of mandates organisations must stay compliant with, and Informatica packages its PHI and PCI policy packs for healthcare and banking respectively (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.79 to 80). GenRocket's column-profiling page says that identifying PII early helps organisations meet requirements "such as HIPAA".

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.5.3 Other regimes, kept general Other privacy rules you will hear about (very general; verify details with your compliance team) Name Where One-line idea PCI DSS Worldwide, by card-brand contract Security standard for anyone handling payment card data. An industry standard rather than a law. CCPA (California Consumer Privacy Act, later amended) California, USA Gives California residents rights over personal information held by businesses, such as knowing what is held and asking for deletion. DPDP Act (Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023) India Consent-centred law on processing digital personal data of people in India. Rules and start dates are phased in, so check the current status before relying on any detail. There are many more (sector rules for banks, national laws in dozens of countries, contract terms from clients). The practical lesson is the same everywhere: personal data in test environments is a liability, and the standard defence is to make sure the test copy no longer identifies anyone.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
h: 2.5.4 Four ideas that repeat across laws
x: 2.5.4 Four ideas that repeat across laws Recurring ideas and what they mean for a TDM engineer Idea Plain meaning What it changes in TDM work Consent / lawful purpose People agree, or the law allows, use for a stated purpose. Testing is a different purpose from running the shop, so real data in test is hard to defend. Minimum necessary / minimisation Use only as much data as the job needs. This is the legal argument for subsetting (see the discovery and subsetting concepts chapter ): do not copy 100 percent when 2 percent will do. De-identification / anonymisation Make the data no longer point to a person. This is the legal argument for masking (see the masking concepts chapter ). Security safeguards Protect what you keep with access control and logging. Applies to the TDM tool itself and to any unmasked staging copy.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
h: 2.6 Data classification: how sensitive is each column?
x: 2.6 Data classification: how sensitive is each column? Data classification means labelling data by how much damage a leak could do, so that you can apply protection in proportion. Organisations choose their own scheme. A typical four-level scheme looks like this: A typical four-level classification (illustrative; your organisation's levels may differ) Level Meaning ShopSphere example Typical test-data action Public Safe for anyone to see PRODUCTS.product_name , PRODUCTS.price Copy as is Internal Fine inside the company, not outside ORDERS.order_date , ORDERS.total_amount Copy as is, or lightly vary Confidential Harms people or the business if leaked CUSTOMERS.email , phone , first_name , last_name , zip_code Mask with realistic replacements Restricted Serious legal or financial harm CUSTOMERS.ssn , tax_id , date_of_birth , card numbers Mask strongly, or never move to test Two things are worth noticing. First, classification is about columns (and sometimes whole tables), not rows. Second, the result of classifying is a plan: each level maps to an action. A column with no label gets no action, so unlabelled sensitive data is the dangerous kind.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.6.1 How the tools record sensitivity Informatica. When you create a data domain you set a sensitivity level for all its columns, chosen from levels that the Administrator defines (User Guide 10.5.10, p.75). Separately, each column in a project has a Sensitive flag. The guide says the flag is "for reference only" and does not affect processing, and that assigning a data domain to a column marks it sensitive automatically (p.89). A different property, Restricted , does change behaviour: the integration service does not write a restricted column's value to the target (p.89). Delphix. A domain ties a category of sensitive data (the terminology page's example is social security numbers) to the way it should be secured. The profiler assigns the domain to a column and, with it, the domain's default masking algorithm (Delphix "Discovering your sensitive data"). Sensitive flag versus masking rule In Informatica, marking a column "sensitive" does not mask it. It documents your decision. Masking happens only when a rule is assigned to the column and a plan runs (see the Informatica data masking chapter ). Beginners often tick "sensitive" and think the job is done. Many laws treat some data as especially sensitive: ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, trade union membership, health, sexual orientation, biometrics. The Delphix ASDD Standard profile set has domains for these (for example ETHNICITY, RELIGIOUS_ORIEN, POLITICAL_ORIEN, UNION_MEMBERSHIP_NO, BIOMETRIC and MEDICAL_CODES), and the default masking method it shows for BIOMETRIC is NullValueLookup. For the most delicate data, blanking a value is often better than faking it.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.7 How sensitive data is found A real production database can have hundreds of tables and tens of thousands of columns. Nobody can read them all, and column names are often cryptic ( COL_17 , FLD_X2 ). So tools look for sensitive data automatically. At concept level they all rely on a small set of signals. The full hands-on process is the subject of the discovery and subsetting concepts chapter , the Informatica discovery and profiling chapter and the Delphix profiling chapter . Here we only need the ideas. Column CUSTOMERS.ssn → Signals name, pattern, list, type → Candidate domain Social Security Number → Human review approve or reject → Protection default rule or algorithm This chain is the same in all three tools, even though each names the boxes differently. Keep it in mind: every feature in the later tool chapters is a way to fill in or control one of these boxes.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.7.1 Three signals The three detection signals (general concept, with where each tool uses it) Signal What it checks Strength Weakness Column name (metadata) Does the name look like ssn , email , phone ? Fast, needs no data access Misses cryptic names. Flags harmless columns with unlucky names. Data pattern Do the values look like an SSN, a phone number, an email? Works even when the name is useless Slower, reads real data. Nine digits may be an SSN or an order code. Dictionary or list of values Are the values found in a list, such as common first names or country names? Finds things with no fixed shape, such as names Lists are language-specific and never complete. A fourth signal, data type and length , is used to rule things out: an SSN cannot live in a column that holds one-character flags.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
h: 2.7.2 What Informatica does: data patterns and metadata patterns
x: 2.7.2 What Informatica does: data patterns and metadata patterns Informatica describes a data domain using regular expressions. A regular expression (regex) is a compact text recipe for a pattern, for example "three digits, a hyphen, two digits, a hyphen, four digits". The guide separates two kinds (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.74 to 75): A data pattern matches the values. Its example for Social Security numbers is [0-9]{3}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{4} . A metadata pattern matches column names. Its examples for Social Security numbers are .*SSN* , .*SOCIAL* and .*SECURITY* . A column joins the data domain if it matches any expression in the domain. When you run a data domain profile you choose to search the data only, the column name only, or both, how many rows to read (default 1,000) and a minimum conformance percent, since not every row has to match the pattern (pp.95 and 100). Data pattern [0-9]{3}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{4} matches 123-45-6789 Metadata pattern .*SSN* matches SSN, CUST_SSN, SSN_NO

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
h: 2.7.3 What Delphix does: profile sets, classifiers and domains
x: 2.7.3 What Delphix does: profile sets, classifiers and domains Delphix calls the detection step profiling . A profiling job examines metadata (column names and types) and possibly the data itself, and when it decides a column is sensitive it assigns the matching domain and that domain's default masking algorithm. It only covers the tables and files in the chosen rule set (Delphix "Discovering your sensitive data", source page ↗ ). The logic is packaged in classifiers , grouped into profile sets . Four classifier frameworks exist, and they map neatly to our signals: Delphix classifier frameworks (Delphix "Discovering your sensitive data") Framework What it examines Level PATH The path to the data; for a database that means table and column name. Uses regex or exact match. Column TYPE Data type and length. Used to reject domain matches. Types: String, Number, Date, Binary. Column REGEX The data itself, using regular expressions to match or reject a domain. Data LIST Whether data values appear in a list of values, to match or reject a domain. Data The recommended built-in profile set, the "ASDD Standard" set, includes list classifiers that can detect domains such as FIRST_NAME and LAST_NAME even when column names are meaningless, though data-level detection is limited to English values (Delphix "Out of the box profiling settings").

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
h: 2.7.4 One real example: how Delphix recognises an SSN
x: 2.7.4 One real example: how Delphix recognises an SSN The ASDD Standard listing (Delphix "ASDD standard profile set", source page ↗ ) shows the SSN domain is defined by three classifiers. In our words: A PATH classifier. A regex on the column path catches names like ssn or social security number with variants such as social_security_no . Its match strength is listed as 0.67. A REGEX classifier on the data. Patterns for the nine-digit format. The dashed or spaced form (123-45-6789) is listed with match strength 0.7, while nine bare digits are listed with only 0.1. The lower number for bare digits fits the idea in the weaknesses table above: nine digits in a row are far more likely to be something other than an SSN. A TYPE classifier. The column must be a Number or String of at least 9 characters. This rejects tiny columns. The excerpt I had does not explain how the strengths are combined into a final decision, so read the product page for your version before relying on the numbers. What matters for a beginner is the design: several weak clues, each with a weight, are combined to decide.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
h: 2.7.5 What GenRocket does: column names only
x: 2.7.5 What GenRocket does: column names only GenRocket's "Data Column Profiling" scans column headers , not the data. It checks whether each column name contains a keyword from a list: 102 built-in names plus any your organisation adds (for example user_email matches email , client_ssn matches ssn ). It then shows you the matches to choose from (GenRocket "PII Discovery with Data Column Profiling", source page ↗ ). It is the "column name" signal on its own. The upside is that the tool never needs to read real values. You will read many patterns in policies, so here is the minimum: [0-9] means one digit, {n} repeats the previous item n times, ? makes it optional, * means zero or more, and a backslash makes a special character literal (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.74 to 75). A data pattern says what a value looks like , not what it is : [0-9]{10} matches a phone number and also a ten-digit order reference. That is the source of false alarms (false positives); a real SSN column stored without hyphens that fails the pattern is a false negative. Dialects differ: Delphix patterns start with (?i) for case-insensitive matching.

x: 2.8 Policies, rules and data domains Now the vocabulary promised at the start. A TDM tool needs one place that records the answer to "what is sensitive here, and how do we protect each kind?". Informatica calls that place a policy . The structure is worth learning exactly, because it explains many menus you will see later. (User Guide 10.5.10, p.71) POLICY (example: ShopSphere_Customer_PII) DATA DOMAIN: Social Security Number Data pattern: [0-9]{3}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{4} Metadata pattern: .*SSN* .*SOCIAL* Sensitivity level: set by the Administrator's list RULE (default): SSN masking technique + parameters (repeatable output, seed ...) Other preferred rules can sit beside it One of them is marked default DATA DOMAIN: Email Address Data pattern: text@text.text shape Metadata pattern: .*EMAIL* RULE (default): Email masking technique + parameters (domain, dictionary ...) Columns found by profiling receive this rule automatically Original diagram: the Informatica structure (policy contains data domains, a data domain holds patterns and preferred rules). The patterns, rule names and parameter lists inside are illustrative, drawn for ShopSphere.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.8.1 What each piece is Policy (Informatica) "A data masking component that describes the methods to maintain the privacy of specific types of source data". It contains data domains. You assign a policy to a data source in a project, and one policy can serve several projects (p.71). Data domain (Informatica) Describes the functional meaning of a column based on its data or its name. It carries data patterns, metadata patterns, a sensitivity level, a status (enabled or disabled) and, optionally, preferred masking and generation rules (pp.73 to 75). Rule (Informatica) "A logic to mask sensitive data or to generate test data": a technique plus its parameters. Rules exist for string, numeric and date data (p.72). Preferred rule and default rule When you attach several rules to a domain they are "preferred rules", and one is the default, applied to all columns in the domain unless you pick another. The guide's example: a Last_Name domain with a shuffle rule as default and a substitution rule as another preferred rule (p.73). Policy pack A ready-made policy shipped with TDM. There are three: PII, PHI and PCI, visible after installation (p.77). The order of work does not matter. The guide says you can create policies, rules and domains in any order, then connect them: create masking rules, define domains, assign rules to domains, create a policy, assign domains to it (p.72). Illustrative ShopSphere policy ShopSphere's TDM engineer, with the compliance officer's approval, builds a policy ShopSphere_Customer_PII from these domains. The domain names echo the PII pack; the rule choices are our example. It is an illustrative process that uses the tool facts from earlier sections where marked. Start with the requirement, in business words. ShopSphere's compliance officer says: "No real customer identity may leave production, in India or Germany. Card data never leaves the payment zone." The reason to write it in plain words is that everything later is traced back to this sentence. A one-page statement of scope: which systems, which data subjects, which laws. Find candidate sensitive columns. Run discovery ( the discovery and subsetting concepts chapter , then the tool chapters). The tool proposes columns and domains from names, patterns and lists. A candidate list of columns with a proposed domain and a match score or conformance percent. Review with the data steward. An approved list, with a short reason for each yes and no. Classify. Give each approved column a level (section 2.6) and decide the action for each level: mask, null out, or exclude. A table like the lab answer below, signed off by the compliance officer. Choose a protection for each domain. Pick techniques that keep data usable for tests (see the masking concepts chapter ). In Informatica, attach them as preferred rules and mark one default per domain; in Delphix, choose the default algorithm for each domain. Each domain has one default protection and a written reason. Bundle into a policy and store it. In Informatica you add the domains to a named policy and assign the policy to a project's data source (p.71). You can export policies, domains and rules to XML files and import them into another TDM repository, so a tested policy can travel from a test setup to the real one (p.80). Importing fails if the object already has assignments, so clear them or rename the file first (pp.80 to 81). A versioned policy and a copy of its exported files. Prove it works. Repeat on change. New columns appear whenever the application changes. Delphix notes that a profiling job only covers tables and files already in the rule set, and that newly reachable objects must be added by hand (Delphix "Discovering your sensitive data"). x: 2.14 Recap Remember Sensitive data is whatever could harm a person or the company if leaked. PII identifies people, PHI ties health facts to a person, PCI covers payment card data. Direct identifiers point to one person. Indirect identifiers (zip, birth date, gender) identify when combined, so deleting names is not enough. GDPR and HIPAA, in plain words, say: have a lawful purpose, use the minimum necessary, secure it, and de-identify where you can. This is the legal case for subsetting and masking. This guide is not legal advice. Classification gives each column a sensitivity level, and each level maps to an action. Tools find sensitive columns by column names, data patterns and value lists, plus type checks. The output is candidates for human review. An Informatica policy contains data domains. A domain holds patterns, a sensitivity level and preferred rules. A rule is a technique plus parameters. Delphix uses domains, classifiers, profile sets and algorithm instances for the same ideas. People decide: the compliance officer sets what is sensitive, the data steward explains the data, the TDM engineer builds and runs the policy. Discovery, profiling and subsetting: the concepts Imagine you have to move a flat. Before you pack, you walk through every room and list what is there: which boxes are fragile, which items belong together, which papers are private. Only then do you decide what to take and how to wrap it. Test data work follows the same order. First you look inside the production database (discovery and profiling). Then you take only what you need (subsetting). After that, you protect what you took (masking, covered in the masking concepts chapter ). This section teaches the two first steps as ideas, without any tool buttons. It builds on the data basics chapter (tables, primary keys, foreign keys) and on the sensitive data chapter (what sensitive data is, and how patterns and names reveal it). The hands-on tool chapters that follow are Informatica discovery and profiling , Informatica data subset and Delphix profiling .

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.15 Words to know first Data discovery The step of finding out what is in a data source: which tables and columns exist, which hold sensitive data, how tables relate. Informatica uses "data discovery" for the whole activity and "profile" for each job inside it. Profile (verb: to profile) A job that scans a data source and reports facts about it. Delphix and GenRocket also say "profiling". Metadata Data about data: table names, column names, data types, lengths, key definitions. The column ssn and its type "string of 11 characters" are metadata. The value 123-45-6789 is data. Primary key (PK) A column (or set of columns) whose values are unique for every row and identify it, such as customer_id . Foreign key (FK) A column whose values point to a primary key in another table, such as ORDERS.customer_id pointing to CUSTOMERS.customer_id . Parent table and child table The table holding the primary key is the parent; the table holding the foreign key is the child. CUSTOMERS is the parent of ORDERS , and ORDERS is the parent of ORDER_ITEMS . Referential integrity The promise that every foreign key value points to a row that really exists. A child row with no parent is an orphan , and it means the data is broken. Data subset A smaller copy of a database that still hangs together: fewer rows, same structure, referential integrity intact. Driving table (driver table) The table you start from when you pick a subset. The tool finds related rows in other tables starting from it. Informatica uses exactly this term for the starting table of an entity. Entity (Informatica) A driving table plus all the tables related to it. It is the unit that Informatica copies to a subset database.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.16.1 What it is Data profiling means scanning a data source with software and producing a report of facts about it. Data discovery is the wider goal: using those facts to decide what to mask, what to subset, and how tables connect. Informatica puts it plainly: run profiles to discover source data for data masking and data subset operations (User Guide 10.5.10, p.86). A profile changes nothing: it measures, lists and flags. Unlike a building survey, its flags are guesses that people must confirm.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.16.2 Why it comes first Masking and subsetting are only as good as your knowledge of the data. You cannot mask a sensitive column you did not know about. Missing one column of SSNs means a leak. You cannot subset safely without knowing the relationships. If you cut ORDERS without knowing it points at CUSTOMERS , you will leave orphans. You cannot choose a masking technique without knowing the column's type, length and shape. Real databases are rarely documented. Old tables, renamed columns and half-forgotten fields are normal. Why it matters Both Informatica and Delphix describe profiling as the step that feeds the next one. Informatica says that before masking you can discover which columns to mask with the same rules, and before subsetting you can discover relationships between tables and the entities for the subset (User Guide 10.5.10, p.86). Delphix says that after connecting data, the next step is discovering which of it should be secured (Delphix "Discovering your sensitive data").

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.16.3 What a profile reports Typically: each column's data type and length; value patterns and their share (99 percent of phone values are ten digits); ranges, minimum, maximum and the share of nulls; the most common values; sensitive-looking columns ( email matches an Email Address domain); primary key candidates ( customer_id is 100 percent unique); and foreign key candidates ( ORDERS.customer_id matches CUSTOMERS.customer_id ).

x: 2.17 Metadata profiling and data profiling A profile can look at two different things, and the difference decides how fast it is and what it can find. Metadata profiling Reads only descriptions : table names, column names, types, lengths, declared keys. Fast, and does not need to read any real customer values. Finds a column called ssn , or user_email . Misses cryptic names such as FLD_X2 , and cannot tell whether notes contains an SSN. Data profiling Reads actual values (often a sample) and measures patterns, counts and uniqueness. Slower, because it reads rows. Finds a column of SSN-shaped values even when its name is meaningless. Needs access to real production data, which is itself a privacy decision. The tools expose the same split under different names. Metadata versus data profiling in the three tools Tool How it splits the two Source Informatica A data domain profile can search for patterns in the data only, in the column name only, or in both. You can run the metadata pass first and then run again for the data. User Guide 10.5.10, pp.95 and 100 Delphix "Column-level" profiling uses regular expressions on column names (metadata). "Data-level" profiling uses regular expressions on the actual data. In the classifier model, PATH and TYPE work at column level, REGEX and LIST at data level. Delphix "Introduction to Delphix Masking" and "Discovering your sensitive data" GenRocket Data Column Profiling scans column headers only, not the actual data, so GenRocket does not need to read production values. GenRocket "PII Discovery with Data Column Profiling"

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
h: 2.17.1 Sampling: a look, not a census
x: 2.17.1 Sampling: a look, not a census Scanning every row of a table with 80 million rows would be slow, so profiles often sample. Sampling means reading only some rows. That is efficient, but it has a catch: a value that appears in only 1 row in 10,000 may not be in the sample. If a few rows of a mostly-clean column hold real phone numbers, a small sample may miss them. Informatica reflects this with options such as "Maximum Rows to Profile" and "Minimum Conformance Percent" (p.95): the second one is the share of profiled rows that must match the pattern before the column is claimed for the domain.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.18 Finding keys and relationships Subsetting needs to know which tables are parents and which are children. Ideally the database declares its primary and foreign keys and the tool simply reads them. In practice many databases declare few or none (for performance, or because the application enforces the links). GenRocket's documentation says this directly: custom referential integrity is added "when referential integrity does not exist between tables in the source database" but the user still needs to subset (GenRocket "How to Add Custom Referential Integrity to Imported Table Schemas"). Discovery fills that gap by inferring the links.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.18.1 Primary key discovery A primary key candidate is a column, or a small set of columns, whose values are unique. Informatica's primary key profile reports the percentage of unique values and lets you limit how hard it searches (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.92 to 93). Its options and defaults: the maximum number of columns combined into a key (3), the maximum rows to profile (1,000) and a conformance criterion, the minimum percentage of unique values allowed (99 percent) (p.93). Why would you allow less than 100 percent? Because real data is messy. If 99.8 percent of values are unique and a few rows are duplicates, the column is probably meant to be a key and the duplicates are data-quality bugs. Informatica notes that a primary key profile is useful to find such non-unique rows (p.92). The result table shows, per candidate, the table, the column or combination of columns, the uniqueness percentage, whether it is verified, any existing constraint and a status of verified, approved or rejected (pp.103 to 104). When you approve a candidate, TDM adds it as a key to the table in its repository, not in the source database. Rejecting a candidate does not affect the subset (p.104). Unique does not mean a good key ssn is 100 percent unique in the table above, yet it would be a poor primary key: it is sensitive, so masking will change it, and every table that used it as a link would need identical treatment. A human picks customer_id , the "meaningless but stable" identifier. Uniqueness tells you what can be a key. A person decides what should be.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.18.2 Foreign key and entity discovery To find parent-child links, Informatica's entity profile "returns a list of possible entities by comparing column names in the source tables" (p.93). In the guide's example, Employee, Employee_Detail and Employee_Address all contain an EmpID column, so the profile suggests Employee as an entity with two child tables. When you later subset, a filter on EmpID applies to every table in that relationship. The profile options show what matters when matching columns (p.94): whether to compare using the datatypes the tool inferred or the documented ones, whether comparison is case sensitive, whether to trim spaces first, the maximum number of foreign key results to return and the minimum confidence percent (the share of foreign key values that match). A coincidental match is the risk: two unrelated integer columns can overlap by chance, so discovery proposes and a person approves. One practical detail: if you choose the entity profile type and the physical database has no primary keys, the profile returns nothing. Run the profile as primary key and entity together, and it can discover both the primary and foreign keys even when the database declares none (p.93). Delphix says its masking keeps referential integrity by scanning metadata and data to identify and preserve the primary and foreign key relationships between elements, so that data is masked the same way across tables and databases (Delphix "Introduction to Delphix Masking"). How keys are defined in a Delphix rule set is covered in the Delphix rule sets and keys chapter .
