h: 2.19 Reading the results: false positives, false negatives and human review
x: 2.19 Reading the results: false positives, false negatives and human review A profile is a set of educated guesses. Every guess can be wrong in two ways: The two kinds of mistake in discovery Mistake Meaning ShopSphere example Cost False positive Flagged, but not actually what the tool thinks order_id flagged as a phone number because it has ten digits Wasted effort, or a harmful change (a key gets masked) False negative Real, but not flagged A contact_no column of real phone numbers not matched by any pattern Real data leaks into test Between the two, false negatives are the more dangerous in a privacy project, because nobody notices them. That is why discovery tools build review into the workflow, and why you should plan for it. In Informatica, each result row has a status, and you can verify, approve or reject it. The guide says the Verified column is for your own tracking and does not affect data subset operations, and that marking the data domain classification as completed does not affect any process either; it simply records that you reviewed everything (pp.104 to 105). The data viewer for a selected column shows the first 200 records, so reviewers can look at real values before approving (p.105).

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.19.1 A review routine that works Sort the results by confidence. Informatica shows % data conformance and whether the column name matched (p.105). High on both is easy to accept. A short list of obvious accepts and a longer list that needs thought. Look at the actual values for doubtful rows. Names alone mislead. Five sample values usually settle it. Ask the data steward about anything ambiguous. "Is tax_id a personal or a company number?" is not something a tool can answer. Scan the unflagged columns too, and record your decisions. Check free-text and generically named columns. A profile only covers the tables it was given, and re-profiling will not remember your reasons. A short list of columns added by hand, and a written list of accepted and rejected findings.

h: 2.19.2 The fourth type: the column profile
x: 2.19.2 The fourth type: the column profile Informatica's column profile measures range, list of values and patterns of columns, mainly to infer rules for generating test data; it runs on Oracle and Microsoft SQL Server databases (p.97). It returns in the test data classification and generation chapter . Lab: profile three mystery columns by hand Goal: practise what a profile computes. The columns come from a ShopSphere table whose column names were lost. Compute for each: the share of nulls, the number of distinct values, the pattern, and your best guess of the data domain. Five rows from a table with cryptic column names row col_a col_b col_c 1 9876543210 123-45-6789 1001 2 9123456780 234-56-7890 1002 3 9988776655 N/A 1003 4 (empty) 345-67-8901 1004 5 9876543210 123-45-6789 1005 Count nulls for each column. Treat "(empty)" as null. Treat "N/A" as a value, because it is text. Count distinct values. Divide by the number of non-null values to get a uniqueness percentage (tools may compute this slightly differently, but the idea is the same). Describe the pattern. Use digits as 9, and spell out hyphens. Guess the domain and the next action. Which column is a primary key candidate? Which is sensitive? Which needs a human decision? Show a worked answer Profile results computed by hand % null Distinct Pattern Guess and action col_a 20% (1 of 5) 3 distinct among 4 non-null, so 75% unique 10 digits in every non-null row Phone. Mask. Not a key: values repeat. col_b 0% 4 distinct among 5, so 80% unique 999-99-9999 in 4 of 5 rows (80% conformance); "N/A" in 1 SSN. Mask. The "N/A" row needs an exception rule; a conformance setting of 100% would reject the column. col_c 0% 5 distinct among 5, so 100% unique 4 digits Primary key candidate (it looks like customer_id ). Handle consistently. The point of col_b: a column can be clearly sensitive even though not all rows match the pattern, which is why tools expose a minimum conformance percent instead of demanding 100.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.20 What is data subsetting? Start with the problem. ShopSphere's production database holds eight years of history: tens of millions of customers, hundreds of millions of orders, terabytes in total. A tester working on the checkout screen does not need all of it. Copying everything to every test environment is slow, expensive and risky. Data subsetting means copying only a slice of the database, small enough to be cheap, and consistent enough to be useful. Informatica describes the goal as a "small, targeted, and referentially intact copy" of production data for use in a nonproduction environment such as development, test or training, and gives the example of financial data for a specific region or time period (User Guide 10.5.10, p.112). GenRocket frames it the same way: production data may contain sensitive data, "you also do not need all that data for application testing, only a subset" (GenRocket "Synthetic Data Masking (SDM) and Data Subsetting Overview").

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.20.1 Why teams subset Size and storage cost: smaller copies need less disk and money (GenRocket lists saved storage as a benefit). Speed: a small copy refreshes overnight instead of over days, and tests and reports run faster. Privacy: fewer real records copied means less exposure and less to mask (the minimum necessary idea from the sensitive data chapter ). Focus: you can pick exactly what a test needs, such as one region or one scenario.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
h: 2.20.2 A subset is not just "the first 1,000 rows"
x: 2.20.2 A subset is not just "the first 1,000 rows" Beginners sometimes subset by taking the first N rows of each table. That breaks the data: the first 1,000 orders belong to customers that may not be in the first 1,000 customers. The result is orphans: orders with no customer, items with no order. A real subset starts from a choice (a set of customers, a time window) and then follows the relationships so that every kept row has all the parents it points to. Everything in the next sections is about doing that correctly.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.21 Types of subset "Type" here means how you choose which rows to keep . Several can be combined. The table lists the kinds I can ground in the documentation, plus two general concepts marked as such. Ways to choose a subset Type How the rows are chosen Informatica GenRocket By filter condition Keep rows that satisfy a condition on a column (zip code, status, region). Entity filter criteria on columns of the driving table, using values or parameters; several criteria combine with AND (pp.116 to 117). Where clause; AND or OR allowed; example address.state = 'CA' (Subsetting how-to). By percentage of rows Keep a given share of the rows, such as 25 or 50 percent. Limit by percentage in the plan (pp.294, 304). "% of rows", usable alone or with a Where clause. By absolute number of rows Keep a fixed number of rows, such as 100. Limit by absolute value (pp.294, 304). "# of rows". By interval of rows Keep a defined interval of rows. Limit by an interval of rows (pp.294, 304). Not described in the pages I read; the overview example starts at customer id 251 and keeps 100 rows. By time window A filter on a date column: last 90 days, a financial year. The guide's example subset is for "a specific region or time period" (p.112); its database-function example uses a date test, HIREDATE > add_months(current_date, -3) (p.119). Full-load tables (How to Select Tables for Full Migration). Random sample Rows picked by chance so the subset resembles the whole. h: 2.22.1 Informatica: the entity and its driving table
x: 2.22.1 Informatica: the entity and its driving table In Informatica, an entity "consists of a driving table and related tables". The driving table is the starting point; TDM finds the tables related to it from physical (declared) and logical (discovered or added) constraints, and adds them to the entity by default. You then define filter criteria on columns of tables in the entity (User Guide 10.5.10, p.114). The guide's example: Employee as the driving table, with primary key EmpID, three child tables holding an EmpID foreign key, and a fourth table, BankAccounts, linked through an account number from one of the children (p.115). The Entity Map shows the star on the driving table. The Entity Map can show all tables, the parents or children of a selected table, or cyclic relationships, and you can disable a relationship; a table left unrelated is excluded (p.115). The guide advises running data discovery before creating an entity so the constraints exist (p.116). The guide's own small example An employee has ID 10 and you want everything about that employee. Employee is the driving table; Employee_History and Employee_Order are related to it by EmpID. Define the criteria "EmpID equals 10". After the plan runs, the target database holds one Employee row for EmpID 10, all of that employee's history rows and all of their orders (p.121).

h: 2.22.2 GenRocket: the subset table and the hierarchy
x: 2.22.2 GenRocket: the subset table and the hierarchy In GenRocket's G-Subset, only one table in a configuration can have subsetting conditions (Where clause and/or row limit). Rows that meet the condition are included, "all records in related tables associated with those meeting the Where Clause condition will be inserted as well" (Subsetting how-to). The Traverse Full Hierarchy page shows what "related" means. Its example database has Organization (1 row), Department (4), Employee (120), Address, Attendance, Payroll and Qualification (120 each) and Project (8). The condition is on Payroll: hours > 10 , limited to 10 rows. Default behaviour: G-Subset goes up from the subset table to the top-most parent to build its queries, then migrates from the top down: Organization, Department, Employee, Payroll. Only the ancestor rows related to the chosen Payroll rows move: 10 employees, the departments they belong to, and so on. Traverse Full Hierarchy enabled: it also brings the other children of those ancestors: Project (2 rows), and Address, Attendance and Qualification rows for the same 10 employees. The same page notes that the option is only available when a subsetting condition has been added to a table, and that masking rules you set for those extra tables are applied to them too. Choose the driving table by the test question If the test is "does the customer page show the right orders?", drive from CUSTOMERS . If the test is "does the monthly report add up?", drive from ORDERS with a date filter and let the parents (customers) and children (items) follow. The table you drive from decides which rows are complete and which are partial.

x: 2.23 Keeping referential integrity Referential integrity is the rule that every foreign key value points to a row that exists. It is the one property a subset must never lose. If it breaks, the application crashes or shows empty pages, and testers blame the data. GenRocket's page defines it in the same plain terms: it "refers to the accuracy and consistency of the defined relationships" between parent and child tables (GenRocket "How to Add Custom Referential Integrity to Imported Table Schemas").

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
h: 2.23.1 How a naive subset breaks it
x: 2.23.1 How a naive subset breaks it Suppose someone takes the first 6 rows of ORDERS and the first 4 rows of CUSTOMERS "to keep it small". Order 5006 belongs to customer 1005, who is the fifth customer and was left out. Order 5006 is now an orphan. SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id FROM ORDERS o LEFT JOIN CUSTOMERS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL; -- any row returned is an orphan order On the naive subset this query returns one row (order 5006, customer 1005). On a correct subset it returns nothing. The same check works one level down ( ORDER_ITEMS to ORDERS , and ORDER_ITEMS to PRODUCTS ). Run these checks after every subset: they are cheap and catch the commonest failure.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.23.2 Integrity options in Informatica plans Informatica goes beyond "no orphans". It also offers several ways to decide how much extra data to pull to keep the subset coherent. You choose the option in the plan's advanced settings, so the same entity can yield different subsets (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.121 to 123). By default all constraint relationships in an entity are "major", which can pull in excess data; you can optimise relations so that the entity has the minimum number of major relations while still covering all tables (p.119). Informatica data integrity options for a subset plan (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.121-123), explained in plain words Option What it does Size of result Notes from the guide Transactional Integrity for Major Relation Type A selected child row pulls in its parents; those parents pull in all of their children; those children may point to more parents, and so on until nothing new is added. Can include extra records Maintains transactional and referential integrity. Criteria apply to the entity as a whole; multiple criteria combine with AND, which can return nothing if they select unrelated tables. Referential Integrity Only Selects the fewest rows needed to keep every foreign key valid. Fewer rows May not include all the children of a parent, so transactional integrity can break. Falls back to the transactional option if the entity has more than one criterion. Two-way Pushes the criteria down, then back up, alternately, until every table in the entity has some data. More than the first two Keeps referential integrity and ensures every table meeting the criteria has data. Requires a staging connection. One-way Applies criteria on individual tables and pushes them downward only; tables above the top-most filtered table are included in full. More than Two-way Aims for the smallest subset that does not break referential integrity while including all data from tables above the filtered one. The guide also says cyclic and self-referencing relationships (a table that points to itself, such as employees pointing to managers) need a staging connection for recursive evaluation (pp.114 and 122).

x: 2.25 Reduced copies and full copies A subset is one way to make a test copy small. There are other ways to get a test copy, and each has a place. The comparison below is a general guide, with the Delphix statements marked. A full physical copy is the most realistic but the slowest and most exposed. A subset is small and quick to refresh but may miss rare cases. A virtual copy looks full but shares storage with its source, so it is cheap to create, but it still holds all the data and needs masking. Delphix describes virtualization as producing "a functioning database or filesystem copy that is lightweight and ephemeral" (terminology page), and its introduction claims that ten virtual copies can fit into the space of one physical copy. The pages I read describe only simple row filters, not key-following subsets, for Delphix, so treat "virtual copy" and "subset" as two different answers to the same cost problem: Delphix makes full copies cheap; Informatica and GenRocket make copies small.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.26 How masking and subsetting combine You rarely do one without the other: subsetting shrinks the set of real records, and masking changes what remains. Three orders are possible. Possible orders of subsetting and masking Order How it works Good Watch out Subset, then mask Select the slice from real data, then mask the slice Less to mask, and filters see real values (for example real zip codes) Unmasked data exists briefly in the slice or staging area Mask, then subset Mask everything, then select the slice from the masked copy Nothing unmasked leaves the masking step Masks the whole database (slow), and filters on masked columns pick different rows than expected Both in one run Select and mask while copying to the target Fast, one job, one schedule Needs a tool that supports it, and careful setup Both Informatica and GenRocket support the third pattern. In Informatica, a plan can contain masking components (policies and rules) and subset components (entities, groups) together (User Guide 10.5.10, p.304; and p.135 for masking plans). The plan also says whether to mask data in place in the source database or in stream into a target database (p.150). In GenRocket, "Mask and subset data set together by providing both the masking and subset parameters in a G-Subset Configuration" (G-Subset Overview). Its sensitive columns are replaced with synthetic values in a temporary file before the rows are inserted, and the sensitive values are never read. The key requirement when you combine them is consistency . The masked customer 1004 in CUSTOMERS must be the same masked customer 1004 that the kept orders point to. Informatica's docs describe "auto cascades" that mask a parent key and its child foreign keys with the same value (p.91), and Delphix says its masking keeps primary and foreign keys consistent across tables and databases (Delphix "Introduction to Delphix Masking"). The masking concepts chapter explains how. Notice too that zip codes were left alone here. As the sensitive data chapter showed, a zip code is an indirect identifier, so whether it stays is a decision for the compliance officer.

x: 2.26.1 GenRocket's subsetting at a glance GenRocket's database subsetting is called G-Subset (formerly G-Migration+). It plans from the source schema, runs in the customer's environment and migrates to a destination database of the same type. Conditions are a Where clause, a percentage or a number of rows, on one table only; related rows follow, other tables can be marked for full load, and custom referential integrity can be added when the source declares none. It does not support composite keys at present (GenRocket "G-Subset Overview", source page ↗ ).

Trusting discovery output without review. Reject coincidental key matches, add missed sensitive columns. Choosing a sensitive column as a key. A unique SSN is a poor primary key because masking will change it. Assuming a percentage limit is random. The documentation excerpts do not say so; verify. Forgetting reference tables. x: 2.28 Recap Remember Discovery and profiling come first: they report types, patterns, sensitive-looking columns, key candidates and relationships, from metadata (names and types) and from data (values, usually sampled). Profiles guess. False positives waste effort or change keys; false negatives leak data. A human reviews and approves. A subset is a small, targeted, referentially intact copy: cheaper to store, faster to refresh and test, and less real data exposed. You choose rows by filter condition, percentage, row count or interval, time window, or by a driving table; tools also copy some tables in full. A driving table is the starting point: related rows are followed down to children and up to parents so there are no orphans. Informatica calls the group an entity; GenRocket follows the hierarchy from the subset table. Informatica offers transactional, referential-only, two-way and one-way integrity options that trade subset size against completeness. Subsetting and masking are partners. Keep keys consistent when you combine them, and check for orphans afterwards. Data masking: the concepts You have found the sensitive columns ( the sensitive data chapter ) and cut the data down to a slice ( the discovery and subsetting concepts chapter ). Now comes the step that makes the copy safe to hand to testers: masking , replacing real sensitive values with realistic fake ones. This section explains the idea and the common techniques in plain words, with before and after values on ShopSphere data. The tool-specific chapters, Informatica data masking and Delphix algorithms and masking jobs , then show where the buttons are.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.29 Words to know first Masking Replacing sensitive values with realistic but fictitious values so test data cannot identify real people. Delphix defines it as iterating through a dataset to identify all sensitive fields and replace them with desensitised values to eliminate risk in lower environments. Technique (Informatica) / algorithm (Delphix) The method that changes a value, such as substitution or date shift. Informatica turns a technique plus settings into a rule . Delphix turns an algorithm framework plus settings into an algorithm instance . Deterministic Always gives the same output for the same input (and same settings). The opposite is non-deterministic or random: a different output each time. Repeatable Informatica's word for deterministic output across runs and tables, switched on with a seed. Seed / key A starting value that controls the output of a deterministic technique. Same seed (Informatica) or same algorithm key (Delphix) gives the same masked values; changing it changes them. Dictionary / lookup file A list of replacement values, such as thousands of first names, that substitution picks from. Collision Two different inputs masked to the same output. Fine for names, harmful for a column that must be unique. Irreversible You cannot get the original value back from the masked one. Format-preserving The masked value keeps the original's shape: a 10-digit phone stays 10 digits, a card number keeps its checksum. In-place and on-the-fly In-place masking changes the data where it sits. On-the-fly masking reads unmasked data and writes masked data to a different place.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.30 Masking and its neighbours People use these words loosely. They mean different things, and the difference decides whether a copy is safe. Obfuscation, masking, encryption, tokenization, anonymisation, pseudonymisation Term What it means Reversible? Keeps data usable for tests? ShopSphere example Obfuscation Umbrella word: make data hard to read or understand, by any method. Masking is one kind. Depends Depends Any of the rows below Masking Replace real values with realistic fake ones, usually permanently, for non-production use. No (by design) Yes Asha Menon becomes Leela Pillai Encryption Scramble data with a key so only key holders can unscramble it. Yes, with the key Only if it preserves format; ordinary ciphertext breaks tests 123-45-6789 becomes q8Zk...== Tokenization Replace a value with a token, keeping a protected way to reverse it later. Yes, by design Partly Send tokens to a vendor; map back afterwards Anonymisation A goal : data that no longer identifies anyone, even in combination. Legal tests are strict. No Varies Masked and generalised so no row is unique Pseudonymisation Replace identifiers with pseudonyms, but a way back exists elsewhere. Still personal data under GDPR. Yes, with the extra information Yes customer_id replaced by a token How the sources use the words: Delphix says tokenization is "the only type of algorithm that allows you to reverse its masking". Its example is masking data before sending it to a vendor and reversing it afterwards to act on the vendor's findings (terminology page). Its introduction labels masking as anonymisation and tokenization as pseudonymisation. It also says unlike encryption, which can be bypassed by obtaining user credentials, masking irreversibly protects data in downstream environments, and that encryption is ill-suited to protecting non-production environments (Delphix "Introduction to Delphix Masking"). Informatica treats encryption as one masking technique. Standard encryption offers AES, CRC and MD5, and format preserving encryption can be decrypted with the same pass phrase and configuration (User Guide 10.5.10, p.161). GenRocket argues that traditional masking "can be reverse engineered" and that its Synthetic Data Replacement generates new values that cannot be traced back (GenRocket "G-Subset Overview" and "What is Synthetic Data Replacement"). Reversible is a risk in test data If a test copy can be turned back into the real data, then stealing the copy plus the key or mapping table is a breach. For ordinary test environments, prefer irreversible masking. Use encryption or tokenization when you truly need to come back, such as a vendor round trip, and guard the key like production data. Anonymisation is a destination, masking is a vehicle Masking is a set of techniques. Whether the masked result counts as anonymous under a law depends on the whole data set (the combinations you saw in the sensitive data chapter) and is the compliance officer's call.

h: 2.31 What good masked data looks like
x: 2.31 What good masked data looks like A tool could blank every sensitive column in a second. That would be safe and useless. Masking has competing goals, and good masking meets all of them. The goals of masking Goal Meaning What goes wrong without it Safe Real values cannot be recovered or inferred A leak of test data is a leak of customers Realistic Looks like real data: names look like names, emails like emails Testers cannot spot UI bugs, and validation rules reject the data Valid Passes the application's rules: format, checksum, length, ranges The card form refuses every masked card number Consistent The same real value maps to the same fake value everywhere it appears Joins break; a customer has different names in two tables Repeatable A re-run gives the same results when it should Test cases that rely on a specific customer fail after each refresh Fit for purpose Keeps the properties the tests depend on (a customer has several orders, a date precedes another) The data is fake but the test no longer tests anything Both vendors state these goals. Informatica: replace source data in sensitive columns with "realistic test data" for nonproduction environments (p.135). Delphix: the data stays "production-like in quality", masking is consistent while "maintaining referential integrity across heterogeneous data sources", and it is irreversible (Delphix "Introduction to Delphix Masking"). Some goals pull against each other. Perfect safety says "change everything completely". Perfect fidelity says "keep it as it was". Every technique in the next section is a compromise somewhere between those poles, which is why choosing is a skill.

x: 2.32.1 Substitution Replace the value with a different, believable one picked from a list. Informatica: it "replaces a column of data with similar but unrelated data from a dictionary", which can be a flat file or a database table (p.176). Delphix Secure Lookup is the same idea: it picks a replacement from a lookup file using a cryptographic hash of the original value, so the output is consistent for each input (terminology page; the framework page says the default hash method is SHA256). Substitution on CUSTOMERS (masked values illustrative) customer_id first_name before after last_name before after 1001 Asha Leela Menon Pillai 1002 Ravi Sanjay Kumar Gupta 1003 Meera Anita Nair Joshi Strengths: very realistic. Limits: the list can run out. Informatica's unique substitution makes the operation fail when the source has more distinct values than the dictionary has (p.176), and Delphix says that two inputs can collide on one output, which is fine for names and a problem for unique columns (terminology page). Informatica also lets you pick names by a lookup column such as gender or country, so female names stay female (pp.177 to 179).

x: 2.32.2 Shuffle Move the existing values of a column between rows. Informatica's own example moves first names between four rows: Tom, Sue, Bob, Eli become Bob, Eli, Tom, Sue (p.173). Delphix SecureShuffle guarantees that each value moves to a different row, but an input can still mask to itself when values repeat (SecureShuffle page). Someone who knows Asha Menon's first name and city could still recognise "Menon" in the column, and a rare value stays rare. Delphix warns that shuffling does not redact or modify any value, so consider carefully whether it meets your security requirements. Informatica offers a constrained shuffle (for example, only within the same city) and a representative shuffle, in which all rows with the same source value get the same shuffled value (p.174).

x: 2.32.4 Encryption and tokenization Informatica offers standard encryption (AES, CRC, MD5, with a key of 16 characters or fewer) and format preserving encryption . The latter can keep the format and length, and can be decrypted with the same pass phrase and configuration. Its example: Abc123@xyz.com becomes Mpz849#dje!kuw , or Mpz849@dje.kuw if the "@" and "." are excluded from encryption (pp.161 to 162). The Delphix Tokenization framework uses AES-128 and produces longer alphanumeric tokens, built for the vendor round trip described in 6.2 (Tokenization page). Because AES and format preserving encryption can be reversed, use them only for that.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.32.5 Nulling and redaction Remove the value, or part of it. Informatica's Nullification replaces a column with NULL, works on all data types and has no parameters (p.168). The simplest safe answer for a column the tests do not use, such as tax_id , is NULL. The cost: NOT NULL columns refuse it and the application paths that read the column go untested. Free text needs smarter redaction: Delphix's Free Text Redaction finds sensitive words and patterns inside a text column (for example "St", "Blvd", or the shape 123-45-6789 for an SSN) and redacts the whole matched word, but it "requires some expertise to use" (Free Text Redaction page).

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.32.6 Date shifting and blurring Move a date by an amount so that the exact date is hidden but the date still looks plausible. Delphix Date Shift masks each date to another within a configured range (for example 3 to 5 days later), based on the algorithm key; a fixed shift (same minimum and maximum) preserves uniqueness and referential integrity, unlike variable ranges. Its docs show 2021-02-03 12:30:00 becoming 2021-02-06 12:30:00 (Date Shift page). Informatica blurs a date within a range of years, months, days or hours: a source of 2 February 2006 with a two-year bound becomes a date between 2 February 2004 and 2 February 2008 (p.170). Date shift of date_of_birth, fixed shift of +3 days (illustrative) customer_id Before After 1001 1990-04-12 1990-04-15 1002 1985-11-02 1985-11-05 Related dates need care. If order_date must stay after date_of_birth , shifting them independently can break the order. Delphix's Dependent Date Shift is a multi-column algorithm that masks two date-times while preserving the interval between them (Algorithms page).

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.32.7 Numeric variance Move a number by a controlled amount. Informatica numeric blurring uses a fixed or percent variance. With the input 66: fixed bounds 10 and 10 give a result between 56 and 76; percent bounds 50 and 50 give 33 to 99 (p.170). A range option returns a number between a minimum and a maximum. Delphix Min Max pulls extreme values toward the middle, because a record with the highest salary may reveal a company's CEO (Min Max Number page). On ShopSphere, a 10 percent blur turns total_amount 1200.00 into something between 1080.00 and 1320.00, which keeps totals plausible but breaks the rule "total equals the sum of its items" unless the items are changed too, so decide whether tests rely on that.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.32.8 Format-preserving masking The masked value keeps the format the application checks. Informatica has built-in formats. Credit card masking returns a number with a valid checksum, leaves the six-digit bank identification number unchanged, and can keep or change the card issuer: 4539 1596 8210 2773 becomes 4539 1516 0556 7067 (p.158). Phone masking keeps the format: (408)382 0658 becomes (408)256 3106 (p.169). SSN masking generates valid numbers that avoid ones the Social Security Administration has issued (p.175). Delphix Payment Card preserves the Luhn check and the leading digits you choose: 5419033646326699 becomes 5419036803270758 when the first six digits are kept (Payment Card page). Format-preserving masking of ShopSphere columns (illustrative) Column Before After phone 9876543210 9412087365 ssn 123-45-6789 561-80-3472 email asha.menon@example.com leela.pillai@example.com

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.32.9 Character replacement Replace characters according to a pattern. In Informatica's key and random techniques you set a mask format : A for letters, D for digits, N for alphanumerics, X for any character, + for "leave as is", and R for the remaining characters (pp.165, 170); and you can mask only chosen source characters or restrict the result to chosen characters. Delphix's Character Replacement framework swaps listed characters (for example vowels to "+") and wraps another string algorithm, and the page notes it has no UI or default instance at present, so it is configured through the API. A ShopSphere use: a tax ID shaped like AKPPM4821Q (five letters, four digits, one letter) masked with format AAAAADDDDA becomes something like TRWQD9037B , same shape, no real content.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.32.10 Algorithm chaining Combine several steps into one result. Informatica's advanced masking uses input, variable and output columns: mask FIRST_NAME and LAST_NAME separately with substitution into variable columns, then output FIRST_MASKED || ' ' || LAST_MASKED as the full name (p.158). Its email masking can build the address from the masked first and last name (p.159). Delphix's String Algorithm Chain runs two to eight string algorithms one after another, and its docs give a reason to chain: with deterministic masking, a very rare input value keeps its low frequency in the output and could be used to infer the original, so a first algorithm can alter such rare values before the main one runs (String Algorithm Chain page). Why chain at all? Real columns are related: the email contains the name, the full name contains the first name. If each is masked independently, the masked email will name someone different from the masked name. Chaining makes the dependent value follow the one it depends on.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
h: 2.33 Same input, same output: deterministic masking and referential integrity
x: 2.33 Same input, same output: deterministic masking and referential integrity This is the idea that separates amateur masking from professional masking. Imagine ShopSphere masks CUSTOMERS.customer_id randomly, and then masks ORDERS.customer_id randomly in a separate step: What happens when the same key is masked independently, versus consistently (illustrative) Column Original Random each time Deterministic (same seed) CUSTOMERS.customer_id (Asha) 1001 48213 48213 ORDERS.customer_id (Asha's order 5001) 1001 90377 48213 Join CUSTOMERS to ORDERS works no match: order 5001 is an orphan works Masking a primary key or foreign key is only safe if every copy of the same real value turns into the same masked value. The same holds across systems: if the billing database and the orders database both hold customer 1001, they must both end up with 48213, or reconciliation tests will fail. This property is called deterministic (Informatica: repeatable ) masking, and referential integrity depends on it.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.33.1 How the tools achieve it Informatica seed and repeatable output. With repeatable output, "John Smith" is masked as "Frank Martinez" in every table, account number 1234 always becomes 6549 and 5678 always becomes 3214, across runs. A seed, a number from 1 through 999 with default 1, is the starting point; use the same seed on the same kind of column in different tables. An administrator can set a central seed that overrides all others, and a seed can come from a parameter file (pp.154 to 155). Informatica cascades. An auto cascade masks a parent key and the related foreign keys in child tables with the same value, applied by default where key constraints exist (p.91). A value cascade does the same for similar columns that are not linked by a key, such as employee_num in one table and EmpID in another, by choosing a driving column (p.90). Delphix key and domain. Most algorithms carry a key; the same algorithm with the same key gives the same output, and changing the key changes every output (the Algorithms page gives an example where "Michelle" becomes "Rachael" and after rekeying "Ben"). Because each domain has one default algorithm, every column found in that domain is masked the same way (Discovering your sensitive data). Delphix across engines. Algorithms can be synchronised between masking engines so that two engines mask the same input the same way. Algorithms that cannot guarantee the same output, such as the variable Date Shift, SecureShuffle and the random Secure Lookup, are called non-deterministic and cannot be used for syncable masking, while a fixed Date Shift is deterministic (Algorithm syncability page). Things that quietly break consistency Different spellings of the same value. Informatica's key masking is case sensitive by default, so "john brown" and "JOHN BROWN" can mask differently unless you convert the source to one format first with a preprocessing expression (p.166). Delphix Secure Lookup has a case-sensitive option and whitespace options with similar effects. The value hiding inside another column. A name in FIRST_NAME may also appear inside FULL_NAME or DESCRIPTION . Informatica's delimited string masking masks such substrings consistently, for example "Donne, John" and "John Donne, General Manager" (pp.166 to 167). Random options. A "random" mode is fine for a column that nothing links to. The Delphix Secure Lookup RANDOMIZE method "does not maintain referential integrity and should never be used" where it is required. Different algorithm or seed for the same data in two jobs. Keep one policy and one seed or key per kind of data (this is what a policy from the sensitive data chapter is for). Repeatable output has a price The same property that keeps joins working also means the mapping can be recomputed by anyone who has the seed or key and the algorithm. For a small value space (an SSN has about a billion possibilities) that is guessable. Treat seeds and keys as secrets, store them outside the test environment, and rotate them when policy says so (Delphix lets you randomise an algorithm key through its API; the Algorithms page gives the endpoint).

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.34 Irreversibility, uniqueness and collisions Irreversible by design. A good masking technique throws the original away. Substitution picks an unrelated value; shuffle and key masking cannot be undone without the seed and source. Encryption and tokenization are the exceptions (section 2.30). Unique by need. Some columns must not repeat: primary keys, SSNs, emails used as login names. A technique that can produce the same output for two inputs (a collision) will break them. Choose by need: When uniqueness matters Need Technique that gives it Source Collisions are fine (names, cities) Secure Lookup / Substitution Delphix and Informatica: names naturally repeat Unique values from a list Informatica unique substitution (fails if the dictionary is too small); Delphix Mapping (each output to one input, but stores an encrypted mapping and tables are masked one at a time) p.176; terminology page Unique short numbers or codes, no collisions Delphix Segment Mapping (no collisions if the allowed set is at least as large as the input; up to 36 characters) or Character Mapping Terminology and Character Mapping pages Unique SSNs Informatica notes SSN masking cannot always return all-unique numbers because it avoids numbers already issued (p.175) p.175

h: 2.35 Static or dynamic, in-place or on-the-fly
x: 2.35 Static or dynamic, in-place or on-the-fly Two different choices are often mixed up. Static versus dynamic asks when data is masked. In-place versus on-the-fly asks where the masked data ends up. Static masking Create a masked copy once. The copy is stored, and from then on anyone using it sees masked data. This is what test data management normally does. Dynamic masking Mask at the moment of reading, depending on who asks. The stored data stays real, and an application or proxy hides values from some users. It protects production views, not test copies. The TDM sources I read do not cover it. A word of caution on vocabulary: GenRocket also uses "dynamically" for masking that happens as rows are inserted into the destination, which is closer to on-the-fly than to the dynamic masking above (GenRocket "SDM and Data Subsetting Overview"). In-place and on-the-fly Method What happens Typical use In-place Updates the data in the source environment itself with masked values You first make a copy (for example a virtual copy), then mask the copy in place. Never point it at production. On-the-fly Reads unmasked data from the source and writes masked data to a different target Producing a masked copy directly from a source, together with subsetting Delphix defines both in its masking job settings: in-place jobs update the source environment with the masked values; on-the-fly jobs read unmasked data from the source and write masked data to the target (create, view, edit, delete, verify jobs page). Informatica says a masking plan indicates whether to mask data in place in the source database or in stream in a target database (p.150). The masked-copy approach fits the rule from the sensitive data chapter : ask at which moment unmasked data exists outside production.

x: 2.36 Risks and what goes wrong Common risks in masking projects Risk What happens Defence Re-identification Masked names, but birth date, zip and gender still single out a person Treat indirect identifiers too: date shift, generalise, subset Sensitive data left in free text An SSN inside a notes column survives column-level masking Free text redaction, or exclude or null the column; search for patterns afterwards Masking a primary key without cascading Joins break, orphans appear Same seed or key everywhere, auto and value cascades, or leave surrogate keys unmasked Non-conformant data left unmasked Delphix: a value that does not fit the algorithm's expected format is by default not masked and only a warning is recorded Check job warnings; set non-conformant handling to fail or null where leaking is unacceptable (terminology page) Masked value too long or wrong type Job fails or truncates. Informatica's Change Metadata encryption needs a larger column precision using a formula given in the guide (p.162); it also does not mask integers over 28 characters (p.152) Check lengths and types; use format-preserving options Null and blank values Treated unexpectedly Informatica exception handling can set constant, ignore, treat as value or log an error (p.155) Collisions on unique columns Duplicate key errors on load Use a unique technique (section 2.34) Performance and memory Large lookup files and parallel jobs need memory; Delphix suggests about 1 GB per job or stream, more for wide rows or big lookups, and about one vCPU per concurrent job Size the engine; mask a subset (best practices page) Realism lost Fake data fails validation or no longer exercises the code Format-preserving techniques; test the rules on a sample first

x: 2.37 Choosing a technique Start from the column, not the technique. Ask four questions: What is it (name, number, date, free text)? Must it stay unique or linked to other tables? Must it keep a format the application checks? Do tests depend on its meaning (for example an age band)? The table gives a reasoned first choice for the ShopSphere columns. (technique names are from section 2.32) Decision table for ShopSphere columns (a starting point, to be confirmed with the compliance officer) Column Constraint First choice Why first_name, last_name Realistic; repeats allowed Substitution from a dictionary Looks real; no uniqueness needed email Valid format; maybe unique; should match the masked name Email masking built from the masked names (chaining) Keeps consistency inside the row phone 10 digits Format-preserving phone masking Keeps the shape the application validates ssn 999-99-9999 format; unique Format-preserving SSN masking, deterministic Valid shape; same output wherever it appears date_of_birth Plausible; age bands matter Date shift or blurring by a few days Hides the exact date, keeps the age band zip_code Valid code; region may matter Substitution from valid codes, or keep the first digits Reduces re-identification, keeps regional logic tax_id Shape like AAAAADDDDA Character replacement with a mask format, or null Same shape, no real content customer_id (key) Joins to ORDERS Leave as is (a meaningless surrogate), or key masking with the same seed in every table A made-up number identifies nobody on its own, but must stay consistent total_amount Must match order items Leave alone, unless amounts are sensitive Masking it breaks arithmetic Free-text notes Unknown content Free text redaction or null Cannot be fixed by column-level rules Not every column needs masking Masking has a cost: it can break realism and arithmetic. x: 2.38 Validating masked data A masking job that finishes without errors is not proof that the data is safe or useful. Check the result against the goals from section 2.31. A validation checklist Check How Nothing sensitive is left Run discovery again on the masked copy. Search free-text columns for SSN-like and phone-like patterns. Compare: no real value from the source should appear in the target for masked columns. Joins still work Run orphan queries between each parent and child table. Consistency The same real value gives the same masked value in every table and system that holds it. Valid format Pattern check on each masked column, for example SSN [0-9]{3}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{4} and card numbers pass the checksum. Uniqueness No duplicates in columns that must be unique. Realism Look at a sample by eye. Null counts and value distributions should be believable. Repeatability Run twice with the same settings; results match when they should. Job logs Read warnings. Delphix shows a yellow warning marker on a job when non-conformant data was found; Informatica logs exceptions per its exception-handling settings. -- duplicates in a column that must be unique SELECT ssn, COUNT(*) FROM CUSTOMERS GROUP BY ssn HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; -- any order without a customer (orphan) SELECT o.order_id FROM ORDERS o LEFT JOIN CUSTOMERS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL; -- any SSN-shaped text left in a notes column (pattern syntax varies by database) SELECT order_id FROM ORDER_NOTES WHERE notes LIKE '%___-__-____%'; Tools help with previewing. Informatica's Rule Simulator shows original and masked values for a standard rule before you assign it, using default sample data, your own sample or a connection, with up to 100 rows and a default of 20 (pp.137 and 140). Delphix says its platform generates reports and email notifications to confirm that sensitive data has been masked (Delphix "Introduction to Delphix Masking"). Neither removes the need to inspect the result yourself. Lab: design and check a mask for the ShopSphere customers Goal: pick a technique for every sensitive column of CUSTOMERS, apply it to the three sample rows by hand, and prove the result is consistent. Write the rule set. For each column in the decision table, choose one technique and say whether it must be deterministic. Decide the seed or key story: one seed, shared by every column that joins elsewhere. Apply it to rows 1001 to 1003. Use made-up values that respect each column's format. Does any masked value equal a real one? Is any value duplicated? Does the masked email match the masked name? Would an orphan appear in ORDERS if customer_id were masked here but not there? x: 2.39 Common mistakes and gotchas Mistakes beginners make Calling encryption "masking". It can be reversed. Use it only when reversal is intended. Masking keys independently. Joins break. Use the same seed or key, or cascades. Ignoring the job warnings. In Delphix, non-conformant values are left unmasked by default and only flagged. Trusting one technique for everything. Shuffle leaves real values in place; substitution can collide; date shifting can reorder dates. Forgetting free text and indirect identifiers. They defeat column-level masking. Sharing the seed or key with the test team. It makes the mapping reproducible by anyone who has it. Declaring success without validating. Run discovery again on the masked data and check joins.

ct: Privacy, discovery, subsetting and masking: the concepts
x: 2.40 Recap Remember Masking replaces real values with realistic fake ones, usually irreversibly. Encryption and tokenization are reversible; anonymisation is a legal goal that masking helps reach. Good masked data is safe, realistic, valid, consistent, repeatable and still fit for the tests. Common techniques: substitution, shuffle, key masking, encryption, nulling and redaction, date shifting, numeric variance, format-preserving masking, character replacement, and chaining several of them. Deterministic masking (same input, same output, from a seed or key) is what keeps keys and joins working across tables and systems. Random masking is for columns nothing links to. Choose by column type, uniqueness, format and test needs. Not every column needs masking, and free text needs special handling. Masking can be in place or on the fly; static copies are the norm for test data. Always validate: rediscover, check joins, formats, uniqueness, repeatability and job warnings.

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
h: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: Test data classification and synthetic data generation So far you have met two ways to get test data. You can copy and cut down real data ( the discovery and subsetting concepts chapter ) and then hide the sensitive parts ( the masking concepts chapter ). This section introduces the third way: make the data up , on purpose, from rules. Before we do that we need a better question than "where do I get data?". The better question is: what is this data for? A tester checking the login screen does not need "a lot of customers". She needs one normal customer, one customer whose account is locked, one with a very long surname, one with no phone number, and one whose date of birth makes them exactly 18 today. Each of those rows has a different job. Naming the jobs is called classifying test data, and it is the starting point for designing any data set, whether you copy it, mask it or generate it. This section is also where the course syllabus phrase "Model, Design, Deploy, Manage" first appears, and where the five "data patterns" of the syllabus (boundary conditions, sequential, random, edge cases, null) are placed on a map. The tool chapters later ( the Informatica data generation chapter and the GenRocket chapters ) assume you have read this one.

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.1 Words to know first Test data Any data the application is fed or finds waiting in its database during a test. It includes both the rows in the database and the values typed into screens or sent in files. Test condition One specific situation a test wants to check, such as "customer with no phone number" or "order with the maximum number of items". Each condition needs data that creates it. Positive (valid) data Data the application should accept and process normally. Negative (invalid) data Data the application should reject or handle gracefully, such as letters in a phone number. Boundary value A value sitting exactly on the edge of what is allowed. If customers must be 18 or older, the boundary values are 17, 18 and 19 years. Edge case A rare or unusual situation outside normal use, such as a surname containing an apostrophe. GenRocket describes it as a rare or unexpected scenario outside the typical usage pattern. Synthetic data Data made by a program following rules, instead of being taken from real events. GenRocket's help centre puts it as data manufactured by an algorithm rather than real-world events. Generator The small piece of logic that produces the values for one column, for example "count up from 1" or "pick a name from a list". Seed A starting number given to a random generator. The same seed gives the same "random" values every time, so a test data set can be rebuilt exactly. Distribution How values are spread: for example, 20% of customers have no orders, 40% have one. Real data is lumpy, and good test data copies the lumps that matter. Referential integrity The promise that every foreign key points at a row that exists. An order whose customer_id has no matching customer breaks it. See the data basics chapter . Parent table / child table The table being pointed at (CUSTOMERS) is the parent; the table holding the foreign key (ORDERS) is the child. Coverage matrix A grid that lists test conditions against the data that covers them, so you can see gaps at a glance.

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
h: 3.2 Why classify test data at all?
x: 3.2 Why classify test data at all? Imagine a kitchen preparing for a cooking class. The chef does not just buy "food". She buys the exact ingredients each recipe needs, in the amounts each recipe needs, and she keeps the allergy-sensitive items (nuts) in a separate, labelled place. Test data works the same way. You prepare the exact rows each test needs, and you keep the dangerous ones (real personal data) away from places they must not be. The analogy stops being accurate in one place: a chef can taste the soup, but nobody can "see" whether a table of 5 million rows has the right mix. That is why we write the classification down, as a plan, before building anything. Why it matters Without classification, teams fall into two traps. Either they copy everything from production (huge, risky, and still missing the odd cases that have never happened yet), or they hand-type five "happy path" rows and discover the bugs in production. Classification gives you a short list of questions to ask for any data request: where does it come from, how sensitive is it, and what must it prove?

h: 3.3 Three ways to classify test data
x: 3.3 Three ways to classify test data You can sort the same piece of data along three independent lines. A single customer row can be "masked production" by source, "restricted until masked" by sensitivity, and "boundary" by purpose. Keep the three lines separate in your head and in your documents. By source where did it come from? + By sensitivity how risky is it if it leaks? + By purpose what must the test prove?

The syllabus groups tool capabilities exactly along this line: subsetting and masking work on production-derived data, while generation makes new data. Source class How it is made Typical risk Where this guide covers it Production copy (raw) Straight copy of the real database Exposes real personal data; not allowed in test for regulated data Why TDM exists Production subset A cut-down, consistent slice of production Still real data until masked the discovery and subsetting concepts chapter Masked production Production (or a subset) with sensitive values replaced Weak masking can leak; masking must stay consistent across tables the masking concepts chapter Synthetic (generated) Created from rules, no real person behind any row May not look like the messy real world unless the rules are good This section Hand-crafted A person types or edits specific rows Slow, hard to repeat, tiny volume This section Hybrid Masked or queried production plus generated rows added Needs a clear plan for which part comes from where Section 3.6 Hybrid is more than a theory. x: 3.3.2 By sensitivity Sensitivity is how much harm follows if the data leaks. the sensitive data and regulations chapter covers PII, PHI and the regulations in depth. For classification purposes you only need a simple ladder. The labels differ between companies; the ladder below is a common shape, not a standard. Level Meaning ShopSphere example Allowed in test? Public Harmless if seen by anyone PRODUCTS.product_name Yes Internal Business data, not personal ORDERS.total_amount with no customer link Yes Personal Identifies or relates to a person first_name , email , phone , zip_code Only masked or synthetic Highly restricted Identifiers regulators care most about ssn , tax_id , date_of_birth Only masked or synthetic, and strongly protected Informatica's own introduction frames the same idea: you identify sensitive information in large volumes of production data, and its profiles can compare data against compliance standards, naming PII, PCI and PHI as examples (User Guide 10.5.10, p.24). The key point for classification is simple: sensitivity decides what you are allowed to do to the data; source and purpose decide what you do with it. Synthetic data has no real person behind it, which is why it needs no masking step.

x: 3.3.3 By purpose This is the line testers care about most. Each purpose answers "what must this row prove?". There are seven that cover almost every request. Purpose What it proves ShopSphere example Positive / valid The normal path works Asha Menon, 560001, valid email, two orders Negative / invalid Bad input is rejected with a clear message Phone 98765abcde ; email with no @ Boundary The edges of each rule behave exactly right Customer aged 17, 18 and 19; surname of 1 and of the maximum length Edge case Rare or odd but legal situations Surname O'Brien , hyphenated name, name with leading spaces, order with 50 items Null / empty Missing values do not crash anything No phone; empty zip_code ; customer with zero orders Volume / performance The system copes with realistic size 2 million customers, 10 million orders Security Hostile input is blocked Name field containing '; DROP TABLE ORDERS;-- Negative data usually does not live in the table A database column with a 10-digit phone constraint will refuse 98765abcde when you try to load it. Negative and security data are normally sent in through the screen, the API or an input file, not inserted straight into the table. Only load invalid values into a table if the table has no constraint and the test is about how the application reads bad stored data (for example a legacy table).

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
h: 3.4 The syllabus "data patterns" on the map
x: 3.4 The syllabus "data patterns" on the map The course syllabus (Day 47) lists five data patterns: boundary conditions, sequential, random, edge cases and null . They are not a separate classification. They are ways of shaping values , and each one serves one or more of the purposes in 7.3.3. the GenRocket data patterns chapter shows them in GenRocket; here we place them on the map. Pattern What the values look like Mainly serves purpose ShopSphere example Boundary conditions Values on and just either side of every limit Boundary Ages 17, 18, 19; quantity 0, 1, max, max+1 Sequential Values that count up (or down) in a fixed step Valid, volume, unique keys customer_id 2001, 2002, 2003 ... Random Values picked unpredictably from a range or list Valid, volume, realism First names picked from a list; zip codes in a range Edge cases Unusual but possible values, placed on purpose Edge case, negative A negative age every fifth record; names over the length limit 25% of the time Null Missing, empty or blank values Null / empty 5 customers with no phone The two documented tools describe these same shapes in their own words. This is the evidence for the table above: GenRocket has a page on Synthetic Data Replacement that lists test scenarios for one column (a Social Security Number): sequential replacement ( 001-00-0001 , 001-00-0002 ), valid-format replacement, character sets that inject invalid characters, boundary values such as 000-00-0000 and 999-99-9999 , missing or null data, illegal-format testing and volume stress testing. What is SDR? ↗ GenRocket's EdgeCaseGen page gives a story where the valid age range is 1 to 120, and a negative age is produced on every fifth record by cycling between a normal-range source and an edge-case source. EdgeCaseGen ↗ Informatica rules have an "exception test data" section where you pick how many rows should be null and how many should hold values that break the rule, each as a percentage with up to two decimal places (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.210 to 211). A rule can also use a sequence technique for ordered numbers or dates and a random technique for random strings, numbers and dates (pp.209 and 220). Worked example: one rule, five patterns Rule: "a customer must be at least 18 years old on the day of registration". Today, in the test, is 2026-10-23. Here is the same date_of_birth column shaped five ways. Illustrative date_of_birth values for the 18+ rule (my example, not from a vendor document) Pattern Values Expected application result Boundary 2008-10-24 (17 years, 364 days), 2008-10-23 (exactly 18), 2008-10-22 (18 years, 1 day) Reject, accept, accept Sequential 1980-01-01, 1980-01-02, 1980-01-03 ... All accepted; useful for volume and unique ordering Random Any date between 1950-01-01 and 2008-10-22 All accepted; realistic age spread Edge case 1900-01-01, 2024-02-29 (a leap day) Application decides: accept, or reject as implausible Null empty Reject with a "date of birth required" message Notice the boundary row. A boundary test needs three values per limit: just inside, on, and just outside. Many bugs are off-by-one mistakes (using "greater than" where "greater than or equal" was meant), and only the exact boundary value catches them. Random data hits the exact boundary almost never. That is the main reason boundary data must be designed , not left to chance.

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.5 What synthetic data is Concept. Synthetic data is data created by a program following rules you set. No row in it was ever a real person's record. Simple explanation. A film set looks like a street, but nobody lives in the houses. Synthetic data looks like customers, but no customer exists. It is built to be good enough to exercise the application , which is a different goal from being a copy of reality. The analogy stops being accurate in one place. A film set is built once and looks right from one angle. Synthetic data must stay correct from every angle the application looks at it: the foreign keys must join, the dates must be in order, and the totals must add up. What the tools say. GenRocket: "Synthetic Test Data" is data manufactured or generated by an algorithm rather than real-world events. Its stated benefit is that companies can maximise test coverage by testing all permutations and combinations. Why Synthetic Test Data? ↗ Informatica: data generation creates realistic test data for test environments, using generation rules that hold the logic. You import the metadata (table and column definitions) so the tool knows which columns to fill, assign rules to columns, then create a plan and run it (User Guide 10.5.10, p.190). Note what both descriptions have in common. The tool needs to know the shape of the target (the metadata) and a rule for each column. It does not need to see any real customer. A real-world example from the Informatica guide The guide's own example is an airline that sells plane tickets. Rules load dictionary values such as names into the customer tables, create random number strings for ticket numbers, create a numeric sequence for identification numbers, and use a reference lookup for values such as airport codes (User Guide 10.5.10, p.191). Map that to ShopSphere and you get: a name dictionary for first_name , a sequence for customer_id , random strings for order references, and a lookup of valid product_code values.

h: 3.6 Synthetic data versus masked production data
x: 3.6 Synthetic data versus masked production data Neither is "better". They solve different problems, and mature teams use both. The table compares them on the dimensions that matter. The ratings are general experience, so each column heading carries the "General concept" badge rather than a product claim. Question Masked production data Synthetic data Realism High. Real shapes, real mess, real correlations between columns As good as your rules. Looks real only for the properties you modelled Coverage of rare or future cases Only cases that already happened in production Any case you can describe, including ones that never happened, and boundary or invalid values on demand Privacy Depends on masking quality. Weak masking, or unmasked columns, can still identify people No real person behind any row, so there is nothing to re-identify Setup effort Discovery, masking rules, consistency checks Modelling the tables, writing rules for each column and relationship Cost to refresh Re-run extract and mask, which grows with production size Re-run the generator; speed depends on the rows asked for, not on production size Referential integrity Comes from the real data, but masking must keep keys matching across tables Must be designed: parent rows first, children point at existing parents (section 3.8) Distributions Real distributions come free You must state them (for example 20% of customers with no orders) Repeatability Same snapshot until refreshed Same output every run if you use a seed Volume on demand Limited by what production holds As many rows as the target can hold Main risk A leaked or unmasked column A model that is too tidy and misses real-world mess GenRocket's SDR page makes one claim worth noticing, which I report as the vendor's view: synthetic data "can produce edge cases that do not currently exist in production" and "can yield more accurate data patterns than exist in production". That is a statement about coverage, and it is true for any generator that supports designed edge cases. It does not mean synthetic data is automatically more realistic than production, which it is not.

x: 3.6.1 Which one should you choose? Is a realistic mix of messy data essential, such as for a new analytics report or a migration rehearsal? Lean towards masked production, because the real mess is the thing being tested. Result: use the subsetting and masking techniques from the subsetting and masking concept chapters. Is the system new, so there is no production data yet, or are you testing a feature with no history? Generate. There is nothing to copy. Result: use rules from this section. Do you need exact boundary, negative or very large data sets? Generate. Production rarely holds the 51st item in an order or a customer aged exactly 18 today. Do you need both realism and designed edge cases? Use a hybrid: masked subset as the base, generated rows added on top, with generated keys chosen so they never clash with the real ones. Generated is not the same as safe by default If a generator copies a real value (for example, picks names from an unmasked production table as its dictionary) the result is no longer purely synthetic. Always check where a generator's source list came from. Dictionaries should be made-up or public lists, never an export of real customers.

x: 3.7 How generation works: rules, generators, seeds and distributions Concept. A generation job has three layers. The target says which tables and columns to fill. A rule (Informatica's word) or an assigned generator (GenRocket's word) says how to fill each column. A run says how many rows and where to put them. 1. Target shape tables, columns, types, keys → 2. Rule per column sequence, random, list, formula → 3. Run settings how many rows, seed, output → 4. Output database, file, message

x: 3.7.2 Seeds: making "random" repeatable Concept. Computers do not produce truly random numbers. They run a formula that produces a long, random-looking list, starting from a number called the seed . Same seed, same list. Why it matters. Suppose a test fails on Tuesday because customer 2003 had a zip code with a leading zero. If the data is regenerated on Wednesday with different random values, you may never see that customer again. With a fixed seed you can rebuild exactly Tuesday's data and debug it. The opposite is also useful: change the seed on purpose to get a fresh data set when you want fresh coverage. GenRocket describes this directly: seeding generates the same set of random data for the same seed value every time, a seed can be set on the domain (a global seed variable) or in an attribute's generator configuration, and two attributes using the same generator and same seed produce the same random series. It also notes that GenRocket can generate the same data as previous runs through a seed on a domain or generator (FAQ). What is Seeding? ↗ The snippet below is my own illustration of the principle in plain Python, not a vendor tool. It builds the 50 customers and orders designed in section 3.10. Run it twice with seed 42 and you get identical data; run it with seed 7 and you get different data. import random def generate(seed): rnd = random.Random(seed) # the seed lives here first = ["Asha","Ravi","Meera","Kiran","Divya","Arjun","Sana","Vikram"] last = ["Menon","Kumar","Nair","Iyer","Rao","Shah","Das","Pillai"] customers = [] for i in range(50): cid = 2001 + i # sequential: 2001, 2002, ... customers.append((cid, rnd.choice(first), rnd.choice(last), "%06d" % rnd.randint(560001, 560099))) # random # exact distribution: 10 customers get 0 orders, 20 get 1, 15 get 2, 5 get 5 counts = [0]*10 + [1]*20 + [2]*15 + [5]*5 rnd.shuffle(counts) # random WHO, exact HOW MANY orders, oid = [], 9001 for cust, n in zip(customers, counts): for _ in range(n): orders.append((oid, cust[0], rnd.randint(1, 4))) # parent id, items oid += 1 return customers, orders c1, o1 = generate(42) c2, o2 = generate(42) c3, o3 = generate(7) print(len(c1), len(o1), sum(x[2] for x in o1)) # 50 75 179 print(c1 == c2 and o1 == o2, c1 == c3) # True False Expected result when I ran it (Python 3.13): the first print shows 50 75 179 and the second shows True False . The first three customers with seed 42 were (2001, 'Ravi', 'Menon', '560095') , (2002, 'Divya', 'Iyer', '560029') and (2003, 'Meera', 'Kumar', '560087') . The item total 179 and these exact names depend on the random generator inside your Python version, so yours may differ. What must hold on your machine is True False .

x: 3.7.3 Distributions: how values are spread If every customer got exactly two orders, the data would be repeatable but unrealistic. Real shops have many customers with none, most with one or two, and a few with many. The snippet above states this on purpose: 10, 20, 15 and 5 customers get 0, 1, 2 and 5 orders. That is a distribution . Both tools let you state percentages rather than writing a loop: Informatica's random technique lets a regular expression create a fixed percentage of the generated values, and pattern percentages must total 100 (User Guide 10.5.10, p.220). Null and invalid-value rows are also set as percentages (pp.210 to 211). GenRocket's MultiWeightGen assigns weights (a percentage and a value) so that, for example, 50% of parents have 2 children, 20% have 3 and 30% have 1. With exactPercentage set to true, ten parents give exactly five, two and three parents of each type. Generate Children based on Weights ↗ Exact or approximate? With "10% of rows null", you can ask for roughly 10% (each row has a 10% chance) or exactly 10% (5 of 50). For small data sets such as 50 customers, always choose exact, otherwise a run can produce zero nulls and your null test silently tests nothing.

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.7.4 Rules that link columns Some values only make sense in combination. A shipped date must come after the order date. A flight cannot leave and arrive at the same airport. Informatica's guide has both examples. It describes a conditional constraint : an expression such as To_City != From_City that restricts values in one column based on another (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.201 to 202). When the rule's own limits make the constraint impossible (for example a modified date that must be later than a created date of 31 July 2014, the last date the rule allows), the rule wins and the tool generates data with warning messages. The lesson for your own designs: when two rules fight, decide which one is the boss, and expect warnings from the other.

h: 3.8 Generating parent and child tables so every key is valid
x: 3.8 Generating parent and child tables so every key is valid Concept. A child row needs a parent that exists. If you generate ORDERS first and pick customer_id values at random, some will point at customers that do not exist, and the database (or the application's joins) will fail. Simple explanation. You cannot write a library card for a member who has not been registered. So you register members first, then issue cards that carry a registered member's number. CUSTOMERS customer_id (PK) 50 rows, made first ORDERS order_id (PK), customer_id (FK) 75 rows, made second ORDER_ITEMS item_id (PK), order_id (FK) 179 rows, made third copies an existing id copies an existing id Generation order: left to right. Arrows show which table each foreign key points at. Original diagram: parents are generated before children, and every foreign key copies an id that already exists. Row counts are from the design in section 3.10.

h: 3.8.1 Two common ways to keep keys valid
x: 3.8.1 Two common ways to keep keys valid A. Child picks from existing parents Generate the whole parent table first. Then, for each child row, choose a parent id from the finished list. Informatica calls this a reference lookup rule: you name the parent table and assign parent columns to child columns (User Guide 10.5.10, p.229). Good when the parent table already exists, for example loading new orders against real or masked customers. B. Children are made inside each parent Loop over parents. For each parent, decide how many children it has, then create exactly that many, stamping the parent's id on each. GenRocket works this way: a parent domain's loop count and the child's count per parent drive the output, and it generates data sequentially along the relationships (see its "Parent, Child, and Sibling Relationships" page). Good when both tables are being created together, and when you want a controlled number of children per parent. GenRocket's page also says every domain has an id or primary attribute that is used to guarantee referential integrity between domains, and its FAQ says it can generate synthetic data with full referential integrity. It introduces a "sibling" idea: a table that merely describes another (the page's example is a role table describing a user table) is marked as a sibling instead of a parent, to avoid generating unnecessary data. Parent, Child, and Sibling Relationships ↗

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.8.2 How many children per parent? Informatica's plan settings for data generation include a minimum and maximum number of child records for each parent record, each with a default of 1 , and percentages for "parent records without children" and "child records without parent" for self-cyclic tables and reference lookup rules (User Guide 10.5.10, p.285). Those last two settings exist because sometimes you want a customer with no orders (a null-style condition) or, rarely, a deliberately orphaned child (for a data-quality test). Do this only on purpose and label it, so nobody mistakes it for a bug. Self-referencing tables A table whose foreign key points at itself (an employee table with a manager id) has no "parents first" order. The tool needs a special rule: the first rows have no parent, later rows point back at earlier ones. Informatica's setting names self-cyclic tables specifically (p.285). ShopSphere has none, so we do not build one here.

h: 3.9 The lifecycle: Model, Design, Deploy, Manage
x: 3.9 The lifecycle: Model, Design, Deploy, Manage The syllabus for Day 46 says "Data generation: model, design, deploy, manage". That is GenRocket's own phrase: its help centre states that GenRocket uses a "Model, Design, Deploy, Manage" methodology and explains it in a video that I could not watch, so the page text is all I can report. The GenRocket Methodology ↗ The four words describe a cycle that any generation effort goes through, in any tool. The table below is my teaching interpretation, built from the pieces I could ground. Phase Question it answers ShopSphere activity What you produce Model What does the data look like? List the tables, columns, types, keys and relationships (CUSTOMERS, ORDERS, ORDER_ITEMS, PRODUCTS) A data model the tool can read, often imported from an existing database definition Design Which values, how many, and why? Choose a rule per column, set the distributions, decide the boundary and null rows (section 3.10) Rules, counts and a coverage matrix Deploy How do the rows reach the test system? Run the generation, write to the QA database or to files, check keys and counts Loaded, verified test data Manage How do we keep it right and reusable? Version the rules, record the seed, handle requests for changes, retire old data sets A catalogue of data sets and a change history Evidence for the pieces. GenRocket's General FAQ says it assigns the more complex test data tasks to a small group of trained "Test Data Engineers" who model test data projects and design the data (the FAQ's examples are integration, load and negative data), while testers and developers only need to learn how to search for the data they need, integrate or deploy it into their test environment, and modify it with a questionnaire tool. Its architecture page adds that GenRocket is hybrid: synthetic data is modelled and designed in a cloud component and generated locally in an on-premises component. GenRocket Architecture ↗ GenRocket also names five building blocks that the phases work on. The reference table on its "Five Key Components" page reads like this in my words: a domain is a noun such as a table or file; an attribute is a characteristic of a domain, such as a column; a generator produces the values for an attribute; a receiver turns generated data into a usable format such as SQL, CSV or JSON; and a scenario holds the instructions for what to generate and how much. GenRocket Five Key Components ↗ Placing them on the cycle is my own reading: domains and attributes are mostly Model work, generators and scenarios are Design work, receivers carry the Deploy step. The GenRocket overview chapter takes this further. Where Informatica fits on the same cycle Informatica's task flow has the same shape: import metadata into a project (model), create generation rules and assign them to columns (design), create a plan, generate a workflow and run it (deploy), then watch it in the Monitor view (User Guide 10.5.10, p.192). The guide does not use the words Model, Design, Deploy, Manage; the mapping is mine.
