x: 3.10 Worked example: 50 ShopSphere customers and their orders The request. The QA team testing ShopSphere's Customer Orders app asks the TDM engineer for a new data set in a QA database: 50 customers, with orders and items, covering the registration rules, the order history page and a customer-search feature. No production data may be used. We follow Model, Design and Deploy; Manage is covered by the lab at the end.

x: 3.10.1 Model The tables are the ShopSphere tables from the data basics chapter. The relationships are the only thing the generator needs to respect: ORDERS.customer_id points at CUSTOMERS , ORDER_ITEMS.order_id points at ORDERS , and ORDER_ITEMS.product_code points at PRODUCTS . PRODUCTS is a small reference table of four rows that we load by hand (P-100 Laptop Stand, P-200 USB Cable, P-300 Phone Case, P-400 Desk Lamp), because it is better to control the catalogue than to invent products. These business rules are invented for this example. They are what the test conditions will aim at: customers must be 18 or older; first and last names are at most 30 characters; phone is 10 digits when present; zip code is 6 digits when present; email is optional; each order has between 1 and 4 items .

x: 3.10.3 The coverage matrix The matrix shows which data group serves which test area. An empty column is a gap. A tick means a row exists that exercises that area. Coverage matrix: data groups against test areas (✓ = covered) Data group Registration validation Customer search Order history page Order total report Privacy export Typical (33) ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Boundary (6) ✓ ✓ Null / empty (5) ✓ ✓ ✓ Edge case (6) ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Customers with 0 orders (10) ✓ ✓ ✓ Customers with 5 orders (5) ✓ ✓ Negative input file (4 rows, not loaded) ✓ Look at the empty cells. Boundary customers have no tick for the order history page, because the design does not say whether they have orders. A good review catches that. Fix it by requiring that at least two boundary customers and two null-phone customers are among the 40 customers who have orders, so the order history page is also tried with them.

x: 3.10.4 Deploy and verify After the run, check three things before you hand the data over. These SQL checks are what I ran against my generated rows in SQLite; the syntax works on most databases. -- 1. No orphan orders (expected: 0) SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL; -- 2. The orders-per-customer distribution matches the design SELECT n AS orders_per_customer, COUNT(*) AS customers FROM (SELECT c.customer_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS n FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id) t GROUP BY n ORDER BY n; -- 3. The null and empty rows really exist (expected: 2, 1, 1, 1) SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN phone IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS null_phone, SUM(CASE WHEN email IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS null_email, SUM(CASE WHEN zip_code = '' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS empty_zip, SUM(CASE WHEN tax_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS null_tax_id FROM customers; Expected result: check 1 returns 0. Check 2 returns four rows: (0, 10), (1, 20), (2, 15), (5, 5); I got exactly this from the snippet in 7.7.2. Check 3 returns 2, 1, 1, 1 once the null and empty overrides from the design table are applied. The snippet in 7.7.2 generates only the typical shape, so I did not run check 3 against it; it is a template for you to run on a real design.

x: 3.11 Test data as a service Concept. "Test data as a service" means test data is something teams can ask for and receive , like a ticket to a service desk, instead of something each team builds in secret. A small group owns the know-how and the rules; many teams consume the results. The phrase itself does not appear in the documentation pages I read, so I use it as a label for what the three tools describe in their own words. Why it matters. Without it, every team writes its own scripts, nobody can reproduce another team's data and the same sensitive columns get masked ten different ways. With it, a request is a small form ("50 customers with orders, boundary included"), and the answer is a catalogued, repeatable data set. Tool What its docs say that fits the idea GenRocket G-Portal is described as part of a distributed self-service platform in which a small group of Test Data Engineers in a Center of Excellence supports large distributed teams. Requesters search for existing test data, create requests, track them and download components. G-Portal Overview ↗ GenRocket Test Data Cases (G-Cases) change the components inside a scenario so the same scenario can produce many permutations for different test cases, organised in suites with categories such as Beta, Unit or Load. G-Cases Overview ↗ Informatica TDM A test data warehouse stores data sets; the guide says multiple teams using different machines that host a Test Data Manager Service in a domain can access a single test data warehouse (User Guide 10.5.10, p.24). Delphix The terminology page describes Delphix Self-Service as a user interface designed for project teams, application developers and testers to manage their virtualised datasets. Delphix masking terminology ↗ What a ShopSphere request might look like Requester: QA engineer. Need: customers with 0, 1, 2 and 5 orders; 5 null-phone customers. Environment: QA2. Refresh: weekly, same seed. Owner: TDM engineer. Delivered as: a named data set "SHOPSPHERE-CUST-50-v3" with the rule version and seed recorded. This record is the "Manage" phase of 7.9 in miniature.

h: 3.12 Hands-on lab: design a smaller data set on paper
x: 3.12 Hands-on lab: design a smaller data set on paper Lab: model and design 20 customers Goal: practise turning a request into a Model, a Design and a coverage matrix. You need pen and paper or a text editor; no tool is required. Write the request. "20 customers with orders for the order history page. Customers must be 18 or older. Zip code is 6 digits." You should have one sentence naming the tables, the count and the rules. Split the 20 customers by purpose. Use typical, boundary, null or empty and edge case. The groups must add up to 20. A table with four rows and a total of 20. Pick an orders-per-customer distribution. Choose counts that add up to 20 customers and state the total orders. Draw a coverage matrix with your groups down the side and the test areas "registration" and "order history" across the top. Mark ticks and find one gap. Write two SQL checks you would run after generation. Show a worked answer Groups: typical 12, boundary 3 (exactly 18; 18 and one day; zip 560001), null or empty 2 (phone NULL; email NULL), edge case 3 (O'Brien; hyphenated surname; leap-day birthday). Total 12 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 20. Orders: 0 orders for 4 customers, 1 order for 8, 2 orders for 6, 4 orders for 2. Total orders = 0 + 8 + 12 + 8 = 28. Gap you should find: the order history column is empty for the groups unless you require some of the boundary and null customers to have orders. A fix: make 2 of the 3 boundary customers and both null customers belong to the groups that have orders. Checks: the orphan-order query from 7.10.4 (expect 0), and a count of customers with exactly 4 orders (expect 2).

x: 3.13 Common mistakes and gotchas Mistakes beginners make Generating children before parents. The foreign keys then point at nothing. Always parents first, or have the child rule read from the finished parent table. All-random data and no designed edges. Random values almost never hit an exact boundary, a null, or a name with an apostrophe. Put those rows in on purpose. Not recording the seed. A failed test cannot be reproduced if the data cannot be rebuilt. Requesting "about 10% null". In a 50-row data set that can come out as zero. Ask for an exact count. Totals that do not add up. Derive total_amount from the items instead of generating it separately. Loading invalid values into constrained columns. The load fails or the constraint is silently dropped. Keep negative data in the input channel. Treating synthetic as automatically realistic. It only mirrors what you modelled. Compare a few generated distributions against real, masked, aggregated figures. Reusing real values as the "dictionary". A name list exported from production defeats the purpose.

x: 3.14 Recap Recap Classify test data along three lines: source (production-derived or synthetic), sensitivity (what harm a leak causes) and purpose (what the row must prove). The seven purposes are valid, invalid, boundary, edge case, null or empty, volume and security. The syllabus data patterns (boundary, sequential, random, edge cases, null) are ways of shaping values to serve them. Synthetic data is created from rules. It gives privacy and designed coverage; masked production gives real-world mess. Hybrids use both. Generation needs a target shape, a rule or generator per column, and run settings. A seed makes it repeatable and a distribution makes it realistic. Generate parents first and make every foreign key copy an existing parent id; control how many children each parent gets. GenRocket's cycle is Model, Design, Deploy, Manage. Test data as a service means requestable, catalogued, repeatable data owned by a small expert group. A coverage matrix shows gaps before the testers find them. ETL from scratch: extract, transform, load Every tool in this guide moves data. Informatica TDM copies a slice of a database, changes some values and writes it somewhere else. Delphix reads a source, masks it and delivers it to a target. GenRocket creates rows and writes them to a database or a file. Underneath, all three do the same three things: get data from somewhere, change it, put it somewhere else . The industry has had a name for that pattern for decades: ETL , which stands for Extract, Transform, Load. This section teaches ETL on its own, with no test data management in it, so that you can recognise the pattern wherever it appears. We will build a small but complete ETL job for ShopSphere using plain SQL, with real input and real output tables, then look at the machinery that real ETL tools wrap around those SQL steps: schedulers, logs, error handling and reusable components. The next chapter on ETL and TDM lays the TDM tools on top of what you learn here. You need to know what a table, a primary key and a foreign key are; if not, read the data basics chapter first.

x: 3.15 Words to know first ETL Extract, Transform, Load: copy data out of one or more sources, reshape and clean it, and write it into a target. Staging area A temporary landing zone, usually a set of tables or files, where extracted data sits unchanged before it is transformed. Operational database (OLTP) The database an application uses to run the business: place an order, update an address. Built for many small, fast reads and writes. Data warehouse A separate database built for reporting and analysis across lots of history. Built for a few big reads. Full extract / incremental extract Reading everything every time, versus reading only what is new or changed since last time. Watermark A saved marker, such as "last order id loaded was 5005", that tells the next run where to start. Change data capture (CDC) Any technique that detects which rows were inserted, updated or deleted in the source so only those are processed. Upsert "Update if the row exists, insert if it does not." Short for update plus insert. Slowly changing dimension (SCD) A way of keeping history in a warehouse table when descriptive data (an address) changes over time. Mapping The definition of how source columns become target columns, including every transformation in between. Workflow, session, job The runnable wrappers around mappings. A job or workflow runs one or more sessions or steps on a schedule. Mapplet Informatica's word for a reusable group of transformations that you build once and drop into many mappings. Metadata Data about data: table definitions, column types, mapping definitions, run history. Reject (error) row A row the job could not process, written aside with a reason instead of stopping the whole run. ELT Extract, Load, Transform: load raw data into the target first and transform it there using the target database's own power.

h: 3.16 What ETL is and why it exists
x: 3.16 What ETL is and why it exists Concept. ETL is a repeatable process that moves data from where it is created to where it is needed, fixing it on the way. Simple explanation. Think of a school canteen. Vegetables arrive muddy from several farms ( extract brings them to the back door), staff wash, cut and combine them in the prep room ( transform ), and trays go to the serving counter ( load ). Each stage has its own place and rules. The analogy stops being accurate here: an ETL job runs many times and must give the same kind of result each time, even if interrupted and restarted. Cooks can improvise; ETL jobs must not. Why it matters Data in real companies lives in many places and many shapes. ShopSphere's orders sit in one database, product prices in a spreadsheet maintained by buyers, and a partner sends a daily file where dates are written day first. A manager who asks "how much did we sell last week, per product?" needs one clean answer. Someone has to collect, clean and combine. ETL is the name for doing that on purpose, automatically, and with a record of what happened. ETL appears in data warehouses and reports (the classic case), system migrations, keeping two systems in step, feeding analytics, and test data provisioning, the topic of the next chapter .

x: 3.17 Operational database versus data warehouse ETL usually connects those two kinds of database, so the difference is worth knowing. Question Operational database (OLTP) Data warehouse Main purpose Run the business, one transaction at a time Answer questions across lots of history Typical work "Insert this order", "update this address" "Total sales per product per month for three years" Table shape Many small tables, tightly normalised to avoid duplication (CUSTOMERS, ORDERS, ORDER_ITEMS) Fewer, wider tables arranged around facts and dimensions History Mostly current values; old values are overwritten History kept, often with dated versions of each row Who writes The application, all day The ETL job, on a schedule A common warehouse shape is the star schema : a central fact table that records events or measurements (one row per order line, with quantity and amount), surrounded by dimension tables that describe the who, what and when (customer, product, date). A fact table is mostly numbers and keys; a dimension table is mostly descriptive text. We will build a tiny star for ShopSphere later in this section.

x: 3.19 Extract: getting data out Concept. Extraction reads data from a source system and hands it to the ETL process, without changing the source. Why it matters. Extraction is where ETL jobs first meet the real world: slow networks, locked tables, files that arrive late or half-written, and sources that must not be slowed down because customers are using them. A good extract takes only what it needs, takes it consistently, and leaves the source as it found it.

x: 3.19.2 Full versus incremental extraction Full extract Read every row, every run. Good: simple; no state to remember; picks up deletions automatically because the target is rebuilt. Bad: slow and heavy as data grows; reads unchanged data again and again. Use for: small reference tables such as PRODUCTS, and first-time loads. Incremental extract Read only rows that are new or changed since the last successful run. Good: fast; kind to the source. Bad: needs a reliable way to know "what changed"; misses deleted rows unless you plan for them. Use for: large, growing tables such as ORDERS.

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.19.3 The watermark technique The simplest incremental method is a watermark : store the highest value you have processed, and next time ask only for rows beyond it. It needs a column whose value only ever grows, such as an increasing order number or a "last modified" timestamp. ShopSphere's order feed has an increasing order_id , so we keep a small control table with one row per job: CREATE TABLE etl_control ( job_name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, last_order_id INTEGER ); INSERT INTO etl_control VALUES ('orders_daily', 0); -- Extract only new orders (the feed holds text, so convert for the comparison) INSERT INTO stg_orders SELECT 1, o.* FROM feed_orders o WHERE CAST(o.order_id AS INTEGER) > (SELECT last_order_id FROM etl_control WHERE job_name = 'orders_daily'); -- After the whole run succeeds, move the watermark forward UPDATE etl_control SET last_order_id = (SELECT MAX(CAST(order_id AS INTEGER)) FROM stg_orders) WHERE job_name = 'orders_daily'; Expected result in my SQLite run: on the first run (watermark 0) five orders (5001 to 5005) were staged and the watermark moved to 5005. On the second run, with orders 5006 and 5007 newly added to the feed, only those two were staged and the watermark moved to 5007. Three ways a watermark goes wrong Moving the watermark too early. If you advance it before the load finishes and the job fails, those rows are never retried. Advance it as the very last step, in the same transaction as the load when possible. A column that is not strictly increasing. If IDs can be assigned out of order by two servers, a late row with a smaller number is skipped forever. A "last modified" timestamp has the same trap when clocks differ. Changes and deletes are invisible. A watermark on order_id sees new orders, not edits to old ones, and never sees a deleted row. For edits use a last-modified column; for deletes use CDC or a periodic full comparison.

h: 3.19.4 Change data capture at concept level
x: 3.19.4 Change data capture at concept level Change data capture (CDC) is the umbrella name for ways to learn what changed. There are four common approaches. Each product implements them differently, so check your tool's documentation before relying on one. Approach How it works Catches deletes? Cost to the source Timestamp or version column Query rows where last_modified > watermark No Low, but the table needs the column Trigger-based A database trigger writes every change into a side table that ETL reads Yes Adds work to every write Log-based Read the database's own transaction log to see inserts, updates and deletes in order Yes Low on the source, but needs special access and tooling Compare snapshots Keep yesterday's copy; compare with today's; the difference is the change Yes High: reads and compares everything

x: 3.19.5 Good extraction habits Record the run. Give every run a batch id and a timestamp, and write both next to the extracted rows. When something looks wrong later, you can say exactly which run brought it in. Read a consistent snapshot. If you extract CUSTOMERS and then ORDERS five minutes later, new orders may point at customers you did not capture. Extract related tables in one transaction or point in time, or cut the orders to a time you know customers cover. What you should see: every order in staging has its customer in staging, or the job knows why not.

x: 3.20 The staging area Concept. The staging area is a temporary landing zone between the source and the final target. Extracted data is stored there in nearly the same form as it was found. Simple explanation. In the canteen, it is the delivery bay where crates are put down before anyone peels anything. Why it matters. Staging gives you four things: A frozen copy. You can transform, check and re-run without hitting the source again. Separation of duties. Extraction only reads; transformation only reshapes; neither depends on the other being fast. Safe restarts. A failure in the transform step does not need a new extract. Informatica's plans give you the same idea in their connection options. When you create a plan, you can choose a staging connection , "a connection to a database for staging data", and the default shown comes from the Preferences view (User Guide 10.5.10, p.276). That is a documented example of a staging area as a configured part of a real tool.

x: 3.20.1 How to design staging tables Mirror the source, with all columns as text. A staged row should never fail because a date has a strange format. Conversion is the transform step's job. Add audit columns. At least batch_id ; often a load timestamp and the source file name. No keys, no foreign keys, no constraints. Staging must accept bad data so that the transform step can decide what to do with it. Empty it each run (or partition by batch). Old staged data is usually not worth keeping beyond debugging. CREATE TABLE stg_customers ( batch_id INTEGER, customer_id TEXT, first_name TEXT, last_name TEXT, email TEXT, zip_code TEXT ); ShopSphere staging, run 1 The extract wrote these rows into stg_customers , and notice it kept the mess exactly as found: the leading space in " Asha ", the upper-case "MENON", the trailing space in the email, the duplicate row for 1002 and the missing email for 1003. stg_customers after extract (batch 1) batch_id customer_id first_name last_name email zip_code 1 1001 " Asha " MENON "Asha.Menon@Example.com " 560001 1 1002 Ravi Kumar ravi.k@example.com 600017 1 1002 Ravi Kumar ravi.k@example.com 600017 1 1003 Meera Nair NULL 682001 The order feed is staged the same way. Two of its rows are traps handled later: order 5004 has a total of "abc", and order 5005 belongs to customer 9999, who does not exist.

x: 3.21 Transform: cleaning and reshaping Concept. Transformation turns staged raw data into the clean, consistent, correctly typed shape the target needs. Why it matters. This is where business rules live. If the transform is wrong, the data is wrong everywhere downstream, and nobody can tell from the target alone. Transformations are therefore the part of ETL most worth documenting and testing. There are nine everyday kinds of transformation: cleaning, type conversion, mapping, deduplication, lookups, filtering, joining, derived columns and aggregation. We cover each in turn using the ShopSphere staging rows from the previous section. Each subsection shows the idea, the SQL, and the before and after.

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.21.1 Cleaning Idea. Make values consistent so that equal things look equal. "MENON", "Menon" and "menon " are the same surname to a person, but three different strings to a database. SELECT UPPER(SUBSTR(TRIM(first_name),1,1)) || LOWER(SUBSTR(TRIM(first_name),2)) AS first_name, UPPER(SUBSTR(TRIM(last_name),1,1)) || LOWER(SUBSTR(TRIM(last_name),2)) AS last_name, COALESCE(LOWER(TRIM(email)), 'not provided') AS email FROM stg_customers; Cleaning, customer 1001 and 1003 first_name last_name email Before (1001) " Asha " MENON "Asha.Menon@Example.com " After (1001) Asha Menon asha.menon@example.com Before (1003) Meera Nair NULL After (1003) Meera Nair not provided Function names differ by database (for example SUBSTR is SUBSTRING in SQL Server). Replacing a missing email with "not provided" is a business choice; some teams keep NULL.

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.21.2 Type conversion Idea. Staging holds everything as text. The target needs real dates and numbers so that sorting, comparing and adding work properly. As text, "9" sorts after "10", and "20/10/2026" sorts before "21/09/2026" only by accident. SELECT CAST(order_id AS INTEGER) AS order_id, SUBSTR(order_date,7,4) || '-' || SUBSTR(order_date,4,2) || '-' || SUBSTR(order_date,1,2) AS order_date, CAST(total_amount AS REAL) AS total_amount FROM stg_orders WHERE total_amount NOT GLOB '*[^0-9.]*'; -- only rows whose amount is numeric Type conversion, order 5002 order_id order_date total_amount Before (text) "5002" "20/10/2026" "250.50" After (typed) 5002 2026-10-20 (date) 250.5 (number) Oracle and PostgreSQL would use TO_DATE(order_date, 'DD/MM/YYYY') ; I sliced the string because SQLite has no date parser with a format string. Confirm with the data owner whether dates are day-first or month-first, and reject dates that do not parse instead of guessing.

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.21.3 Mapping and standardising The word mapping has two meanings in ETL, and both matter. In the broad sense a mapping is the whole definition of how source columns become target columns (we meet this in 8.11). In the narrow sense, value mapping means translating codes: the order system stores S , P and C , and reports want the words. CREATE TABLE status_map (status_code TEXT PRIMARY KEY, status_name TEXT); INSERT INTO status_map VALUES ('S','Shipped'),('P','Pending'),('C','Cancelled'); SELECT o.order_id, COALESCE(m.status_name, 'Unknown') AS order_status FROM stg_orders o LEFT JOIN status_map m ON m.status_code = o.status_code; Value mapping of status codes order_id status_code (before) order_status (after) 5001 S Shipped 5003 P Pending 5006 (run 2) C Cancelled 5007 (run 2) Z Unknown The unmatched code Z becomes "Unknown" because of the LEFT JOIN plus COALESCE . An inner join here would silently drop order 5007 altogether, which is one of the most common ETL bugs: a lookup that loses rows when it fails to match .

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.21.4 Deduplication Idea. Keep one row for each real-world thing. Customer 1002 arrived twice in the staging data. SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name, email, zip_code FROM ( SELECT s.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id) AS rn FROM stg_customers s ) t WHERE rn = 1; ROW_NUMBER() numbers the rows inside each customer id (1, 2, ...); keeping only number 1 removes the extras. The ORDER BY inside the window decides which duplicate survives. Here the two copies were identical so it did not matter. In real data the copies often differ, and you must choose a rule such as "keep the latest by modified date" or "keep the one with the most filled-in columns". Deduplication result (batch 1) rows for customer 1002 total rows Before 2 4 After 1 3

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.21.5 Lookups Idea. A lookup enriches a row by finding a related value in a reference table. Order items carry only product_code . A lookup in PRODUCTS adds the product name. SELECT i.item_id, i.product_code, COALESCE(p.product_name, 'UNKNOWN PRODUCT') AS product_name FROM stg_order_items i LEFT JOIN products p ON p.product_code = i.product_code; Product lookup, with one miss item_id product_code product_name (after lookup) 1 P-100 Laptop Stand 4 P-400 Desk Lamp 8 (run 2) P-999 UNKNOWN PRODUCT Choose deliberately what a miss does: use a default such as "UNKNOWN PRODUCT" and report it, or reject the row. Never let it vanish. Real ETL tools provide a ready-made lookup transformation for this and handle caching, because looking up a million rows one at a time would be slow. In the Informatica guide, lookup transformations appear among the restrictions on mapplets used for Hadoop masking (User Guide 10.5.10, p.137), which confirms that lookup is a standard kind of transformation in that product.

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.21.6 Filtering, validating and rejecting Idea. Some rows should not reach the target. Filtering removes rows that are valid but unwanted (for example, test orders). Validating checks rows against rules and rejects those that fail, keeping them aside with a reason so someone can fix them. CREATE TABLE reject_orders (batch_id INTEGER, order_id TEXT, reason TEXT); INSERT INTO reject_orders SELECT 1, o.order_id, CASE WHEN o.total_amount = '' OR o.total_amount GLOB '*[^0-9.]*' THEN 'total_amount is not a number' ELSE 'customer ' || o.customer_id || ' not found' END FROM stg_orders o WHERE o.total_amount = '' OR o.total_amount GLOB '*[^0-9.]*' OR NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dim_customer d WHERE d.customer_id = CAST(o.customer_id AS INTEGER)); reject_orders after run 1 batch_id order_id reason 1 5004 total_amount is not a number 1 5005 customer 9999 not found The valid orders carry on. This is the key design choice: one bad row must not stop the whole run, and must not vanish . It goes to a reject table with a batch id and a human-readable reason.

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.21.7 Joining and derived columns Joining combines rows from different inputs. To build the sales fact table we join order items to their orders for date, customer and status. Ask of every join: "what happens to a row with no match?" An inner join drops it; a left join keeps it with empty columns. That is a business decision, not a technical one. Derived columns calculate values that do not exist in the source, such as line_amount as quantity times unit price (item 2: 2 × 100.00 = 200.0).

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.21.8 Aggregating Idea. Summarise many rows into fewer, such as a daily sales table for dashboards. SELECT order_date, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders_count, SUM(quantity) AS units, SUM(line_amount) AS revenue FROM fact_order_line GROUP BY order_date; agg_daily_sales after run 1 order_date orders_count units revenue 2026-10-20 2 4 1749.5 2026-10-21 1 1 75.0 Hand check: on 20 October, 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 units and 1499 + 200 + 50.5 = 1749.5 revenue.

x: 3.22 Load: writing into the target Concept. Loading writes the transformed rows into the target tables, in a way that is correct, repeatable and fast enough. Why it matters. A load that half-finishes leaves the target in a state nobody understands: some rows from tonight, some from yesterday. Loads must either complete or leave things as they were, and they must be safe to run again.

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.22.1 Load strategies Strategy What it does Good for Danger Truncate and load (full refresh) Empty the target table, then insert everything Small tables, reference data, test databases Target is empty or partial during the load; slow for big tables Append (insert only) Add new rows, never touch old ones Event or fact data that never changes Running twice duplicates rows Incremental Load only the rows extracted incrementally Large tables Depends on a correct watermark Upsert (merge) Update rows that exist, insert those that do not Dimensions and master data Needs a reliable key to match on History-keeping load (SCD) Close the old version of a row and insert a new one Dimensions where history matters More complex; the table grows What the tools say about these ideas, all in their own terms: Informatica's plan has update strategy options: treat source rows as Insert or Update , and an "Update as" choice of Update , Insert or Update else Insert , which updates a row if it exists in the target and inserts the rest (User Guide 10.5.10, p.284). That is the upsert strategy, named. Informatica lets you run SQL before and after writing to a target. Its example is TRUNCATE TABLE $OWNERNAME.$TABLENAME; , which deletes all rows from the target table first (pp.277 to 278). That is truncate and load. Delphix on-the-fly masking jobs have a Truncate option that sets whether target database tables are emptied before the masked data is loaded, and a Batch Update option for loading in batches sized by the commit size. Create, view, edit, delete, verify jobs ↗ GenRocket's FAQ says that for very large volumes you do not want to connect through JDBC; you generate data in the database's native bulk load format using bulk load receivers. GenRocket General FAQ ↗

x: 3.22.2 Upsert in SQL Suppose Asha Menon's zip code changes in the next feed. A plain insert would collide with the existing row. An upsert updates it: -- SQLite and PostgreSQL syntax INSERT INTO dim_customer_simple (customer_id, full_name, email, zip_code) VALUES (1001, 'Asha Menon', 'asha.menon@example.com', '560002') ON CONFLICT (customer_id) DO UPDATE SET full_name = excluded.full_name, email = excluded.email, zip_code = excluded.zip_code; -- Oracle and SQL Server use MERGE instead Upsert effect on one row customer_id full_name zip_code Before 1001 Asha Menon 560001 After 1001 Asha Menon 560002 Notice the property that makes upserts valuable: running the same load twice gives the same result . A property like this is called idempotence , and it is what lets you safely re-run a failed job.

h: 3.22.3 Keeping history: a slowly changing dimension
x: 3.22.3 Keeping history: a slowly changing dimension An upsert overwrites. After it, the warehouse says Asha always lived in 560002, so a report on October 20 sales would attribute them to the wrong zip. If history matters, keep both versions with validity dates. This pattern is commonly called a Type 2 slowly changing dimension . The pattern needs two statements, which you will run in Lab 2: first close the current row of any customer whose data changed (set valid_to and is_current = 0 ), then insert a new current row for every customer who has none. The table gets a surrogate key ( customer_key ), an artificial id, because the business key customer_id now appears more than once. dim_customer after run 2 (real output from my SQLite run, 1002 and 1003 omitted) customer_key customer_id zip_code valid_from valid_to is_current 1 1001 560001 2026-10-23 2026-10-24 0 4 1001 560002 2026-10-24 9999-12-31 1 A fact row can then be joined to the customer version valid on the order date. The date 9999-12-31 is a common convention for "still current".

x: 3.22.4 Making a load safe Transactions and commit size. Rows are written in groups; each group is committed. Informatica's plan lets you set a source-based or target-based commit (target-based is the default) and a commit interval whose default is 10,000 rows (User Guide 10.5.10, p.285). Delphix masking jobs have a Commit Size field with the same meaning. Recovery. Decide in advance what a failed load does: roll back and stop, skip the bad row, or resume from a checkpoint (see 8.13).

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
h: 3.23.1 Batch versus streaming at a glance
x: 3.23.1 Batch versus streaming at a glance Batch collects data for a period (an hour, a night) and processes it as one group. It is easy to reason about and to re-run, and results are always "as of the last run". Most ETL, and nearly all test data provisioning, is batch. Streaming processes each event within seconds of arrival. Results are fresh, but you must handle duplicates and out-of-order events, so it is used where the answer must be current, such as fraud alerts. A middle path, micro-batching , runs a small batch every minute or so.

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.23.2 ETL versus ELT In ETL , transformations run in the ETL engine, on its own servers, before data reaches the target. In ELT , raw data is loaded into the target first (often a powerful cloud warehouse) and transformed there using its SQL engine. ETL ELT Where transforms run Separate ETL engine Inside the target database Strength Sensitive data can be cleaned or masked before it lands in the target Uses the target's power; raw data can be re-transformed later Weakness The engine can become a bottleneck Raw (maybe sensitive) data sits in the target Look at the last row, because it matters for test data. If raw data holds real personal details, ELT would place them in the target before masking. That is why test data work usually follows the ETL order: mask first, then load. The ShopSphere example in this section is really a hybrid: staging is a lightweight "EL" step and the transformation is done by SQL. Many practical systems mix both styles.

x: 3.25 Mappings, sessions, workflows and jobs Every ETL tool has a few layers of "thing you can define and run". Names vary, so learn the layers and then the names. Transformation. One operation on rows: filter, lookup, aggregate. The smallest piece. Mapping. A diagram or definition that connects a source to a target through a chain of transformations. It describes what happens to the data, but does not run by itself. Session (or task). A runnable instance of one mapping, with the run settings: which connections, commit size, error rules. Workflow (or job, or pipeline). A set of sessions and other steps with an order and conditions: "run session A; if it works, run B and C; if it fails, send an email". Schedule or trigger. When the workflow starts: a time, a file arriving, another workflow ending. These layers in the Informatica TDM guide When you generate a workflow from a plan, "the PowerCenter Repository Service generates mappings for the workflow"; when you start it, the PowerCenter Integration Service does the subset, masking and generation tasks defined in the plan (p.308). You can view the sessions that run from each workflow, with statistics for affected rows, rejected rows and rows written to the target (p.275, "Session Details" tab). A plan can run a chosen workflow before ("pre workflow") and after ("post workflow") the main one: its example copies files from production to test area first, then masks, then runs statistics on the tables (p.277). The guide also warns that if you edit components generated from Test Data Manager in the PowerCenter Client, "the session might generate unexpected results" (p.150).

x: 3.26 Reusable components and the mapplet Concept. A reusable component is a piece of ETL logic you build once and use in many places, like a function in programming. Why it matters. Without reuse, the same rule (clean a phone number, standardise a country name) is copied into twenty mappings. When the rule changes, someone must find and fix twenty copies, and will miss one. In Informatica's world, the reusable group of transformations is called a mapplet . A mapplet has input and output ports (named connection points), contains one or more transformations, and can be placed into many mappings. Think of it as a small mapping with sockets at each end. Input port FIRST_NAME → Transformations inside trim, fix case, reject blanks → Output port FIRST_NAME_CLEAN What the TDM guide says about mapplets (the rest of the product is not needed to follow this): Test Data Manager can create a masking rule from a mapplet . The mapplet holds the logic that masks the input columns and returns data to the target columns (User Guide 10.5.10, p.137). You import the mapplet from an XML file exported from the PowerCenter repository or the Model repository, and the mapplet can contain "any passive transformations" (p.137). A passive transformation is one that does not change the number of rows. A mapplet can have multiple input and multiple output columns; at least one input and one output must be marked required. When you assign the rule to a column you map the mapplet's column names to the real table columns (p.137). The TDM repository stores the mapplet logic when imported, and you cannot change the mapplet inside Test Data Manager. The guide also says that if you change the name or type of a field of a custom masking rule, you must import the mapplet again (p.144). Data generation uses the same idea: a custom generation rule is based on PowerCenter mapplet logic, for example one that joins first and last name into a full name (pp.192 and 211). The syllabus mentions "mapplet creation" on Day 54; the Informatica data masking chapter returns to this. This guide has no documentation excerpt on building a mapplet in PowerCenter itself.

x: 3.27 Error handling Concept. Error handling is the plan for what the job does when something goes wrong, decided before it goes wrong. Why it matters. Something will go wrong. A file will arrive empty, a database will be down for maintenance, a date will say 31 February. The question is whether you find out from an alert at 2 a.m. with a clear row count, or from an angry tester at 10 a.m. with a half-loaded database.

x: 3.27.2 Strategies Reject and continue for data errors, as in 8.7.6. Each reject row has a batch id and a reason. Threshold stop. Continue unless more than N errors occur. A file where 40% of rows fail is a broken file, not 40% bad customers. All-or-nothing. Load inside a transaction so a failure undoes everything. Checkpoint and resume. Remember how far you got, and on restart continue from there. Retry with a limit. Temporary glitches (a dropped connection) often pass on a second attempt. Real settings in the Informatica TDM plan Under "Error and Recovery Options" in a plan (User Guide 10.5.10, p.285) the guide lists these, which are a concrete menu of the strategies above. Stop on Error: how many non-fatal errors the session tolerates before it stops. Zero means the session never stops for non-fatal errors; zero is the default. Suspend on Error: pause the workflow when an error occurs so you can fix it and restart; default No. Rollback Transactions on Error: roll back at the next commit point on a non-fatal write error; default Yes. Recover Strategy: resume from the last checkpoint, restart the task, or fail the task and continue the workflow (the default). Enable High Availability Recovery: default No. Commit type and interval: target-based commit by default; interval default 10,000 rows. Delphix gives a second example of the same ideas for masking jobs. Data that does not fit what an algorithm expects (non-conformant data) can, at job level, make the job fail, leave the value unmasked, or set it to null (jobs page; terminology page). It also warns that when a masking job fails, the target database or files may be left in a partially masked or unmasked state (job monitoring page). Job monitoring ↗ That sentence is a good reminder: after a failed job, never assume the target is usable.

x: 3.27.3 Reprocessing rejected rows Run 1 rejected orders 5004 and 5005, and the watermark moved past them, so nothing picks them up again. Rejected rows need their own path: group the reject table by reason, have the owner fix the cause (the "abc" amount; whether customer 9999 arrives tomorrow), then re-stage the corrected rows as a new batch and run transform and load again. Idempotence and restarts A safe job can be run twice with no harm. Achieve this with upserts, with "delete the target rows of this batch, then insert them" loads, and with watermarks moved last. Without it, every failed run needs a careful human cleanup, and humans make mistakes at 2 a.m. In my SQL, the fact load used INSERT OR REPLACE keyed on item_id for this reason (other databases: MERGE or delete-then-insert).

x: 3.28 Data quality and reconciliation Concept. Data quality checks are tests on the data itself, run as part of the job, that prove the result is what you expected. Why it matters. The most dangerous failure is a job that "succeeds" and loads the wrong thing. Only checks find logic errors. Quality dimension Question Example check Completeness Is anything missing? Rows read = rows loaded + rows rejected Validity Do values follow the rules? Amounts are numeric and not negative; dates parse Uniqueness Is anything duplicated? One current row per customer; no repeated item_id Consistency Do related values agree? Every fact row has a customer; line amounts add up to order totals Timeliness Is it fresh enough? Latest order date in the target is yesterday or later

x: 3.28.1 Reconciliation queries Reconciliation means comparing counts and totals between two stages to show nothing was lost or invented. These are the queries I ran after run 2 of the ShopSphere job. -- Completeness: orders read = orders loaded + orders rejected SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM feed_orders) AS read_total, (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) FROM fact_order_line) AS loaded_orders, (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) FROM reject_orders) AS rejected_orders; -- Consistency: no fact row without a customer version (expect no rows) SELECT DISTINCT f.customer_id FROM fact_order_line f LEFT JOIN dim_customer d ON d.customer_id = f.customer_id WHERE d.customer_id IS NULL; Expected result from my run: the first query returned 7, 5 and 2 (7 = 5 + 2); the second returned no rows. Keep the checks with the job Write checks once and run them every time, with results stored in a table. Then the question "was last Tuesday's load complete?" has an answer. The Informatica guide shows the same idea at the product level: TDM can be used with the Data Validation Option so that target data can be validated and compared against production to show the transformation process did not introduce errors (User Guide 10.5.10, p.24).

x: 3.29 Performance ideas Performance tuning is its own craft, and the right fix depends on measurement. These are the ideas that help most often, in the order I would try them. Think in sets, not rows. One SQL statement that updates a million rows is much faster than a program that updates them one by one. Many ETL tools give you a row-by-row feeling in their diagrams, but good ones process rows in streams and batches. Use bulk loading for big loads. See 8.8.1 for the documented examples from GenRocket's FAQ. Tune commit size. A commit after every row is slow; a commit after 50 million rows risks a huge rollback. Informatica's default of 10,000 rows is a hint at the ballpark, not a rule. Handle indexes and constraints during the load. Maintaining an index for every inserted row costs time. Some loads drop indexes first and rebuild afterwards. Delphix exposes this as the "Drop Indexes" job option and warns that multiple update threads can cause deadlocks, advising fewer threads if that happens (jobs page). Run in parallel. Independent tables can load at the same time. Delphix jobs have "Number of Streams", described as the number of parallel streams, so several tables are processed at once; some streams finish before others, so the number of active streams falls during the job (jobs page). Informatica allows up to eight concurrent workflows (p.276).

x: 3.32 Hands-on labs You need any SQL database. I used SQLite because it is free and has no setup: install the SQLite command-line tool or use an online SQLite playground, open a new empty in-memory database, and paste each block. If you use another database, adjust the function names as noted in section 3.21. Lab 1: ETL by hand with SQL Goal: run extract-staged data through clean, deduplicate, reject, convert, look up, derive, aggregate and reconcile, and compare your results with mine. The staged data is the ShopSphere batch 1 from section 3.20. Create the staging and target tables. Staging holds the raw text; the targets are empty until the transform runs. CREATE TABLE stg_customers (customer_id TEXT, first_name TEXT, last_name TEXT, email TEXT, zip_code TEXT); INSERT INTO stg_customers VALUES ('1001', ' Asha ', 'MENON', 'Asha.Menon@Example.com ', '560001'), ('1002', 'Ravi', 'Kumar', 'ravi.k@example.com', '600017'), ('1002', 'Ravi', 'Kumar', 'ravi.k@example.com', '600017'), ('1003', 'Meera', 'Nair', NULL, '682001'); CREATE TABLE stg_orders (order_id TEXT, customer_id TEXT, order_date TEXT, total_amount TEXT); INSERT INTO stg_orders VALUES ('5001', '1001', '20/10/2026', '1499.00'), ('5002', '1002', '20/10/2026', '250.50'), ('5003', '1001', '21/10/2026', '75.00'), ('5004', '1003', '21/10/2026', 'abc'), ('5005', '9999', '22/10/2026', '303.00'); CREATE TABLE stg_order_items (item_id TEXT, order_id TEXT, product_code TEXT, quantity TEXT, unit_price TEXT); INSERT INTO stg_order_items VALUES ('1', '5001', 'P-100', '1', '1499.00'), ('2', '5002', 'P-200', '2', '100.00'), ('3', '5002', 'P-300', '1', '50.50'), ('4', '5003', 'P-400', '1', '75.00'), ('5', '5004', 'P-200', '1', '100.00'), ('6', '5005', 'P-300', '6', '50.50'); CREATE TABLE products (product_code TEXT PRIMARY KEY, product_name TEXT, price REAL); INSERT INTO products VALUES ('P-100', 'Laptop Stand', 1499.00), ('P-200', 'USB Cable', 100.00), ('P-300', 'Phone Case', 50.50), ('P-400', 'Desk Lamp', 75.00); CREATE TABLE dim_customer (customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, full_name TEXT, email TEXT, zip_code TEXT); CREATE TABLE reject_orders (order_id TEXT, reason TEXT); CREATE TABLE fact_order_line (item_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_id INTEGER, order_date TEXT, customer_id INTEGER, product_code TEXT, product_name TEXT, quantity INTEGER, line_amount REAL); CREATE TABLE agg_daily_sales (order_date TEXT, orders_count INTEGER, units INTEGER, revenue REAL); No output. Check with SELECT COUNT(*) FROM stg_customers; , which should return 4. Clean, deduplicate and load customers. Trimming and case fixes make equal things equal; ROW_NUMBER() keeps one row for customer 1002. The customer table has three rows: Asha Menon, Ravi Kumar, and Meera Nair with email "not provided". Reject bad orders. Bad rows are parked with a reason, not dropped. Two reject rows: 5004 "total_amount is not a number" and 5005 "customer 9999 not found". Build the fact table. This converts text to dates and numbers, looks up the product name and derives the line amount. Four fact rows (items 1 to 4). Item 2 has line_amount 200.0 (2 times 100.00). Aggregate, then reconcile. The summary shows revenue per day, and the reconciliation proves nothing was lost. Revenue 1749.5 for 2026-10-20 and 75.0 for 2026-10-21. x: 3.33 Common mistakes and gotchas Mistakes beginners make Transforming while extracting. Business logic buried in the source query is invisible and slows the source. Inner joins on lookups. A failed match silently deletes rows. Use left joins with a default, or an explicit reject. Moving the watermark before the load finishes. A failure then loses data forever. Overwriting when history matters. Upsert is right for corrections; a history-keeping load is right when reports must show "as it was". Letting one bad row stop everything, or letting bad rows disappear. Reject with a reason, and set a threshold for when to stop. No reconciliation. A job that "succeeds" with the wrong totals is worse than one that fails loudly. Forgetting that deletes are invisible to a watermark. Plan for them, or accept and document the gap.

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.34 Recap Recap ETL moves data from sources to targets in three steps: extract (read), transform (clean, convert, enrich, combine, summarise) and load (write), usually through a staging area that keeps a raw copy. Extraction can be full or incremental; a watermark or change data capture tells an incremental run what is new. Transformation covers cleaning, type conversion, value mapping, deduplication, lookups, filtering and rejecting, joining, derived columns and aggregation. Lookups and joins must decide what happens when nothing matches. Loads can be truncate and load, append, incremental, upsert, bulk, or history-keeping (slowly changing dimension). A safe load can be run twice without harm. An ETL architecture has sources, an integration engine, a metadata repository, a scheduler, monitoring and logs, and targets. Tools add layers: mappings, sessions, workflows, schedules. A mapplet is Informatica's reusable group of transformations. TDM can import mapplets as masking and generation rules. Good ETL rejects bad rows with reasons, tolerates a set number of errors, reconciles counts, and records every run. ELT loads raw data first and transforms inside the target; test data work usually transforms (masks) before loading. ETL and TDM: how they relate You now know what ETL is ( ETL from scratch ) and what test data management has to achieve ( subsetting , masking and generation ). This section joins the two. The short version: a TDM job is an ETL job whose output is a safe, small, consistent copy of production for testing . Seeing the shared skeleton makes each tool in the next parts easier to understand, because you can ask of every screen: which ETL stage is this? It also tells you what is not the same. A person who treats a TDM job as an ordinary ETL job will load unmasked data, break foreign keys or leave no record of what was done. The differences are where TDM engineers earn their pay.

x: 3.35 Words to know first TDM pipeline The chain of stages that turns production (or a generator) into a usable test data set: find sensitive data, cut it down, mask it, load it, check it. Provisioning Delivering a prepared data set to a test environment so testers can use it. In-place masking Masking that changes the values inside the database you point it at. Delphix describes in-place jobs as updating the source environment with the masked values. On-the-fly masking Masking while copying: unmasked data is read from the source and only masked data is written to the target. This is the ETL order. Deterministic (consistent) masking Masking that turns the same input into the same output every time, so the same customer is masked identically in every table and every run. Driving table The table whose rows decide which rows are copied. Informatica uses the term for the starting point of a subset. Audit trail A record of who ran what, when, and with which settings, kept so that compliance questions can be answered later. Refresh Re-running the pipeline to replace old test data with a new copy. Receiver GenRocket's component that receives generated data and writes it into a usable format at a destination. It plays the role of the load stage. Workflow (Informatica) The runnable job that Test Data Manager generates from a plan.

x: 3.36 The same underlying idea Concept. Both ETL and TDM move data and change it on the way . Both read from a source, apply rules, and write to a target. Both are driven by definitions that tell the engine what to do, both run as repeatable jobs, and both need logs, error handling and connections to databases. Evidence from the products. The strongest proof is in the Informatica guide itself. The PowerCenter repository, it says, stores the workflows and mappings generated from Test Data Manager and "information required to extract, transform, and load data" (User Guide 10.5.10, p.26). The workflows that perform data subset, data masking and data generation are run by the PowerCenter Integration Service (p.27). In other words, Informatica TDM is an ETL engine with a test-data front end. ETL extract, transform, load = TDM job extract a subset, mask, load to test The analogy is useful but incomplete: a photocopier that blacks out names is a good picture of masking, and a photocopier is not an ETL engine. TDM adds purpose-built rules (find the sensitive columns, hide them consistently, keep keys valid) on top of the same moving parts.

x: 3.37 How they differ The seven differences below explain why you cannot take an everyday ETL job and call it a TDM job. Dimension Typical ETL TDM Purpose Make data usable for reporting, integration or migration Make data safe and suitable for testing Direction and shape Many sources converge into a reshaped target (warehouse tables) One source copied to one or many test environments, usually with the same shape Output consistency Consistent with business meaning (totals are right) Relationally intact: every foreign key still matches, even after values are hidden Privacy Protect access to the target; data stays real Sensitive values must not reach the target at all Size As much data as the business needs, often all of it As little as the tests need (a subset), or newly generated Repeatability Scheduled, usually nightly; results are the latest facts On demand or per release; results should be reproducible and resettable Who uses it Data engineers, BI developers TDM engineers, QA engineers, developers, with data stewards and compliance officers as approvers

x: 3.37.1 The differences in more detail Shape. ETL changes shape because the target has a different purpose (a star schema, as in the previous chapter). TDM keeps shape because the application under test expects its own tables. The documents show this: GenRocket's G-Subset can only migrate between databases of the same type, for example MySQL to MySQL (G-Subset overview); Delphix on-the-fly masking supports Oracle to Oracle or delimited file to delimited file, and database to delimited file (jobs page). Consistency. A warehouse can lose the original keys and use surrogate ones. A test database cannot, because the application joins on the real keys. Masking must keep joins working: if customer_id in CUSTOMERS is masked differently from customer_id in ORDERS, the join returns no rows. Delphix's terminology page shows how its algorithms deal with this: a secure lookup algorithm picks replacements by a cryptographic hash of the original value, "so masking output is consistent for each input"; mapping algorithms guarantee no collisions; segment mapping permutes short values with no collisions and is suggested for unique columns such as Social Security Numbers and keys. Delphix masking terminology ↗ Size. Informatica describes a data subset as a "small, targeted, and referentially intact copy" of production for nonproduction use (User Guide 10.5.10, p.112). Small matters because test environments are cheap and many; but small must still be whole , meaning parents and children come together. Section 3.40 shows the integrity options. Repeatability. Informatica lets you use criteria parameters so the same workflow produces different subsets by changing values at run time (p.113). Delphix jobs can be multi-tenant, so the same rule set masks identical schemas through different connectors chosen when the job runs. GenRocket can regenerate the same data with a seed (General FAQ). Success measure. A broken ETL job is noticed when a report is wrong. A broken TDM job may produce a data set that looks fine and leaks a real phone number. Its success has to be proven by checks for leakage as well as for counts, which is why section 3.41 ends with a test step.

x: 3.38.1 Masking really is a transformation Look back at the previous chapter's cleaning transformation: LOWER(TRIM(email)) changes a value row by row, according to a rule. A masking rule such as 'user' || customer_id || '@example.test' does exactly the same. The only difference is the reason: cleaning makes a value better ; masking makes it safe . In the Informatica guide, masking rules that come from mapplets are literally PowerCenter transformation logic imported into TDM (User Guide 10.5.10, p.137). The same is true of generation: a custom generation rule is built from mapplet logic (p.192).

h: 3.38.2 Subsetting really is a filtered extract
x: 3.38.2 Subsetting really is a filtered extract The Informatica guide defines an entity as a driving table plus the tables related to it through constraints. Define a filter, such as EmpID equal to 10, and the workflow loads the Employee row, its history rows and its orders into the target (pp.114 and 121). In SQL that is WHERE on the parent plus joins down to the children. Delphix rule sets offer the same at table level: each table can carry a Filter , "a WHERE clause to filter or subset the data", or a custom SQL SELECT (Managing rule sets). Managing rule sets ↗ GenRocket's G-Subset offers a "Where" clause, a percentage of rows, or a number of rows (G-Subset overview).

x: 3.38.3 Provisioning really is a load Loading rules from the previous chapter apply directly: load parents before children, decide truncate versus append, use commit sizes, handle constraints. Delphix on-the-fly jobs expose a Truncate checkbox, Commit Size , Batch Update and Disable Constraints . Informatica's plan has an update strategy and a commit interval (p.284 to 285). Provisioning adds one thing ETL rarely has: a path back . Informatica's test data warehouse stores versions of data sets and lets you reset a target to any version (pp.236 to 237).

h: 3.39 A reference architecture for a TDM pipeline
x: 3.39 A reference architecture for a TDM pipeline Here is the picture to keep in your head for the tool chapters. Every stage is something you met in the ETL chapter; the two extra boxes at the ends (profile and test) are TDM additions. Production or a generator (read only) 1. Profile find sensitive columns and relationships 2. Extract subset, following foreign keys 3. Mask transform values, keep keys consistent 4. Load write to the test database or files 5. Verify, then test no orphans, no leaks, counts match; then testers use it Boxes 2, 3 and 4 are the ETL core (accent border). Mask before the data reaches the target. Rules repository policies, rule sets, entities Orchestrator plans, jobs, schedule, queue Audit and logs who ran what, row counts Test data store versions, reset, self-service Original diagram: a TDM pipeline built from ETL-style stages. Solid arrows are the data path; dashed boxes are the supporting services.

x: 3.39.1 Stage by stage Profile. Reason: you cannot mask what you have not found. Profiling scans columns for patterns (SSN-like, phone-like) and learns which tables relate. Output: a list of sensitive columns and a relationship map, approved by a data steward. Covered in the Informatica profiling chapter and the Delphix profiling chapter . Extract the subset. Reason: copying everything is slow and expands the exposure. Choose driver rows, then pull in all related rows so the subset is whole. Output: a consistent slice in staging or in a stream, still containing real values. Mask (transform). Reason: this is the stage that removes risk, so it must happen before data lands anywhere testers can read. Output: the same rows with sensitive values replaced consistently. Load. Reason: put the result where tests run, in the right order and within the target's constraints. Output: a populated test database or set of files. Verify, then test. Reason: nobody should trust a TDM job on its exit code. Check keys, counts and, crucially, that no original sensitive value survived. Output: pass or fail evidence, stored with the run. The supporting services mirror ETL architecture: a rules repository (metadata), an orchestrator (scheduler), logs (monitoring), plus a place to keep versions of data sets. Informatica provides the last as the test data warehouse, which stores multiple versions of test data in a central location, shareable across teams (User Guide 10.5.10, p.236). Why the order extract, mask, load matters If you load first and mask afterwards (an ELT-style order), there is a time window in which real personal data sits in the test database, copies may be taken, and a failed masking job leaves the original data behind. Delphix says it plainly for in-place jobs: when a masking job fails, the target "may be in a partially masked or unmasked state" (Job monitoring), and stopping a running job results in semi-masked data (Running and Stopping Jobs). On-the-fly masking avoids the window by never writing unmasked data to the target.

h: 3.40.1 Informatica TDM: a plan that becomes a PowerCenter workflow
x: 3.40.1 Informatica TDM: a plan that becomes a PowerCenter workflow Core idea. You do not draw an ETL mapping. You describe what you want in a plan, and TDM generates the ETL objects for you. A plan defines a data subset, masking or data generation operation and holds the components it needs (User Guide 10.5.10, p.274). When you generate a workflow, "the PowerCenter Repository Service generates mappings for the workflow"; when you start it, the PowerCenter Integration Service does the subset, masking and generation tasks (p.308). The guide lists what the Integration Service creates for masking: mappings, transformations, mapplets, sessions and workflows (p.150). Rules, entities, policies in the TDM repository → Plan specification → Generated workflow mappings and sessions in the PowerCenter repository → Run PowerCenter Integration Service Where each pipeline stage lives, from the pages I read: Extract subset. An entity has a driving table, and TDM adds the tables related to it through constraints; you attach filter parameters to columns. The workflow loads the matching subset into a target database (pp.112 to 114). Three data integrity options decide how whole the subset is: Transactional Integrity for Major Relation Type (a selected child pulls in its parents, the parents pull in all their children, and this repeats until no more related rows are found), Referential Integrity Only (the least rows needed to keep keys valid, so some children of a parent may be missing) and Two-way (criteria propagate down and then up until every table has some data). Recursive evaluation and Two-way need a staging connection (pp.121 to 122). Staging. A plan lets you choose source, target, staging, lookup, storage and dictionary connections (p.276). A staging connection is a database used for staging data, and cyclic tables in an entity require one (p.114). Mask. Masking rules (standard, advanced, or imported from a mapplet) are assigned to columns, data domains and policies. Subset and masking can share a plan: "the subset component gets priority", so TDM subsets first and then masks the subset, and does not mask data outside the subset (p.275). That is the extract-then-transform order of the reference architecture. Load. The target is a database, flat file, or the test data warehouse, which keeps versioned data sets that can be reset to a test system (pp.236 to 238, 275). Plan settings add update strategy (insert, update, or update else insert), commit type and interval, and error and recovery options (pp.284 to 285). A pre workflow and post workflow, and SQL before and after writing to the target, are available (pp.277 to 278). Operate. The Monitor view shows progress, and the Session Details tab shows affected, rejected and written rows (p.275). Up to eight workflows run at once (p.276). Architecture reminder (pp.25 to 27): Test Data Manager is the web front end; the TDM repository stores rules, projects and entities; the PowerCenter Repository Service and Integration Service hold and run the generated workflows. The Informatica architecture chapter covers this in full, and the plans and workflows chapter covers the plan screens.

h: 3.40.2 Delphix Continuous Compliance: connectors, rule sets and masking jobs
x: 3.40.2 Delphix Continuous Compliance: connectors, rule sets and masking jobs Core idea. Delphix's masking engine models the pipeline as four objects you configure once and reuse: a connector (how to reach a source or target), a rule set (which tables or files), an inventory (which columns get which algorithm) and a job (the thing that runs). The terminology page defines masking as iterating through a dataset to find sensitive fields and replace them with desensitised values, and a rule set as a group of tables or flat files on which profile, masking or tokenization jobs run. Delphix masking terminology ↗ Connector source and target access → Rule set tables or files, optional filter → Inventory domain and algorithm per column → Masking job in-place or on-the-fly Extract subset. In a database rule set each table can have a Filter (a WHERE clause) or a custom SQL SELECT, and a logical key that uniquely identifies a row (Managing rule sets). Mask. The inventory lists table or file, column or field, classification and chosen algorithm; an optional setting lets a profiling job update the assignment or lets the user's choice override it (Managing inventories). Managing inventories ↗ Load: the two job methods. This is the clearest ETL parallel in any of the tools. In-place jobs update the source environment with the masked values. On-the-fly jobs read unmasked data from the source and write masked data to the target, and require a source environment and source connector as well as the target. Supported pairs are same-type databases or files, and database to delimited file (Create, view, edit, delete, verify jobs). Create, view, edit, delete, verify jobs ↗ Load options. Commit Size, Update Threads, Batch Update, Truncate (on-the-fly only), Drop Indexes, Disable Triggers, Disable Constraints, a Pre SQL and Post SQL script, Number of Streams for parallel tables, Row Limit, Feedback Size, memory settings and email notification. Multi-tenant jobs choose connectors at run time (same page). Operate. A submitted job is run or queued depending on memory and a limit on simultaneously running jobs (default 7); a stopped running job leaves semi-masked data, and indexes, constraints or triggers that the job dropped are not recreated (Running and Stopping Jobs). Running and Stopping Jobs ↗ Job executions show states such as Queued, Running, Succeeded, Failed and Cancelled (Job monitoring). Provisioning. A masking job can be marked eligible for masked provisioning of virtual databases under a feature called Selective Data Distribution (jobs page); the connectors and VDB chapter covers it.

h: 3.40.3 GenRocket: generators feed receivers; G-Subset is an ETL job
x: 3.40.3 GenRocket: generators feed receivers; G-Subset is an ETL job Core idea. GenRocket's main product creates data, so in the pipeline it replaces the "source". Its five key components give each ETL stage a name: a domain (like a table) with attributes (like columns), a generator that creates values, a receiver that "receives the data from an Attribute's Generator and morphs it into a usable format", and a scenario with the instructions for what to generate and how much. GenRocket Five Key Components ↗ Load = receiver. The Receivers overview describes 120+ receiver types that format and deliver generated data: SQL and NoSQL databases, web services, fixed and delimited files, big data formats such as Parquet and Avro, message formats such as Kafka and MQ, packaged applications, EDI, documents and images, and cloud environments. More than one receiver can be attached to a domain, and data is generated for each in order. Receivers Overview ↗ The FAQ adds that a receiver does not know whether it delivers to a mainframe or a PC; it only knows its format and destination. For large volumes, native bulk load receivers are preferred over JDBC. Pre and post SQL runs through the SQLUpdateReceiver. Where it runs. The Runtime executes scenarios on premises, behind your firewall (General FAQ). General FAQ ↗ This is the ETL engine; the cloud part is where you model and design (Architecture page). Synthetic replacement as a masking transform. "Synthetic Data Replacement" replaces sensitive values with generated ones and is used in G-Subset and file masking. What is SDR? ↗ G-Subset as an ETL job. G-Subset is GenRocket's subsetting and masking feature for databases. Its description reads like our reference architecture. G-Subset Overview ↗ Import the schema. You upload only the source database's metadata, not customer data. This is the "model" step and the source profile. Define subset conditions. A "Where" clause, a percentage of rows or a number of rows, and the sensitive columns to replace. Download the configuration. The files are the instruction set. The actual work runs in your environment. Extract into temporary dump files. Rows to be subset are read from the source tables into temporary files on the machine doing the migration. This is the staging area. In default mode, sensitive columns are never read: the dump file marks them "to be masked" and fills them with synthetic data from an automatically created domain and scenario. Load. The data is inserted into the destination tables, directly via JDBC with bulk files or using SQL insert files, and the temporary files are removed afterwards. Result: a smaller, masked copy in a destination database of the same type as the source. Here the ETL parts are named: extract into staging, transform (replace), load, clean up. Note one design difference from most masking tools: by default the sensitive values are not read at all, which is a privacy advantage over reading and then hiding them. The overview also describes an optional conditional masking feature, disabled by default, that does read the actual values.

h: 3.41 An end-to-end ShopSphere story: profile, subset, mask, load, test
x: 3.41 An end-to-end ShopSphere story: profile, subset, mask, load, test The request. The ShopSphere QA team needs a test copy of "Customer Orders" for a release. They need customers who ordered on 20 October 2026, with all of their orders and items. The compliance officer adds one rule: no real SSN, phone, email, tax id, name, date of birth or exact zip code may reach the test database. You are the TDM engineer. Here is the plan, with every step labelled as ETL-style or TDM-specific. Step What happens ETL-style? TDM-specific part 1. Profile Scan CUSTOMERS columns for SSN-like and phone-like patterns Partly (source profiling) Classifying columns as sensitive; steward approval 2. Subset Choose the customers with an order on 2026-10-20 Yes (filtered extract) Children and parents must travel together 3. Mask Replace names, email, phone, SSN, tax id, birth date and zip Yes (transformation) Deterministic, format-preserving, nothing real left 4. Load Insert customers, then orders, then items into the test tables Yes (load, parents first) Target must be a non-production system 5. Test No orphans, no leaked values, counts match, rerun gives same output Reconciliation is ETL-style The leak check is TDM-specific The SQL below is a hand-made miniature of the pipeline. A tool would do the same work from rules and plans, with logging; the goal here is to see each stage with your own eyes. Mark which statements are extract, transform and load as you go. Lab: run the ShopSphere TDM pipeline by hand Goal: profile, subset, mask, load and verify, and confirm that the test tables contain no original SSN or email. Use an empty SQLite database (or adapt the function names for another database). All data is fake. Create the fake production tables, the staging helper, a name dictionary and empty test tables. Production stays read only for the whole lab; we only ever select from it. -- "Production" (fake data, as in the shared ShopSphere example) CREATE TABLE customers (customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, first_name TEXT, last_name TEXT, email TEXT, phone TEXT, ssn TEXT, date_of_birth TEXT, zip_code TEXT, tax_id TEXT); INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1001, 'Asha', 'Menon', 'asha.menon@example.com', '9876543210', '123-45-6789', '1990-04-12', '560001', 'AAAPM1234C'), (1002, 'Ravi', 'Kumar', 'ravi.k@example.com', '9123456780', '234-56-7890', '1985-11-02', '600017', 'BBBPK5678D'), (1003, 'Meera', 'Nair', 'meera.n@example.com', '9988776655', '345-67-8901', '1999-07-23', '682001', 'CCCPN9012E'); CREATE TABLE orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER REFERENCES customers, order_date TEXT, total_amount REAL); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (5001, 1001, '2026-10-20', 1499.00), (5002, 1002, '2026-10-20', 250.50), (5003, 1001, '2026-10-21', 75.00), (5004, 1003, '2026-10-21', 100.00); CREATE TABLE order_items (item_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_id INTEGER REFERENCES orders, product_code TEXT, quantity INTEGER, unit_price REAL); INSERT INTO order_items VALUES (1, 5001, 'P-100', 1, 1499.00), (2, 5002, 'P-200', 2, 100.00), (3, 5002, 'P-300', 1, 50.50), (4, 5003, 'P-400', 1, 75.00), (5, 5004, 'P-200', 1, 100.00); -- Staging area, test target and a dictionary of fake first names CREATE TABLE subset_keys (customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY); CREATE TABLE mask_names (slot INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, first_name TEXT); INSERT INTO mask_names VALUES (0,'Anil'), (1,'Bina'), (2,'Chitra'), (3,'Dev'); CREATE TABLE t_customers AS SELECT * FROM customers WHERE 0; CREATE TABLE t_orders AS SELECT * FROM orders WHERE 0; CREATE TABLE t_order_items AS SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE 0; No output. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers; returns 3. Profile. Count values that match an SSN pattern and a 10-digit phone pattern. Real profilers do this across all columns and also check column names. Both counts are 3, which tells you these columns are fully populated with sensitive-looking data. Extract the subset keys. The driver is customers with an order on 2026-10-20. The keys go into a small table that later steps join to; that is our staging area. Customers 1001 and 1002. Customer 1003 is not selected, since their only order is on the 21st. Transform and load customers. Each sensitive column gets a rule built from the customer id, so the same input always produces the same output. The name comes from a four-name dictionary chosen by customer_id % 4 . Two masked rows, for example 1001 becomes Bina Tester1001, user1001@example.test, SSN 900-00-1001, zip 560000. Extract and load the children. Orders of the subset customers, then items of those orders. Parents were loaded first. Orders 5001, 5002 and 5003. Customer 1001 brings order 5003 although it is dated the 21st: the subset follows the customer, not the date. Test. Check for orphans, leaks and counts. Orphans 0, leaked SSNs 0, leaked emails 0, and counts 2 customers, 3 orders, 4 items. Repeatability.
