x: 3.42 Pitfalls: where ETL habits hurt TDM

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
h: 3.42.1 Masking after load instead of before
x: 3.42.1 Masking after load instead of before The ETL reflex "land the raw data, then clean it" is wrong for sensitive data. Between the load and the end of masking, real values sit in an environment with wide access, and a failure leaves them there. Prefer on-the-fly or pre-load masking, or in-place masking inside a protected staging environment that testers cannot reach, and copy onward only after verification. Informatica's plan masks data inside the same workflow that loads the target, with subset first (p.275); Delphix on-the-fly jobs never write unmasked rows to the target; GenRocket G-Subset replaces sensitive values in the dump file before insertion.

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.42.2 Consistency across ETL and masking When keys are masked, they must be masked identically wherever they appear. I tested this with the three ShopSphere customers and four orders by adding 70000 to the key. -- Customer keys masked, order keys left alone: the join breaks SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o JOIN (SELECT customer_id + 70000 AS customer_id FROM customers) c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id; -- returns 0 -- The same rule applied to both tables: the join works SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT order_id, customer_id + 70000 AS customer_id FROM orders) o JOIN (SELECT customer_id + 70000 AS customer_id FROM customers) c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id; -- returns 4 Two further consistency risks come from ETL-style staging. First, if the same person appears in two systems (CRM and billing) and each is masked by a separate job with a random rule, the person gets two different fake identities and cross-system tests fail. Use deterministic rules and share the algorithm and its key across jobs. Delphix algorithms differ in this respect: some are non-deterministic and "cannot guarantee the same output for the same input across masking jobs", while others are fixed ( Algorithm syncability ↗ ); the terminology page also notes that a secure lookup can collide, which matters when a column must stay unique. Second, a reversible method such as tokenization (the only algorithm type that allows reversing, per the terminology page) is a deliberate exception, not a default.

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.42.3 Performance Masking adds work to every row, and subsetting adds joins. Plan for it as you would for ETL: choose commit sizes, parallelism and index handling, and expect trade-offs. Delphix's guidance includes number of streams, update threads (reduce them if you see database deadlocks), and the option to drop indexes during a job; Informatica allows up to eight workflows at once. A subset reduces volume, which is usually the biggest performance win, so extract less before you optimise anything else.

ct: Synthetic data, ETL from scratch, and how ETL meets TDM
x: 3.42.4 Audit trails An ordinary ETL log says whether the job ran. A TDM log must also help answer: who masked this, with which rules, and when? What the tools provide, from the pages I read: Informatica: an Audit Trail Report listing recent activities in Test Data Manager (type of activity, object, user, date and time, with filters and CSV download), a Data Masking Report listing columns with their assigned rules and policies, a Plan Audit Report, and a Row Count Report (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.321 to 322, 324). The Monitor view shows job types such as Generate Workflow, Execute Workflow and Reset Data Set from Test Data Warehouse (p.316). Delphix: audit logs record user actions in the UI or REST API: the action, user and time, with action categories such as Create, Edit, Run, Login; the UI page is for admin users and can export a PDF. Audit logs ↗ GenRocket: the pages I read do not describe an audit log for the G-Subset feature, so check your version. Other gotchas Treating the exit code as proof. A job can finish and still have left a column unmasked. Always run the leak check. Masking only some copies of a value. The same SSN in a notes column or a file export remains. Profile every column and every file. Letting a rerun double-load. Use truncate, upsert or a reset path so a rerun does not duplicate rows. Overwriting masked data with a refresh by accident. Name and version data sets, as the test data warehouse does.

x: 3.43 Recap Recap A TDM job is an ETL job with a different purpose: safe, small, consistent test data. Informatica TDM is built on a PowerCenter ETL engine. The seven differences: purpose, direction and shape, output consistency, privacy, size, repeatability, and who uses it. Overlaps: masking is a transformation, subsetting is a filtered extract, provisioning is a load, generation is a source. Reference pipeline: profile, extract subset, mask, load, verify, supported by a rules repository, an orchestrator, logs and a test data store. Mask before data lands where testers can read it. Informatica: plan to generated PowerCenter workflow. Delphix: connector, rule set, inventory, then an in-place or on-the-fly job. GenRocket: generators feed receivers; G-Subset extracts into dump files, replaces sensitive values and loads. Keys must be masked identically everywhere; use deterministic algorithms. Verify leaks as well as counts, and keep audit evidence.

x: Informatica TDM: what it is and how it is built Part I ( the start-here chapter through the ETL and TDM chapter ) explained why test teams need safe, small, realistic data and which techniques produce it. From here on we look at tools. This section opens Part II with Informatica Test Data Management, usually shortened to TDM . Before you click anything in it, you need a mental map: what the product is for, which pieces run behind the web page, where each kind of information is stored, and what order of work the product expects. That map matters because almost every error message and permission problem you meet later is really a "this piece cannot reach that piece" problem. The Informatica discovery and profiling chapter goes deep on discovery and profiling.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.1 Words to know first Test Data Manager (TDM) The web page you work in. The same name is also used for the whole product, which is confusing. In this guide, "Test Data Manager" with spaces means the web client, and "TDM" means the whole product. Policy A named bundle that says "these kinds of data must be protected, and this is how". It holds data domains and holds no actual data. Data domain A group of columns that mean the same thing, for example "all columns that hold a Social Security number", found by looking at column names or at the values. Project The workspace for one job: it holds your imported source tables, profiles, masking assignments, subset definitions and plans. Plan The final recipe: which tables, which rules, from which connection to which connection. You turn a plan into a workflow and run it. Workflow The runnable job that actually copies and changes data. TDM generates it from a plan, and a PowerCenter service runs it. Application service A background program in the Informatica installation that does one job, such as running profiles or running workflows. You never see it on the Test Data Manager screens, but TDM calls it. Repository A relational database where Informatica keeps its own working information (definitions, metadata, results). It is not your business data. Metadata Data about data: table names, column names, data types, keys. Importing "metadata" copies this description, not the rows. Informatica domain The family of Informatica services installed together and managed as one unit, with a shared set of users.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.2 What Informatica TDM is for Start with ShopSphere's problem. The online retailer has a production database, SHOPSPHERE_PROD , with real customers. Testers need data that behaves like it, but real names, phone numbers and SSNs must never reach the test lab. Copying the whole database is slow and risky. Writing test rows by hand is slow and unrealistic. The guide describes TDM as a product that works with PowerCenter, PowerExchange and other Informatica applications to manage nonproduction data (anything that is not the live system: test, development, training) (User Guide 10.5.10, p.21). With it an organisation can make a smaller copy of production data, mask the sensitive parts, find the sensitive columns in the first place, or build test data that never touched production. It can also store test data in a central place and reset it later. The capabilities TDM groups under Test Data Manager (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.21-23), with a ShopSphere example for each Capability What the guide says it does ShopSphere example Data discovery Run profiles to find sensitive columns and key relationships; define data domains to group sensitive columns by pattern. Find that ssn and tax_id in CUSTOMERS hold identity numbers. Data subset Build a small test database, for example by time, function or geography. Copy only customers from the last 6 months with their orders and items. Data masking Apply rules such as substitution, shuffle, key masking and encryption; results can be repeatable; several rules can go on one column. Replace first_name and last_name with believable fake names, always the same fake for the same real person. Data generation Create test data from rules, with no production data involved, in a schema you can test against. Create 5,000 brand-new customers for a load test. Data sets (test data warehouse) Store versions of test data, edit them, and reset a test system to a version. Save "clean masked set v1" and restore it after a destructive test run. Self-service portal A simpler screen for users who only use stored data and do not create it. A tester who only needs to reset data, not design masking. Data coverage analysis Check, across pairs of columns, whether the data set has enough variety for the test cases. Check that there are customers in every zip-code band with orders of every size band. Two more things are worth knowing now. TDM also includes a command-line program, ilmcmd , which can do a subset of the Test Data Manager tasks without the web page (User Guide 10.5.10, p.23). And users have roles and privileges (rules about who may do what) that an administrator manages in the Informatica Administrator, so two people can log in to the same Test Data Manager and see different things. Other items in the guide's overview, which we only name here: exporting flat-file results to an HP ALM test-management server, and masking or moving data on Hadoop clusters (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.22-23). They are real features of the 10.5.10 guide but not part of the ShopSphere path in this book. Why it matters The guide's own motivation (p.21) is blunt: organisations guard production tightly but protect test copies far less. TDM exists to close that gap without making developers rewrite code to create test data. When someone asks you "what does TDM do?", the short honest answer is: find the sensitive data, shrink the data, mask it, or generate it instead, and keep versions of the result .

h: 4.3 Use cases: performance, security, and verified data
x: 4.3 Use cases: performance, security, and verified data The guide groups what TDM is used for into three families (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.23-24). Seeing them as three goals helps you choose the right feature later.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.3.1 Performance in testing environments Here "performance" means the testing team's speed and agility, not database speed. The guide lists these ways TDM helps (p.23): Subsets keep primary and foreign key relations, so the smaller data is still referentially intact (every child row still finds its parent row). Flat file results can be copied straight to an integrated test tool. Generated data serves teams who are not allowed to see production at all. The test data warehouse keeps several versions of test data in one shared place, and teams on different machines that host a Test Data Manager Service in one domain can share it. Data sets can be edited , with row-level tags to track changes, and restored to return a test system to an earlier state. ShopSphere example The Customer Orders team runs a "refund" test that deletes orders. After the run, the test environment is in a strange state. Without TDM, someone re-copies the database (hours). With a stored data set, a tester resets the environment to "masked set v1" from the Data Sets view. This restore idea is the guide's "restore a data set version" use case. The refund story is ours, not the guide's.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.3.2 Security and compliance The guide frames the challenge as finding sensitive information in huge volumes of production data and making sure it does not appear in test data (p.24). Its three suggestions: Run profiles to find sensitive columns, comparing against PII, PCI or PHI regulation standards. (Those three names are explained in the sensitive data and regulations chapter .) Run a data masking operation to remove sensitive values, with standard formats (such as credit card or Social Security numbers) or custom formats. Store results in the test data warehouse so fewer uncontrolled copies exist.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
h: 4.3.3 Verified test data with Data Validation Option
x: 4.3.3 Verified test data with Data Validation Option Data Validation Option (DVO) is a separate Informatica solution used with PowerCenter to check that target data is accurate and that the transformation did not introduce errors (p.24). Used with TDM, it can compare production and development data. The guide's example is a team that must send compliance reports for test data made from production, and needs "verifiable proof" that the test data holds no sensitive values. The documentation excerpt I used mentions DVO only at this level. It does not describe how DVO is configured, so this book does not either. If your project uses it, ask your trainer or read the DVO guide. Goal: performance "Give testers the right data quickly, and let them get it back." Features: subset, flat-file copy to test tool, data generation, test data warehouse, restore. Goal: security and compliance "Prove sensitive data is not in the test lab." Features: profiles with PII, PCI, PHI domains, masking, a single controlled warehouse, DVO for proof.

Tool What it is What you use it for in TDM Test Data Manager Web-based client Configure masking, subset, generation and discovery profiles; configure connections; manage project permissions; manage data sets. Informatica Developer Client application ("thick client", installed on a computer) Create and export profiles for data discovery, and run them. Informatica Administrator Web-based client for a domain administrator Manage application services; create users and user groups. PowerCenter Client Client application Manage the repository and design mappings, mapplets and sessions; set permissions on folders and on connection objects of the PowerCenter repository. A mapplet is a small reusable piece of transformation logic built in PowerCenter. In TDM you can create a data masking rule from a mapplet that has been imported (p.31). Later chapters return to this.

x: 4.4.2 The TDM Server One sentence in the guide: the TDM Server is the interface between Test Data Manager and the application services (p.27). Elsewhere the guide says "the TDM Server sends a request to the Data Integration Service" when you run a profile, and that the Test Data Manager Service "creates and manages the TDM repository" (pp.27-29). The guide does not say in one place how the "Server" and the "Service" relate. In the figure on p.25 only the Test Data Manager Service appears. I treat them as the same hub, and you should read "TDM Server" as "the part that takes your click and calls the right service". That is my reading, so check it with your administrator.

Here is the list with the plain-English job of each. Service Its job (from the guide) When you notice it Test Data Manager Service Creates and manages the TDM repository; runs Test Data Manager and manages connections between service components and users (pp.26, 28). Every login and every click. Data Integration Service Performs data discovery; stores profile metadata through the Model Repository Service; loads results to the profiling warehouse you chose when creating it; also runs data coverage tasks for the test data warehouse (p.27). When a profile runs. Model Repository Service Manages the Model repository for data discovery (p.27). Behind profiles; also when you import metadata or data domains from the Model repository. monitoring Model Repository Service A Model Repository service that monitors statistics for Data Integration Service jobs (p.27). Rarely, as an administrator. PowerCenter Repository Service Manages the PowerCenter repository and accepts requests from the PowerCenter Integration Service when a workflow runs (p.27). Generating a workflow; importing metadata from PowerCenter. PowerCenter Integration Service Runs the data subset, generation and masking workflows. Test Data Warehouse Service Manages the test data warehouse repository and the warehouse; copies the metadata created with a data set and creates the data set tables (p.27). x: 4.4.4 The TDM databases (repositories) These are the "recipe books and pantries". The guide lists seven relational databases that TDM connects to for metadata, profiling, TDM configuration, domain configuration and the test data warehouse (User Guide 10.5.10, p.28). Notice that only one of them holds a copy of test data ; the rest hold Informatica's own working information. Database What it stores ShopSphere reading TDM repository The components you define in Test Data Manager (policies, projects, entities, rules) plus source or target metadata you imported (pp.26, 28). The masking policy, the "Customer Orders" project, the imported structure of CUSTOMERS and ORDERS . Model repository Table metadata for data discovery profiles; connection information for connections made in TDM; optionally mappings saved for Hadoop operations (p.28). The profile's view of the tables. PowerCenter repository Metadata for PowerCenter sources and targets and for the workflows generated from plans; also permissions and privileges for its users (pp.26, 28). The generated masking workflow. Profiling warehouse Profile results for data discovery (p.28). " ssn looks like an SSN domain" lives here until you approve it. Domain configuration repository Connections and metadata for the Informatica domain, including users (pp.26, 28). Who can log in. Test data warehouse repository Project and source table metadata for stored data sets (p.28). The description of the stored "masked set v1". Test data warehouse The source data of stored data sets (p.28). The masked customer rows themselves. Do not confuse these with SHOPSPHERE_PROD Your business database (the source SHOPSPHERE_PROD and any test target) is not on the list above. TDM needs a connection to it, but it is not one of TDM's own repositories. Beginners often mix this up and look for "their data" inside the TDM repository. The guide says that importing copies source metadata into the TDM repository (p.31), and that constraints you add in a project are stored in the TDM repository while the TDM server does not update the data sources (p.32).

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.4.5 TDM connections TDM needs connections to databases, repositories and services, and what it needs depends on what you run (User Guide 10.5.10, p.28): Discovery needs a database source connection and a Data Integration Service. Subset and masking workflows need connections to services, the TDM repository, external database sources, and Informatica sources and targets. Workflows that store data in the test data warehouse need external database sources, the test data warehouse repository and the test data warehouse itself. To copy flat file results to a test tool, you first integrate the test tool server with TDM. The guide splits them into service, repository and database connections. The table below keeps its meaning and shortens the words. Connection kind Examples and purpose (pp.29-30) Service connections Data Integration Service (discovery); Model Repository Service; PowerCenter Integration Service (running generated workflows; you pick its name when you generate the workflow); PowerCenter Repository Service (extracts source metadata from the PowerCenter repository on import); Analyst Service; Test Data Warehouse Service; Test Data Manager Service. Repository connections TDM repository (a masking, generation or subset workflow needs it); Model repository; profiling warehouse (the Data Integration Service loads profile results there); PowerCenter repository; test data warehouse repository and test data warehouse. Database connections A database source for discovery, a database target for generation, relational sources and targets for subset and masking, and a source plus the test data warehouse for storing data sets. You configure them in the Administrator view of Test Data Manager and do not need a separate driver. You pick them when creating a plan; TDM tests them when it generates the workflow, and the Integration Service uses them when it runs it.

h: 4.4.6 A readiness checklist before your first job
x: 4.4.6 A readiness checklist before your first job Putting the connection rules together gives a practical checklist. Most items belong to an administrator, but as a TDM engineer you should know to ask for them. Each item is drawn from the guide pages cited; the order is mine. A user in the Informatica domain with the right roles and privileges. Users and groups are created in the Informatica Administrator, and roles and privileges decide which views you can open (pp.23, 27). A connection to the source database. Needed for discovery, and for subset and masking sources. Created in the Administrator view of Test Data Manager, with no extra driver to install (pp.28-30). Connections to the Data Integration Service and Model Repository Service. Needed before any profile can run (p.92). A PowerCenter Integration Service chosen for workflows. Selected when the Test Data Manager Service is created, and again each time you generate a workflow from a plan (pp.27, 29). A target connection to a test schema. For masking, subset and generation plans. Never the production database (p.31). The test data warehouse and its repository, if you will store data sets. Needed for plans that target the warehouse (p.28). Folder and connection permissions in the PowerCenter repository. Configured with the PowerCenter Client (p.27). What you should be able to say afterwards: for each job I plan to run, which service runs it and which connections it needs.

h: 4.4.7 Following a click through the pieces
x: 4.4.7 Following a click through the pieces The guide describes three journeys in words. Putting them side by side shows how the pieces cooperate (pp.29-32). 1. Run a profile Test Data Manager → TDM Server asks the Data Integration Service to extract source data → Model Repository Service loads table metadata into the Model repository → Profiling warehouse receives the results 2. Import metadata from a database → TDM Server extracts table metadata → TDM repository holds it 2b. Import from PowerCenter → TDM Server asks the PowerCenter Repository Service → TDM repository receives a copy of the metadata 3. Run a plan's workflow → PowerCenter Integration Service runs it using the chosen connections → Target database receives masked or generated data The practical lesson (my reasoning from the three journeys, not a quote): a failed profile points at the Data Integration Service, its connection, or the profiling warehouse. A failed workflow points at the PowerCenter Integration Service or the connections you picked in the plan. A missing table in a project usually means the metadata import did not finish or was rejected.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
h: 4.5 The TDM process, end to end
x: 4.5 The TDM process, end to end The guide gives a ten-step outline: run a profile against source data, create a subset, mask it (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.30-31). Steps 1 to 3 prepare, steps 4 to 8 define, steps 9 and 10 run. Not every project does every step. Step 3 is explicitly optional, and data generation is a separate path from subset and masking. Create policies. Decide which types of data to mask and which rules to use. Create a project and import data sources. Bring the table descriptions into TDM. Optional: discover information about the source data. Profiles find primary keys, entities and data domains. Optional: create parameters. Global parameters for use across Test Data Manager, or project parameters (criteria, connection and owner) so one plan can make different test data on demand. Define subset and masking operations. Choose tables and relationships for the subset; assign masking rules to columns. Define data generation operations. Choose tables and assign generation rules to target columns. If needed, enter test-tool (HP ALM) integration properties in the plan. To copy flat file results to the integrated test tool server. If needed, choose the test data warehouse as the target in the plan. To store the result as a data set. Generate and run the workflow for masking, subset or generation. The PowerCenter Integration Service does the work. Monitor the workflow. Check status and logs. Policy who and what to protect → Project import metadata → Discover profiles (optional) → Define subset, mask, or generate → Plan connections and options → Run and monitor workflow Notice the split of roles in this order. The policy is design work (the guide's example gives it to a compliance officer). Everything from the project onward is build work (a project developer). Reviewing profile results and validating the output goes back to compliance. Keep that hand-off in mind for the example in the example section .

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.5.1 Create a data masking policy A policy contains data domains that describe what you want to mask. It has no data source, so one policy can serve many projects (p.31). A data domain groups sensitive fields by column name or by the data inside, using patterns written as regular expressions (a compact way to describe text shapes; the guided tour of Test Data Manager has a short primer). A domain also holds masking rules. A rule is a built-in masking technique plus specific settings; rules can also be built from imported mapplets. ShopSphere: a policy named for customer personal data, with domains for SSN, email, phone, first name and last name. (the policy name and domain list are ours).

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
h: 4.5.2 Create a project and import metadata
x: 4.5.2 Create a project and import metadata A project organises everything for discovery, masking, subset and generation. You import metadata for the sources you want to subset or mask, and target metadata if you want to generate data. You can import from a PowerCenter folder, from the Model repository, or from an external database. You also create a target schema, and the guide warns that TDM overwrites any data that already exists in the target schema (p.31). Target schema warning Point your plan at a schema made for test data. "TDM overwrites data that already exists in the target schema" is the guide's own wording (p.31). Never aim a target connection at SHOPSPHERE_PROD .

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.5.3 Discover source information Profiles can discover three things (pp.31-32): Primary keys , when a source has none. A primary key profile suggests candidates. Entities (related tables), when the project has several sources. An entity profile suggests possible relationships between tables. You select entities from the results to shape the subset. Data domains . A data domain profile searches columns that fit each domain, so you can mask all of them with the same rules. Running a profile makes the TDM Server ask the Data Integration Service to extract source data, and the results go to the profiling warehouse. Constraints you add are stored in the TDM repository. The TDM server does not update the data sources (p.32). All of this is the subject of the Informatica discovery and profiling chapter .

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
h: 4.5.4 Define data masking and data subset operations
x: 4.5.4 Define data masking and data subset operations For subset , you define which tables to include and how they relate (p.32). Three building blocks appear: Block Meaning in the guide ShopSphere reading Entity A set of tables related by physical or logical constraints. CUSTOMERS with its ORDERS and ORDER_ITEMS . Group A set of unrelated tables. PRODUCTS , copied whole as reference data (our design choice). Template Optional container holding entities and groups. "Customer Orders subset kit". You also assign masking rules to source columns, create a subset plan from entities, groups and templates (with optional filters on parent-table columns), and create a masking plan that carries the policies and rules. Rules outside policies are allowed too. TDM stores projects, entities, groups, templates and plans in the TDM repository (p.32). The Informatica data subset chapter and 14 teach these in detail.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.5.5 Define a data generation operation Three tasks (p.32): create the entities for the plan, create generation rules and assign them to target-table columns, then create a generation plan with entities and tables, assigning default generation rules to columns that have none. The Informatica data generation chapter covers it.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.5.6 Create plans A plan holds what a workflow needs. Two rules matter for planning (pp.32-33): A masking operation and a subset operation can share one plan or have separate plans. A data generation operation cannot be combined with masking or subset in the same plan. It needs its own plan. In either plan you can choose the test data warehouse as a target connection to save the result as a data set, and you can enter test tool integration properties to copy flat file results to an integrated HP ALM server. A generation plan also asks for the number of records. Then you generate the workflow and run it. The Informatica plans, workflows and warehouse chapter covers plans and the warehouse.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.5.7 Monitor the workflow Each workflow appears as a job in the Monitor view, together with jobs such as metadata imports and profiling (p.33). You can run the Row Count Report on a successfully run workflow to see how many rows the plan affected, and open the TDM job log to troubleshoot. In ShopSphere terms: after the masking run, the compliance officer checks that the row counts in the test target match the intended subset, and the QA lead opens the job log if the workflow failed.

h: 4.6 The guide's TDM example, retold with ShopSphere
x: 4.6 The guide's TDM example, retold with ShopSphere The guide's example (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.33-34) is about an organisation that wants to mask sensitive employee stock data for a new employee stock plan. Its test database needs data from several applications: personal data, salary, stock purchases and job information. Several teams must share it and be able to put the original test data back. The company builds a policy and keeps the result in the test data warehouse. The table maps each of the guide's 13 steps onto ShopSphere. The first column is the guide. The second column is our retelling, and it is illustrative (the guide never mentions ShopSphere). The guide's 13 steps and a ShopSphere version # Guide (employee stock) Who ShopSphere version (illustrative) 1 Create an Employee_Stock policy. Compliance officer Create a customer-data policy listing what must be masked. 2 Define data domains; columns named like Employee_Salary, Yearly_Salary, Salary_History share a "Salary" domain. Compliance officer An "SSN" domain for ssn , tax_id ; a "Phone" domain for phone . 3 Define masking rules: substitution from a dictionary for names, random masking for salary, Social Security masking for SSNs. Compliance officer Substitution for names, Social Security masking for ssn . 4 Define a project; import sources. Project developer Project "Customer Orders"; import the four ShopSphere tables. 5 Run a data discovery profile; it fills the data domains. Project developer Run a data domain profile; email , phone , ssn appear against their domains. 6 The database has no primary or foreign keys, so run a profile for primary keys and entities; create logical keys. Project developer Suppose the test copy of the metadata lacks declared keys; profile them and add customer_id as a logical primary key. 7 Create entities and a group (Employee, JobHistory, Salary, Employee_Stock as an entity; Stock_History in a group). Project developer Entity: CUSTOMERS , ORDERS , ORDER_ITEMS . Group: PRODUCTS . 8 Approve or reject profile results. Compliance officer Approve ssn to SSN domain; reject any wrong match. 9 Verify all sensitive fields are masked, using reports. Compliance officer Check that every personal-data column has a rule. 10 One plan for subset and masking; add entities, groups and the policy; run the workflow. Project developer A plan that copies a masked subset into a test schema. 11 Validate results in the subset database. Compliance officer Spot-check masked names and SSNs in the test schema. 12 Plan with the subset database as source and the test data warehouse as target; run to create a data set. Project developer Store the masked subset as "masked set v1". 13 Reset a data set from the test data warehouse to a required connection. Project developer Restore "masked set v1" into a QA schema after a refund test. What the example teaches Two things. First, the order : design (policy, domains, rules) before build (project, profile, entities, plan) before run (workflow, data set). Second, the hand-offs : the same person does not do everything. The people who understand the regulations choose and approve; the people who understand the tables build. In a real engagement ( the chapter on planning real engagements ) the same split shows up as roles on your team.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.7 Advanced parameterization at a glance Here is a problem you will meet within a week of working on a real project. ShopSphere's QA team needs test data for sprint 14 regression (orders from this month, in schema QA1 ), then for performance tests (orders from last year, in schema PERF , on a different server). Making a new plan for each request is slow. Editing one plan every time is error-prone. The guide's answer is parameters : placeholders in the plan that point to a value, and the value is read when the workflow runs (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.35, 51). You change the value and run the same plan again to get different test data.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.7.1 Three kinds of parameter Type Placeholder for ShopSphere use Connection Source or target connections "QA database" today, "PERF database" tomorrow. Owner Source or target schema owner names QA1 versus PERF . Criteria Values in filter criteria of an entity The order_date cut-off used to choose which orders to copy. You can create parameters inside a project , or an administrator can create global parameters usable across Test Data Manager. Global parameters are marked with an asterisk (*) in parameter lists. If you import a global parameter into a project, you get a copy: changes you make to the copy do not touch the global parameter (p.35). One rule to remember now You must import source metadata from every source connection you might need into the project. A workflow whose parameter value points at metadata the project does not contain cannot run (p.35).

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.7.2 The sequence in the guide The guide lists 16 tasks. Grouped into five phases they read like this (pp.35-36): Prepare the project. Create a project and import the required source metadata. Create connection, owner and criteria parameters in it with default values, and choose whether the default may be overridden. Optionally import global parameters. Use parameters in the entity. Create an entity with the required tables and add filter criteria that use parameters. You can add several criteria; they can be project or global parameters. Use parameters in the plan. Create a plan using parameters. On the Plan Settings page, add the source and target connection types as variables and choose the connection parameters. You must enter a parameter file name and the path to that file on the machine that hosts the PowerCenter Integration Service. In Advanced Settings, add schema owners as variables and select the owner parameters. Save the plan. Optional: use a parameter file. From the plan's Properties tab, Actions > Create Parameter File downloads a file listing every parameter in the plan. You may edit values, and set the "ignore" flags of criteria parameters to "Y" to leave them out of a run. Run. From the plan Properties page, Actions > Generate and Execute, then pick how values are supplied. Choose Default (the file entered in Plan Settings), Use Parameter File (a different file), or Add Parameter Values (edit values in Test Data Manager, and use the Select Parameter button to include criteria parameters). Click Generate and Execute and monitor the workflow. What you should see: the same plan, different data each time you change values. The guide's two examples: change owner and criteria values to get data in the same connection but a different schema, or change connection parameters and include different criteria to get data between different connections (p.36). ShopSphere example Plan "Customer Orders masked subset" uses an owner parameter for the target schema and a criteria parameter for the order date. Sprint run: owner value QA1 , criteria "this month". Performance run: owner value PERF , criteria "last year". One plan, two results. The names and values are ours; the mechanism is the guide's. Details such as parameter naming prefixes, rules, and editing steps are in the guided tour of Test Data Manager . Using parameters inside plans is covered again in the Informatica plans, workflows and warehouse chapter . Lab: trace three ShopSphere problems to the right piece Goal: practise using the architecture map. This is a paper exercise, no software needed. The failures are invented by us; the pieces and their jobs come from the guide (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.25-30). Problem A. A data domain profile on CUSTOMERS finishes, but no results appear in Test Data Manager. Which service ran it, and where should the results be stored? Problem B. A masking plan generates a workflow successfully, but the run fails to start. Which service runs workflows, and which connections did you choose in the plan? Problem C. A tester cannot see the "Customer Orders" project in the list. Which kind of setting decides this, and where does an administrator manage users and roles? Show a worked answer A. The Data Integration Service performs discovery and loads profile results to the profiling warehouse. Check that service and the profiling warehouse connection. The guide also says to close and reopen a profile to see its results (p.103), so try that first. B. The PowerCenter Integration Service runs the generated workflows (p.27). In the plan you selected source and target connections, and TDM tests them at generation (p.30). Check that service and those connections. C. Project permissions. If a user has no permission on a project it does not appear in the list (p.68). Roles and privileges are managed in the Informatica Administrator (p.23). The guided tour of Test Data Manager explains the Read, Write and Execute levels.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.8 Common mistakes and gotchas Watch out Looking for business data in the TDM repository. The repositories hold definitions, metadata, results and stored data sets. Your source and target databases are separate and need their own connections. Treating "the TDM Server", "Test Data Manager" and "TDM" as three products. They are the web client, the go-between, and the product name respectively. When a document is ambiguous, ask which piece is meant. Planning generation and masking in one plan. The guide says a generation operation needs its own plan (p.33). Forgetting the overwrite. TDM overwrites existing data in the target schema (p.31). Use a dedicated test schema. Skipping discovery on a database with no declared keys. The guide's example had none, so profiles created the logical keys the subset needed (p.34). Importing only one connection's metadata, then parameterizing the connection. The workflow cannot run (p.35). Assuming every feature in the guide exists in your installation. Licences, privileges and version differ. Confirm in your version.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.9 Recap Key points Informatica TDM finds sensitive data, makes smaller copies, masks, generates data, and stores versions of test data (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.21-22). Use cases fall into performance, security and compliance, and verified data with DVO. Four tools (Test Data Manager, Developer, Administrator, PowerCenter Client), a TDM Server, about ten application services, and seven databases make up the architecture. Your business databases need connections ; they are not TDM's repositories. The process is: policy, project and import, optional discovery, define, plan, generate and run, monitor. Generation needs its own plan; masking and subset can share one. Parameters (connection, owner, criteria) let one plan produce different test data. A guided tour of Test Data Manager The Informatica overview and architecture chapter gave you the map. This section tours the part you touch: the Test Data Manager web page, then the three areas where beginners spend their first week, namely projects (your workspace), data sources (the tables you bring in) and policies (what to protect, and how). The aim is to know where things live, why each task exists and what you should see afterwards. The discovery and profiling chapter then uses all of it. What this section is based on The Informatica Test Data Management 10.5.10 User Guide, PDF, February 2026, 455 pages : chapter 2 "Test Data Manager" (pp.37-48), chapter 3 "Projects" (pp.49-70) and chapter 4 "Policies" (pp.71-85), read in full, with the figures on pp.38, 41, 43, 45, 47 and 49 viewed. The guide's screenshots have no image address, so I use visual reference boxes and one schematic sketch I drew. Menu names are quoted from the guide; if your version differs, trust your screen. What you will learn How to log in, what each view does, and the helpers on every screen (search, filter, Actions menu, Expression Builder). What a project holds, and how to create, copy, export and import one, set permissions and import source tables. What policies, rules and data domains are, how patterns find columns, and how to create and manage each.

x: 4.10 Words to know first View One of the main screens of Test Data Manager, chosen from the tab bar at the top (for example Policies or Projects). Content panel and Details panel The two areas of most screens. The Content panel lists items (rows). The Details panel shows more about the row you selected. Actions menu A menu that changes with the view. Almost every task in this section starts with "click Actions". Data source (in a project) A set of source tables whose descriptions (metadata) you imported into the project. Not a copy of the rows. Data domain A named group of columns that mean the same kind of thing, such as "Social Security Number", recognised by column name or by value shape. Regular expression A short text code that describes a shape of text. [0-9]{3}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{4} describes "three digits, a dash, two digits, a dash, four digits". Data pattern and metadata pattern Two kinds of regular expression on a data domain. A data pattern describes what the values look like. A metadata pattern describes what the column name looks like. Sensitivity level A label you give a data domain to say how sensitive it is. An administrator defines which levels exist. Policy pack A ready-made policy installed with TDM, covering PII, PHI or PCI data. Impacted Objects dialog A warning window that lists what will break when you delete or change something that is already used.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.11 Who uses which view The guide ties each view to a typical person (User Guide 10.5.10, p.37). A compliance officer uses Policies to create policies, rules and data domains. A developer uses Projects to import sources, run profiles, define subset, masking and generation, and generate and run workflows, and uses Monitor to check job status. A test data specialist or test engineer uses Data Sets for the test data warehouse. An administrator uses Administrator for connections, pass phrases, workflow options and server management. By default an administrator can open the Administrator view; other users need privileges for the other views (p.39).

h: 4.12 Logging in to Test Data Manager
x: 4.12 Logging in to Test Data Manager You use a normal web browser and the user name and password defined in Informatica Administrator (User Guide 10.5.10, p.48). Open the address https://hostname:portnumber/tdm/ (or http:// if Transport Layer Security is off). hostname is the machine with the TDM Server. The guide's default port is 6643 with TLS and 6605 without. The Login dialog box appears. Enter your user name and password and choose the security domain, then click Login. If the domain uses LDAP, the default security domain is Native. Test Data Manager opens. Click Logout to leave.

Most screens have a Content panel (a list of rows) and a Details panel (more about the selected row). Visual reference Informatica TDM 10.5.10 User Guide, p.38, Figure "Test Data Manager" (the Policies view). What to look for: the tab bar, a list of policies above, and Properties and Data Domains tabs below with a pie chart the guide describes as showing unmasked data, a compliance risk. h: 4.14.1 Search, filters, Quick Links and preferences
x: 4.14.1 Search, filters, Quick Links and preferences Search field. Finds projects, plans, assignments, data sets and data set tables in the TDM and test data warehouse repositories. It cannot find connections. Results include the object plus what it contains and what contains it (p.39). Advanced text filter. In column filters (Discover > Columns, Define > Data Masking, Define > Data Generation, profile results) type "FIRST_NAME" in quotes for an exact match, ORDER* for starts with, *_ID for ends with, or plain PHONE for contains (p.39). x: 4.15 The Overview view Overview is a read-only "management view" of summary dashboards (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.41-42). The main ones: Project Risk Analysis (percentage of columns at each domain sensitivity level and the percentage in no domain), Project Assignments and Project Objects (counts for the last 10 projects), Recent Activities (the last 10 changes, with an Audit Trail report you can download), Plan Execution (plans in progress or completed on a date), Global Components (share of policies, rules and domains) and Recent Projects (the last 10 projects you modified). A sensitive-data distribution graph appears only if sensitivity levels are set. Visual reference Informatica TDM 10.5.10 User Guide, p.41, Figure "Overview view". What to look for: a plan-execution timeline, a Global Components pie chart and a Recent Projects table.

h: 4.16 Data Sets, Monitor, Parameters and Administrator
x: 4.16 Data Sets, Monitor, Parameters and Administrator The Policies and Projects views get their own sections below. The others, briefly (pp.43-46): Data Sets lists stored data sets. A version has Overview, Tables and Components tabs, and the Actions menu can reset a version to a target, delete or lock it (the plans, workflows and warehouse chapter covers this). Monitor lists jobs with ID, name, status, project, times and user. Select a job and use Actions. Parameters holds global parameters, usable directly in a plan or added to a project first. Administrator covers default settings, sensitivity levels, connections, dictionaries, application logs and log levels, test tool integration and pass phrases.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.17 The Expression Builder An expression is a small formula, like a spreadsheet formula. The Expression Builder lists functions by category and columns, so you can build one without memorising names (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.46-47). You open it with the Expression button when you create an Expression-type masking rule, add pre- or post-processing to a rule, create advanced masking rules, assign rules to a column, configure an ad hoc generation rule or set advanced expressions in plans. A Validate Expression button checks your formula. Visual reference Informatica TDM 10.5.10 User Guide, p.47, Figure "Expression Builder". What to look for: function categories on the left, an Expression box and a Join Condition box, and OK, Cancel and Validate Expression buttons. Example from the guide, with ShopSphere names An advanced masking rule has two variable ports holding the masked first and last names. The output port joins them with a space: CONCAT( CONCAT( VAR1, ' ' ), VAR2 ) VAR1 would hold a masked first_name and VAR2 a masked last_name , giving a full name such as "Priya Das". The expression is the guide's; the names are ours. Function syntax is in the Informatica Transformation Language Reference, which I did not read.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.18 Projects A project is the top-level container for everything you do to one set of data: discovery, masking, subset and generation (User Guide 10.5.10, p.49). Think of a project as a folder on your desk for one job, "Customer Orders for QA". Inside it you keep the table descriptions, your profile results, which rule goes on which column, the subset recipe, and the plans. The analogy has one flaw: in TDM the project folder is also a real folder in the PowerCenter repository with the same name as the project, which is how workflow information lands in the right place (p.60).

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
h: 4.18.1 The six views inside a project
x: 4.18.1 The six views inside a project Open a project and you see a second row of tabs (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.49-50). Project view What you do there Overview Edit properties; add policies and rules; import data sources (from PowerCenter, the Model repository or a database; you can mix source types); create project parameters. Discover Find primary keys, table relationships and data domains (the discovery and profiling chapter ). Define Assign masking rules and policies to columns; define entities, groups and templates for subset; assign generation rules. Execute Define a subset, masking or generation plan; generate and run a PowerCenter workflow. Monitor Status of import, profiling, workflow and data jobs; refresh, abort, stop or recover them. Permissions Set who can do what in the project (see the permissions section ). Visual reference Informatica TDM 10.5.10 User Guide, p.49, Figure "a project in Test Data Manager". What to look for: the project tab bar, a General block of project facts and a Data Sources list at the bottom.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.18.2 Project components A project has at least one data source. The other components depend on the work (pp.50-51): Entity : a set of related tables (subset, generation). Group : a set of unrelated tables copied to the subset (subset). Both are made in Define. Parameters : values for connections, criteria and schema owners. Plan : defines the operations; a PowerCenter workflow is generated from it. Made in Execute. Policy assignments : assigning a policy gives the project its data domains and masking rules. Rule assignments : which rule applies to which column. Profile : suggests keys, relationships and data domains. Made in Discover.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.18.3 Parameters in a project The Informatica overview chapter explained why parameters exist. Details (pp.51-52, 57-58): the tool adds the name prefix for you: connection parameters begin $DBConnection , owner parameters $Param , criteria parameters $$ . With a connection parameter on an Oracle source, you cannot enable the Oracle Rowid property. Connection parameters rule out batch updates for in-place masking , because that needs a staging connection and a staging connection cannot be a parameter. If a plan uses one connection parameter as both source and target, Update Strategy does not change to Update. Tick Use Source Connection as Target Connection, or set it by hand. Open the project, click Parameters, then Add. A project parameter is usable only in this project. Enter a name and choose the type (criteria, connection or owner) and a data type (String, Numeric or Date). For Date, enter an expression such as TO_DATE($$CRIT1,'MM-DD-YYYY') so a function knows how to use it. Enter a default value and choose whether to allow override, then click OK. If you do not allow override, nobody can change the value when running the workflow, so a default is then required. The parameter appears in the project's list. To edit, click the row (not the checkbox), change values and Save; the parameter and data types cannot change. To delete, tick the box and click Delete; you see the entities and plans that use it and must regenerate and run them again. To import a global parameter, click Add Global Parameter; changes to the copy do not affect the global one (pp.57-58). Global parameters export to CSV from the Parameters view (Actions > Export).

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.18.4 Project logs PowerCenter writes workflow and session logs when you run a plan from a project. Unless you set locations, it uses defaults from the PowerCenter Integration Service: $PMWorkflowLogDir\ , $PMSessionLogDir\ and $PMBadFileDir\ (reject files hold rows that could not be written) (p.52). You can set them in the Edit Project dialog but not when creating the project: open the project, Actions > Edit, Default Log File tab, fill in the three directories with a trailing slash, Save (p.59). The directory must already exist. A wrong workflow log directory makes the workflow fail without an error log.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.18.5 Data masking transformation session properties You can tune run-time properties of the masking session (pp.52-53). The guide ties better performance to a bigger Cache Size (the dictionary cache in memory; default 8 MB, at least 32 MB recommended for 100,000 records) and a bigger Storage Commit Interval (rows committed per batch to the storage table; default 100,000). Other properties: DMO Cache Directory (default $PMCacheDir , needs write permission), SSN High Group File (path to the Social Security Administration high-group list) and Shared Storage Table (default disabled; share it only when two masking instances or ports use the same dictionary column, connection, seed and locale). The Informatica masking chapter explains the techniques.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.19 Managing projects When you create a project you become its owner and have access to its folder by default. You can edit its name, description, folder location and associated sources, and the place where its logs are stored (User Guide 10.5.10, p.53). You can also export a project, with its components, to an XML file and import it elsewhere. People do this to back a project up or to move it from a development system to a production system.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.19.1 Creating a project Task: create the "Customer Orders" project Goal: make an empty workspace for the ShopSphere work. The steps and field list are from the guide (pp.53-54). The project name and values we choose are illustrative. Click Projects. The Projects view lists existing projects. Always check here first that a project for this job does not already exist. A list of projects appears. Click Actions > New. This opens the Create Project dialog. Fill in the properties. Use the table below. For ShopSphere: Name CustomerOrders (no spaces, which the guide requires if you will use Hadoop sources), a short description, keep the default Folder (the project name), and keep the default Target Conflict Resolution Strategy (Rename) unless your team says otherwise. Click OK. The project opens in a new page. Show the property table Option Meaning in the guide Name The project name. Must not contain spaces if you plan TDM operations on Hadoop data sources. Description The project description. PowerCenter Repository The PowerCenter repository that stores the project folder. Folder The project folder in the repository. Default is the project name; you can choose another. Owner The user who owns the folder, with all permissions on it. Default is the creator; you can pick another user. Target Conflict Resolution Strategy What to do about duplicate target table definitions made when you regenerate a plan: Rename (rename and create another definition), Replace (overwrite the definition and use it in the mapping), Reuse (reuse the existing definition; a workflow fails if the target table metadata changed). Default Rename. Target Empty Value Optional. A value to use in place of empty values in target non-null columns. A workflow fails if that non-null column is also a unique column.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.19.2 Editing a project Click Projects and click the project name. It opens in its own tab, with properties and data sources. Click Edit, change options, click Save. You can change name, description, folder, owner, target conflict resolution strategy and target empty value (the PowerCenter Repository field is not in the edit list). You cannot remove a source that entities or groups in the project use. (pp.54-55)

x: 4.19.3 Project default property configuration An administrator with the Manage Preferences privilege can add default fields to every new project, on Administrator > Preferences > Project Configuration (p.55). Two examples from the guide: Enable Old Dictionary Optimization (True keeps the pre-10.5 substitution-masking optimisation so output stays the same; False or unset uses the new algorithm, pp.55-56) and Target Empty Value (a replacement for empty strings that would break a non-null target column, for example when resetting an Oracle-based data set to SQL Server; the workflow still fails if that column is unique, p.56).

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.19.4 Copying and deleting a project Copy: in Projects click a project description to select it without opening it, then Actions > Duplicate, rename, Save. The copy does not import the metadata or objects (p.56), so it starts as an empty shell. Delete: select it the same way, Actions > Delete, Yes. All sources associated with the project are deleted (p.57).

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.19.5 Exporting and importing a project An exported project is an XML file containing source information, connections, constraints, data domains and assignments (p.59). Export: Projects, click a project, Actions > Export, choose the XML file name and path, OK. Import: Projects, Actions > Import, browse for the XML file, click Finish. Before importing, import all the global components that the project assigns (policies, domains and rules; see the policies section ). Otherwise the project refers to objects the target repository does not have (p.59). Test Data Manager imports the project.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.20 Data sources A project cannot do anything until it knows what tables it is working on. To do subset, masking or discovery, you import source metadata into the TDM repository. To generate data, you import target metadata instead (User Guide 10.5.10, p.60). A project can hold more than one type of source, for example a flat file and a relational database, and you can create constraints that relate them and add filter criteria for subset and masking. A numeric precision limit If a numeric column has a precision above 28, you cannot apply a masking or subset condition to it. The Integration Service passes that row and column to the target without applying the condition (p.60). Check unusual numeric columns before you trust a run.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.20.1 TDM source definitions You can import source metadata from PowerCenter, from the Model repository, or directly from the source database (p.60). The guide's points: The TDM project and the repository folders share the same name, so workflow information goes to the correct folder. If the source is relational and has many tables , importing straight from the database is faster than going through PowerCenter or the Model repository. Importing from the PowerCenter or Model repository brings in the definitions Informatica services support, by importing the repository folder that holds them; TDM makes a copy of that folder in the TDM repository. MongoDB sources imported into PowerCenter need unique column names of at most 80 characters. Flat files must come from the PowerCenter or Model repository; you cannot create flat file connections in Test Data Manager. rowid is a reserved keyword. You cannot import Oracle sources that use it as a column or table name.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.20.2 Importing data sources Task: import the ShopSphere tables into the project Goal: have the four tables visible in the project's Data Sources view. The steps are the guide's (pp.66-67). The choice of "Datasource Connection" and of the schema is our illustration; it assumes an administrator already created a connection to the ShopSphere database. Click Projects, then click your project to open it. Imports belong to a project, so the tables arrive in the right workspace. Click Actions > Import Metadata. The Import Metadata window appears. Choose the source type. Options: PowerCenter Repository , Model Repository , or Datasource Connection . For a plain relational database, Datasource Connection is the direct route. To import metadata from a flat file or a JDBC connection, you must use the Model repository. Decide whether to review metadata changes before the import. If you choose to review, TDM shows the metadata and its impact on rules and domain assignments, or entities and groups. You can skip this option. Reviewing is wise when re-importing into a project that already has assignments. Click Next and choose where to import from. For PowerCenter or the Model repository, pick the folder (filter by name or description). For Datasource Connection, pick the schema (filter by name). Click Next. Select the tables or files to import and click Next. You can filter by data source, table name or description. For a Hive database, do not select temporary "junk" tables created when mappings run. Choose when to import and click Finish. Import Now (tick Run import in the background if you want to keep working) or Schedule Later (pick a date and time). The Import Progress dialog box shows a progress bar. If you chose to review, the Impact Review dialog box appears with metadata, assignments and project objects; click Approve to import or Reject to cancel. Afterwards the tables are in the Data Sources details view. Show what ShopSphere should look like afterwards Illustrative, not from the guide: four tables in the project's data source, CUSTOMERS , ORDERS , ORDER_ITEMS and PRODUCTS , all under the schema you picked. A job for the import is listed in the project's Monitor view while it runs. If a table is missing, check the table selection step and the Monitor view for a failed import job.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
h: 4.20.3 Special source types in the guide
x: 4.20.3 Special source types in the guide The guide spends several pages on source types that a ShopSphere beginner will not meet on day one. Know that they exist and what the headline rules are. Source type Headline facts (pp.60-66) Hive and HDFS You can do data movement, data domain discovery and masking. A cluster configuration must exist in the Administrator tool. Use a Hadoop plan . You cannot do subset or generation on Hive and HDFS. Do not select temporary junk tables. Data domain discovery works, but primary key and entity profiles do not run on Hive. Before in-place masking on Hive, back up the source tables, because a failed move from staging can truncate them. Avro and Parquet Semi-structured formats for single-level hierarchy files, usable when you choose an HDFS target. With Parquet you cannot use null or repeated constraints. You cannot run profiles on Avro and Parquet. XSD (XML) sources Subset, masking and generation work on XML. Import the XSD source definition from the PowerCenter repository; importing the XML itself makes the workflow fail. View files under Discover > Files. On a file page, the Properties, View and Details tabs let you assign data domains, mark elements Restricted or Sensitive, and assign masking rules, generation rules or subset criteria. You cannot delete XML files after import. PowerExchange nonrelational Adabas, IMS unload, Sequential, and hierarchical and nonhierarchical VSAM. Define datamaps in PowerExchange, import into PowerCenter, then import into the project. You cannot import a PowerExchange source directly into the TDM repository.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.20.4 Identity columns An identity column is one the database fills in automatically with a counter. Three rules from the guide (p.67): On Sybase , you cannot move data from a source DBO schema to a target non-DBO schema if the data has an identity column and indexes. If auto identity is enabled in Sybase and a table has no primary or unique keys, Sybase adds a SYB_IDENTITY_COL column. Mark it Restricted (restricted means the Integration Service does not write the value to the target), or the workflow fails. To disable an identity column on Microsoft SQL Server , the database user needs execute permission on sp_help .

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.20.5 Deleting a table You can remove a table from a project if you added too many or no longer need some (pp.67-68). Rules: an orphan table (related to no other table and with no assignments) deletes directly. If the table is part of profile results, a warning appears and it is removed from them too. If it is part of an entity, group, masking plan or generation plan, the Impacted Objects dialog lists what will be affected; a table in a template that is part of a plan does not list the template and plan. You delete one table at a time. Open the project and click Discover > Tables. Select the table and click Actions > Delete Table. A confirmation message appears if the table has no assignments; otherwise the Impacted Objects dialog appears. Click Continue to confirm. Delete only tables not used in a TDM operation. Regenerate and run affected plans afterwards.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.21 Project permissions and security When you create a project you become its owner and can add users and user groups with permission levels. The domain administrator can also add and edit project permissions (User Guide 10.5.10, p.68). A project you have no permission on does not appear in your list, and you cannot open it even from search results. There are three levels, and they sit on top of privileges: you need the permission on this project and the minimum privilege for the task (p.50). Permission levels and tasks (p.69) Permission What you can do Minimum privileges (as listed) Read Open and view the project; monitor logs for project workflows. View project, Monitor project, Audit project Write Everything in Read, plus import metadata, delete tables, create entities, groups and templates, assign rules, generate workflows, run profiles, copy the project, delete the project. View, Monitor, Audit, Import metadata, Generate project, Manage project, Discover project Execute Open and view the project; monitor logs; run workflows. View, Monitor, Audit, Execute project Notice that "run workflows" is separate from "generate workflows". That lets a team give a QA engineer Execute to re-run a prepared plan without letting them change it. Write does not list Execute in the guide's table; if a developer must both build and run, grant both. Open the project and click Permissions. Lists of users and user groups with their permissions appear (Users and User Groups tabs). Click Edit on the Users or User Groups tab. The Edit Project Permissions dialog opens. Change, delete or add. To change, select the user or group and edit the permission; save for each user or group. To delete, select and click Delete. To add, click Add Users or Add User Groups, select one or more, optionally pick the permission to give all selected, then OK; if you did not pick, select each one and set permissions, saving each. Click OK. Changes take effect from the user's next login .

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.22 Policies A policy is a data masking component that describes how to protect specific types of source data (User Guide 10.5.10, p.71). It is built from three smaller things that you can create separately, in any order: Rule one masking (or generation) technique with specific settings → Data domain a group of columns that mean the same thing, plus its preferred rules → Policy a set of data domains → Project you assign the policy to a data source The ShopSphere reading: a rule is "replace first names from a dictionary of fake names". A domain is "First Name", the group of every column that holds first names. The policy is the compliance officer's list of domains that must be masked in any customer-data project. Once the policy exists, the Customer Orders project simply receives it and every first-name column gets the first-name rule. You can apply one policy to many projects (p.71). Policies task flow (p.72): create masking rules, define data domains that describe which columns can receive the same rules, assign the rules to the domains, create a policy, assign the domains to the policy. The order is flexible; you can create a policy first and fill it later.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.22.1 Rules A rule defines logic to mask sensitive data or to generate test data (p.72). You can create rules for string, numeric and date data types. You can add rules to data domains and then use the domains in policies and plans. After you add rules to a project, you still assign them to columns, matching the column's data type. The built-in masking techniques (substitution, shuffle, key masking and so on) are the subject of the Informatica masking chapter ; generation rules are in the Informatica data generation chapter .

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.22.2 Data domains A data domain represents the functional meaning of a column, based on its data or its name. Assign a masking rule to the domain and all columns in that domain are masked with the same rule . You can also give it generation rules so generated data follows the same logic (p.73). The guide says to assign at least one masking rule to each domain. The guide's Social Security example: the number might be in a column called SSN , in a column called SOCIAL_SECURITY in another table, or buried in a COMMENTS column. One domain describes all three: a data expression for the format 999-99-9999 and metadata expressions for the likely column names such as SSN or Social (p.73). If you do not have Data Discovery, you can still use domains to group data, but you must associate columns with domains manually (p.73). With discovery, a profile does the assignment for you ( the discovery and profiling chapter ). Preferred rules and the default rule Rules you attach to a domain are called preferred rules . If there are several, you mark one as the default , which applies to every column in the domain. You may change an individual column to another preferred rule, and you can even apply more than one rule to a column (p.73). Guide example, with a ShopSphere twist The guide's Last_Name domain has a shuffle rule as default and a substitution rule as another preferred rule: shuffle for customer last names in one table, substitution in another (p.73). In ShopSphere: last_name in CUSTOMERS uses the default, while a hypothetical shipping_contact_last_name in another table uses the second preferred rule. Generation rules work the same way: in the guide, Date_of_Birth defaults to date random generation and also offers date sequence generation (p.74). The ShopSphere column is ours.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.22.3 Data patterns and metadata patterns A regular expression (regex) is a text string that describes a search pattern; it matches strings of characters in the source data (p.74). TDM uses regexes in two ways, and a domain may hold several of each. A column belongs to the domain if any expression matches (pp.74-75). Data pattern (look at values) Describes what the data looks like. SSN example from the guide: [0-9]{3}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{4} . Use when you do not trust column names (an SSN hidden in a COMMENTS column). Metadata pattern (look at column names) Describes the column name. Guide example: .*Name* matches Name, Employee_Name and Organization_Name; .*SSN* , .*SOCIAL* , .*SECURITY* find SSN columns. Use when names are reliable and values vary. A regex primer, using only what the guide lists Regexes are case sensitive . The guide lists these building blocks (pp.74-75), and gives a tutorial site for more. I added the ShopSphere reading. Piece Guide's meaning Reading Ordinary characters All except [\^$.|?*+() match themselves; abc matches abc. ssn matches the letters s, s, n in order (and not SSN, because of case). \ Escapes a special character so it loses its special meaning. \. means a real dot. * Matches the previous token zero or more times. .*SSN* style names. [ ] One character from a set; a hyphen gives a range, such as [a-zA-Z0-9] . [0-9] is one digit. ? Makes the previous item optional. -? an optional dash. {n} Repeats the previous item n times (n is 1 or more). [0-9]{4} is four digits. Case and shape traps Because regexes are case sensitive, a pattern in capitals may not match a lower-case column name such as ssn . Whether TDM treats metadata expressions case-insensitively is not stated in the part of the guide I read, so test it on your own data. And a 10-digit phone pattern also matches any other 10-digit column. This is why you review profile results rather than approving everything blindly.

x: 4.22.4 Data domain options A data domain has four options (p.75): Name ; Sensitivity level , applied to every column in the domain and chosen from the levels the administrator defines (the Overview dashboards use it); Description ; and Status , enabled or disabled, where an enabled domain is included in discovery profiles (default enabled).

x: 4.22.5 Creating a data domain Task: create a "Customer SSN" data domain Goal: a domain that finds SSN-like data and SSN-like column names in ShopSphere. Steps are from the guide (p.76); the name, pattern and rule choice are our illustration. Assume a Social Security masking rule already exists (see the Informatica masking chapter ). Click Policies. The Policies view lists policies, data domains and rules in the TDM repository. Click Actions > New > Data Domain. This starts the domain wizard. Enter the name, sensitivity level and description, then click Next. For example Name Customer_SSN , a high sensitivity level (your administrator's list decides what exists), description "US-style SSN in customer data". On the data pattern page, optionally enter a regular expression; click the + icon to add more. Enter [0-9]{3}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{4} . This finds the SSN even when the column name is odd. Click Next for the column-name page (or Finish to stop here), then enter name expressions. Enter .*SSN* and .*SOCIAL* . You can add several. Click Next to add preferred rules, or Finish to stop. To add rules, click Add Rules, select masking and generation rules in the Add Rules dialog, click OK. Enable one default masking rule and one default generation rule, then click Finish. The new data domain appears in the Policies view. Show a worked answer Result (illustrative): domain Customer_SSN , status Enabled, one data pattern, two metadata patterns, one preferred masking rule marked default. When you later run a data domain profile on CUSTOMERS , ssn should appear as a candidate for this domain, with both the column name and values matching. tax_id may or may not match depending on its format, which is the kind of question you review in the discovery and profiling chapter .
