h: 4.22.7 Policy packs: PII, PHI and PCI
x: 4.22.7 Policy packs: PII, PHI and PCI You do not have to start from an empty Policies view. TDM includes three ready-made policy packs : PII, PHI and PCI. After installation they are visible in the Policies view, with the data and metadata patterns of their domains, so you can read the actual regular expressions (User Guide 10.5.10, p.77). To view and work with policies you need the Test Data Manager Service View Policies and Manage Policies privileges, and without View Policies you cannot see policies at all. The three names are explained in the sensitive data and regulations chapter : PII is personally identifiable information, PHI is protected health information, PCI is payment card information. Policy packs and their data domains with default rules (pp.78-80) Pack Industry focus (guide) Data domains (each has a default rule of a matching name) PII Personal information Age; Birth Date; Birth Place; Country; Credit Card; Drivers License Number; Email Address; First Name; Full Address UPPER; Full Name; Gender; Grades; IP Address; Job Position; Last Name; Organization Name; Passport; Phone; Salary; School Name; Social Security Number; State; Street Name; UK National Identifier; Vehicle Registration Number; ZIP PHI Healthcare and pharmaceutical Account Number; Birth Date; Certificate License Number; Device Identifier Serial Number; Email Address; First Name; Health Plan Beneficiary Number; IP Address; Last Name; Medical Record Number; Phone; Primary Account Number; Social Security Number; State; Unique Identifier; Web URL; ZIP PCI Banking and finance Account Number; Birth Date; Credit Card; Expiration Date; First Name; Last Name Look at how this fits ShopSphere. The PII pack already has First Name, Last Name, Email Address, Phone, Social Security Number, Birth Date and ZIP, which cover almost every personal column in CUSTOMERS ( first_name , last_name , email , phone , ssn , date_of_birth , zip_code ). Nothing in the packs obviously covers tax_id : that is a case where you would add your own domain or assign one manually. The guide's pack tables do not list a "tax ID" domain.

x: 4.22.8 Importing and exporting policy components You can export policies, domains and rules to XML files and import them into another TDM repository (pp.80-81). The details matter: Exporting a policy exports references to its domains. Exporting domains exports references to rules. Neither exports the referenced objects unless you choose to export them as well. Policies, domains and rules go into separate XML files , each with a default name and a date number such as Policy_121112141309.xml or Domain_121112141309.xml . You can rename them. If a rule or policy in the target TDM already has assignments , you cannot import the file. Clear the assignment or change the name in the file first. If the object already exists, import overwrites it. Export: in the Policies view tick the objects, click Actions > Export, then Open or Save. Test Data Manager prompts once for each type of file. Import: in the Policies view click Actions > Import, browse for the XML file, click Finish. Importing data domains from the Model repository Data domains created in the Informatica Developer tool live in the Model repository. Import them before you import a data domain profile (pp.81-82). Click Policies, then Actions > Import Data Domains. A window lists data domains in the Model repository. Select the domains, set a sensitivity level for each in the Sensitivity Level column, click Save, then Import. If a same-name domain exists, you can overwrite or cancel. What comes across: name, description and links to business terms . What does not : data patterns, metadata patterns and preferred rules. So an imported domain is a shell that you finish in Test Data Manager. If you overwrite, TDM updates the description and linked terms but keeps the patterns and rules you set in TDM. Linked business terms are merged, and a term deleted in Developer is kept in TDM until you delete it by hand (p.81).

A business term has a business definition and examples of use, stored centrally so people can look things up. Link a term to a TDM object and you can see the object from the term in the Analyst tool. You need an Analyst Service configured in the Test Data Manager Service properties, as the Informatica architecture chapter listed. A copy contains the rules and domains of the original, and a policy can be exported to XML and imported elsewhere (p.83). Task: create the ShopSphere customer-data policy Goal: one policy holding the domains your project will mask. Steps are from the guide (p.83); the policy and domain choices are ours. In the Policies view, click Actions > New > Policy. The New Policy dialog box appears. Enter a name and optional description, click Next. For example ShopSphere_Customer_PII , "Personal data in customer tables". A clear name matters because projects choose policies by name. Click Add Data Domains and select domains from the list. For Copy and Delete, select the row by clicking its Description or Created On column and do not open it (pp.56-57). Expecting a project copy to contain the tables. x: 4.24 Recap Key points Test Data Manager has seven views: Overview, Policies, Data Sets, Projects, Monitor, Parameters and Administrator, with search, quick links, preferences, an Actions menu, a data filter and an Expression Builder on top. You log in with an Informatica domain user at http(s)://host:port/tdm/ ; the guide's defaults are ports 6643 (TLS) and 6605. A project holds data sources, entities, groups, parameters, plans, policy and rule assignments and profiles, and has six views including Permissions. Import metadata with Actions > Import Metadata from PowerCenter, the Model repository or a database; importing does not copy rows. Permissions are Read, Write and Execute, and each task also needs a minimum privilege. A policy is a set of data domains; a domain finds columns by data patterns and metadata patterns (regular expressions) and carries preferred masking and generation rules, one marked default. Informatica: discovering and profiling your data Before you can protect data you have to know where it is. ShopSphere's CUSTOMERS table has nine columns, so it is easy to see that ssn is sensitive. A real production database has hundreds of tables, and a Social Security number can hide in a column called NOTES . Data discovery is Informatica's name for the automatic search that finds sensitive columns and table relationships. This section covers the discovery and profiling material of the guide: the profile types, how to run them, how to review and approve results, primary keys and logical relationships, and three labs matching the syllabus items TDM_Handson1, 2 and 3. It builds on the discovery and subsetting concepts chapter , the data basics chapter (for keys) and the guided tour of Test Data Manager . What this section is based on The Informatica Test Data Management 10.5.10 User Guide, PDF, February 2026, 455 pages , chapter 5 "Data Discovery" (PDF pages 86 to 111), read in full, with supporting facts from chapters 1, 3 and 4; the figures on pp.88 and 103 to 106 were viewed. Figures have no image address, so I use visual reference boxes. All ShopSphere numbers and results are illustrative. The syllabus gives only the titles of the three hands-on items, so the labs are my reconstruction, with guide steps cited by page. What you will learn The four profile types: primary key, entity (foreign key), data domain and column. What a primary key is and how to discover, review and approve keys. How data domain discovery finds sensitive columns and how to curate its results. Constraints, major and minor severity, and cascades. Three labs: profiling, profiling plus masking, profiling plus subset.

x: 4.25 Words to know first Profile A saved search definition: which tables, which kind of analysis, which sampling limits. You can run it again later. Profiling Reading the data (or the column names) to describe it: which columns are unique, which look like SSNs, how many are empty. Primary key (PK) A column, or combination of columns, whose values uniquely identify each row. No empty values, no duplicates. Like a library card number. Foreign key (FK) A column in a child table that holds the primary key value of a parent row, such as ORDERS.customer_id pointing to CUSTOMERS.customer_id . Referential integrity The rule that every foreign key value has a matching parent row. Without it you get orphan orders. Logical key or constraint A key relationship defined only inside TDM, not in the real database. The guide stresses that TDM does not update the source tables. Entity A set of related parent and child tables, used to define a subset. Uniqueness percentage The share of values in a column that are unique. 100 means no duplicates. Conformance The percentage of rows that fit a rule or pattern. A threshold lets a few rows disagree. Curation (review) Looking at suggested profile results and approving or rejecting each one.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.26 What data discovery is for The guide's overview (User Guide 10.5.10, p.86): you run profiles to discover source data for masking and subset . Before masking, you discover which columns to mask with the same rule. Before building a subset, you discover relationships between tables and the entities that shape the subset database. You can then apply the results instead of configuring entities by hand or applying a masking rule one column at a time. Why it matters Discovery turns "someone remembers which columns are sensitive" into a repeatable, reviewable record. A compliance officer can see which columns were found, with what confidence, and who approved them. It also supplies the keys that subsetting needs when the database does not declare them.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.26.1 The profile types The guide names four types on p.86-87. In the screens you will see three of them listed as the options when you create a profile (primary key, entity, data domain) plus column. Note a naming wrinkle: the overview calls the relationship profile "Foreign key", while the creation steps and result screens call it an entity profile. They describe the same relationship discovery. Profile Question it answers What you get Used for Primary key Which column (or combination) could uniquely identify rows? Candidate keys with a uniqueness percentage. You approve those you want, and TDM adds them to the table in the TDM repository, not to the source database. Subset, relationships Foreign key / entity Which tables are related, and which could be entities? Possible entities and logical constraints; you select entities and approve constraints. TDM stores logical constraints in its repository and does not apply them to source tables. Subset with referential integrity Data domain Which columns hold data of a given kind (SSN, phone, name)? Column-to-domain suggestions based on column values or names. Masking, sensitive-data inventory Column What do the values in this column look like (range, patterns, lists)? Inferred rules (range, pattern, list of values) you can reuse to generate data. Data generation You can run data domain and primary key profiles at the same time, and you can import and run profiles you built in Informatica Developer (p.87). Source tables imported into project → Profile PK, entity, domain or column → Results candidates with percentages → You review approve or reject → Applied keys, constraints, domain assignments

x: 4.26.2 Which sources can be profiled Profiles run on relational sources : Oracle, Microsoft SQL Server, IBM DB2 for Linux, UNIX and Windows, MySQL, Sybase and Teradata (ODBC for MySQL, Sybase and Teradata). Data domain profiles also run on Hive and HDFS (User Guide 10.5.10, p.87). Rules (pp.87-88, 94): You cannot profile nonrelational sources, but you can profile in PowerCenter or Informatica Data Quality, export the results and import them into TDM. Imported mapplet-based results must use simple regular expressions (no labeler, tokenizer, content set or reference tables). A table must use the same connection in the profile as when imported, or results may be unexpected. One profile cannot hold two tables with the same name ; make a profile per table. No primary key or entity profiles on Hive, and no profiles on Avro or Parquet.

x: 4.27.1 Column properties Discover > Columns shows Table Name, Column, Owner (the schema), Data Type, Domain , and three flags (p.89): Restricted : the Integration Service does not write the value to a target. Computed : the value is calculated from other columns, for example Net_Pay = Basic_Salary + Allowances - Tax_Deduction . You cannot assign masking or generation rules or cascades to it, and TDM does not copy data into it because the database recomputes it (p.90). Sensitive : a label for people only; it does not affect processing. Assigning a data domain marks the column sensitive automatically. A Similar Value Columns count shows how many columns share a value cascade with this one.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.27.2 Value cascades and auto cascades Both make sure the same original value becomes the same masked value in several places. That is the difference between a customer whose id looks right everywhere and one whose id no longer matches across tables. Auto cascade (keys exist) Masks a parent table's primary key and the related foreign keys in child tables with the same value. Applied by default to tables with key constraints; you can enable or disable it. It needs key constraints between parent and child. Not available for XSD, MongoDB and Cassandra sources (p.91). ShopSphere: mask CUSTOMERS.customer_id and ORDERS.customer_id receives the same masked value. Value cascade (no keys) Masks similar columns in different tables the same way when they are not linked by key constraints. You group similar columns and mark one as the driving column ; a rule assigned to it goes to all the others. The columns must have the same type (p.90). ShopSphere: an email column in CUSTOMERS and a contact_email column in some marketing table. The guide's example: employee_num in one table and EmpID in another are similar value columns, with employee_num driving. Assign a rule to it and EmpID receives the same rule (p.90). The driving column shows a number in Similar Value Columns; the others show none. Create: in Discover > Columns select the columns, click Actions > Set as similar value columns, and click the driving-column checkbox to change No to Yes for one column (p.90). Change: select the driving column (it has a number), open the Similar Value Columns view in the Details panel, click Edit Similar Value Columns. Set Driving Column to Yes on another column (the previous one switches to No), use Add to add columns or Delete to remove them (p.91). Delete the group: select the driving column, open Similar Value Columns, select any column in the group, click Delete, confirm (p.91).

h: 4.29 Primary keys: the basics, then discovery
x: 4.29 Primary keys: the basics, then discovery The syllabus calls out primary key basics and "data integrity maintained in primary and foreign key columns" (Days 43 and 51). Nearly every later task, subset above all, depends on keys, so spend time here.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
h: 4.29.1 Primary and foreign keys in plain words
x: 4.29.1 Primary and foreign keys in plain words A library gives each member a card number. No two members share one, and no member is without one. That number is a primary key : a column (or combination of columns) that uniquely identifies each row. The guide's rule for keys you add by hand: a primary key column cannot contain null (empty) or duplicate values, and a table has only one primary key constraint (User Guide 10.5.10, p.109). When a library loan record stores the member's card number, that stored number is a foreign key : it points at a row in another table. In ShopSphere: CUSTOMERS (customer_id PK) 1 ----< ORDERS (order_id PK, customer_id FK) ORDERS (order_id PK) 1 ----< ORDER_ITEMS (item_id PK, order_id FK) PRODUCTS (product_code PK) (ORDER_ITEMS.product_code refers to it) Data integrity means these links stay true: every ORDERS.customer_id exists in CUSTOMERS , every ORDER_ITEMS.order_id exists in ORDERS . Test data that breaks this is useless. A subset that copies an order but not its customer produces an orphan. Masking that changes CUSTOMERS.customer_id but not ORDERS.customer_id breaks the link. TDM relies on keys to avoid both: subset follows constraints "to create subset data with referential integrity" (p.86), and auto cascades mask parent and child keys together (p.91). Why discovery of keys matters Real source systems often have no declared keys, for performance or legacy reasons. In the guide's own example (pp.33-34), the database "does not contain primary and foreign keys", so the project developer runs profiles to find them and then creates logical keys. If ShopSphere's imported tables came with no declared keys, you would have to do the same.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.29.2 Primary key discovery To discover possible keys, create a primary key profile (p.92). It also helps find data quality problems: a profile that finds non-unique rows where you expected unique ones shows duplicates. It is useful when the key is a combination of columns that together identify a row. After discovery you can add keys to the source table in the project. The guide's example: an Employee table has an EmpID column that is 100% unique, so the profile identifies it as a possible primary key to add to the project table (p.92). ShopSphere equivalent: CUSTOMERS.customer_id . Primary key profile options The Data Integration Service infers candidates and you can limit them (pp.92-93). Option (guide label) Meaning Default Primary Key Rows Maximum number of columns the profile may combine to form a primary key. (The label says "rows", but the description says columns.) 3 Max Rows Maximum number of rows to profile. 1,000 Conformance Criteria Minimum percentage, or maximum number, of key violations allowed. Minimum percentage 99 Creating and running a primary key profile Open the project, click Discover, then click Profile. You are in the profile list of this project. Click Actions > New Profile. The New Profile dialog box opens. Enter a name and description and choose to create a primary key profile. For ShopSphere: pk_shopsphere . A clear name makes it findable later. Click Next, select the tables to profile, click OK, then Next. Include every table you want keys for. On the Sampling Options page, enter the maximum number of columns in the key, the maximum rows to profile, and the minimum conformance (or the maximum number of rows that may violate). Fewer columns in the key means a faster, simpler search. Click Finish, then Actions > Execute. The run is a job you can follow in Monitor (p.92). After it completes, close and reopen the profile to see results. Reading primary key results Click the Profile > Primary Key view. Each row is a candidate (pp.103-104). Visual reference Informatica TDM 10.5.10 User Guide, p.103, Figure "sample primary key profile results". What to look for: a table of candidates with columns for table, column, relationship type (Primary Key), uniqueness percentage, verified status (NOT_VERIFIED), existing constraints, and status (for example Approved), with a Properties pane below for the selected row. Field Meaning Table Name The table holding the candidate. Column Name The column or combination inferred to be a primary or unique key. Relationship The column's role: primary key. Uniqueness Percentage of unique values. 100 means all unique. Use it to decide. Verified Whether the candidate has been verified as not containing another constraint (for tracking). Existing constraints Any primary or foreign key constraint already on the column. Status Whether a user verified, approved or rejected the candidate. Illustrative primary key results for ShopSphere (invented numbers, shaped like the guide's fields) Table Column Uniqueness Existing constraints My decision CUSTOMERS customer_id 100 none Approve. It is the identifier and ORDERS points to it. CUSTOMERS email 100 none Reject as key. Unique today, but a customer can change email, and it is sensitive. CUSTOMERS ssn 100 none Reject as key. Sensitive; it will be masked, so it is a poor link. CUSTOMERS phone 99.6 none Reject. Not fully unique and not an identifier. ORDERS order_id 100 none Approve. ORDER_ITEMS item_id 100 none Approve. PRODUCTS product_code 100 none Approve. Unique is not the same as a key A profile only tests uniqueness within the sample. email and ssn may score 100 on a small sample and still be unsuitable keys. Pick the column that is the business identifier and is what child tables refer to. That judgement comes from you, not the tool. (My reasoning, not a guide quote; the guide's decision aid is the uniqueness percentage plus your own knowledge of the data.) Applying the primary key results Select a row and choose Verify, Approve or Reject from the Actions menu (p.104). Approve: TDM adds the primary key to the table in the TDM repository. Reject: does not affect the subset operation. Verified column: only for tracking your review; it does not affect subset operations. Expected result: approved keys appear on the table in Discover > Tables, under Constraints as primary key constraints. The source database is unchanged. (The location under Constraints follows from the constraint steps on pp.109-110 and the statement that TDM does not add keys to the source tables, p.87.) You can skip discovery and add keys by hand. The guide says when you manually add keys, you do not need a primary key discovery profile, and you define constraints for subset, masking and generation without updating the source database (p.109). The step list is in the manual keys section below.

x: 4.30 Entity (foreign key) discovery An entity is a parent table plus its related child tables. An entity profile finds possible entities by comparing column names in the source tables, and returns a list you choose from. The entities you define for a subset determine the structure and content of the subset database (User Guide 10.5.10, p.93). The guide's example: Employee, Employee_Detail and Employee_Address all contain an EmpID column, so the profile suggests Employee as an entity with two direct relationships and two child tables. You select Employee as the entity. Later, a subset filter on EmpID (for example EmpID less than 2000) filters each table in the entity relationship (p.93). ShopSphere reading (illustrative): customer_id appears in CUSTOMERS and ORDERS ; order_id appears in ORDERS and ORDER_ITEMS ; product_code appears in ORDER_ITEMS and PRODUCTS . The profile can therefore suggest CUSTOMERS to ORDERS to ORDER_ITEMS as a chain, and ORDER_ITEMS to PRODUCTS as another link. Needs keys, or run both together If you choose the Entity type and the physical database has no primary keys , the profile returns no results . If you run it as a primary key and entity profile, it discovers possible primary and foreign keys and returns results even without physical keys (p.93). The creation steps repeat the advice: select primary key and entity profile if the database has no primary keys (p.99).

x: 4.30.1 Entity profile options and creation TDM infers foreign key candidates, and options limit the results (pp.93-94, 99): Datatypes used in comparisons (inferred or documented), Comparison case sensitivity (the guide warns it can slow the profile), Trim spaces before comparison (None, Both, Leading or Trailing), a minimum confidence or conformance percent and Regenerate signature (clears existing object information in the profiling warehouse first). The p.94 summary and the p.99 dialog list slightly different options, so read the labels on your screen. Create it like a primary key profile (Discover > Profile > Actions > New Profile, choose entity, select tables, set sampling options, Save, Actions > Execute). Select primary key and entity if the database has no primary keys (p.99).

x: 4.30.2 Reading entity results Close and reopen the profile, then open Profile > Entity (p.104). Each row is a possible entity. Select one to see the Constraints view (parent columns, child columns, relationship) and approve the constraints and the entity you want. Visual reference Informatica TDM 10.5.10 User Guide, p.104, Figure "results of an entity discovery profile". What to look for: a list of profiled relationships, an Actions menu (Approve, Reject, Clear status, Verify checked items) and a Constraints tab with parent and child key columns. ShopSphere (illustrative): you would approve CUSTOMERS.customer_id to ORDERS.customer_id , ORDERS.order_id to ORDER_ITEMS.order_id and PRODUCTS.product_code to ORDER_ITEMS.product_code . Approved relationships become logical constraints : TDM stores them in its repository and does not apply them to the source tables; a subset plan uses them to keep referential integrity (p.86).

x: 4.31 Data domain discovery A data domain profile finds the source columns that hold similar data and assigns each the same data domain name, so you can apply the same masking rules to all of them at once (User Guide 10.5.10, p.94). Domains are defined with regular expressions on data and on column names (see the data domains section of the Test Data Manager tour ). A project must contain policies before you create a data domain profile, because policies hold the domains the profile can search for (p.100).

h: 4.31.1 Sampling options for a domain profile
x: 4.31.1 Sampling options for a domain profile Option Meaning (p.95) Data Search for patterns in the data only. Column Name Search for patterns in the column name only. Data and Column Name Search both. Maximum Rows to Profile Limit rows profiled. Default 1,000. Minimum Conformance Percent Minimum percentage of rows in which the data or metadata matches the domain. Why a conformance percent? Real data is messy. If 97 of 100 rows look like SSNs and three are blank or mistyped, a threshold lets the column still match. The guide says all rows might not conform, so you enter the minimum percentage of profiled rows that must (p.100).

x: 4.31.4 Assigning domains by hand, and by CSV Discovery only suggests, so you can correct it (pp.95-96). For one column, click its Domain cell in Discover > Columns. x: 4.32 Column profile (for data generation) A column profile reports the range of values, list of values and data patterns of the columns you choose, so you can generate test data that looks like the real data without copying it (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.87, 97). It runs on Oracle and Microsoft SQL Server. TDM infers three kinds of rule: Range (min and max, first and last values, percent null; numeric and date), Patterns (patterns with percentage distribution, summing to 100%; string and numeric) and List of Values (unique and non-unique values with distribution; string, numeric and date). Inferred rules become auto rules you can assign in Define > Data Generation (the Informatica data generation chapter uses them). Sampling options (p.98): minimum conformance for patterns (default 5), maximum rows (default All), minimum data coverage to show List of Values (default 80) and maximum values in the list (default 20). With a cap of 20 values, those 20 must cover at least 80% of the data.

You can rename it (not change its type), add or remove tables, override key inference options, or change domains, policies and what to search. Delete: select the row without opening it, Actions > Delete, Yes (pp.101-102). Import a profile from the Model repository (p.102), for example one run in Informatica Developer on a flat file. x: 4.34 Constraints and relationships Discovery suggests; constraints are what TDM actually uses. Foreign key constraints define parent-child relationships between source tables, and TDM uses them to decide which tables go into a subset and to limit the values in subset columns (User Guide 10.5.10, p.107). When you create an entity you pick one table as the driving table , and TDM adds other tables based on the constraints of that table (p.107). The Informatica data subset chapter builds on this.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.34.1 Table classification In Discover > Tables you can classify tables as Temporary, Master, Configuration, Transactional, Log or Seed . It does not affect profiles, but you can filter tables by it when creating entities or plans. The guide's reason: knowing which tables are master helps you decide driving tables, and transaction and log tables are candidates for extra filter criteria (p.107). ShopSphere reading: CUSTOMERS and PRODUCTS look like master tables; ORDERS and ORDER_ITEMS look transactional (our classification).

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.34.2 Constraint types Type Meaning (pp.108-109) Notes Primary Key Column or combination that uniquely identifies a row; a table can have one. No nulls or duplicates. Foreign Key A column or combination in a table related to a parent column. Defined on the child table. Logical Manual Parent-child relationship based on columns that are not keys. Either accepted from discovery profiles or defined in TDM. You can delete both kinds. Unique Key Column(s) that define a unique key; may contain nulls; you can add more than one. Also helps bulk generation rule assignment. Conditional An expression that restricts generated data in a column based on another column. For data generation; becomes part of the target table metadata.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.34.3 Major and minor constraint severity When you define a foreign key constraint you choose a severity , which decides how much data a subset pulls in (pp.108-109). The severity does not change the structure of the entity; you can change it after creating an entity and at run time in a subset plan (the run-time change does not change the entity). Major Moves in both directions, child to parent and parent to child. If a filtered child row selects a parent, all other children of that parent come along too . This honours referential and transactional integrity. You can apply a major constraint only from within an entity. Minor One direction only, child to parent. The parent row is included, but not all its other children . The guide's example: Customer is the parent of Leads. You filter Leads to high-quality leads. With a major constraint the subset includes the customer for each high-quality lead and all that customer's leads. With a minor constraint it includes the high-quality leads and their customers only (pp.108-109). ShopSphere version (illustrative): you filter ORDERS to total_amount > 500 . Major: you get those orders, their customers, and all other orders of those customers. Minor: you get those orders and their customers only. Selecting more records in the child can pull in more parents, which pull in more children, and so on until no related records remain (p.108). For a smaller subset, choose the Referential Integrity Only option in a plan at run time. The data stays referentially intact, but it may not include every child of a parent, so transactional integrity might not be kept. If constraints form cycles , or an object has more than one major parent constraint, TDM does recursive evaluation and needs a staging connection . Using the source connection as the staging connection is recommended (p.109).

Steps from the guide (pp.109-110); table and column choices are ours. Primary key on CUSTOMERS. In the project click Discover > Tables, click CUSTOMERS , click Constraints, then Create New Constraint. Select Primary Key, Next, click Add, choose customer_id , Finish. The constraint appears in the table's Constraints list. Foreign key on ORDERS. Click ORDERS , Constraints, Create New Constraint. Enter a Name, set Constraint Type to Foreign Key, choose Severity Level (Major or Minor), choose Parent Table CUSTOMERS , and keep Enable Constraint ticked. Click Next. Map the columns. In the left pane click the child column customer_id , in the right pane click the parent column customer_id , click the Link icon, then Finish. The relationship shows in the table's Relationship Overview. Show a worked answer Illustrative result: CUSTOMERS has primary key constraint on customer_id ; ORDERS has a foreign key constraint to CUSTOMERS with severity Major if you want a customer's other orders to come with a filtered order. Repeat for ORDER_ITEMS.order_id to ORDERS.order_id . For the ORDER_ITEMS.product_code to PRODUCTS link, Minor is a reasonable choice because you do not want every item that uses a product. That severity choice is a design judgement of ours. For a unique key , choose Unique Key instead of Primary Key and add columns (pp.110-111). h: 4.35 Performance and accuracy tips from the guide
x: 4.35 Performance and accuracy tips from the guide The guide has no dedicated discovery performance section; these tips are scattered through it. Cap the sample. Primary key and data domain profiles default to 1,000 rows; column profiles default to All , the heaviest setting (pp.93, 95, 98). A small sample is fast but can call a column "unique" or "an SSN" wrongly (my reasoning). Limit key columns (default 3, p.93) and avoid case-sensitive entity comparisons, which can slow the profile (p.99). Search names first, then data. You can run a domain profile on column metadata and then on the data (p.100). Pick only the domains you need : disabled domains are skipped (p.75), and choosing a policy includes all its domains at once. Import metadata directly from the database when there are many tables (p.60), and use the same connection for import and profile (p.88).

x: 4.37 Common mistakes and gotchas Watch out Not reopening the profile. Results only show after you close and reopen it (User Guide 10.5.10, p.103). Running an entity-only profile on tables without keys. It returns nothing. Combine it with a primary key profile (p.93). Approving every unique column as a key. Uniqueness is evidence, not proof. Choose the real identifier that child tables use. Trusting a domain match without a preview. Use the Data Preview tab (first 200 records) and the conformance percentage before approving (p.105). Expecting profiling to change the source database. Keys and constraints live in the TDM repository only (pp.86-87, 109). x: 4.38 Recap Key points Discovery profiles find what to mask and how tables relate before you configure masking or subset (User Guide 10.5.10, p.86). Four profile types: primary key, entity (called foreign key in the overview), data domain and column. Primary key and entity, or primary key and data domain, can run together. Primary keys uniquely identify rows; foreign keys point at them. Discovery proposes keys with a uniqueness percentage, and you approve or reject. Data domain profiles match column values or names to domains defined by regular expressions; sampling options set the rows and the conformance threshold. Results are suggestions: preview, approve or reject, correct by hand or by CSV, and close and reopen the profile to see them. Constraints you approve or add (primary, foreign, logical, unique, conditional) live in the TDM repository. Major severity brings all siblings; minor does not. Auto cascade keeps parent and child keys masked the same way; value cascades do it for similar columns without keys. Labs 1 to 3 chain profiling into masking and subset on ShopSphere. Their menu paths are from the guide; the data and results are illustrative. Informatica: creating a data subset the discovery and subsetting concepts chapter explained why a team would shrink a production database before using it for testing. Then the Informatica discovery and profiling chapter showed how to find the tables, keys and sensitive columns in a source. This section is where you actually build the smaller copy in Informatica Test Data Management (TDM). A data subset is a small slice of production data that still hangs together: if you keep a customer, you also keep that customer's orders and the order lines inside them. Why do you care? A full copy of production is slow to load, expensive to store and full of real people's data. A random sample of rows is cheap but useless, because a sampled order may point to a customer that was not sampled. A subset gives you the middle path: small and consistent. In the syllabus this is Day 44 ("types of subset, driver tables") and the subset half of the hands-on exercise TDM_Handson3 (data profiling and subset). What this section is based on Everything marked comes from the Informatica Test Data Management 10.5.10 User Guide (PDF, February 2026, 455 pages) : User Guide chapter 6 "Creating a Data Subset" (pages 112 to 134) in full, plus the related parts of User Guide chapter 3 "Projects" (parameters, p.57), User Guide chapter 5 "Data Discovery" (constraints, p.107 to 109) and User Guide chapter 13 "Plans and Workflows" (plan settings, criteria and workflow generation, p.274 to 310). Page numbers are written as (User Guide 10.5.10, p.NN). The ShopSphere tables, the numbers and the 10 percent target are my own illustrative example ( or labelled "illustrative"), not from the guide. Where the guide does not say something I say so. Menu names can differ slightly between TDM versions, so confirm against your install. What you will learn What a data subset is and the three kinds of source TDM can subset (relational, flat file, XSD). What an entity, a driving table, a group and a template are, and when to use each. How filter criteria, operators, parameters and the plan-level Limit (percentage, absolute value, interval) decide which rows are picked. How TDM pulls related rows: major and minor constraints, and the four data integrity options. The full workflow from an empty project to a running subset plan, with the reason for every step. A worked ShopSphere example that cuts 20 customers down to 2 (10 percent) with their orders, items and products, and a lab you can repeat.

x: 4.39 Words to know first Data subset A small, targeted copy of production data that keeps related rows together, so it can be used in development, test or training. Referential integrity The rule that every foreign key points at a row that exists. An order whose customer is missing breaks it. Entity In TDM, a set of tables that are related by physical or logical constraints, built around one starting table. You filter the entity to say "which customers". Driving table The one table you pick as the starting point of an entity. The guide says "driving table"; the syllabus says "driver table". They mean the same thing. People also say "root table", but the guide does not use that word. Group A set of tables that are not related to each other (or that you want copied without filtering), added to a plan as they are. Template An optional container that holds entities and groups. The guide mentions it but gives almost no detail (see 13.5). Constraint A rule linking two tables, usually a foreign key from a child table to a parent table. It can be physical (declared in the database) or logical (added in TDM because the database does not declare it). Major / minor constraint A severity setting on a foreign key. Major moves in both directions (child to parent and parent to child). Minor moves only child to parent. Criteria parameter A named placeholder (for example $$CRITERIAVALUE ) used in an entity filter so the value can change at run time without editing the entity. Plan / workflow A plan lists what to do (which entities, groups, rules, connections). A workflow is the runnable job TDM generates from the plan.

x: 4.41.2 The three component types A component is a building block you define before you build the plan. The guide names three (User Guide 10.5.10, p.113 to 114) : Component What it defines Source types Use it when Entity A set of tables related by physical or logical constraints, starting from a driving table Relational, flat file You want related data copied together, filtered by criteria Group A set of unrelated tables Relational, flat file You want some tables copied with no filtering, or tables with no relationship to the entity XSD files Criteria applied to elements or attributes, plus a "scope" XSD You subset XML data

x: 4.42.1 What an entity is An entity is a shape : "start at this table, and include everything connected to it". The guide says an entity "consists of a driving table and related tables" (User Guide 10.5.10, p.114) . The driving table is the starting point. TDM works out the other tables from the constraints that involve the driving table and adds them by default. You then put a filter on columns of the tables in the entity to say which rows you want. Here is the same idea on ShopSphere. We choose CUSTOMERS as the driving table because the business question is "give me some customers and everything they did". ORDERS points at CUSTOMERS through customer_id , ORDER_ITEMS points at ORDERS through order_id , and ORDER_ITEMS points at PRODUCTS through product_code . (The first two links are in the shared ShopSphere model. The product_code link is my assumption for this example: in the source it is a column that names a product, so I treat it as a foreign key.) ★ CUSTOMERS driving table ORDERS child of CUSTOMERS ORDER_ITEMS child of ORDERS PRODUCTS parent of ORDER_ITEMS major major minor (our choice, see 13.11) Solid line: enabled relationship. Dotted line here shows the relationship we will set to minor. (In TDM's own map, a dotted line means a disabled relationship.) Original diagram: the ShopSphere entity with CUSTOMERS as the driving table. The star marks the driving table, as the guide says TDM does in its own entity map. The dotted line is my drawing style for "minor"; in the real tool, dotted means disabled (p.120).

h: 4.42.2 The three views of an entity
x: 4.42.2 The three views of an entity Once saved, an entity can be seen three ways in the Define | Data Subset view of a project (User Guide 10.5.10, p.114 to 116) . View What it shows What you can do there Entity Map A picture of the tables and links. The driving table has a star. Click a table to edit its filter. Click a link to edit the constraint. Enable or disable relationships. Pick a sub-view (below). Tables A list: table name, description, database name, and a status (included or excluded). Edit filter criteria for each table. Relationships A list of constraints: parent table, child table, database names, and enabled or disabled status. A table with more than one relationship appears more than once. Enable or disable relationships. Select a relationship and set minimum and maximum child records (the guide ties this to generating test data). The Entity Map can show All tables, All parents of the selected table, All immediate relationships (one level up and down), All children , or All cyclic relationships (TDM shows at most 1000). By default it shows only enabled relationships; tick Show excluded tables to see disabled ones (p.115). Selecting a link in the map highlights the matching row in the Relationships view, and the other way round.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
h: 4.42.3 Where the relationships come from: physical and logical constraints
x: 4.42.3 Where the relationships come from: physical and logical constraints TDM can only follow links it knows about. Those links are the constraints stored in the project (User Guide 10.5.10, p.107 to 109) . Foreign keys that already exist in the database are physical. If the database does not declare a foreign key (common in older systems), you can accept one that data discovery inferred (see the Informatica discovery and profiling chapter ), or add one by hand as a logical constraint. Adding keys in TDM does not change the source database (p.109). The guide's advice before you build an entity is: run data discovery to identify constraints, and add constraints to the source to define the child tables (p.116).

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
h: 4.42.4 Creating an entity, step by step
x: 4.42.4 Creating an entity, step by step This is the guide's procedure (User Guide 10.5.10, p.116 to 117) , with the reason for each step. Open the project, then click Define > Data Subset. The Define area is where all the "design" objects live: subset components here, masking assignments in Define | Data Masking (see the Informatica masking chapter ). You see a list of entities and groups in the project, possibly empty. Click Actions > New > Entities. This starts the New Entity dialog. Enter a name and an optional description. Names matter later: plans list components by name. Something like ShopSphere_Customer_Entity beats Entity1 . Click Select Table, choose the driving table, click OK. This is the key decision. Choose the table that answers your business question: "customers" for ShopSphere. Click Save. TDM now looks at the constraints of the driving table and adds every related table. A diagram of the tables and their relationships appears, and you can switch to the list views. To filter, click Edit in the Properties pane. The Edit Criteria dialog opens. Without a filter, the entity copies everything it reaches. The filter is what makes it a subset. On the Entity Criteria tab, click Add Criteria, select the columns to filter on, click OK. The columns you chose now appear in the list. For each column, pick the attribute: Value (type a value) or Parameter (pick a parameter). Pick an operator. Then type the value or choose the parameter. Click Save for each criterion. Parameters let you change the value later without editing the entity (13.7). Click Save to leave the Edit Criteria dialog. The entity is ready to add to a plan. When you have several criteria in one entity the guide says the filter conditions act as "AND" (p.117). So customer_id <= 1002 and zip_code = '560001' together would keep only rows that satisfy both.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.43.1 Groups A group is "one or more unrelated tables" you want copied to the subset database. The guide gives two uses: add unrelated tables to a plan, or "copy unfiltered data to a target" (User Guide 10.5.10, p.116) . When you add tables to a group you can include residual tables : tables that are not yet in any group or entity. Tick them when you want every table of the source to be in the subset plan. An entity only reaches tables linked by constraints, so unlinked tables go in a group. The guide's example: an employee-skills table and an organization-location table are unrelated, you want both, so you put them in one group and add the group to the plan (p.116).

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.43.2 Creating a group In the project, open Define | Data Subset and click Actions > New > Groups. Same place as entities, different menu item (User Guide 10.5.10, p.123). In the Create Group dialog, enter a name and optional description, then Next. Click Add Tables, optionally filter the list to search, select tables, click OK. The filter box helps when a schema has hundreds of tables. Click Save. The group appears in the Define | Data Subset list next to your entities. Editing a group later lets you add or remove tables (p.124).

x: 4.43.3 Templates: what the guide actually says The guide mentions templates only in passing: "an optional component that contains the entities and groups" (User Guide 10.5.10, p.32 and p.293) . Chapter 6 has no section on creating a template and I found no steps elsewhere, so I give none. Ask your trainer if your course uses them.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.44 How related rows are pulled This is the part that makes subsetting more than a filter. When your filter selects customer 1001, which other rows must come with it? The answer depends on the constraint severity and on the data integrity option you pick in the plan. Both are covered in the guide (User Guide 10.5.10, p.108 to 109, 119 to 123).

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.44.1 Major and minor constraints When a foreign key is defined, you give it a severity. The guide's rules : Major constraints move in both directions, child to parent and parent to child. A selected child pulls in its parent, and the parent then pulls in all of its children. This keeps referential and transactional integrity (p.108). Minor constraints move one way only, child to parent. The parent row comes along, but the parent's other children do not (p.108 to 109). You define the constraint on the child table. Severity does not change the entity's structure. You can change it after the entity exists, and also at run time in a subset plan, which leaves the entity unchanged (p.108). By default every constraint in an entity is major (p.119). The guide's own example (p.108 to 109) uses Customer as parent and Leads as child, with a filter on Leads that keeps only high-quality leads. With a major constraint, the subset receives each qualifying lead, its customer, and all leads of that customer. With a minor constraint it receives only the qualifying leads and their customers. MAJOR (both ways) MINOR (child to parent only) CUSTOMER 1001 CUSTOMER 1001 | ^ ^ v | parent pulls ALL its children | parent comes along, ORDER 5001 (selected) | siblings do not ORDER 5002 (comes along) ORDER 5001 (selected) ORDER 5003 (comes along) ORDER 5002 (left out)

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.44.2 The loop that surprises beginners With major relations the pulling can chain. The guide describes it (p.108, p.122): a selected child record pulls in its parents; each parent then selects all its related children; those children might point to other parents not yet in the subset, which pull in more children, "in a loop until there are no more related records to select". This is how a small filter can grow into a big subset. You will see exactly this in the ShopSphere example when PRODUCTS is related by a major constraint (13.11). For schemas with cycles, or objects that have more than one major parent, TDM uses recursive evaluation to compute the subset, and that needs a staging connection. The guide recommends using the source connection as the staging connection (p.109).

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.44.3 The four data integrity options The entity says how tables are connected. The data integrity option in the plan says how aggressively TDM follows those connections at run time. This lets you reuse one entity to produce different subsets. You choose it in the Advanced Settings area of the Plan Settings page when you create the plan; the field is called Data Integrity for Subset and its default is Transactional Integrity for Major Relation Type (User Guide 10.5.10, p.121, p.287) . Two terms first. (A staging connection , mentioned below, is a database connection TDM uses for temporary working tables.) Referential integrity means no child row points at a missing parent. Transactional integrity goes further: if a parent is in the subset, all of its children are too, so a business transaction (a customer with all their orders) is complete. Option What it does (guide, p.122 to 123) Size of result Needs / caveats Transactional Integrity for Major Relation Type (default) Follows major constraints both ways in a loop until no more related rows. Applies criteria to the entity as a whole, not each table. Several criteria are ANDed. Can be large Recursive evaluation (cycles, more than one major parent) needs a staging connection. If criteria hit mutually exclusive tables the result can be empty; you can switch to OR at plan time (Advanced on the Custom tab). Referential Integrity Only Picks the fewest rows needed to keep foreign keys valid. A parent may arrive without all of its children. Smaller Meant for an entity with one criterion. With more than one criterion TDM uses the Transactional option anyway. Self-cyclic relations or objects with more than one major parent also fall back to Transactional. Two-way Criteria propagate downward, then upward, alternately, until every table is covered; the upward step uses OR. Every table that meets the criteria has some data in the result. Larger than the first two Needs a staging connection (it may or may not be used). Ignores optimized or manually changed relationship types. Not available with custom Advanced or Limit criteria. With a cyclic relationship it falls back to Transactional. One-way Applies criteria to individual tables, not the entity as a whole, and propagates downward only. Tables above the topmost filtered table are included in full. More than Two-way Same caveats as Two-way about optimization and custom criteria. Falls back to Transactional for cyclic relationships. Recursive evaluation for self-cyclic relations needs a staging connection. A wording puzzle in the guide The One-way description (p.123, repeated in the plan settings table on p.287) says One-way returns more data than Two-way, and in the same breath recommends it for "the smallest required subset that does not break referential integrity". Those two statements only fit together if "smallest" means "smallest among the ways that keep every row of the tables above the filtered table". When size matters, run a trial plan and count rows rather than trust the labels.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.44.4 Which option for ShopSphere? One criterion on CUSTOMERS, want complete customer histories: keep the default Transactional option. Every order and line of a selected customer comes along. Same criterion, want the smallest consistent database for a quick smoke test: Referential Integrity Only. You may get a customer with only some of their orders. For a test that checks "order total equals sum of lines" that is fine; for one that counts "all orders for this customer" it is not. Criteria on both CUSTOMERS and ORDERS (for example zip code and order value): consider Two-way so that both tables end up with data, or edit the criteria to OR (see the table). These are my suggestions built on the guide's descriptions, . Always verify on a trial run.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.44.5 Optimizing relations Because every relationship starts as major (p.119), a subset can pick up more rows than you need. Optimize Relations asks TDM to analyse the entity and propose which relationships can be minor while still reaching every table. The guide's procedure (User Guide 10.5.10, p.119 to 120) : Make sure the entity already has a criterion. TDM raises an error if you optimize an entity with no criteria at entity level (p.119). Open the entity and click Actions > Optimize Relations. TDM analyses the constraints. The Optimize Relationships page lists each parent and child with the current and the proposed type. Optional: Download Optimizations. Saves the proposal as a CSV so you can review it with a colleague. Click Optimize to accept all proposals. You cannot accept some and reject others (the guide says results cannot be applied selectively). A list of plans that include the entity appears; regenerate and rerun them. Click Continue. The entity is updated. You can still edit single constraints by hand afterwards. You can also optimize at run time in the plan (the "Optimize Relationship Type for Entities" setting, p.283). That changes the run, not the saved entity, and it also requires criteria at the plan level (p.283). When you choose Two-way or One-way integrity, optimization is ignored (p.122 to 123).

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.44.6 Disabling and enabling relationships Sometimes you do not want TDM to follow a link at all, for example a link to a huge audit table. In the Entity Map or the Relationships view you can disable a relationship (p.120) . In the map, choose to view all relationships and show excluded tables; enabled links are solid, disabled links are dotted. Click the link, then Disable Relationship or Enable Relationship. If a table loses every link to the entity this way, it is excluded from the subset database (p.115). If you still want its data, put it in a group.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
h: 4.44.7 When constraints change after you built the entity
x: 4.44.7 When constraints change after you built the entity Entities do not update themselves. If you add a constraint after building the entity, the entity list marks it as having a change impact. Open it, click Review Changes , accept the relationship changes you want, then use Actions > Mark Changes Review as Complete so the notice goes away (p.120 to 121) . The guide's figure on p.121 shows a dialog with Added, Changed and Deleted groups and an Accepted action.

x: 4.45 Choosing rows: criteria, operators, parameters and limits

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.45.1 Entity filter criteria and operators You met entity criteria while creating an entity (13.4). A criterion is: a column, an attribute (Value or Parameter), an operator , and the value or parameter. The guide's examples use "greater than", "equals" and "IN" (p.118, p.119, p.127). The excerpt I had does not print the full list of operators in the drop-down, so do not assume more than those three; look at your own dialog. ShopSphere examples (illustrative) customer_id <= 1002 : keeps the first two customers. Easy to predict, good for a lab. zip_code = '560001' : keeps all customers in one postal area, a "region" subset like the guide's financial-data-for-one-region example. customer_id > $$CRITERIAVALUE : the same, but the number comes from a parameter (next section).

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.45.2 Subset with parameters Typing the value into the entity means editing the entity every time the requirement changes. A criteria parameter lets you change the value when you run the workflow. The guide (User Guide 10.5.10, p.113, p.118, p.57) says: Create criteria parameters in the project (Projects, open the project, Parameters tab, Add) or use global parameters an administrator created. Global ones show an asterisk (*) in lists, and you can import one into the project first (p.57 to 58). Parameter types are criteria, connection and owner. Criteria parameter names begin with $$ , connection ones with $DBConnection , owner ones with $Param . Data types are String, Numeric or Date. For a Date parameter you enter an expression that says how it is used, for example TO_DATE($$CRIT1,'MM-DD-YYYY') (p.57). You choose a default value and whether overriding is allowed. If you do not allow override, you cannot change the value when you run the workflow (p.57). Values can live in the project or in an external parameter file . The guide's example: a parameter CRITERIAVALUE , a parameter file line $$CRITERIAVALUE=100 , and an entity criterion EMPID > CRITERIAVALUE . To get EMPID greater than 500, change the file to 500 and run the same workflow (p.118). For a string or date parameter on a relational source, put the value in single quotes in the parameter file (p.118). Ignore flags. If you keep values in a parameter file you create yourself, add a flag for each criteria parameter, for example $$CRITERIAVALUE_IGNORE . "N" means use the criterion, "Y" means the workflow skips it. A file created from Test Data Manager already contains the flags, set to "N" (p.118, p.309 to 310). To make the plan accept parameter values, tick Treat the subset criteria as a variable in the plan's connection options and give the parameter file name and path (p.279) . At run time, in the Execute Workflow window, you choose where values come from (p.310 to 311): the default file named in the plan settings, a parameter file you browse to, or Add Parameter Values from the project. Criteria parameters do not appear in that list by default: click Select Parameter and add them, because "a workflow does not include parameters that do not appear in the list" (p.311). Two silent ways to get the wrong subset (1) You forget to select the criteria parameter in the Execute Workflow window, so the criterion is not included. (2) You edit a parameter that was created without "allow override": the change does not take effect and the workflow uses the default value and logs an error (p.311). Check the workflow log if the row counts look wrong.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.45.3 Database functions in entity criteria You may want a date rule such as "hired in the last three months". The guide (p.118 to 119) warns that writing a database function directly in the criterion makes workflow generation fail, because TDM does not recognise it as a function and cannot pass it on. The documented workaround: choose the operator IN and write a SELECT query in the Value field, for example select HIREDATE from <table> where HIREDATE > add_months(current_date, -3) . TDM then passes the query to the database. The ShopSphere version of this idea would be a query on ORDERS.order_date .

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.45.4 Filtering again inside the plan You can also set criteria in the plan itself without editing the entity (User Guide 10.5.10, p.294, p.304) . In the plan's component list you pick a subset component, then a column in the Criteria panel. TDM shows existing criteria, which you can change or add to. You then choose a method: Method Option What it does Custom Basic A simple expression with an operator and an operand. You can use parameters. Custom Advanced An expression typed in the Expression Editor. It can use several columns, functions and parameters, including global ones (a global parameter inside an expression is written without the asterisk). Limit (a limit type) Limit the subset result by percentage , by absolute value or by an interval of rows to write to the target. The plan creation steps put it like this: "To limit the subset results, click Limit and choose to limit by percentage, by absolute value, or by defining an interval of rows to create" (p.304). You cannot override the subset criteria of an XSD component in the plan (p.304). What the guide does not tell you about Limit The excerpt I had names the three limit types and nothing more. It does not say which table the percentage applies to, how rows are chosen (first N, random?), what the "interval" arithmetic is (every Nth row? a range?), or how a Limit interacts with parent-child pulling. So I describe the three types by their names only: percentage means a share of rows, absolute value means a fixed row count, interval means "a set of rows defined by an interval". Test on a small table and count the result before relying on it. The guide also says Two-way and One-way integrity are not available when a plan uses custom Advanced or Limit criteria (p.123). Percentage: for example 10 percent. Natural fit for the ShopSphere goal, but check how TDM applies it to related tables. Absolute value: for example 500 rows. Handy when the test environment has a hard size cap. Interval: a defined interval of rows. The guide gives no example. Syllabus link: Day 44 "types of subset". In practice, the guide supports these ways of choosing rows: by condition (entity criteria and plan Basic/Advanced criteria), by parameterised condition , and by quantity (Limit). I label this grouping as my own summary, , not a list taken from the guide.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
h: 4.45.5 Subset and masking in one plan
x: 4.45.5 Subset and masking in one plan A plan can hold both subset components and masking components. The guide says the subset component gets priority: TDM does the subset first, then applies masking rules to the columns of the subset data. Masking is not applied to source data that is outside the subset, "even if the data is part of a cascade" (User Guide 10.5.10, p.275) . You can also keep them in separate plans (p.304). the Informatica masking chapter covers the masking half.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
h: 4.46 Subsetting XML: XSD sources in brief
x: 4.46 Subsetting XML: XSD sources in brief XML data is a tree, not a set of tables, so entities and driving tables do not apply. Instead you put a filter on an element or attribute and set a scope : the level of the tree at which the filter is applied. You can apply one filter per hierarchy, and the scope changes the outcome (User Guide 10.5.10, p.114, p.124) . The procedure (p.124): import the XML source definition from the PowerCenter repository into the project; click Discover > Files; open the XSD file; select an element or attribute; on the Criteria tab of the Details tab click Edit; choose an operator; enter a value (you cannot use a parameter here); choose the scope; click OK. Then add the XSD file to a plan and run it. The guide's worked example (p.127 to 134): a master XML file lists departments, each with an address, employees and contractors, each with a name, address and skill. Test group A wants employees skilled in Java; group B wants departments located in BLR. Group A: criteria on the element Skill on the Employee branch, operator Equals, value JAVA, scope Employee. The output has all Java employees. Because Department is an ancestor of Employee, the departments that have such employees come along with all their child elements. Group B: delete the Skill criterion, then put a criterion on City : Equals, BLR, scope Department. The output has every department whose address city is BLR, with all child elements. Visual reference Informatica TDM 10.5.10 User Guide, p.127, Figure (Criteria tab of the file page). What I saw: a dialog titled "Edit - Skill" with tabs General, Data Masking, Data Generation and Criteria. Criteria is selected and shows three fields: Operator set to Equals, Value set to JAVA, Scope set to Departments/Department/Employee, with OK and Cancel buttons. The lesson carries over to relational data: the level where you filter decides which ancestors and descendants appear. For the ShopSphere tables the equivalent of "scope" is your choice of driving table and relationship types.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.47 Managing subset components Components live in the TDM repository and are reused by plans, so changing them has side effects. The guide's housekeeping tasks (User Guide 10.5.10, p.124 to 126) : Task How Watch out for Edit Define | Data Subset, open the entity or group, Actions > Edit. General tab: name, description, status. Entity Criteria tab (entity) or Tables tab (group). After saving, a list of plans that use it appears. Those plans must be generated and run again to pick up the change. Optionally Export the list to CSV. Export In the project, tick the component, Actions > Export, choose a file name and path. Output is an XML file; the default name has the component type, date and time. Use it to move a component to another TDM repository. Import In the Projects view select the target project without opening it, Actions > Import, browse to the XML, Finish. The guide says to import into a different TDM repository's project. Copy Select the component without opening it, Actions > Duplicate, change name and description, Save. Good for creating a "10 percent" and a "1 percent" variant. Delete Select, Actions > Delete, OK. If the component is assigned to a plan, that plan becomes invalid. A list of affected plans is shown, which you can export.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
h: 4.48 The whole workflow, start to finish
x: 4.48 The whole workflow, start to finish The guide's own summary of "Creating a Data Subset" is seven steps (User Guide 10.5.10, p.126) . Here they are with the reason and what you should see. Create a project and add the data sources. A project is the workspace that holds sources, parameters, components and plans. The guide advises separate projects for XSD sources and relational sources. If you ran discovery in the Informatica discovery and profiling chapter , it is the same project. The tables of the source appear in the project, with constraints from physical keys. Optional: create connection, owner or criteria parameters. Do this now if you want the same plan to serve different values later (13.7). Create the subset components for your source type. Relational and flat file: entities and groups. XSD: criteria with scope on elements and attributes. Entities and groups listed under Define | Data Subset. Optional: optimize the relationships in the entity. Reduces over-pulling by turning unneeded major relationships into minor ones (13.6). Create a plan and add the subset components and data sources. The plan ties together what to copy, where from and where to. Choose the integrity option, connections (source, target and a staging connection if needed), and any plan-level criteria or Limit. Run the workflow. Generate a workflow from the plan (the PowerCenter Repository Service generates the mappings) and execute it (the PowerCenter Integration Service does the extraction and load). You can do both in one step with Actions > Generate and Execute (p.308, p.310). Monitor progress. Watch status in the Workflow Executions view: In Queue, Running, Success or Error. Click the Job ID to open the workflow log (p.311 to 312). 1 Project → 2 Parameters → 3 Entities / groups → 4 Optimize → 5 Plan → 6 Run → 7 Monitor Plans and workflows get a full chapter of their own: see the Informatica plans and workflows chapter . For connections and the profile that finds constraints, see the Informatica discovery and profiling chapter . The tour of the TDM screens is the Informatica TDM tour .

x: 4.49.1 The goal ShopSphere's QA team wants a test database with about 10 percent of customers, with all their orders and order lines, and the products on those lines. The source has 20 customers (1001 to 1020), 36 orders, 80 order lines and 12 products (illustrative). Target: 2 customers.

x: 4.49.3 Steps Confirm the constraints exist. An entity follows constraints. Open the project's tables and check that ORDERS to CUSTOMERS, ORDER_ITEMS to ORDERS and ORDER_ITEMS to PRODUCTS are listed. If the PRODUCTS link is not declared in the database, add it as a logical foreign key in TDM (p.109 and p.116; this does not alter the source). Three relationships visible, each with Input Type physical or logical. Create a criteria parameter. Projects, open the project, Parameters, Add. Name MAX_CUST_ID , type criteria (TDM builds the name $$MAX_CUST_ID ), data type Numeric, default 1002, override allowed (p.57). The parameter is listed in the project. Setting 1002 gives 2 of 20 customers, which is 10 percent. Create the entity. Define | Data Subset, Actions > New > Entities, name ShopSphere_Customer_Entity , Select Table = CUSTOMERS, Save (p.116 to 117). The map shows a star on CUSTOMERS and links to ORDERS, ORDER_ITEMS and PRODUCTS. Every link is major by default (p.119). Add the filter. Edit, Entity Criteria, Add Criteria, choose customer_id . Attribute Parameter, operator less-than-or-equal, parameter MAX_CUST_ID . Save (p.117). Deal with PRODUCTS before you run anything. See "Option A versus a major relationship" below. Set the ORDER_ITEMS to PRODUCTS relationship to minor by clicking the link in the Entity Map and changing Type (p.117), or use Actions > Optimize Relations (p.119). The link is marked minor; the entity needs a criterion first for Optimize Relations to work. Create the plan. Execute, Actions > New, enter a name, click Add Subset Components, select the entity, Next. Set source and target connections and a staging connection (recommended: the source connection). Tick "Treat the subset criteria as a variable" and give the parameter file name and path. Keep Data Integrity for Subset at its default, Transactional Integrity for Major Relation Type (p.279, p.287, p.304 to 305). The plan appears in the project. Generate and execute. Open the plan, Actions > Generate and Execute, choose the Integration Service and run now. In the parameter section, select MAX_CUST_ID using Select Parameter so it is included, and keep the value 1002 (p.310 to 311). Status moves from In Queue to Running to Success in the Workflow Executions view. Verify the target. Count rows and check there are no orphans (SQL below). TDM's job is to keep integrity, but you confirm. -- Row counts in the target (general SQL, adjust schema names) SELECT 'CUSTOMERS' t, COUNT(*) n FROM CUSTOMERS UNION ALL SELECT 'ORDERS', COUNT(*) FROM ORDERS UNION ALL SELECT 'ORDER_ITEMS', COUNT(*) FROM ORDER_ITEMS UNION ALL SELECT 'PRODUCTS', COUNT(*) FROM PRODUCTS; -- Orphan check: order lines whose order is missing (expect 0) SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ORDER_ITEMS i LEFT JOIN ORDERS o ON o.order_id = i.order_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;

h: 4.49.5 Option A versus a major relationship
x: 4.49.5 Option A versus a major relationship Why did I insist on changing PRODUCTS to minor? With the default (all major), the loop from 13.6 applies: line 9001 pulls in its parent product P-100. As a major parent, P-100 then selects all order lines for P-100, from every customer. Those lines pull their orders, the orders pull their customers, and so on, until nothing new is added. A popular product like P-100 can connect nearly everyone, so "10 percent of customers" turns into most of the database (the right-hand column above, illustrative counts). Minor means: bring the product along, but do not let the product pull its other lines. Major PRODUCTS link Minor PRODUCTS link customer 1001 customer 1001 order 5001 -> line 9001 order 5001 -> line 9001 product P-100 --pulls--> product P-100 (stops here) ALL lines with P-100 -> other orders -> other customers

h: 4.49.6 Option B: reference table as a group
x: 4.49.6 Option B: reference table as a group PRODUCTS is small and looks like reference data. Another valid design: disable the ORDER_ITEMS to PRODUCTS relationship in the entity (p.120) so the entity is just customers, orders and lines, then create a group containing PRODUCTS (tick it from the residual tables, p.116) and add both the entity and the group to the plan. The target gets all 12 products (unfiltered) and still has no orphan lines. The trade-off: 8 unused products travel along, which is harmless here but would matter for a 2-million-row table. Pick Option A for big parent tables and Option B for small reference tables. the discovery and subsetting concepts chapter covers why test teams usually want reference data complete and transactional data small; the Informatica masking chapter shows masking the customers you just selected, so the 2 customers in this subset do not carry real names or SSNs.

x: 4.50 Lab: TDM_Handson3 (profiling and subset), ShopSphere version Lab: subset ShopSphere to about 10 percent of customers Goal: after profiling the source for constraints (the profiling half of TDM_Handson3 is in the Informatica discovery and profiling chapter ), build an entity with CUSTOMERS as the driving table, filter with a parameter and run a plan so the target has the first 10 percent of customers with their orders, order lines and products. Everything below on ShopSphere is illustrative; the screens are from the guide, so use your lab environment's real database and its real table names. Check the source. Query counts on the four tables and write them down. You need them for the before and after comparison. For example 20, 36, 80, 12 on the sample, or your lab's own numbers. Confirm or add the constraints. Open the project's tables and check the three relationships. Add any missing logical foreign key. Create parameter MAX_CUST_ID , then the entity and its criterion. Follow steps 2 to 4 above. In your lab replace 1002 with the 10th percentile ID of your own data. Switch the PRODUCTS link to minor (or use Option B). Record which you picked and why. Create the plan, generate and execute it. Use Generate and Execute and select the criteria parameter in the run window. Status Success. Verify. Run the count and orphan queries on the target and fill in a before/after table. Experiment. Change the parameter value to 1004 and rerun the same workflow: the point of parameters is that nothing else needs editing. Then try the default (all major) PRODUCTS link and note how the counts change. If a Limit-based alternative interests you, replace the criterion by a plan-level Limit of 10 percent and compare counts; the guide does not say how it treats related tables, so measure it.
