x: 4.51 Common mistakes and gotchas Watch out for these No criterion, huge subset. An entity without a filter copies everything it reaches. Everything is major by default, so a popular parent table can balloon the result (p.119, 13.11). Optimize relations or set minor. Missing constraints. If the database does not declare a foreign key, TDM will not follow it until you add a logical constraint (p.109, p.116). Editing without rerunning. After you edit or delete an entity, group or rule, the plans that use it do not pick up the change until you generate and run them again (p.124, p.275). Using a database function directly in a criterion. Workflow generation fails; use IN with a SELECT clause (p.118 to 119). Parameter not selected or not overridable. Criteria parameters must be added in the Execute Workflow window, and non-overridable ones ignore your edit (p.311). Forgetting quotes on string or date parameter values in the parameter file (p.118). Cycles and a missing staging connection. Cyclic or multi-major-parent structures need one (p.109, p.122). Mutually exclusive criteria give an empty subset. Several criteria are ANDed; use OR in the plan's Advanced criteria if you want either (p.122). Treating the Limit like a magic 10 percent. The guide does not describe how it interacts with related rows. Test it.

ct: Informatica TDM (1): architecture, the tool tour, discovery and subsetting
x: 4.52 Recap Key points A data subset is a small, referentially intact copy of production data; TDM can build one from relational, flat file or XSD sources. An entity is a driving table plus the tables related to it by constraints; a group is a set of unrelated tables copied as they are; a template is an optional container the guide barely describes. Filter criteria, with an operator and either a value or a parameter, choose rows. A plan can add Custom (Basic, Advanced) criteria or a Limit by percentage, absolute value or interval. Major constraints move both ways and can pull in far more than you expected; minor constraints go child to parent only. Optimize Relations suggests which can be minor. Integrity options (Transactional, Referential only, Two-way, One-way) trade completeness against size. The workflow: project, parameters, components, optional optimization, plan, run, monitor.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
h: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: Informatica: masking data, rules and mapplets The previous chapters showed how to find sensitive columns ( the Informatica discovery and profiling chapter ) and how to cut production down to a small consistent slice ( the Informatica data subset chapter ). This section covers the step that makes the slice safe to hand to testers: data masking , replacing real sensitive values with realistic fake ones, so a tester sees "Divya Iyer" where production has "Asha Menon". The general idea is in the masking concepts chapter ; here is exactly how Informatica TDM does it. In the syllabus this is Day 44 (substitution, shuffle, key masking, encryption), Day 54 (masking rules, algorithms, mapplet creation, transformations), Days 55 and 56 (mask first name; alphanumeric text, SSN, telephone number) and the masking half of TDM_Handson2. What this section is based on Everything marked is from the Informatica Test Data Management 10.5.10 User Guide (PDF, February 2026, 455 pages) : User Guide chapter 7 (p.135 to 150) and chapter 8 (p.151 to 189) read in full, plus chapter 4 "Policies" (p.71 to 85), cascades in chapter 5 (p.90 to 91), Data Masking transformation properties in chapter 3 (p.52 to 53) and plan settings in chapter 13 (p.275, p.281, p.286 to 287). Citations look like (User Guide 10.5.10, p.NN). ShopSphere data, before and after values and labs are my illustrations ; real masked values will differ. The guide says little about building a mapplet in PowerCenter, and section 5.9 says where its coverage stops. Menu labels can differ between versions. What you will learn How rules, data domains, policies and column assignments fit together, and the flow from creating a rule to running a masking plan. The three kinds of rule: standard, advanced and mapplet, and how to preview a standard rule in the Rule Simulator before using it. The common parameters: repeatable output, seed, exception handling, override. Every masking technique in the guide (credit card, email, encryption, expression, IP address, key, nullification, phone, random, shuffle, SIN, SSN, substitution, URL, plus advanced and mapplet/custom): what it does, its parameters, ShopSphere before and after, gotchas. A decision table for choosing a technique. What the guide says about mapplets and the PowerCenter Data Masking transformation, and where it says nothing. Labs for TDM_Handson2, Day 55 (first name) and Day 56 (alphanumeric text, SSN, phone).

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.1 Words to know first Masking technique The logic that replaces a value, such as "pick a name from a list" (substitution) or "swap values between rows" (shuffle). Masking parameters The options of a technique, such as the dictionary to use, the seed, or the range of dates allowed. Masking rule A technique plus its parameters, saved under a name. "FirstName_Substitution" is a rule. The same technique with different parameters is a different rule. Data domain A named group of columns that mean the same thing (for example "Social Security Number"), found by patterns in the data or in column names. You can attach preferred masking rules to it. Policy A bundle of data domains (and so their rules) that you reuse across projects. It holds no data source itself. Deterministic / repeatable The same input always gives the same masked output, so "Asha" becomes the same fake name in every table and in every run. Seed A starting number that makes repeatable output reproducible. Same seed, same rule, same input, same result. Dictionary A flat file or database table of replacement values used by substitution, for example a list of first names. Mapplet A reusable group of PowerCenter transformations with input and output ports. TDM can import one as a custom masking rule. Value cascade / auto cascade Ways to make related columns receive the same masked value: a value cascade for similar columns you group by hand, an auto cascade for primary and foreign keys.

h: 5.2.1 Six objects and how they connect
x: 5.2.1 Six objects and how they connect Start with the ShopSphere problem. Your CUSTOMERS table has first name, last name, email, phone, SSN, date of birth, zip code and tax ID, all sensitive. You do not want to configure "how to mask an SSN" nine times in nine projects. TDM lets you define it once and reuse it. The guide's building blocks (User Guide 10.5.10, p.71 to 73, p.135 to 138, p.149 to 150) : Object What it is ShopSphere example Rule A masking technique, an optional rule qualifier and masking parameters. Can have an override option. "SSN_Rule" using SSN masking Data domain The functional meaning of a column, identified from data patterns and column-name patterns; holds one or more preferred rules, one of them the default. "Social Security Number Domain": data pattern for 999-99-9999 and column names matching SSN or SOCIAL Policy A collection of data domains. Contains no data source; can be applied to many projects. "ShopSphere_PII_Policy" Assignment A rule attached to a column, either directly (column assignment) or through a data domain (domain assignment). CUSTOMERS.ssn uses SSN_Rule Plan Defines the masking operation and whether to mask data in place in the source database or in stream into a target. "ShopSphere_Mask_Plan" Value cascade Masks similar columns in different tables with the same rule so the values match. A customer_ref column in another system masked like customer_id You can create rules, domains and policies in any order. The guide's high-level policy task flow (p.72): create masking rules, define data domains, assign the rules to the domains, create a policy, assign the domains to the policy. You can apply the rules to source columns, data domains, policies and plans (p.136). Column CUSTOMERS.ssn 123-45-6789 Data domain Social Security Number pattern: [0-9]{3}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{4} Preferred rule SSN_Rule (default) technique + parameters Plan workflow run matches offers added to Policy: ShopSphere_PII_Policy contains data domains (and through them, rules) assigned to a project's data source Original diagram: how a column ends up with a masking rule. A column is matched to a data domain (by data pattern or by column name), the domain offers a preferred rule, and the rule is added to a plan. The policy groups domains so the setup can be reused across projects. The Social Security pattern shown is the one the guide gives (User Guide 10.5.10, p.74 to 75).

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.2.2 Data domains and preferred rules A data domain (User Guide 10.5.10, p.73 to 76) "represents the functional meaning of a column based on the column data or the column name". The guide's SSN example: social security numbers may sit in a column called SSN , in another table's SOCIAL_SECURITY and even in a COMMENTS column. You define a data expression for the format (regular expression [0-9]{3}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{4} ) and metadata expressions for column names such as .*SSN* and .*SOCIAL* . Data discovery profiles (see the Informatica discovery and profiling chapter ) use these patterns to assign domains to columns; without Data Discovery you assign columns by hand (p.73). Link back to discovery: profiling finds the sensitive columns, domains carry the rule to them. When you attach masking rules to a domain they are called preferred rules . If you attach several, one is the default rule , applied to all columns of the domain, and you can change an individual column to another preferred rule (p.73). The guide's example: a Last_Name domain with shuffle as the default and substitution as another preferred rule for a different table. TDM ships three policy packs, PII , PHI and PCI , each listing domains with a default rule (p.77 to 80). The PII pack, for example, pairs First Name Domain with First Name Rule, Phone Domain with Phone Number Rule and Social Security Number Domain with Social Security Number Rule. The guide does not say which technique each default rule uses, so open a rule in your install to see.

x: 5.2.3 The task flow A masking plan must contain at least one rule or one policy (User Guide 10.5.10, p.135). The PowerCenter Integration Service does the masking when the workflow runs. If a plan has both subset and masking components, subsetting happens first (p.275), as in the Informatica data subset chapter . Plans are explained in the Informatica plans, workflows and warehouse chapter , and the screens in the Informatica TDM tour .

x: 5.3 Creating masking rules A rule is created in the Policies view, then added to a project, then assigned to columns. The guide recognises three kinds (User Guide 10.5.10, p.136 to 138) : Kind What it is Columns Use it when Standard A built-in technique with parameters. One masking technique per rule. One input column, one output column Most cases: mask a name, an SSN, a date Advanced A combination of techniques; masks multiple source columns, or one column based on more than one input. Input, variable and output columns A full name built from masked first and last name; conditional masking; dependent columns Mapplet Logic imported from a mapplet exported from PowerCenter or the Model repository. Multiple input and output columns You need a PowerCenter masking technique TDM does not offer natively

x: 5.3.1 Creating a standard rule Click Policies, then Actions > New > Masking Rule. The Rule Wizard opens (User Guide 10.5.10, p.139). Enter a name and optional description. Pick the datatype of the column the rule will be applied to. Techniques depend on datatype: you cannot blur a string by a percentage. A rule can be created for string, numeric and date types (p.72). Select the Standard masking rule type. Tick Override Allowed if users may change parameters when they assign the rule. Click Next. Override is described below. The next screen changes depending on the masking technique you select (p.139). Enter the masking parameters. These decide exactly how values are masked: dictionary, seed, range, mask format and so on. Section 5.6 lists them per technique. Enter the exception handling options. Decide what to do with nulls, empty spaces and errors (14.5). Click Finish (p.139 to 140). The rule appears in the Policies view and can be edited, copied (Actions > Duplicate) or deleted there (p.139, p.146).

h: 5.3.2 Previewing a rule: the Rule Simulator
x: 5.3.2 Previewing a rule: the Rule Simulator The guide describes a built-in preview so you do not have to run a full workflow to see what a rule does (User Guide 10.5.10, p.137, p.140) . It works for standard rules only (the text says "simulate the output of a standard rule"). Policies view, click a masking rule name to open its Rule Properties, then click Rule Simulator. This opens the simulator tab. Choose a source in Source Details: Default, My Test Data or Connection, then click Edit. Default uses sample data supplied by TDM. My Test Data lets you type rows (up to 100). Connection reads real rows (the Configure Source Details page opens). If Connection: open the Connection tab, pick connection and owner, Browse to the table, choose the column. By default up to 10 random columns are listed; type the column name if yours is missing. Enter the number of rows: default 20, maximum 100. Click OK. Click Go. The Rule Simulator tab lists original values beside masked values. Adjust the rule and run the simulation again on the same data. The latest simulation configuration is stored in the browser cache, and clearing the cache deletes it (p.137).

x: 5.3.5 Creating an advanced rule Policies, Actions > New > Masking Rule. Enter a name and description, choose Advanced, click Next. Advanced rules combine techniques (User Guide 10.5.10, p.141). In Input Columns click Add New. Give the name, datatype, precision and scale. Choose whether assigning it is mandatory in every project. You cannot enter masking properties on input columns, because input columns just receive the source value. In Variable Columns click Add New. For each, enter an expression, a masking rule or a dependent column. Variable columns are scratch fields for intermediate results. If you apply a masking rule, say which input column feeds it. In Output Columns click Add New. Enter an expression, a masking rule or a dependent column. The output column receives the final value written to the target. Click OK and finish. The column names in the rule do not have to match source column names; you map them at assignment time (p.156 to 157). The full parameter tables for advanced rules are in 14.8.

x: 5.4.3 Assigning a standard rule, step by step Open the project, click Define | Data Masking, select a column. Choose the column that needs masking, for example CUSTOMERS.first_name . If Domain is blank, click the Policy column and pick a policy that contains the rule you want. The list of rules comes from the data domain's preferred rules, then the policy's rules (p.142, p.145). Click inside the Masking Rule column and pick a rule. Domain preferred rules are at the top; the rest of the policy's rules are below. For a substitution rule you can set the rule assignment parameters (lookup condition, unique substitution column, see 14.6). For a mapplet or advanced rule you map columns (below). Click Save for each column. If you move to another row without saving, TDM discards the assignment (p.145). This is the most common beginner loss. If you changed an assignment that other objects use, the Impacted Objects dialog lists plans, columns and domains. Click Export for a CSV, Continue to save. Regenerate and rerun the affected plans (p.142). No rules appear in the list? No rules listed? Check that a rule exists for the column datatype, that the project has a policy with masking rules, and that the domain's preferred rule is in a policy assigned to the project (p.145). The Integration Service does not mask integers longer than 28 characters (p.145, p.152).

x: 5.4.4 Assigning a mapplet or advanced rule (port mapping) These rules have named input and output ports, so you map source columns to them (User Guide 10.5.10, p.142 to 143) . Pick the rule in the Masking Rule column; a Custom Rule Assignment or Advanced Rule Assignment dialog opens. Select a source column and a same-datatype rule input port, click Link (or Show Simple), then Next, link rule output ports to source columns, Save. For an expression cascade in an advanced rule, Add Associated Table lets you combine two tables with a join condition. Sybase to Hadoop limits a custom rule to 20 columns (p.143).

Clearing: select the column and click Clear Assignment, confirm, and Continue if the Impacted Objects dialog appears (p.148).

h: 5.4.6 Cascades: keeping values consistent between tables
x: 5.4.6 Cascades: keeping values consistent between tables The ShopSphere customer_id is a primary key in CUSTOMERS and a foreign key in ORDERS . If you mask the key but the foreign key keeps its old value, the join breaks. TDM handles this with cascades (User Guide 10.5.10, p.90 to 91) : Auto cascade: masks a primary key in a parent table and the related foreign keys in child tables with the same value. Applied by default to tables with key constraints; can be switched off or on. Needs key constraints between parent and child. Not available for XSD, MongoDB and Cassandra sources. Value cascade: for similar columns not linked by key constraints (the guide's example: employee_num in one table and EmpID in another). Select the columns in Discover | Columns, Actions > Set as similar value columns, and choose a driving column. A rule assigned to the driving column is assigned to all the group. The columns must have the same type. In the masking view the driving column shows the number of other columns in the cascade. Not for computed columns: you cannot apply masking or generation rules to computed columns or build cascades on them (p.90).

h: 5.4.7 Changing or deleting rules after assignment
x: 5.4.7 Changing or deleting rules after assignment Editing or deleting a rule shows an Impacted Objects dialog, but changes do not flow into plans: regenerate and rerun them. Deleting a rule does not remove it from the columns, domains and plans using it. If you change a custom rule's field names or types, import the mapplet again (p.144 to 146) . For XSD sources you apply rules to XML elements and attributes in Discover > Files (p.144); shuffle is not allowed for XSD (p.135).

x: 5.5.1 Repeatable output and the seed Repeatable output returns deterministic values: the same input gives the same masked value, every time you generate and run the workflow. Use it when the same value occurs in several tables and the target tables must show the same masked value. The guide's example: customer John Smith has account numbers 1234 and 5678 in many tables; masking turns John Smith into Frank Martinez everywhere, 1234 into 6549, 5678 into 3214, on every run. The seed is the generator's starting point: 1 to 999, default 1 (p.154; the key masking string table says 1,000, p.168, so I use 999). Give the same seed to columns that must match, such as Cust_ID in four tables. You can put the seed in a parameter file variable. A TDM administrator can set a central seed that overrides every other seed (p.155). Substitution and expression masking keep a storage table of source and masked value pairs; you name the storage connection in the plan (p.286: IDM_SUBSTITUTION_STORAGE , IDM_EXPRESSION_STORAGE ), and expression masking fails without it (p.163). Key masking is deterministic from source, rule and seed (p.164). Repeatable means "same in, same out", not "reversible".

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.5.2 Exception handling Every rule has an Exception Handling section that decides what happens with nulls, blanks and errors (p.155): Option What it does Preprocessing Expression Optional expression applied to the data before masking Post processing Expression Optional expression applied to the masked data before it is written Null and Empty Spaces Constant (mask with a value you give); Log error and continue; Treat as value (mask the space or null as a valid value); Ignore (leave it unmasked). For dependent masking columns there is no separate rule: they follow the column they depend on. Error Handling Constant; Log exception and continue; Ignore and continue; Error (log and stop) Trim Leading or Trailing Spaces When on, " Jones", "Jones" and "Jones " are the same value

x: 5.6 The masking techniques, one by one The guide lists these techniques (User Guide 10.5.10, p.152 to 153): Advanced, Credit card, Email address, Encryption, Expression, IP address, Key, Mapplet, Nullification, Phone, Random, Shuffle, SIN, SSN, Substitution and URL. Advanced and Mapplet are in 14.8 and 14.9; the other fourteen follow, each with what it does, parameters, a ShopSphere before and after, and gotchas. How to read the before and after tables "Before" values are the fake ShopSphere sample data. "After" values are illustrations I made up ; the tool generates its own. Where ShopSphere has no suitable column (credit card, IP address, URL) I use the guide's example.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.6.1 Substitution masking What it does. Replaces a value with a "similar but unrelated" value looked up in a dictionary , a flat file or database table of replacement values (User Guide 10.5.10, p.176 to 177) . Works on date, numeric and string columns. The guide calls it an effective way to replace production data with realistic test data; its examples are a dictionary of addresses, or the InvalidSSN dictionary of Social Security numbers that are not valid. Where Parameter Meaning Rule assignment Lookup Condition (optional) Column of the source table to match against a column of the dictionary, for example match on gender so a female first name gets a female replacement Rule assignment Unique Substitution Column (optional) Source column to substitute with unique data Rule Repeatable Output Same result between sessions; masked values saved in the storage table Rule Seed Start number for deterministic results. Required for deterministic output Rule Unique Substitution Data Every unique source value gets a unique masked value. Fails if the source has more distinct values than the dictionary. Default is nonunique, "for security" Rule Dictionary Information (required) Dictionary (the file or table); Masked Value (column returned); Lookup Column (source column used in the lookup); Serial Number Column; Sort Column (to keep results deterministic if a relational dictionary is moved and its row order changes) ShopSphere example. A flat file dictionary FIRSTNAMES.csv (illustrative): SNO,GENDER,FIRSTNAME 1,F,Divya 2,M,Arjun 3,F,Latha 4,M,Karthik Substitution on first_name (illustrative output) customer_id first_name before first_name after 1001 Asha Divya 1002 Ravi Arjun 1003 Meera Latha Gotchas. Choose Unique Substitution Data only if the dictionary is bigger than the number of distinct values in the column. A dictionary of 4 names cannot uniquely replace 20 customers; the operation fails. Two customers with the same first name get the same replacement only if Repeatable Output is on (the storage table remembers pairs). Without repeatability, each row can get a different value. Repeatability. Tick Repeatable Output and set a seed. Name the storage connection in the plan.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.6.2 Shuffle masking What it does. Swaps values of one column between rows of the same table. The guide's example (p.173) uses four rows: Tom Bender, Sue Slade, Bob Bold, Eli Jones. After a shuffle of the first-name column they read Bob Bender, Eli Slade, Tom Bold, Sue Jones. You can restrict which values may be swapped by a lookup condition or a constraint. Works on date, numeric and string columns . Parameter Meaning (p.174) Shuffle Type: Random Values move from row to row without checking that target values are unique per source value. 12345 may become 65432 in one row, and 33333 may become 12345 in another. Shuffle Type: Representative All source rows with the same value get the same shuffle value (if 12345 becomes 65432 once, it does everywhere). Does not save values between workflow runs; use repeatable masking to get the same values across runs. Seed 1 to 999, default 1. Enabled only when Representative is selected. Constrained Restrict shuffling to rows constrained by another column, such as shuffle employee names within gender, or addresses within the same city. You choose the constraint column when you assign the rule to columns. Shuffle on last_name (illustrative output; the values come from the same column) customer_id first_name last_name before last_name after 1001 Asha Menon Nair 1002 Ravi Kumar Menon 1003 Meera Nair Kumar Gotchas. It cannot be used for XSD sources, and not when both source and target are Hadoop HDFS connections (p.135, p.173). A Spark engine cannot do it (p.62). Empty strings: set Null and Empty Spaces to Treat as Value, or the empty columns are skipped (p.173).

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.6.3 Key masking What it does. Produces deterministic results: the same source value, rule and seed always give the same masked value. Works on date, numeric and string columns (User Guide 10.5.10, p.164 to 168) . Parameter Meaning Seed Start number that makes output deterministic. Apply the same seed to columns that must match (string table: 1 to 1,000; see the note in 14.5) Seed value is a parameter Tick if a plan parameter supplies the seed Mask Format (string) What kind of character may replace each input character (table below) Source String Characters (string) Which characters to mask. Options: Mask Only (mask just these) or Mask all except (mask everything but these). Blank means all characters. Case sensitive Result String Replacement Characters (string) Characters allowed in the output. Options: Use only or Use all except Case Insensitive (string) Treat upper and lower case as the same input character Delimited String Masking and Delimiters (string) Also mask the value when it appears as a substring in other columns, splitting on delimiters you list The mask format characters (shared with random masking; p.165): Char Means A Alphabetical, ASCII a to z and A to Z D Digit 0 to 9 N Alphanumeric X Any character + No masking at that position R Remaining characters can be any type; must be the last character of the mask If no mask format is given, each source character is replaced with any character. A mask format longer than the input is truncated; shorter than the input means the characters at the end are not masked . Lowercase letters you type are converted to uppercase (p.164). Key masking of an alphanumeric tax_id with mask format AAAAADDDDA (illustrative; tax_id is a ShopSphere column, the values are made up) customer_id tax_id before tax_id after 1001 ABCPM1234K QWZRT5820M 1002 ZZTPK9087L HNBXC4413D Other forms the guide describes. Delimited strings: the guide's example masks "John Donne" consistently when it appears as the strings John and Donne in two columns and as "Donne, John" or "John Donne, General Manager" in two more. Assign delimited string masking with comma and space as delimiters to the last two (p.166 to 167). Dates: output dates fall between 1753 and 2400 and are always valid. A leap year maps to a leap year; a 31-day month to a 31-day month; February stays February (p.167). Give the same seed as another column to get matching dates. Numbers: to keep a primary-key to foreign-key relationship intact between two tables, give the key column in each table the same seed . Deterministic output means 1001 in CUSTOMERS and 1001 in ORDERS both become the same new number (p.167). Gotchas. Output is not guaranteed unique when there are fewer source characters than result characters (p.165). By default a masked character may differ from the original only in case ("x" to "X"); Case Insensitive treats both cases as one character so it cannot. To get identical output for "John Brown" and "JOHN BROWN", convert to one case first with a preprocessing expression (p.166).

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.6.4 Random masking What it does. Produces random, non-repeatable output: the same source value and rule can give a different result each run. No seed. Works on date, numeric and string columns (User Guide 10.5.10, p.169 to 173) . Option For Meaning Range date, numeric, string Output between a minimum and maximum. For strings it is a range of lengths. For dates the maximum must be later than the minimum Blurring date, numeric Output within a fixed or percent variance of the source value Mask Format string Same A, D, N, X, +, R characters as key masking Source String Characters string Which characters to mask: Mask Only or Mask all except Result String Replacement Characters string Use only or Use all except Numeric blurring with a source value of 66 (guide table, p.170): Type Low High Result Fixed 0 10 between 66 and 76 Fixed 10 0 between 56 and 66 Fixed 10 10 between 56 and 76 Percent 0 50 between 66 and 99 Percent 50 0 between 33 and 66 Percent 50 50 between 33 and 99 Bounds must be zero or greater. Date blurring takes a unit (year by default), a low and a high bound: unit year, bounds 2 and 2 on 02 February 2006 gives a date from 02 February 2004 to 02 February 2008 (p.170). The unit list differs between p.170 (to hour) and p.172 (to second); check your drop-down. Random masking on ShopSphere columns (illustrative output) Column Setting Before After date_of_birth Blurring, unit year, low 2, high 2 1990-04-12 1991-03-30 (somewhere in 1988-04-12 to 1992-04-12) zip_code Mask format +++DDD 560001 560417 (first three digits kept) Gotchas. No seed, so reruns differ and the same customer will not match across tables. A short mask format leaves trailing characters unmasked: +++DD on a 6 digit zip leaves the last digit as it was. If you need repeatability use key masking.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.6.5 Encryption masking What it does. Applies an encryption algorithm to a string column (User Guide 10.5.10, p.161 to 162) . Two families: Type Options Notes Standard Encryption AES (Advanced Encryption Standard, 128-bit), CRC (cyclic redundancy check, a checksum for finding transmission errors), MD5 (one-way hash, 128-bit value) You enter an encryption key of 16 characters or fewer Format Preserving Encryption Preserve Format and Metadata; Preserve Metadata; Change Metadata Can be decrypted later with the same pass phrase and the same rule configuration. Not usable if the data has UTF-8 four-byte characters The three format preserving options in the guide's own words (p.161 to 162): Preserve Format and Metadata: keeps format and length. Upper case becomes upper case, lower case lower case, digits digits, special characters special characters. Example: Abc123@xyz.com may become Mpz849#dje!kuw ; with "@" and "." set as Do Not Encrypt Characters, Mpz849@dje.kuw . Preserve Metadata: keeps only length. Alexender may become jl6#HB91v . Change Metadata: length and format change. London may become Xuep@8f5 or 6ky#ke33h*we . Before using it you must raise the column precision in the database (and in TDM) using: Required Precision = (1.33 x Original Precision) + 24, rounded up. After changing the database column, reimport metadata or edit the precision in Test Data Manager. Parameter Meaning (p.162) Encryption Type Standard Encryption or Format Preserving Encryption Encryption Technique The technique to encrypt or decrypt the data Encryption Key Input key for standard encryption, 16 characters or fewer Publish Rule Makes a format preserving rule read-only; only domain administrators can make it editable again or delete it Do Not Encrypt Characters Characters left as they are. A leading or trailing space is respected but not displayed in the field Use it when you must be able to get the original back (decryption is described only for format preserving encryption) or the application checks the shape of a value. Reversibility is also a risk: anyone with the key or pass phrase and the rule can recover production values (my note, ). The excerpt does not say where the pass phrase is entered; check your version. Same key and configuration give the same output for the same input.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.6.6 Expression masking What it does. Applies a PowerCenter-style expression to a column to create or change data. You build the expression in the Expression Builder by clicking columns, functions, variables and operators. Any datatype (User Guide 10.5.10, p.162 to 163) . Guide example: to join first names with the text ABC, enter CONCAT(FirstName,'ABC') . On ShopSphere Asha becomes AshaABC, a poor mask on its own but it shows the idea; a better use builds a value from other pieces, such as 'CUST' || customer_id . Parameter Meaning Repeatable Output Keeps the masked value for a given column value; you must enter a seed if you enable it Alphanumeric Seed Any text. Use the same seed in several rules that must return the same masked values Expression A PowerCenter expression working on values in a single row Gotchas (p.163): use it for one column (use advanced masking for several); make the expression return the column datatype, or you get zero (numeric) or NULL (string); one expression's output cannot feed another; repeatable output needs a storage table in the plan or the operation fails; no repeatable expression masking for Hadoop.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.6.7 Nullification masking What it does. Replaces the value with NULL. Works on binary, date, numeric and string data. No parameters (p.168) . Use it for columns the test environment does not need: the strongest privacy result. The target column must allow NULL, and the application may expect an SSN to exist.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.6.8 SSN masking What it does. Applies a built-in mask for Social Security numbers on string columns (User Guide 10.5.10, p.175) . It generates valid-looking numbers and tries to avoid numbers the US Social Security Administration has actually issued, using the High Group List. The service reads that file from the PowerCenter installation's infa_shared/SrcFiles directory; you can download the latest version from the Social Security Administration. Any nine-digit input is accepted, with any delimiters. Parameters. Repeatable Output with a seed value; an SSN randomization option, based on the method the Social Security Administration developed to remove the geographic meaning of the first three digits. The excerpt does not give more parameter names. SSN masking (illustrative output) customer_id ssn before ssn after 1001 123-45-6789 612-73-4410 1002 234-56-7890 478-09-2231 1003 345-67-8901 559-21-7068 Gotchas. TDM "cannot return all unique" SSNs, because it cannot return numbers already issued, so test for duplicates if ssn has a unique constraint. Any delimiter style is accepted; check the output style suits your validation. Repeatability. Tick Repeatable Output, tick Seed, enter a value.

x: 5.6.9 SIN masking SIN is the Canadian Social Insurance Number (general background). The technique handles a nine-digit SIN with any delimiters on string columns (p.175) : no delimiters in gives none out, otherwise xxx-xxx-xxx . Start Digit forces the first digit; Repeatable Output takes a seed. ShopSphere has no SIN column.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.6.10 Phone masking What it does. Changes phone numbers while keeping the original format; string columns only (p.169) . The guide's example: (408)382 0658 becomes (408)256 3106 . Input may contain digits, spaces, hyphens and parentheses; alphabetic and special characters are not masked. Illustration: 9876543210 might become 9876012345. The excerpt lists no parameters, and does not say which digits are preserved; in the example the first three stayed, but I would not assume that rule holds for every format.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.6.11 Credit card masking What it does. Applies a built-in format to credit card numbers on string columns, producing a logically valid number with a valid checksum (User Guide 10.5.10, p.158 to 159) . The source must be 13 to 19 digits with a valid checksum under card industry rules. It may contain numbers, spaces and hyphens. Invalid characters or length: the service logs an error in the session log and applies a default credit card mask. The six-digit Bank Identification Number (BIN) at the front is not masked. The guide's example: 4539 1596 8210 2773 may become 4539 1516 0556 7067 . Parameter Meaning Repeatable Same masked value across runs and across tables Seed Start for repeatable output, 1 to 999, default 1 Keep card issuer Output has the same card type (Visa in, Visa-format out) Replace card issuer Output has a different type: choose AMEX, VISA, JCB, MASTERCARD or ANY (default ANY)

x: 5.6.12 Email masking What it does. Generates realistic email addresses on string columns. It can build the user name from the masked first and last names, and use a constant or a dictionary-chosen domain (p.159 to 161) . Output is always ASCII. It can be repeatable between workflows or within one workflow. Group Parameter Meaning General Repeatable output, Seed Same email masked the same way; seed 1 to 999, default 1 General Standard Replaces the string with characters; user and domain names are not realistic General Advanced Builds from names and domains in a dictionary or mapping General Columns to form email From mapping (assign columns when you assign the rule) or From dictionary User name Dictionary for columns A dictionary containing first and last names User name Expression For From mapping: build the user name from parts of first and last name; names in the expression need not match source columns User name First name column, First name length Dictionary column and how many characters to use (first letter, first 4); default 10 User name Delimiter Period, underscore or hyphen between first and last name User name Last name column, Last name length Same for the last name; default 10 Domain Constant Every address gets the same domain Domain Random, Domain lookup dictionary, Domain name column Pick domains at random from a flat file or relational dictionary, naming the column Advanced email masking, user name from masked names, delimiter period, constant domain (illustrative) Masked first/last name email before email after Divya Iyer asha.menon@example.com divya.iyer@example.com Arjun Das ravi.k@example.com arjun.das@example.com Gotchas. The From mapping option needs the masked name columns, which usually means one advanced rule that masks the names and builds the email (14.8). h: 5.7.1 Choosing a technique: questions to ask
x: 5.7.1 Choosing a technique: questions to ask Does the test environment need this column at all? If not, nullification is the simplest and safest. Does the application check a format (SSN pattern, card checksum, phone layout, URL)? Use the matching built-in technique (SSN, SIN, credit card, phone, email, IP, URL) so the checks pass. Does it need real-looking text such as names and places? Substitution (new values from a dictionary) or shuffle (existing values moved between rows). Is the value an identifier that appears in several tables and must stay joinable? Use key masking with the same seed, or rely on auto cascade for keys with constraints, or repeatable substitution with the same seed (14.4, 14.5). Is it a number or date where only "near the original" matters? Random masking with blurring. Do you need to undo the masking later? Format preserving encryption, knowing the privacy trade-off. Does a masked value depend on more than one column? An advanced rule, or a mapplet if PowerCenter logic already exists.

x: 5.8 Advanced masking rules in depth An advanced rule is a small program built from columns of three types (User Guide 10.5.10, p.137 to 138, p.156 to 158) : input (receives the source value), variable (a scratch column that holds an intermediate result from an expression or a masking technique, so you can combine several techniques) and output (the target column that receives the final value). Column names inside the rule are your own; at assignment time you map them to real columns. Property For Meaning Column Name, Column Type, Datatype, Precision, Scale, Mandatory input, variable, output General properties. Mandatory means the column must be assigned to a source column in every project (input and output only) Expression variable, output An expression built in the Expression Builder Masking Rule variable, output Apply an existing rule to an input column and write the result to this column. Sub-options: Condition (if true, mask the column), Rule , Override properties (if the rule owner allowed it), Input column Condition Input output only Pick a condition applied earlier on an input column Dependent variable, output Dependent masking: replaces a column's value with the value from the same dictionary row that another column's substitution returned. You must define substitution on another column first. Sub-options: Input column (the column configured for substitution) and Dictionary column

h: 5.9 Custom rules: mapplets and the Data Masking transformation
x: 5.9 Custom rules: mapplets and the Data Masking transformation This is the Day 54 topic "masking rules, algorithms, mapplet creation, using transformations". I will separate three things: what the guide says, what it does not say, and the general idea.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.9.1 What the guide says Purpose. Mapplet rules let you use PowerCenter masking techniques that are "not available in Test Data Manager" (User Guide 10.5.10, p.150). The mapplet holds the logic to mask the input columns and return data to the target columns (p.137, p.152). How it gets in. You export the mapplet to an XML file from the PowerCenter repository or the Model repository, then import it in Test Data Manager as a rule (p.137, p.140). To mask Hadoop data you import mapplets built in the Developer tool (p.137). The TDM repository then stores the mapplet logic, and you cannot change the mapplet inside Test Data Manager (p.137). What it must contain. One or more Data Masking transformations , and all transformations must be passive (they must not add or remove rows) (p.137, p.150). It can have multiple input and multiple output columns (p.137). Required ports. Mark at least one input and one output column as mandatory; mandatory columns need source and target assignments when you assign the rule (p.137, p.141, p.155). Custom masking parameters (p.156): Column Name, Column Type (input or output), Data Type, Precision, Mandatory, Group Name (input, output or another name you gave in the mapplet). Exporting the other way. You can also export rules as PowerCenter mapplets (p.150). Assignment. Select the rule in the Masking Rule column, then link source input columns to rule input ports and rule output ports to source columns (p.142 to 143). Sybase to Hadoop limit: 20 columns. Hadoop engine limits. A Blaze engine allows Expression, Data Masking, Case Converter, Comparison, Decision, Labeler, Merge, Parser, Weighted Average, Standardizer and Java Passive transformations in a mapplet rule; Spark allows Expression, Data Masking and Java Passive; Hadoop mapplets cannot use sequence generator, lookup or classifier (p.62, p.137). Changes. If you change the name or type of a field of a custom rule, existing assignments do not see it; import the mapplet again (p.144). Data Masking transformation session properties (User Guide chapter 3, p.52 to 53): SSN High Group File path, DMO Cache Directory, Cache Size (default 8 MB), Shared Storage Table (default disabled) and Storage Commit Interval (default 100,000).

h: 5.9.2 What the guide does not say
x: 5.9.2 What the guide does not say The guide tells you to export a mapplet containing Data Masking transformations; it does not teach building one in PowerCenter Designer or the Developer tool, and gives no list of the transformation's port properties and no finished example. "Mapplet creation" as a click-by-click task is outside this guide; ask your trainer which PowerCenter material your course uses.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.9.3 The general idea (not from the guide). A transformation in PowerCenter is one processing step on rows of data (calculate, look up, mask). A mapplet is a reusable bundle of such steps with input and output ports, like a function you write once and call from many mappings. A Data Masking transformation applies masking techniques to a port. A mapplet rule therefore means "run my own bundle of steps instead of one built-in technique", for example mask phone numbers differently per country. Day 54 mapping: masking rules are 14.3 and 14.4, algorithms are 14.6 and 14.7, mapplet import and assignment are 14.9 (building the mapplet is not in the guide), and "using transformations" is 14.8 (expressions) and 14.9 (Data Masking transformation). The architecture behind this, with PowerCenter running the workflows that TDM generates, is in the Informatica overview and architecture chapter . x: 5.10.1 Running the masking operation: the guide's steps The guide's list for performing a masking operation (User Guide 10.5.10, p.148 to 149) , with reasons: Create a data masking rule. The rule is the recipe (14.3). Preview it in the Rule Simulator. Create a project and import metadata. The project knows the tables and columns. Use separate projects for XSD and relational sources. Optional: create parameters or import global parameters. For example a seed variable in a parameter file, so you can change the seed without editing the rule (p.155). Add the rule to the project. Projects only see rules you add (14.4). Assign the rule to a target column (or to an XML element). This is where you say "mask ssn with SSN_Rule". Save each row. Create a plan, add the rule, and configure source and target connections. A plan holds at least one rule or policy. It states whether data is masked in place in the source database or in stream into a target (p.150). Add a storage connection if any rule is repeatable substitution or expression masking (p.286). Generate and run the workflow. PowerCenter creates mappings, sessions and a workflow and runs them (p.150). Use Actions > Generate and Execute, then pick parameter values (p.310 to 311). Monitor the workflow. Check Workflow Executions for Success, then open the logs if not (p.311 to 312). Target columns hold masked values; source untouched (when masking in stream into a target). Plans and workflow settings are in the Informatica plans, workflows and warehouse chapter . If you also subset, masking runs on the subset result (p.275), as in the Informatica data subset chapter .

x: 5.12 Common mistakes and gotchas Watch out for these Forgetting to click Save after each assignment; TDM discards unsaved assignments (User Guide 10.5.10, p.145). Not rerunning plans. Edits to rules, assignments or domains do not change existing plans until you regenerate and run them (p.144 to 148). Different seeds on columns that must match. The same seed gives the same output across columns (p.154, p.167). Different seeds give different values, and joins break. Repeatable substitution or expression masking with no storage table. Expression masking fails; substitution cannot remember pairs (p.163, p.176, p.286). Unique substitution with a short dictionary. The operation fails (p.176). Short mask formats. Trailing characters stay unmasked (p.164). Masking the primary key but not the foreign key. Use auto cascade, value cascade or the same seed (p.90 to 91, p.167). Shuffle on XSD or Spark, expression repeatable on Hadoop, flat-file dictionaries on Hadoop. Documented as unsupported (p.62, p.135, p.163, p.176). Expecting reversibility from the wrong technique. Only format preserving encryption is described as decryptable (p.161).

x: 5.13 Recap Key points A rule is a technique plus parameters. Rules attach to columns directly or through data domains, which a policy groups for reuse. Always preview a standard rule in the Rule Simulator. Three rule kinds: standard (one input, one output), advanced (input, variable, output columns with expressions, conditions and dependent masking) and mapplet (imported PowerCenter logic made of passive transformations including Data Masking transformations). Repeatable output and a seed make masking deterministic. Substitution and expression masking also need a storage table. Substitution gives realistic values from a dictionary; shuffle moves real values between rows; key masking keeps character types deterministically; random masking uses ranges and blurring; encryption can be reversible; nullification empties the column; SSN, SIN, phone, credit card, email, IP and URL are built-in formats. Choose by what the application needs: realism, format validity, joinability across tables, reversibility, or nothing at all. The guide covers importing and assigning mapplet rules but does not teach building the mapplet in PowerCenter. Masking happens after subsetting when both are in one plan. Informatica: generating test data So far in Part II every operation started with real production data: discovery looked at it, subsetting shrank it and masking disguised it. This section does something different. Data generation builds test data from nothing but rules, so no production row is read, copied or at risk. If you have read the generation concepts chapter , you know why teams want this. Here you learn how Informatica TDM does it. The chapter has one running goal, taken from the Day 45 syllabus item "generate test data using the Informatica ILM tool": by the end you should be able to describe how a generation job is defined, choose a technique for every ShopSphere column, and generate 50 customers with valid orders. The plan, workflow and monitoring side is shared with masking and subsetting, so it is covered in the plans, workflows and warehouse chapter .

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.14 Words to know first Data generation Creating new, realistic but fictional rows by following rules, instead of copying real rows. Also called synthetic data creation. Generation rule A saved recipe for one kind of value, for example "ten random digits starting with 6 to 9". It names a technique and sets its parameters. Assignment The link between a rule and a target column: "column phone uses rule Phone_10_digits ". Global rule A named rule created once in the Policies area and reusable in every project. Standard, custom and advanced rules are global. Ad hoc rule An unnamed rule created inside one project directly on a column. It cannot be moved to another project. Default rule The rule TDM applies to a column you did not assign anything to, chosen per data type. Entity A set of tables linked by keys (a parent with its children) that TDM treats as one unit. You met entities in the Informatica subsetting chapter . Dictionary A file or table of ready-made values, such as first names, that a rule can pick from. It must be added to TDM by a user with the right permission before a rule can use it. Exception test data Deliberate nulls and deliberately invalid values mixed into the output, so that tests also see bad data.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.15 What data generation is for Picture ShopSphere's performance team. They want to test the "Customer Orders" app with 500,000 customers, ten times more than production holds. Subsetting can only shrink what exists. Masking keeps the same number of rows. Neither can invent rows. Generation can, and since it never touches production, there is nothing to leak. The guide defines it plainly: use data generation to create realistic test data for test environments, using rules that define the logic (User Guide 10.5.10, p.190). You import the target table definitions (the metadata ) into a project to say what shape of data you want, assign rules to columns, then run a plan. Three ways to get test data, side by side (concept view; the Informatica terms are from the guide) Subset Masking Generation Reads production rows? Yes Yes No Number of rows Fewer than production Same as input Whatever you ask for Real values at risk? Yes, unless masked Disguised None exist Realism comes from The real data The real data plus substitutes Your rules (dictionaries, patterns, distributions) Typical ShopSphere use A small regression database A realistic UAT copy Load tests, new features with no production data yet Why it matters Generated data is the safest test data there is, and it is the only kind that can reach any volume you like, or hit awkward cases (nulls, invalid values, boundary dates) on purpose. Its weakness is realism: it only looks as real as your rules. A rule that makes every email "name@example.com" will not exercise your duplicate-email checks. Most of this section is about writing rules that are realistic enough.

h: 5.16 The building blocks and the order of work
x: 5.16 The building blocks and the order of work The guide names five components you create or use for generation (User Guide 10.5.10, p.191): Data generation components Component What it is ShopSphere example Rule A technique plus its parameters. May allow overriding. Phone_10_digits Assignment The allocation of a rule to a column. CUSTOMERS.phone gets Phone_10_digits Table The target table where rules are assigned. CUSTOMERS Entity Tables related by physical or logical constraints. CUSTOMERS with its children ORDERS and ORDER_ITEMS Plan Defines the generation operation: which tables or entities, how many records, which connections. PLAN_GEN_CUSTOMERS_50 The order matters, because each step needs the one before it. The guide's task flow (User Guide 10.5.10, p.192): 1. Rules create global rules and defaults → 2. Project import target metadata → 3. Parameters optional → 4. Constraints optional conditional rules → 5. Assign rules to columns → 6. Plan add tables or entities → 7. Run generate workflow, watch Monitor Steps 1 to 5 are design time : you are only describing data, and no row exists yet. Step 6 packages the description, and step 7 is the first time anything is written. This mirrors the ETL and TDM chapter : the plan is the specification, and the workflow that TDM generates from it is the ETL job. One detail from the overview is easy to miss: if a table name or column name contains special characters, the data generation workflow fails (User Guide 10.5.10, p.190). Check your target names before you import metadata. Where you click In the Test Data Manager web client, global rules live under Policies . Inside a project, the tabs are Overview, Discover, Define, Execute, Monitor and Permissions (older screenshots say Security). Generation rules are assigned under Define | Data Generation , plans are built under Execute (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.50, 203). The next chapter tours plan building in detail.

h: 5.17 Rule types: standard, custom, advanced and ad hoc
x: 5.17 Rule types: standard, custom, advanced and ad hoc A rule can be created in four ways. The difference is mostly how many columns it touches and where it lives (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.192-193). The four generation rule types Type Scope What it does Created in Standard Global, one output column Uses one predefined technique. You can assign the same rule to many columns. Policies Custom Global Generates data from the logic of a PowerCenter mapplet. Policies Advanced Global, several columns Combines techniques and uses more than one input column. Policies Ad hoc One project, no name Created straight on a column. Can use extra techniques that global rules cannot. Define | Data Generation of a project Global rules appear in every project and carry a name. Ad hoc rules have no name, cannot be moved, and are defined by the target columns you pick when you create them (p.193). The three techniques that exist only as ad hoc are reference lookup , effective dates and expression ; conditional is also listed as ad hoc in the technique table (p.209).

h: 5.17.1 Editing and deleting rules: the "impacted objects" check
x: 5.17.1 Editing and deleting rules: the "impacted objects" check If you edit or delete a global rule that is already assigned somewhere, TDM shows an Impacted Objects dialog listing affected columns, plans and data domains. You can export that list as a .csv file, then click Continue to save. The change does not reach a plan until you generate and run that plan again (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.195-196). The same dialog appears when you edit an ad hoc rule, assign a rule, or clear an assignment (pp.199, 204-206).

x: 5.17.2 Creating a standard rule Open Policies and choose Actions > New > Generation Rule. Creating it in Policies, not inside a project, makes the rule global and reusable. Enter a name, pick the column's data type, select the standard type and optionally tick Override Allowed. The data type decides which techniques the wizard offers, so choose it first. Click Next, fill in the parameters, set the exception test data options and click Finish. The options choose whether to allow nulls or empty spaces and whether to produce invalid data (see exception test data ). The rule appears in the Policies list and can be assigned in any project (p.195).

x: 5.17.3 Override: one rule, small variations If a rule has Override Allowed set, whoever assigns it can change its parameters for that one column without touching the global rule. The guide's example: a rule that makes random dates from 2011 to 2012 with override on; a user assigns it and adds Saturday and Sunday as excluded days, so that column gets weekday dates only (p.193). To do it, select the column in Define | Data Generation, choose Actions > Override, edit the values and Save. The Override column then reads Yes-Overridden (p.196).

x: 5.17.4 Custom and advanced rules, in brief A custom rule imports a PowerCenter mapplet. You must mark at least one input and one output column as required. The guide's use: combine first and last name into a full name, or use PowerCenter transformations such as an SQL or Stored Procedure transformation (User Guide 10.5.10, p.196). An advanced rule has input, variable and output ports and can mix techniques. Both get their own sections in the technique tour .

h: 5.18 Default rules: what happens to columns you ignore
x: 5.18 Default rules: what happens to columns you ignore Columns without an assigned rule receive the default rule for their data type (User Guide 10.5.10, p.193). The defaults (Numeric, String, Date and Binary, plus separate primary key and unique key defaults for each type) are visible on a project's Overview | Properties tab (pp.193-194). Keys get their own defaults because a primary key must never repeat or be empty. The administrator configures the initial defaults (p.193), and in the plan's Data Generation Properties you can adjust them again and tick Apply Default Rule to columns without rules (p.285). Two more shortcuts the guide mentions (pp.194, 205): Default data domain rule. You set this when you create and run a data domain profile ( the Informatica discovery and profiling chapter ), so discovery can feed generation. Auto rule. After a column profile you review and finalise results. Columns whose Inferred Rule shows Yes can take the Auto Rule, which fills the column from the approved profile results. Do not apply an auto rule to a primary key column, because a primary key cannot contain nulls. Default rules are not a plan The guide notes that default rules are not filled in if the rules are not part of the project. If the default boxes in the plan are blank, you must choose the default rules yourself (p.284). Random defaults are fine for a column nobody tests, not for one with business meaning such as email .

x: 5.19.1 How each kind of rule is assigned Standard rule: click inside Generation Rule for the column, choose the rule, click Save (p.204). x: 5.20 Tables, entities, relationships and keys Real data is not a pile of independent tables. Every ShopSphere order must point to a customer that exists, and every order item to an order that exists. If you generate each table separately with random numbers, the foreign keys will point nowhere and the app will fail for reasons unrelated to what you wanted to test. TDM gives you two tools for this.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
h: 5.20.1 Entities: generate a parent with its children
x: 5.20.1 Entities: generate a parent with its children An entity defines tables related by physical or logical constraints, and keeps the hierarchy (User Guide 10.5.10, p.277). You can add entities (and plain tables) to a generation plan. You create the entity in the project's Define area, pick a driving table, and TDM finds related tables from the constraints. If your database has no declared foreign keys, add a logical foreign key on the Discover | Tables | Constraints tab, mapping the child column to the parent column ( the Informatica subsetting chapter ; User Guide 10.5.10, pp.110, 116). For each relationship in an entity map there are Minimum and Maximum properties: the fewest and most child records to generate for each parent record (p.117). The plan-level Data Generation Properties repeat this as Minimum and Maximum (guide default 1 for each), plus Parent Records Without Children and Child Records Without Parent percentages for self-cyclic tables or reference lookups (p.285). A link between XML elements works the same way. A range set on an individual relationship takes priority over the plan-level ratio (p.207). CUSTOMERS customer_id 1001 ORDERS order 5001, cust 1001 ORDERS order 5002, cust 1001 ORDER_ITEMS item 9001, order 5001 ORDER_ITEMS item 9002, order 5002 min 1, max 3 orders min 1, max 4 items Original diagram: the fan-out an entity describes. Each generated parent receives a random number of children between the minimum and maximum, and every child carries its parent's key. The numbers are my ShopSphere illustration.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
h: 5.20.2 Reference lookup: borrow values from a table that already exists
x: 5.20.2 Reference lookup: borrow values from a table that already exists The second tool is the reference lookup technique (see Reference Lookup ). Instead of making values, it reads them from an existing parent table, so a child column can only receive keys that exist there. The plan then needs a Reference Lookup Connection , a connection to the database that holds the parent tables (User Guide 10.5.10, p.280). Use it for static reference data: ShopSphere's PRODUCTS table is the natural example for ORDER_ITEMS.product_code . What I could and could not confirm The guide says entities keep parent-child hierarchy and lets you set child counts per parent. It does not spell out, in the pages I read, exactly how TDM copies the parent key into the child's foreign key column, or whether a reference lookup may read a parent table generated in the same plan rather than one already loaded in the database. After a first run, always check keys with a quick join query (the lab does).

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.20.3 Primary keys and unique values A computed column as primary key blocks generation for an entity: you cannot run generation that includes an entity whose primary key column is a computed column (p.191). For multirecord IMS sources imported from PowerCenter, the table sequence is not imported, so you must supply it with the Manage Sequence button on the entity's Entity Map tab (pp.191-192). This is a mainframe case you can skip for ShopSphere. Many techniques have a Generate Unique Values checkbox. It cannot be combined with regular-expression patterns, and cannot be used for binary or flat-file dictionary rules (pp.216, 222-223). For ids, the cleanest choice is the Sequence technique. A sequence never repeats within a run, and "Start Sequence from Last Value" lets a second run continue where the first stopped (p.231).

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
h: 5.21 How many records? And exception data
x: 5.21 How many records? And exception data The number of rows is not part of a rule. It is set in the plan : the field Number of Records to Generate is marked Required for generation plans (User Guide 10.5.10, p.280). In the plan wizard it is step 14: "enter the number of records that you want to generate" (p.305). You can also give criteria per entity on the generation criteria step (p.305). For a parent-child set, the Minimum and Maximum child settings decide how many children each parent gets, so total rows in the child tables are not a round number. My reading, flagged because the guide gives no worked example of totals: with 50 customers and 1 to 3 orders each, expect between 50 and 150 orders. Confirm with the Row Count report ( the plans, workflows and warehouse chapter ).

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
h: 5.21.1 Exception test data: nulls and invalid values
x: 5.21.1 Exception test data: nulls and invalid values Almost every technique ends with the same two settings, Null Values and Invalid Values (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.210-211). Each takes a rule (an existing global rule, or "Default") and a percentage, which may have up to two decimal places. Null Values: the percentage of rows that will contain a null in this column. Cannot be generated for MongoDB sources (p.210). Invalid Values: the percentage of rows that deliberately break the rule, where "invalid" means whatever does not conform to the rule: outside the numeric range, wrong length, not in the dictionary and so on. The guide's trick: make a rule "Recent_Dates" for 2012 to 2013 and, in its Invalid Values setting, choose a second saved rule "Dates_2005" (2005 to 2010) at 15 percent. Now 85 percent of dates are recent and 15 percent are old (p.210). So "invalid values" is really a way to mix in a second population. Why would I want bad data? Good testing needs negative cases. If ShopSphere's checkout rejects a customer with no phone number, you need rows with no phone number. Ten percent nulls in phone and two percent invalid zip_code values give your tests something to reject, without hand-crafting rows.
