h: 5.22 The generation techniques, one by one
x: 5.22 The generation techniques, one by one A technique is the method a rule uses to produce values. The guide lists eleven (User Guide 10.5.10, p.209). Which ones you may choose depends on the column's data type, and some are ad hoc only , meaning you can use them only when you create a rule directly on a column inside a project (pp.208-209). All eleven generation techniques (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.209-235) Technique Kind Data types One-line purpose Sequence Standard Numeric, date Values in order with a start and an increment Random Standard String, numeric, date Random strings, numbers or dates, optionally from a pattern Set of Values Standard String, numeric, date A short list of values with a percentage for each Dictionary Standard String, numeric, date, binary Values picked from an imported dictionary Credit Card Standard String only Card numbers by network, passing the Luhn check Reference Lookup Ad hoc String, numeric, date Values taken from an existing parent table Expression Ad hoc String, numeric, date Values computed from other columns Conditional Ad hoc String, numeric, date Different rule depending on another column's value Effective Dates Ad hoc Date Consecutive start and end dates in two columns Advanced Combination String, numeric, date Several techniques and several columns in one rule Custom Mapplet String, numeric, date Logic imported from a PowerCenter mapplet For each technique below you get what it does, when to reach for it, its parameters and a ShopSphere example. The example outputs are my illustrations of what such a rule would produce, not captured TDM output, unless I say the guide shows them.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.22.1 Sequence A global or ad hoc rule that makes numeric or date values in a sequence. You pick a beginning value and an increment (User Guide 10.5.10, p.230). When: ids and anything that must be ascending: customer ids, ticket numbers, consecutive dates. The guide's example is a TICKET_NUMBER column with start 1000 and increment 1 (p.231). Parameters (pp.231-232): numeric rules take Start Value, Increment Value and Start Sequence from Last Value , which makes the next run continue from the previous output (on a string column it restarts from the beginning). Date rules take Start Date and Increment by (a number plus year, month, day, hour, minutes or seconds). Null Values and Invalid Values apply, where invalid means below the start for a positive increment. ShopSphere: customer_id with start 1001, increment 1 gives 1001, 1002, 1003 and so on. A date sequence for order_date with start 2026-01-01 and increment 1 day gives one order per consecutive day. Limits: you cannot add a conditional constraint to a sequence column (p.201) or put conditions on a sequence rule (p.234).

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.22.2 Random A global or ad hoc rule that creates random strings, numbers and dates, for things like salary and birth dates (p.220). For strings you give a minimum and maximum length; for numbers a minimum and maximum value; for dates a range. You can instead supply a regular expression (a compact pattern language for text shapes) and say what percentage of rows follow it. If you use several patterns the percentages must total 100. Visual reference Informatica TDM 10.5.10 User Guide, p.210, figure "random string generation rule". The rendered page shows a wizard step titled "New Generation Rule: Step 2 of 2" with a Random option (Minimum Length, Maximum Length), a From Regular Expression option with a Pattern box and a Distribution % box, a Generate Unique Values checkbox, and an Exception Test Data area with Null Values and Invalid Values drop-downs set to "Default" beside percentage boxes showing 0. What to look for: the two radio choices are mutually exclusive ways of making a string. Parameters (pp.221-223): strings take Minimum Length (default 1) and Maximum Length (default the column maximum); numbers take Minimum Value (default 0) and Maximum Value (default the column maximum); dates take Start and End Date/Time and Exclude (up to two different weekdays). Strings and numbers can instead use From Regular Expression with a Pattern and Distribution. Generate Unique Values is not available with a pattern, and neither are invalid values. Null Values and Invalid Values apply as usual. Writing patterns For strings the usable operators are . , \d , \w , alternation (a|b|c) , {n} repeat counts and [ ] sets. To make numbers that contain special characters, use the string technique. To make plain numbers use the numeric technique, which allows \d , alternates like (1|2|3) and [0-9] , and alternates cannot be nested (p.223). ShopSphere pattern examples (my illustrations, using the operators the guide lists on p.223) Goal Technique Pattern Example output ShopSphere mobile, 10 digits starting 6 to 9 Numeric (6|7|8|9)\d{9} 9123456780 ShopSphere SSN-like String \d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4} 234-56-7890 ShopSphere tax id String [A-Z]{3}\d{6} KQM481926 ShopSphere test email String [a-z]{8}@example\.(com|org) qkdmpzra@example.org Read a pattern left to right as slots: \d is one digit, {n} repeats the previous piece, [A-Z] is one character from a range, (a|b) is a choice and \. is a literal dot. So (6|7|8|9)\d{9} is a first digit 6 to 9 followed by nine digits. This reading aid is general knowledge. Test a pattern by generating a few rows into a scratch table first. Patterns cannot make valid checksummed numbers For credit card, Social Security and Social Insurance numbers the guide warns that pattern-made values might not be valid, because real numbers follow algorithms that a pattern cannot reproduce (p.224). That is fine for "SSN-like" test data, and it is why the Credit Card technique exists. Date example: a random date rule from 1950-01-01 to 2005-12-31 for date_of_birth gives values such as 1990-04-12 and 1999-07-23. Set Exclude to Saturday and Sunday and no value falls on a weekend; "invalid" for dates means outside the range or on an excluded day (p.221).

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.22.3 Set of Values You type the values you want and the percentage of rows for each; the percentages must total 100 (decimals allowed). Works for string, numeric and date, and can be global or ad hoc (pp.232-233). Best for columns with a handful of values, such as membership status. Parameters: Value (one row per value, add rows as needed), Distribution% , and the usual Null Values and Invalid Values. For this technique "invalid" means anything not in the list (p.233). The guide's example is a PAYMENT_TYPE column with Visa 60, MasterCard 30, Paypal 10. ShopSphere: zip_code with 560001 at 40, 600017 at 35 and 682001 at 25. Of 50 customers, about 20, 17 or 18, and 12 or 13 will get each zip code. Percentages are targets, so expect small rounding differences.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.22.4 Dictionary Loads values from a dictionary (a flat file or relational table of values) into a column. Good for columns with realistic but finite values: names, states, countries. Before you create the rule, someone with permission must add the dictionary under Administrator | Dictionaries . Works for string, numeric, date and binary data; flat file or relational source; binary only from relational (p.215). Parameters (p.216): Dictionary Name; Dictionary Column (longer values are truncated to the target size); an optional Dictionary Lookup Column plus Table Column to match rows; Serial Number Columns (relational dictionaries, needed for binary); Generate Unique Values (not for flat-file dictionaries or binary); Null and Invalid Values (invalid means not in the dictionary). If both lookup and table columns are of double data type the process generates nulls (p.216). The guide's example makes two string rules from one names dictionary: one picks the first-name column, one the last-name column (p.215). ShopSphere: first_name uses dictionary NAMES column FIRST, last_name uses column LAST. Sample output: Meera, Nair; Ravi, Kumar; Asha, Menon. The dictionary's name and column names here are placeholders I made up. Because the two rules pick independently, "Ravi Menon" is as likely as "Ravi Kumar", which is fine for testing and wrong for anything that needs a believable family name.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.22.5 Credit Card Creates card numbers by issuing network. Output is a string (not numeric, date or binary), and numbers must pass verification using Luhn's algorithm, the check-digit formula real cards follow (pp.226-227). Formatted output looks like XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX . Parameters (pp.227-228): Issuing Network (required: American Express, Discover, JCB, Mastercard or Visa); an optional Issuer Identification Number of up to six starting digits (a value invalid for the network makes the workflow fail; blank lets TDM use valid ones); Distribution % (must total 100); Generate Formatted Values; Generate Unique Values; Null and Invalid Values. Valid starting digits include Visa 4, Mastercard 51 to 55 and American Express 34 and 37. ShopSphere: the four tables hold no card numbers, so imagine a later PAYMENTS.card_no column. A rule with Visa at 60 percent and Mastercard at 40 percent, formatted, gives values shaped like 4666-1760-3137-2159 and 5122-3307-9244-0268 . I computed those two to pass the Luhn check, but TDM would produce its own digits.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.22.6 Reference Lookup An ad hoc rule that takes column values from an existing table, for string, numeric and date columns. You name the parent table and map parent columns to child columns. The same rule can fill several child columns from the same parent table (p.229). The guide's example: use the same customer ids that exist in another table. Parameters (p.230): Minimum (default 1) and Maximum (default 3) child records per parent; Data Source (connection to the parent table); Parent Table; pairs of Child Column and Parent Column; a Parent Table Filter; the percent of parent records without children and of child records without a parent (if that is 0 you must give a Default Value to write instead of nulls). ShopSphere: ORDERS.customer_id reads CUSTOMERS.customer_id with minimum 1 and maximum 3, so each existing customer gets one to three orders. Set "Parent records without children" to 10 and about one customer in ten has no orders, a useful edge case. Remember the plan needs a Reference Lookup Connection (p.280), and see the note on reference lookup about where the parent rows must already live. Reference lookup is not for XML targets You cannot use reference lookup or effective dates rules for an XSD (XML) source (p.206).

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.22.7 Expression An ad hoc rule that computes a value from an expression you build in the Expression Builder, choosing columns and functions from lists. Works for string, numeric and date (p.219). Parameters: Expression, Null Values, Invalid Values (invalid = does not follow the expression) (p.220). If you tick "Override Data Type to Numeric" on a string column, you cannot enter a numeric expression (p.219). The guide's example builds a Name column from FirstName and LastName with CONCAT (FirstName+'/'+LastName) . ShopSphere: imagine a display_name column built as CONCAT(CONCAT(first_name,' '),last_name) , giving "Asha Menon". I mirrored the nested CONCAT style the guide uses in its advanced example; check the exact function list in your Expression Builder. When: any column that is a function of other columns in the same row. The dependent column must still be assignable after its inputs, so assign rules to the inputs too.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.22.8 Conditional An ad hoc rule with one or more rows of " if this condition, then use this generation rule ". Conditions are applied in the order listed (reorder with the up and down arrows). Works for string, numeric and date, but you cannot apply conditions to effective dates or sequence rules (p.234). The guide's example: DEPT_ID 11 gets a 5 percent hike, 22 gets 10, 33 gets 15. The column that the condition reads (DEPT_ID) must itself have a rule, and TDM generates it first, then the dependent column (p.234). ShopSphere (hypothetical city column): if zip_code = '560001' then city is "Bengaluru", if '600017' then "Chennai", if '682001' then "Kochi". Each "then" is a one-value Set of Values rule. The guide does not describe a catch-all "else" row, so make sure every possible input value has a condition.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.22.9 Effective Dates An ad hoc date rule that fills two related columns, an effective start date and an effective end date, so that periods follow one another without overlap. It makes a random start in a range, an end after it, and the next start right after that end. A grouping column decides how many dates are in each sequence: the number of rows sharing the same grouping value (pp.217-218). You create the rule on either the start or the end column and name the other. Parameters: Start Date/Time, End Date/Time, Exclude (up to two different weekdays), Effective Start Date column, Effective End Date column, Grouping Column, Invalid Values (percent of rows breaking the sequence; the rule is fixed to Default) (pp.218-219). ShopSphere: a hypothetical CUSTOMER_ADDRESS_HISTORY table with grouping column customer_id gives each customer a chain of addresses with no gaps. Good for testing "address on the order date" logic.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.22.10 Advanced A combination of techniques that fills one or several target columns from one or more input, variable and output ports (pp.199, 212). Use it when one column needs two techniques, or the value depends on other columns. You can generate string, numeric and date data. An input port (optional) takes a target column or a parameter. A variable port holds intermediate values and uses either Conditional or Generation Rule Set (rules with distribution percentages, optionally grouping records by foreign key). An output port receives the data and needs an Expression built from the inputs and variables. Port names need not match column names; you map them when you assign the rule (pp.199, 214-215). Visual reference Informatica TDM 10.5.10 User Guide, p.200, figure "advanced rule parameters". The rendered page shows "New Generation Rule: Step 2 of 2" with a Columns pane listing one input column (Ip_1, string, 10), a variable column (Var_1) with Configure Rule and two default numeric sequence rules, and one output column (Out_1), plus a Properties pane showing the output expression CONCAT(Ip_1,Var_1). What to look for: the three port groups stacked in one list. The guide also shows 50 "Invoice-n" plus 50 "Order-n" ids built from a conditional sequence (pp.199-200). ShopSphere: realistic emails (my adaptation of the guide's example) Input in_FirstName mapped to first_name . Variable var_Domain with a Generation Rule Set: example.com 50 percent, example.org 50 percent. Output out_Email with the expression above. Result: Asha@example.com, Ravi@example.org. Two customers called Asha share the same name before the @. The guide does not say whether an input port reads the value generated for another column in the same run, so check that first_name is generated before the email.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.22.11 Custom A global rule built from a PowerCenter mapplet . You import it, and mark at least one input and one output column as required. Works for string, numeric and date (pp.196, 211). Use it when you need PowerCenter transformations (SQL, Stored Procedure) or logic that the built-in techniques cannot express. You map your table columns to the mapplet's input ports and its output ports to target columns (p.204). ShopSphere: a mapplet that takes first and last name and returns "Asha Menon" for a display_name column. Building mapplets is covered in the Informatica masking chapter .

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.23 Conditional constraints: rules between columns Techniques fill one column at a time. A conditional constraint is a table-level rule that restricts what may appear in a column based on another column. It becomes part of the target table's metadata (User Guide 10.5.10, p.201). The guide's example: a flight table with From_City and To_City both filled by the same dictionary rule, plus the constraint To_City != From_City so no ticket flies from a city to itself (p.202). A ShopSphere analogue with hypothetical columns: delivery_date > order_date . To create one, open Discover > Tables, click the table, open the Constraints tab, choose Create New Constraint, set the type to Conditional and build the expression in the Expression Builder (pp.110-111). Where the constraint cannot be used: numeric sequence, date sequence and random data patterns (p.201). On XSD sources you cannot constrain an element that allows more than one child per parent (p.201). When the rule and the constraint disagree, the rule wins The guide's example: both Created_Date and Modified_Date use a random date rule ending 31 July 2014, with the constraint Modified_Date > Created_Date . When Created_Date is 31 July 2014 no later date is allowed, so TDM writes a date within the rule's range anyway and generates warning messages (p.202). The constraint was broken, quietly. Read the warnings in the Monitor logs ( the plans, workflows and warehouse chapter ) and loosen the rule's range, not just the constraint.

h: 5.25 From rules to a running job: the generation plan
x: 5.25 From rules to a running job: the generation plan Rules and assignments are only a description. A plan turns them into something that runs. The plan lists which entities and tables to generate, how many records, and which connections to use; then TDM generates a workflow from it and the workflow does the work (User Guide 10.5.10, p.207). The plan screens are shared with masking and subsetting, so the full tour is in the plans, workflows and warehouse chapter . Here is the generation-specific part.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.25.1 Creating a generation plan From the guide's wizard (User Guide 10.5.10, p.305), with the reason for each step: In the project, click Execute, then New Plan, and name it. Plans live in Execute, the project's "run things" tab. Click Next twice to skip the masking and subset pages. The wizard offers all three operation types on one path. You are skipping the two you must not use. Click Add Generation Components and choose entities and tables (or the XSD file for XML output). Only components with generation rule assignments make sense here. The chosen entities and tables appear in a list. Review table names, set generation criteria for an entity if you want, click Next. Criteria are where you can restrict which rules apply for a test. Enter the number of records to generate and set connections and target properties. The count is required (p.280). Optionally edit data generation, error and recovery, and advanced settings. Click Next and Finish. Defaults are usually fine for a first run. The plan appears in the project's Execute tab. It has not run yet. You can also make a quick ad hoc generation plan for a single column: in Define | Data Generation select the column, choose Actions > Generate and Execute, name the plan, pick the Integration Service, enter the number of records and answer Yes at the prompt (p.306). It is the fast way to try one rule before you commit to a full plan.

h: 5.25.2 Connections and settings that matter for generation
x: 5.25.2 Connections and settings that matter for generation The settings that matter for generation (pp.280-285): the target connection (a relational database, a flat file or the test data warehouse); Number of Records to Generate (required); a Reference Lookup Connection if any reference lookup rule is assigned; a Dictionary Lookup Connection if the plan has a dictionary rule or a mapplet rule with a transformation; the default Numeric, String, Date and Binary rules with Apply Default Rule to; Minimum and Maximum child records (default 1); and the percentages of parents without children and children without a parent. Target options such as Truncate Table (off by default) and Disable Constraints are covered in the plans, workflows and warehouse chapter . If the target is a flat file you can use the test tool integration properties to copy the output to an integrated HP ALM server. If the target is the test data warehouse , you fill in data set properties (name, application, version, tags) and the generated data is stored as a versioned data set (pp.190, 281). That is how generated data gets reused, see the plans, workflows and warehouse chapter . Heap space and special characters If a "Java heap space" exception occurs while setting an ad hoc rule, ask the administrator to increase the heap size (p.198). Remember also that special characters in table or column names make the generation workflow fail (p.190); the plan setting "Enable special characters in metadata" defaults to No (p.289).

h: 5.26 Why a generation plan stands alone
x: 5.26 Why a generation plan stands alone The guide is firm: when you add data generation components to a plan, you cannot add data masking or data subset components, and the reverse holds too (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.274-276, 305). It repeats the rule in the plan overview, the task list, the component table and the creation steps. A Hadoop plan likewise cannot do subset or generation (p.306). The guide states the restriction but does not explain it. My explanation, as a concept and not a quote: masking and subsetting both read existing rows from a source, then change or filter them. Generation has no source rows; it builds new rows from rules. A plan that tried to do both would have to decide what the masking rule should act on. Keeping them apart avoids that. One plan: subset and masking Source connection to target connection. The guide says you can combine them in one plan, or keep separate plans (p.304). If both are present, subset runs first and masking applies only to the subset rows (p.275). Another plan: generation Only entities, tables or XSD files with generation rule assignments. Number of records to generate. No source data is masked or subsetted in this plan. What to do when you need both. Use two plans: Masked copy of old customers plus brand-new ones: run a masking plan into the test database, then a generation plan into the same schema. Make the generation sequences start above the existing ids, or continue with "Start Sequence from Last Value", so keys do not collide. Generate once, then make small slices: send the generation plan to the test data warehouse, then create a related data set , a subset of that data set built from an entity or group (pp.248-251). That is subsetting generated data without breaking the rule. Why it matters This restriction is a favourite interview and review question, and it shapes how you design a data pipeline: generation is its own track, not a masking option. Lab A: generate 50 ShopSphere customers with valid orders Goal: end with 50 rows in CUSTOMERS plus linked ORDERS and ORDER_ITEMS in an empty test schema, then prove the keys are valid. The steps follow the guide's task flow (pp.192, 195-205, 305); names and values are my illustration. You need an installed TDM, an empty test schema SHOPSPHERE_TEST with the four tables, and a PRODUCTS table already holding a few products (P-100, P-200, P-300). Ask an administrator to add a names dictionary under Administrator | Dictionaries. Dictionary rules refuse to be created until a dictionary exists (p.215). A file with a FIRST and a LAST column is enough. The dictionary appears in the list. In Policies, create standard rules with Actions > New > Generation Rule. Make the seven rules in the table of the earlier rule table: Seq_Cust (Sequence from 1001), Dict_First , Dict_Last , Phone_10 ( (6|7|8|9)\d{9} , 10 percent nulls), SSN_like , DOB_Range , Zip_Set (40/35/25) and TaxId_Pattern . Pick the data type first, since it decides which techniques you see. The rules appear in the Policies list. Create a project and import metadata for the four tables. Click Projects, Actions > New, name it, open it, then Actions > Import Metadata and choose Datasource Connection to the test schema (pp.53, 66). Metadata tells TDM what columns exist; it copies no rows. The four tables appear under the project's data sources. Create an entity for the parent-child tables. In Define, create an entity with CUSTOMERS as driving table so TDM pulls in ORDERS and ORDER_ITEMS (pp.116, 277). If the foreign keys are not declared in the schema, add logical foreign keys first on Discover | Tables | Constraints (p.110). Set the relationship minimum and maximum to 1 and 3 for CUSTOMERS to ORDERS, and 1 and 4 for ORDERS to ORDER_ITEMS (p.117). A diagram shows the three tables joined. Add the rules to the project and assign them in Define | Data Generation. Assign the seven rules to the matching CUSTOMERS columns. Click Save after every assignment (p.203). Also give the order and item tables sequences for ids, Random ranges for dates, amounts and quantities, and a Set of Values rule (P-100, P-200, P-300) for product_code . Every row has a rule name, and nothing is left to the default rule except columns you chose to ignore. Add the advanced email rule. In Policies create an advanced rule with input in_FirstName , variable var_Domain (Generation Rule Set: example.com 50, example.org 50) and output out_Email with the expression CONCAT(CONCAT(in_FirstName,'@'),var_Domain) . Assign it to email and map the input port to first_name (pp.200-201, 204-205, 213). The email cell shows the advanced rule's name. Create the plan. Execute > New Plan, name it PLAN_GEN_CUSTOMERS_50 , skip masking and subset, add the entity as a generation component, enter 50 records, choose the target connection SHOPSPHERE_TEST , and set the Reference Lookup Connection only if you used a lookup rule (p.305). Tick Truncate Table (p.282) if you may want to rerun. The plan appears in the Execute

x: 5.27 Common mistakes and gotchas Things that go wrong Forgetting to Save each assignment. The earlier assignment is discarded (p.203). Editing a rule and expecting a finished plan to change. Regenerate and rerun the plan (pp.195-196). Combining masking or subset components with generation components in one plan. Not allowed (pp.274-275). Use two plans. Using a pattern and "Generate Unique Values" together. The guide says uniqueness is unavailable with a regular expression (pp.222-223). Use sequences for keys. Re-running into a table that already has ids from 1001. Key collisions. Truncate the target, or continue the sequence from its last value (p.231). Believing pattern-made SSNs or card numbers are valid. They might not be (p.224). Use the Credit Card technique when validity matters. Ignoring warnings. A rule that conflicts with a conditional constraint wins quietly and only logs a warning (p.202).

x: 5.28 Recap Recap Generation builds new rows from rules and never reads production data. It is set up in a project, run from a plan, and executed as a generated workflow. Rules come as standard, custom, advanced (global) and ad hoc (per project). Unassigned columns get the default rule for their data type. The eleven techniques are Sequence, Random, Set of Values, Dictionary, Credit Card, Reference Lookup, Expression, Conditional, Effective Dates, Advanced and Custom. Reference Lookup, Expression, Effective Dates and Conditional are ad hoc. Null and invalid values are mixed in by percentage through the Exception Test Data settings. Entities with minimum and maximum child counts, and reference lookups, keep parent-child keys consistent. Always verify keys with a join. The number of records is a plan setting. A generation plan cannot contain masking or subset components. Conditional constraints restrict one column using another, but a conflicting rule wins and only produces a warning. Informatica: plans, workflows, monitoring and the Test Data Warehouse Every earlier Informatica chapter ended the same way: "then you put it in a plan and run it". The discovery , subsetting , masking and generation chapters described what to do to data. This section covers the machinery that actually does it, and what happens afterwards: the plan that packages the work, the workflow TDM generates from it, the Monitor where you watch it, the reports that prove what happened, and the Test Data Warehouse where the result can be stored, versioned and restored. If you already know ETL from the ETL from scratch chapter and the ETL and TDM chapter , here is the key idea in one line: a TDM workflow is an ETL job that TDM writes for you. You describe the data and the rules; TDM builds the mappings and runs them. The Day 45 syllabus asks you to understand generation in Informatica; the plan and workflow side is what turns your rules into rows.

x: 5.29 Words to know first Plan The saved definition of one operation: which components, which source and target connections, which settings. It does nothing until you generate and run a workflow from it. Workflow The runnable job generated from a plan. It contains PowerCenter mappings and sessions and is run by the PowerCenter Integration Service. Parameter A named placeholder (for a connection, an owner or a filter value) whose value you supply at run time, so one plan serves many runs. Test Data Warehouse (TDW) A central store for versions of test data, so teams can save a known-good state and restore it later. Data set A named collection of one or more tables stored in the warehouse. Each time you store it again, a new version is created. Reset Copying a data set version from the warehouse back to a target so a test environment returns to a known state. Data pack A data set published to the self-service portal for testers who do not use Test Data Manager. Data coverage A check of whether a data set has enough rows for each combination of values your test cases need.

h: 5.30 Plans and workflows: the big picture
x: 5.30 Plans and workflows: the big picture A plan defines a data subset, data masking or data generation operation, and includes the components you need to generate a workflow (User Guide 10.5.10, p.274). When you start a workflow, the PowerCenter Integration Service completes the operations in the plan (p.275). Project tables, rules, entities → Plan components + settings → Generate mappings + workflow → Execute sessions run → Monitor jobs, logs, reports → Target database, file or warehouse ETL ideas and their TDM names. This mapping is my teaching aid; the TDM terms and who does what come from the guide (pp.275, 308). ETL idea (earlier chapters) In Informatica TDM Who creates it Job specification Plan You, in Test Data Manager Transformation logic Mappings with masking, subset or generation logic PowerCenter Repository Service generates them from the plan Job run Workflow and its sessions PowerCenter Integration Service runs them Source and target connections Connections named in the plan Administrator creates, you choose Run-time inputs Parameters and parameter files You Job scheduler and monitor Run now or schedule; Monitor view You Staging area Staging connection (temporary tables) Chosen in plan settings The analogy stops at one point. A hand-written ETL job is a thing you maintain. A TDM workflow is disposable: change the plan, generate again. The guide says so directly: when you update or delete a plan component you must generate and run the plan again to apply the change (p.275).

h: 5.30.1 Plan types and what each can contain
x: 5.30.1 Plan types and what each can contain Plan components by operation (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.274-277, 306) Component What it is Used in Rule A masking rule, assigned to a policy or standalone Masking plan Policy A set of data domains, each with rules Masking plan Entity Related tables with a parent-child hierarchy and filter parameters Subset or generation plan Group A set of tables to copy to a target subset database Subset plan Template A bundle of subset components; see the Informatica subsetting chapter (named with entities and groups on p.293) Subset plan Table Target table columns that have generation rule assignments Generation plan XSD file An imported XML source definition Subset, masking or generation plan The practical plan types are: Masking, subset, or masking plus subset in one plan. If both kinds of component are present, subset has priority: TDM subsets first, then masks columns in the subset data that have assignments. It does not apply masking to source rows outside the subset, even if they are part of a cascade (p.275). Generation plan. Only entities, tables or XSD files. You cannot add masking or subset components to the same plan, and the reverse (pp.274, 276). See the Informatica generation chapter for the reasoning. Hadoop plan. Groups and masking components for Hadoop sources and targets. No subset or generation (p.306). Data set (related data set) plan. Created from a data set in the warehouse to cut a smaller data set from it (p.251). Reset and restore plans appear in the guide's notes about pre and post workflows (p.277); resets are covered in the warehouse section below.

h: 5.31 The ShopSphere story we will follow
x: 5.31 The ShopSphere story we will follow ShopSphere's QA team needs a safe, small, realistic copy of SHOPSPHERE_PROD for the next release of Customer Orders. They want to refresh it quickly after every destructive test run. The path through this section: Discovery. A profile has already tagged ssn , tax_id , phone , email , first_name and last_name as sensitive data domains ( the discovery chapter ). Masking plus subset plan. An entity with CUSTOMERS as driving table pulls in its orders and items. A limit keeps about 5 percent of customers. Masking rules disguise the sensitive columns in that small slice. Workflow. Generate and run it. The target is the Test Data Warehouse. Monitor and reports. Watch the job turn to Success, read the session counts, run the Row Count report for the audit file. Store. The warehouse now holds data set SHOPSPHERE_MASKED , version 1. Reuse. After a test run damages the data, testers reset version 1 back into the test database, cut a smaller related data set for a hotfix, and check coverage.

h: 5.32.1 A data masking and data subset plan
x: 5.32.1 A data masking and data subset plan You may combine subset and masking in one plan or keep separate plans; generation needs its own (User Guide 10.5.10, p.304). The wizard, with reasons: Open the project, click Execute, then Actions > New. Enter a plan name and optional description. Plans belong to a project so they can use its rules, entities and parameters. Click Add Masking Components and select policies and rules. Click Next. Pick only what this run needs. You may add rules assigned to a policy and rules that are not. Click Add Subset Components and select entities, groups, templates or XSD files. Click Next. This is where you say which tables to copy. If an entity is already inside a chosen template, you cannot add the same entity again (p.277). Skip the generation step with Next. Generation cannot be combined here. Switch off any masking rule you want to skip, using the check box and Off. A cheap way to test one rule at a time. Filter subset components: choose a basic or advanced expression, or click Limit and choose percentage, absolute value or an interval of rows. Click Next. An XSD subset component cannot have its criteria overridden. Details in the Informatica subsetting chapter . Configure connections and other properties. For a flat-file target you can set test tool integration. If you choose the test data warehouse as the target you enter the data set properties. With an XSD source you cannot add other source types. Click Next. Optionally override plan settings for one data source, or data source settings for one table. Click Finish. Overrides handle the one table that needs special treatment. The plan appears in the project's Execute list. Nothing has run. Steps from User Guide 10.5.10, pp.304-305.

x: 5.32.2 A data generation plan The wizard is the same, but you skip the masking and subset pages, add generation components (entities and tables), enter the number of records and set connections (p.305). The full walk-through, with ShopSphere examples, is in the Informatica generation chapter . There is also a one-column ad hoc generation plan reached from Define | Data Generation with Actions > Generate and Execute (p.306).

x: 5.33.1 Masking and subset components Masking components are policies and rules. You may restrict a run to some of them, and turn masking on or off per column in the plan criteria. A plan that decrypts with a Format Preserving Encryption rule cannot include other masking rules (p.292). Subset components are entities, groups, templates or XSD files (p.293). Component criteria. For each column of a subset component, choose a filter method in the Plan Components panel: Custom (a Basic expression with an operator and operand, or an Advanced expression with several columns, functions and parameters) or Limit (percentage, absolute value or interval of rows). To disable masking for a column click the masking component, select the column in the Criteria panel and click OFF (or ON) (p.294). ShopSphere: shrink to about 5 percent The plan holds one entity (driving table CUSTOMERS , children ORDERS and ORDER_ITEMS ) and one policy PII_Policy . For the entity's customer criteria choose Limit by percentage and enter 5. Subset runs first, so only the customers in the slice, and their orders and items, are masked (p.275). Check the Row Count report after the first run to see how the limit applied to the entity. What subset-then-mask does to three rows My illustration of the rule on p.275: subset runs first, so customer 1002 never reaches the target, and masking then changes only the rows that arrived. Illustrative: before and after a plan with an entity and a PII policy customer_id In production In the subset? In the target 1001 Asha Menon, 123-45-6789 Yes Meera Joshi, 456-78-9012 (masked) 1002 Ravi Kumar, 234-56-7890 No not present 1003 Meera Nair, 345-67-8901 Yes Kiran Rao, 567-89-0123 (masked)

x: 5.33.2 Connections A workflow connects to the Integration Service, the TDM repository and one or more connection objects. You choose them in the plan (p.276): Connections you can set in a plan (User Guide 10.5.10, p.276) Connection Purpose Source Where data is read from Target Where data is written: relational, test data warehouse, flat file or Hadoop HDFS, or a variable Staging A database for temporary staging tables; a default comes from Preferences. Recommended to be the source connection for cyclic subsets and similar cases (p.286). Lookup A database that holds lookup tables Storage A database for storage tables used for repeatable masking (substitution and expression); default from Preferences Teradata An ODBC connection to Teradata Dictionary A database with a dictionary table for substitution, email masking and data generation Plans also need connections to repositories, and this has a hard limit. An offline job needs three connections to the TDM repository, each workflow in a multi-workflow plan needs one more, and you can run at most eight workflows at a time (eight workflows need 11 connections). Extra workflows wait in the queued state (p.276). The guide also states that Use Source Connection as Target Connection is for in-place masking, where data is changed in the same database it came from (p.279). That is risky; we never do it on ShopSphere's production copy.

h: 5.33.3 Pre and post workflows, and target SQL
x: 5.33.3 Pre and post workflows, and target SQL You can run another existing workflow in the project's PowerCenter folder before the TDM workflow (it must finish successfully first) or after all TDM workflows complete successfully. Example from the guide: copy files from production area to test area, mask them, then run database statistics. You can disable triggers before and enable them after. Not available for Hadoop, reset and restore plans (p.277). You can also run target pre SQL and post SQL in the plan's Advanced Options, using the variables $OWNERNAME , $SCHEMA and $TABLENAME . Example from the guide: TRUNCATE TABLE $OWNERNAME.$TABLENAME; deletes all rows before the load (pp.277-278). Use these variables so one statement works across environments.

x: 5.35 Source, table and file overrides Many plan settings can be overridden for one data source or one table; where a property is not offered at that level, the plan-level value applies (p.295). Examples: connections, flat-file name, delimiter and encoding, schema names, pre and post SQL, batch size, table name overrides and partitioning (pp.295-301). For flat-file sources you can supply a file list , a text file naming one source file per line; all listed files must share the same properties (p.303).

x: 5.36 Parameters and parameter files Parameters let one plan serve many runs. You may use project parameters and global parameters (created by an administrator, shown with an asterisk) in connections, owner names and filter criteria (pp.275, 279). In an entity or plan you can use a parameter instead of a fixed value in a criterion. A parameter file lists every parameter used in a plan with its default value. Criteria parameters carry an ignore flag that defaults to "N" (include); set it to "Y" and save to ignore that criterion in a run. Parameters you cannot override do not change, and the workflow logs an error (pp.309-311). Create one with Actions > Create Parameter File on the plan. If you use parameters for connections, the parameter file must be on the node that runs the Test Data Manager Service, in the same path on every node (p.279). When you execute the workflow you choose how values are supplied (pp.310-311): Parameter value options at execution Option Behaviour Default Use the parameter file named in the plan settings Use Parameter File Browse to a different file for this run Add Parameter Values Type values in a list. Criteria parameters are not listed by default; use Select Parameter to add them or the workflow ignores them. ShopSphere: one plan, three regions Make the subset criterion on zip_code a criteria parameter p_zip . Run the same plan with 560001 for the Bengaluru team, 600017 for Chennai, 682001 for Kochi. No plan edits, three different data sets. This is the guide's "test data on demand" idea (p.309) in ShopSphere clothes.

x: 5.37 Plan management After you create a plan you can edit it, copy it, export it to XML, import one exported from another TDM repository, or delete it (User Guide 10.5.10, p.304). Plan management tasks (pp.304-308) Task How Notes Copy Execute tab, click the plan's Description or Status field (do not open it), Actions > Duplicate Default name "Copy of <original name>". Edit the copy. Export Select the plan the same way, Actions > Export, save the XML Default file name starts with "Plan_" plus date and time Import On the Projects list select the project (do not open it), Actions > Import, browse to the XML, Finish For moving plans between TDM repositories Delete Select the plan, Actions > Delete, confirm Yes Deleting the plan also deletes its workflow Why export and import? ShopSphere has a development TDM and a production-grade TDM. A plan proved on the first is exported to XML and imported into the second, with connections and parameters adjusted. The command line tool ilmcmd , covered below, can do the same export and import without the web page (pp.330-332).

x: 5.38 Generating and running a workflow You generate a workflow from a plan to perform subset, masking and generation. When you generate, the PowerCenter Repository Service creates the mappings. When you start, the PowerCenter Integration Service performs the work. You can generate and start in a single step (User Guide 10.5.10, p.308). Generate: in the project click Execute, select a plan, Actions > Generate Workflow. This builds mappings and stores them. Do it again whenever the plan changes. Choose whether to run now or later. You may generate now and execute on a schedule. Execute: Actions > Execute Workflow from the Plan properties or Workflow view. If the plan has several workflows, open the Workflow view, select one and execute it. A workflow name contains the project, plan, connection and table names (p.309). Pick the Integration Service and run now or schedule. You must select the service configured in the Test Data Manager Service. Choose parameter values if the plan has parameters. See the parameters section . If the target is the warehouse, optionally publish to the self-service portal, then click Generate and Execute. Publishing creates a data pack for testers who cannot use Test Data Manager. The workflow appears in the Workflow Executions view and in Monitor. Steps from User Guide 10.5.10, pp.308-311. To do both in one go use Actions > Generate and Execute on the Plan | Properties page. Constraints that will not turn back on If you ran the workflow with Disable Constraints and TDM then fails to re-enable them after loading, the workflow fails. Enable the constraints in the database by hand and run the workflow again (p.311).

After fixing the cause Abort (a job) Stops a non-workflow job immediately A stuck profile or import. Workflows are stopped or aborted with the two tasks above, not this one. x: 5.39.3 Reading the logs Select a job and open the Logs tab. The TDM server writes TDM logs; the PowerCenter Integration Service writes session and workflow logs (a Data Integration Service does for Hadoop). TDM always writes console logs when a job is triggered, so if job logs are missing, read the console log (User Guide 10.5.10, p.318). Each message has a Date/Time, a Severity and a Description that explains the error, its cause and the solution. Severity levels (p.319): Error (the TDM server failed an operation; start here), Warning (an operation that might cause an error), Info (normal), Debug and Trace (increasingly detailed server operations, mostly for support). Click Monitor, then the job ID, then the Logs tab. The log belongs to that job only. Filter by severity Error, and by date range or a keyword. Real logs are long; the first Error line is usually the cause and the rest are knock-on effects. Select a message and click Download to keep the log file. Attach it to a ticket. To see console logs, select the job ID and use Actions > View Console Logs. For a workflow, click its job ID to open the workflow details, then the Sessions tab. Look for a session whose Target Rows Failed is not zero. Click the Session ID to see tables processed, affected and rejected rows, error messages and the session log. This is where "which table broke" is answered. You can name the failing session, table and message. Steps from User Guide 10.5.10, pp.319-320. For Hadoop plans you see mapping logs only: no workflow logs and no row counts (p.320). On a clean copy run the Source and Target Rows Succeeded counts match and both Failed counts are zero; a non-zero Failed count means rejected rows, so read the session's last error message.

h: 5.41 Data coverage analysis, at overview level
x: 5.41 Data coverage analysis, at overview level Having a data set is not the same as having enough of the right data . Data coverage analysis checks whether a data set holds a minimum amount of data for specific test cases. It is pairwise : you choose two columns and see how many rows exist for every combination of their values, drawn as a grid (User Guide 10.5.10, p.259). Cell colour shows density: white means no data, light blue is below the minimum threshold you set, dark blue is above it (p.261). Visual reference Informatica TDM 10.5.10 User Guide, p.266, figure "data coverage analysis page" (rendered and viewed). A grid with one column's values along the bottom and another's up the side, mostly white cells with some light and dark blue, a green-bordered selected cell and a side panel of task columns. What to look for: white cells are the gaps. Open the data set, click Data Coverage, Actions > New, name the task and set a minimum threshold. The threshold is the least number of rows you accept as "dense enough". Select a master table (and optionally related tables), then create task columns. Columns can be Use as is (individual values), Range (numeric or date ranges) or Mapping (group values, such as states into regions); binary columns are not allowed (pp.260-263). Put one column on each axis, optionally add up to two filter columns, and click Analyze. The grid shows density. Fix gaps: mark meaningless cells invalid, or select a gap and use Fill to move rows from dense cells. Fill runs a separate job per source cell. If a needed parent row is missing, a dialog asks you to type values (pp.267-269). Coverage grid (schematic, ShopSphere) threshold = 5 customers total_amount band zip band under 500 500-2000 over 2000 56xxxx 9 7 0 <- gap 60xxxx 6 2 1 <- below threshold 68xxxx 0 8 5 <- gap Schematic illustration drawn for this guide, not an official screenshot. Numbers are mine. Here "large order from a Bengaluru customer" has no data. Fill moves rows in, or you generate more. Fill changes the data set itself (p.268), so keep a version first. Coverage jobs show in Monitor as Data Coverage Analysis and Fill Cell, run by the Data Integration Service (pp.26, 316-317).

h: 5.42 Command-line tools: ilmcmd, tdwcmd and tdwquery
x: 5.42 Command-line tools: ilmcmd, tdwcmd and tdwquery TDM ships three small command-line programs (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.326-350). Scripts and schedulers can call them, so a nightly refresh needs no human clicking. Names of commands, options and objects are case sensitive, and -h shows the syntax. The three tools at a glance Tool Purpose ilmcmd A subset of Test Data Manager tasks: import and export XML objects, search, validate, delete, generate and run workflows, show workflow status, reset data set versions, and run data set subset plans tdwcmd List test data warehouse details: repository, warehouse, connections, data sets, versions and version tables (it lists and changes nothing) tdwquery Run SELECT queries (joins, aggregates, WHERE) on the tables of one data set in the warehouse Examples printed in the guide for ilmcmd (pp.329-338): generate a workflow, get its status, run it, export a policy, and reset a data set version from a reset file. It cannot search data generation objects (p.333), and over HTTPS you must first set up a keystore (p.327). ilmcmd -wf -g -Project Infa_Project -pn Plan_NameMasking ilmcmd -wf -gs -JobId 360 ilmcmd -wf -ex -Project TDM -pn Plan_NameMasking -is PCInteg ilmcmd -r -dvn "RESET Version1" -rf "C:\Documents\ResetObject.json" -ris PIS For tdwquery you first fill in userConfig.ilm (service URL, user, domain, warehouse and data set version), then run for example tdwquery "SELECT * FROM td_empdetails" (pp.348-349). Passwords on the command line The guide's tdwcmd examples put the password in the command ( -pd Administrator ), where shell history can expose it. Follow your organisation's secret-handling rules. That advice is mine, not the guide's.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.43 The Test Data Warehouse Test data goes stale and gets damaged. A tester deletes orders to check a refund flow; a batch job rewrites prices; another team starts testing on the same tables. Re-running the whole subset and masking plan each time is slow. The Test Data Warehouse solves this: it is a central location that stores multiple versions of test data, and multiple Test Data Manager services can use the same warehouse, so teams share one store (User Guide 10.5.10, p.236). The guide's scenario: before any tests, store the original data as a data set. After each team finishes, store the modified data as another version. To return the environment to its original state, restore the version holding the original data. You can restore any version (p.237).

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.43.1 What is behind it You create a Test Data Warehouse Service in the Informatica Administrator tool. That application service manages two relational databases (pp.26-28, 236): the test data warehouse repository , which holds project metadata (plan information, version, tags) and source table metadata of each data set; the test data warehouse itself, which holds the actual source data you put in data sets. The service copies the metadata created when you make a data set and creates the data set tables in the warehouse (p.27). Workflows that store data in the warehouse need connections to the external source databases, the repository and the warehouse (p.28). Data coverage tasks run on the Data Integration Service (p.26). Source DB SHOPSPHERE_PROD PowerCenter Integration Service Test Data Warehouse Service Test Data Manager Service (plan, Monitor) TDW repository metadata, tags Test Data Warehouse (rows) Original diagram, simplified from pp.26-28 and 236: a map of who holds what, not a network drawing. A plain database backup Restores a whole database, usually needs a DBA, and carries no test metadata. Hard for a tester to find "the data from the refund tests". A warehouse data set (concept view) Holds chosen tables, with application name, version and tags you can search. Testers with Execute permission can reset it, or pick it up from the portal. The analogy to a backup stops here: a data set can also be edited and sliced into related data sets.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.44 Data sets, versions and tags A data set is a collection of one or more tables from one or more data sources, and generally matches one or more test cases (User Guide 10.5.10, p.238). You create one when you subset production, make a masked copy, or generate data, by selecting the test data warehouse as the target when the plan runs. It stores source table metadata and plan metadata, and you can search by those properties.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.44.1 Creating a data set Check the tables first. You cannot create a data set from tables with user-defined data types; mark such columns Restricted under Discover > Columns. Tables without primary keys need logical keys, or a reset might fail. More than two character columns with precision 4000 should be edited to 3,999 or less (p.239). Build a plan (masking, subset or generation) and in the plan settings select Test Data Warehouse from the target connections. The Data Set Properties section appears. Enter a data set name (default: the plan name), application name, application version and tags. A new name creates version 1. TDM fills in the version number (p.240). Finish the plan and click Actions > Generate and Execute. Optionally publish to the self-service portal in the same step. Monitor shows the job. On success the data set appears in the Data Sets view. Condensed from User Guide 10.5.10, pp.239-240.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.44.2 Versions and tags Test data changes during testing. You make a new version in two ways (p.238): rerun the same plan without changing the data set name; or create and run a different plan and enter the same data set name. Tags are comma-separated words (test case name, ticket number) used to filter and search data sets. Row-level tags mark individual rows, to track edits or to select rows for a related data set (p.239). Tag text may include spaces and special characters but not a comma (pp.247, 255). ShopSphere: naming Data set SHOPSPHERE_MASKED , application CustomerOrders , application version 2.4 , tags baseline, masked, 5pct . After the regression run, rerun the plan or run a different plan with the same data set name to get version 2 tagged after-regression . Visual reference Informatica TDM 10.5.10 User Guide, p.237, figure "tasks for storing and using warehouse data" (rendered and enlarged). A left-to-right flow: create project, optional parameters, plan with the warehouse as target, generate and run, view the data set, then optional steps (edit metadata, permissions or lock, edit data, coverage, reset, publish to the portal). What to look for: only the first four boxes are mandatory.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.45 Restoring: the reset Reset moves data from a data set version in the warehouse to a target, so a test environment goes back to a known state (User Guide 10.5.10, p.240). You can make the reset delete everything in the target and replace it, which suits tables you do not share. Or you can keep other testers' data in the target and replace only the part that overlaps the data set. In selective resets TDM runs an SQL script that backs up the deleted data in the target (p.241).

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.45.1 Master and transactional tables Reset behaves differently per table, according to how you classify it (p.241): Table classification and reset behaviour (pp.241-242) Class Meant for Reset action by default ShopSphere Master Records shared by all testers No deletes. Upsert: update rows that exist in both, insert rows that exist only in the data set. CUSTOMERS, PRODUCTS Transactional Descendants of master tables; rarely shared Insert. If a record already exists the insert fails. Deletes cascade from top-level transactional tables (direct children of master tables). ORDERS, ORDER_ITEMS Unclassified tables are treated as transactional. To classify: open the data set, Plan Components tab, Tables tab, Edit Table Type. When you mark a table as master you must choose to mark all descendants as transactional, or all other tables (pp.241-242). Verify the classification before every reset.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.45.2 Reset options Open the data set version you want and click Actions > Reset. The source is fixed: the warehouse. Select the target connection. Usually your test database. Choose reset settings. Truncate Tables deletes all target data and loads the data set, disabling constraints and indexes; no backup is made. Disable Constraints and Indexes speeds things up. Upsert in Transactional Tables avoids insert failures when parents changed. Insert in Master Tables skips the existence check but needs all tables to be master and no overlapping records. Enter reset recovery properties if you are not truncating: a Backup Recovery Prefix and the Backup Recovery User Name (schema) for backup tables named <prefix>_<tablename> . This is your undo. Review Error and Recovery and Advanced Settings; optionally override at data source or table level; choose the PowerCenter Integration Service; run now or schedule. Then follow the job in Monitor. A "Reset Data Set from Test Data Warehouse" job reaches Success and the target matches the version. Steps from User Guide 10.5.10, pp.243-244. Visual reference Informatica TDM 10.5.10 User Guide, p.245, figure "reset process". I rendered this page. It is a flowchart: Reset leads either to "Full restore" (truncate tables, insert tables from the data set, success message) or to "Reset with default settings", which validates table classification (not valid: exit with error), creates staging tables to find candidates for cascade delete, then asks whether to disable constraints and indexes. Yes goes to a parallel transactional cascade delete and insert; No goes to a sequential one. Both then upsert master tables in parallel, re-enable constraints, and show the success message. What to look for: a note says the backup tasks are not drawn.

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.45.3 Speed versus downtime Disabling constraints lets TDM load several tables in parallel, so resets finish sooner. But constraints are disabled for the entire table, and while they are off, other testers' tests that use those tables might fail. If tables are shared, a slower reset may be better than downtime; if no one else is using them, disable constraints (pp.242-243). As good practice, create an index on foreign keys in the target so child-record deletes are quick (p.243).

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.45.4 Failure and special cases Failed reset: if recovery was enabled, backups are kept. Restore with a separate plan: put the backed-up tables in a group, add it as a subset component, use the backup schema as source and the real database as target, disable constraints and indexes, set Treat Source Row As Update and Update As "Update else Insert", and put the backup prefix in the Reset Recovery Prefix advanced field (p.247). On success TDM deletes the backup tables (p.246). Empty strings in non-null columns: a reset fails if it must copy empty strings into a non-null column, for example from an Oracle warehouse to SQL Server. The project can supply default values, but a reset fails if the non-null target columns are unique (p.243). PWX NRDB Batch target: you must delete the target files yourself first; the reset only copies (p.243).

ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.46 Managing data sets Permissions. Whoever runs the plan owns the data set. Owner and domain administrator can grant Read (view, monitor, create coverage tasks, run related data set plans), Write (create, edit metadata and data, classify, delete, create related plans) and Execute (reset). Users also need matching privileges such as View Data Set or Reset Data Set (pp.252-253). Lock and unlock. Owner and administrator can lock a data set so nobody edits or resets it, for example while you check it first. The owner and administrator can still reset it (p.254). View and edit data. From the Tables tab you can browse, or run SQL in the SQL Query field and edit the grid, add or delete rows and add row-level tags. DML only, no DDL. Restrictions: no aggregates, GROUP BY or joins in SELECT; no table aliases or owner names; dates in WHERE need TO_DATE; Oracle BLOB and RAW data cannot be viewed or edited (pp.255-258). Related data sets. A related data set is a subset of a data set, cut by an entity or group built inside the data set and run in a plan. A lineage window shows parent and child data sets (pp.248-252). ShopSphere use: a hotfix needs only the Kochi customers. Self-service portal. Publish a data set as a data pack . Testers without Test Data Manager can then view and restore the data. You cannot delete a published data set until you delete the data pack (pp.239, 247-248). Delete. From the Data Sets view, delete whole data sets or single versions, Actions > Delete. Data and metadata are removed (p.248).

x: 5.48 Common mistakes and gotchas Things that go wrong Changing a plan and expecting the old workflow to follow. Generate and run again (p.275). Mixing generation with masking or subset in one plan. Not allowed (p.274). Forgetting the eight-workflow limit. Extra workflows queue (p.276). Criteria parameters silently missing. They are not in the run list by default; add them with Select Parameter or the workflow ignores them (p.311). Leaving tables unclassified before a reset. They are treated as transactional (p.241). ct: Informatica TDM (2): masking, generation, plans and workflows
x: 5.49 Recap Recap A plan defines a masking, subset or generation operation; TDM generates a workflow (an ETL job) from it and the PowerCenter Integration Service runs it. Subset plus masking can share a plan (subset first); generation cannot share a plan with either. Connections, target options, update strategy, error and recovery and parameter files control where and how the run happens, with overrides per source or table. Monitor shows each job's status (In Queue, Running, Success, Error, Terminated), its logs by severity, and sessions with row counts. Start at the first Error. Reports: Audit Trail, Data Masking, Plan Audit, Plan Detail and Row Count. The Test Data Warehouse stores versioned data sets. Reset restores a version, with master and transactional classification deciding what is deleted or upserted. Data coverage analysis finds gaps in a data set; ilmcmd, tdwcmd and tdwquery script and inspect the same objects.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: GenRocket: what it is and how it works The earlier part of this guide explained why teams need test data and how to make it safely: copy a slice of production ( subsetting ), hide the sensitive parts ( masking ), or build data from nothing ( generation ). The Informatica part showed one commercial tool for all three. This part turns to a tool that is built around the third way: GenRocket . It does not copy your production data at all. You describe the shape of the data you want, and it manufactures as many rows as you ask for, already consistent with each other. This first GenRocket chapter is the map. You will learn the five building blocks the whole product is made of, where each piece runs (some in a cloud web site, some on your own machine), what a "project" is, and how the syllabus phrase Model, Design, Deploy, Manage (Day 46) lines up with real screens. The two chapters after this one go deep on the building blocks: domains, attributes and generators , then receivers and scenarios . Nothing here needs a licence to understand; you only need to know what a table and a column are. What you will learn What "synthetic test data" means and why GenRocket's own pages argue it improves test coverage. The five key components (domain, attribute, generator, receiver, scenario) with an everyday analogy, and how they map to the ShopSphere tables. What "Test Data Automation" and the Model, Design, Deploy, Manage cycle mean in GenRocket's documentation. The hybrid architecture: design in the cloud web platform, generate on your own machine with the GenRocket Runtime. What the runtime is made of, the requirements the docs list, and the shape of the setup, including Docker and Jenkins at overview level. Projects, project versions, project types, project categorization and the Project Dashboard. Who can do what: users, roles and the licensing idea in the documentation.
