ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.1 Words to know first Synthetic test data Data manufactured by an algorithm instead of captured from real events. GenRocket's page defines it in nearly those words. Nobody's real name or card number is in it. Domain One "thing" you want data for, such as a customer. For a database it is a table. For output it can also be a file, message, JSON or XML document. Attribute One characteristic of a domain, such as firstName or email . For a database it is a column. Generator The small engine attached to an attribute that decides what value to produce, for example "a first name from a list" or "count up from 1". Receiver The component that takes the raw generated values and puts them into a usable form: a CSV file, a JSON file, SQL insert statements, a database table and many more. Scenario A saved instruction sheet: which domains to generate, how many rows of each, in what order. Running it is what actually produces data. Test Data Automation (TDA) The phrase GenRocket's pages use for its approach: test data defined once as components and then generated automatically, in real time, whenever a test needs it. Web platform GenRocket's web application in the cloud, where you model and design. Also called GenRocket Cloud. GenRocket Runtime A set of Java programs installed on your own computer or server. It reads a downloaded scenario and generates the data there, inside your firewall. Project and project version A project holds the data model for one application or database. A version is one release's copy of that model, with its own domains, receivers and scenarios. Referential integrity The promise that every foreign key points to a row that exists. See the data basics chapter .

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.2 What GenRocket is and why synthetic data
x: 6.2 What GenRocket is and why synthetic data GenRocket's welcome pages are short and to the point. They define synthetic test data as data "manufactured or generated by an algorithm rather than real-world events", and argue that companies can maximise test coverage by using it to test all permutations and combinations. The CI/CD page describes the product as a component-based platform for defining and provisioning test data for high-volume, automated testing. Think of a bakery that has to supply cupcakes for a hundred different tasting events. One approach is to buy finished cakes from a rival shop, scrape off the logos and send them out (that is masked production data). The GenRocket approach is to own the recipe and the oven. You write down "chocolate, 12 per tray, nut-free, one tray with a deliberately burnt top" and the oven makes exactly that on demand. The analogy stops being accurate in one respect: a recipe produces cakes that taste alike, while a GenRocket recipe can be told to vary values, include edge cases and keep related trays consistent with each other. Why it matters A tester for ShopSphere's "Customer Orders" app needs a customer with 0 orders, one with 1, one with 200, one whose email is missing and one whose surname is 60 letters long. Production rarely contains all of these, and copying production brings real names along ( see why TDM exists ). Because GenRocket's data is manufactured to a rule, you can ask for the odd cases directly and rebuild the same set tomorrow. The documentation is also frank about the work involved. The FAQ says the harder data-design tasks are assigned to a small group of trained "Test Data Engineers", while testers and developers mainly search for the data they need, deploy it into their test environment and tweak it. That is the "TDM engineer" role this guide is aimed at. The Test Data Workflow page starts from the same person: it says the workflow begins with a Power User, a Test Data Engineer. One more design choice matters for privacy. The Test Data Projects page says a project contains no customer data . It holds your data model and the five components that describe how to generate data. The architecture diagram (below) labels the cloud part "No Customer Data Stored".

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.3 The five key components The help centre says the whole platform is built on five key components, and every other feature is a derivative of them. Learn these five words and the rest of GenRocket becomes vocabulary. Here is the official reference table in my words, with the ShopSphere example added. The five key components, with ShopSphere examples (the examples in the last column are mine) Component Think of it like Official examples ShopSphere example Domain A noun: a person, place or thing Database table, file, image, message, JSON, XML CUSTOMERS , ORDERS , ORDER_ITEMS Attribute A characteristic of the noun Id, FirstName, LastName, Phone, SSN, DOB first_name , email , zip_code Generator The recipe for one attribute's values NameGen, PhoneNumberGen, SSNGen, DateGen, QueryGen A name generator for first_name , a counter for customer_id Receiver The packaging that turns raw values into a usable format JDBC, SQL, CSV, Image, XML, JSON, VSAM, REST, SWIFT A CSV file of customers, SQL inserts for orders Scenario The instruction sheet: what to generate and how much "Generates data into a typical test case in about 100 milliseconds" (the vendor's claim) "50 customers, then their orders" DOMAIN CUSTOMERS (a table, a file, a message) ATTRIBUTES first_name, email, ... (the columns) GENERATORS one per attribute (raw values) RECEIVER CSV, SQL, JSON ... (usable output) SCENARIO Which domains? How many rows of each? In what order? The GenRocket engine follows it when you run it. Original diagram: how the five components relate. A domain has attributes, each attribute has a generator, a receiver packages the values, and a scenario (dashed arrows) draws on the domains and receivers to tell the engine what to produce. One rule to remember from the Generators Overview: generators only generate values; receivers format them. The split is deliberate. You can change CSV to JSON by swapping the receiver, without touching any generator. The five-component page adds a small note: the components can also be managed through the Runtime Application Interface (API). The CI/CD page, quoted later, uses that to change a scenario while a pipeline runs. Worked example: one customer row Take the ShopSphere row 1001 | Asha | Menon | asha.menon@example.com | 9876543210 | 123-45-6789 | 1990-04-12 | 560001 from the earlier chapters. In GenRocket terms: the domain is CUSTOMERS. The attributes are customer_id , first_name , last_name , email and so on. A generator on first_name produces "Asha" (then a different name for the next row), a generator on customer_id counts 1001, 1002, 1003. A receiver writes the lines into a file. A scenario says "make 3 of these". Every value is fake, so the row can go to any test environment.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.4 Test Data Automation and "Model, Design, Deploy, Manage"
x: 6.4 Test Data Automation and "Model, Design, Deploy, Manage" GenRocket calls its platform a Test Data Automation platform. The CI/CD page explains the idea with a short list of things any generator of data must know, and then shows how GenRocket captures each one: What the generator must be told Where GenRocket records it The object to create (a User, a Customer) Domain The properties of the object (name, id number, phone) Attributes What each property should look like (Swedish names, a national id) Generators The format of the result (CSV, JSON, XML) Receivers How many, in what order (implied) Scenario Something to carry out the instructions (added later) GenRocket Runtime Notice that the runtime has now joined the list as a sixth piece. The five components are the design ; the runtime is the engine that executes it. The docs describe the runtime as a secure Java program that executes encrypted scenarios inside the customer's firewalled environment.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.4.1 The four steps The course syllabus for Day 46 says "Data generation: model, design, deploy, manage". GenRocket's Methodology page says the product uses exactly this "Model, Design, Deploy, Manage" methodology, and the CI/CD page gives each step a plain meaning. Official screenshot: The vendor's "Synthetic Data Lifecycle" ring: Model, Design, Deploy and Manage chase each other in a circle. The circle matters: after Manage, the next release of your application sends you back to Model. Source page ↗ Step What the docs say Where it happens in the product ShopSphere version Model Import the data model. Done in the web platform (many import and create methods) or by API at runtime. Project Dashboard: New Domain menu (import from DDL, XTS, CSV, JSON and others) or manual creation Import the CUSTOMERS, ORDERS and ORDER_ITEMS definitions as three domains Design Create test data designs that match each test case: how much data, which variations. Self-service features exist for positive, negative, pattern, permutation, boundary, dynamic and load data. Generators, receivers, scenarios, and the self-service "Test Data Case" family Pick generators per column, a CSV receiver, a scenario for "50 customers" Deploy Generate and deliver the data in real time. Over 100 receivers format and deliver it. Triggered from a CI/CD script or a REST request to a GenRocket server component. Download the scenario, run it with the runtime A pipeline job runs the scenario before the order tests start Manage Manage multiple releases of test data projects with version control. A repository component keeps managed artifacts in sync. Project versions, categories, G-Repository Release 2.0 of the shop gets its own project version The Deploy row says "more than 100 receivers", while the receivers overview page says "120+" and the architecture is described in terms of a growing list. Treat all such counts as approximate and growing ; I quote them only to show scale. The same page also lists the self-service vocabulary used in the Design step, in a table from the vendor's screenshot below. These names matter later ( data patterns chapter ), so recognise them now. Official screenshot: The vendor's table of design-time terms. A Test Data Case specifies the exact data one test needs (for example 100 customers), a Rule filters the data to what you want, a Query pulls specific production values to blend with generated data, Stories combine cases, and Epics combine stories. Source page ↗ Do not confuse the stages with the five components Model, Design, Deploy and Manage are phases of work . Domain, attribute, generator, receiver and scenario are things in the product . Several components appear in more than one phase: generators are chosen while designing, but a generator's output is only produced while deploying.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.5 Architecture: a cloud for design, your machine for generation
x: 6.5 Architecture: a cloud for design, your machine for generation The Architecture page says GenRocket is built on a hybrid architecture. The cloud component is where synthetic data is modelled and designed . The on-premise component is where synthetic data is generated locally . The cloud itself is offered as a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) or a Dedicated Private Cloud (DPC). Official screenshot: The architecture diagram. Top: the GenRocket cloud, where test data cases are designed, marked "No Customer Data Stored". Bottom: your premises (and your own cloud facilities), behind your firewall, where the GenRocket Runtime on a dev or test machine produces SQL, XML, JSON, PDF or Excel output. Connections are labelled HTTPS with TLS 1.2, and users (Org Admin, Dev User, Test User) reach the web platform over HTTPS 443. Source page ↗ Read the diagram from top to bottom. A designer logs in to the web platform and builds the design. The design is then sent to the customer side as an encrypted scenario file. On the customer side, the runtime runs it and writes data into databases and files that never leave your network. Official screenshot: The same idea as three steps: create designs in the cloud, download them securely, generate synthetic data on your premises on Windows, Mac or Linux. Source page ↗ Why it matters For a bank or hospital, the question "does our data leave the building?" decides whether a tool may be used at all. In this design, the cloud holds only the design (a data model and rules, not data). The only place rows are created is on a machine you control. Compare this with a masking tool ( Informatica masking chapter ), where real data is read and transformed. The Architecture page links onward to security, team permissions, the runtime overview and "G-Repository", the component that keeps scenarios and configuration files synchronised across a company's machines. There is also a downloadable PDF, "Components and Ports Configuration Guide", which the docs call a vital resource for core components, diagrams, port configurations and deployment advice. I did not open that PDF; if your organisation deploys GenRocket, that is the document to ask for.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.6.1 What it is The runtime is a set of Java jar files, downloaded from GenRocket Cloud and installed wherever data generation is needed: a laptop, a shared machine, a server, a virtual machine or a container. The pages list these jars. Jar Job (docs wording, shortened) genrocket.jar Reads the command line, checks the user's licence, launches the engine gr-engine.jar The core engine that runs scenarios (and supports components such as the multi-user server) gr-generators.jar The generator classes gr-receivers.jar The receiver classes gr-grepository-servers.jar Creates and runs a G-Repository server gr-grepository-clients.jar Creates a G-Repository client Official screenshot: The runtime overview page's picture: the runtime sits "in the customer environment" (the blue box), next to the machine that needs the data. Three setup styles are listed: a local user machine , a shared central machine where many people log in, and a local or remote server , including one used for automated testing in CI/CD.

h: 6.6.3 Profiles: how the runtime knows who you are
x: 6.6.3 Profiles: how the runtime knows who you are A scenario file is encrypted and tied to your organisation. To run it, the runtime must find a profile file (extension .grp ) in a hidden folder named .genrocket in your home directory. The profile ties the machine to a GenRocket licence. Profile Used for User Profile Every person who runs the runtime. It matches the scenario to your organisation and checks that you have an enabled account Server Profile A server with no particular person, typically a CI/CD machine. An organisation administrator must first add the server in the web platform Both are downloaded from the web platform. Whenever a resource value changes, the docs say you must download your profile again and replace the old one.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.6.4 Port 443, online mode and the offline certificate
x: 6.6.4 Port 443, online mode and the offline certificate The runtime runs in online mode by default: when you run a scenario, it contacts GenRocket Cloud over port 443 to confirm the licence. The "Verify Port 443" page gives a quick test: open https://app.genrocket.com/license/check in a browser, or run curl on the same address. If the port is open you see a short JSON message saying a valid user or server was not found. That odd-looking "failure" is the proof that the connection works. If your company blocks that port, the docs offer an offline certificate : download a file from the web platform, put it in the .genrocket folder, and run scenarios without internet. The certificate is specific to one organisation and lasts 24 hours, so you download a fresh one each day. Offline certificate pitfall from the docs If the home directory stored in your resource.home.directory resource does not match the machine's real home directory, you get "Unable to validate license". The fix on the page is: correct the resource value, download the certificate again and retry.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.6.5 Setting it up: the shape of the steps
x: 6.6.5 Setting it up: the shape of the steps You will not install the runtime in this guide's labs (the hands-on chapter assumes a trainer or lab machine has done it), but you should know what the steps look like. The three operating-system articles are long and similar. Here is the Windows article's skeleton, in my words. Details such as folder paths and the exact variable names belong to the vendor page for your system. Check the prerequisites. An active GenRocket user account and access to the cloud address from your network, port 443 open, admin rights on the machine, and Java installed. What you should see: java -version prints one of the supported versions. Download the runtime zip from the web platform. Log in, open the Options menu, and choose the download for the current runtime version. The docs also show a curl or wget way to fetch it. What you should see: a zip file named with the runtime version number. Extract it into your home directory and name the folder genrocket . The page warns that you must not end up with a nested folder such as genrocket\genrocket-3.5.x , and that the user name in the path must not itself be "genrocket". What you should see: a genrocket folder with bin and lib inside. Set the environment variables. Point the home variable at the folder, add its bin directory to PATH , check JAVA_HOME , and for Java 11 or later add the documented JAVA_OPTS value. What you should see: after opening a new terminal window, the word genrocket is recognised. Run genrocket once. This downloads the other jars into lib and creates the hidden .genrocket folder. What you should see: no error. If you see "genrocket is not a recognized command", the troubleshooting page says to check the folder name, the home variable and PATH . Download the helper libraries and your user profile. The page uses genrocket -lib for libraries. The profile comes from the Download menu in the Resources pane and goes into .genrocket . What you should see: a .grp profile file inside .genrocket . Fill in your organisation resources. Three default resources hold folder paths for you (home directory, JDBC config directory and output directory; the screenshots in the next section show them). Set them to real folders, and enter N/A for the JDBC one if you do not connect to a database. What you should see: your own paths in the Resources pane of the web platform. Typing genrocket alone, or genrocket -h , prints the list of runtime command-line options. That is the quickest way to see what your installed version supports.

h: 6.6.6 Updates, Docker and Jenkins at overview level
x: 6.6.6 Updates, Docker and Jenkins at overview level Updates. The docs distinguish a full runtime update (replace the whole genrocket folder) from a jar-only update (done from the command line, and sometimes without re-downloading the runtime). Release notes say which is needed, and users see a pop-up after login when a new release arrives. Docker. For teams that run containers, GenRocket provides a Docker image you download from the web platform (or with curl ) and load with docker load . The page's basic idea is that a container forgets everything when it stops, so you mount folders from the host for the runtime, the scenarios, the configuration files, the .genrocket profile folder and the output. The page also notes that the runtime must be set up when using a container, and describes a custom-image option. Jenkins (continuous integration). Jenkins is a popular tool that runs build and test jobs automatically. The Windows and Mac/Linux Jenkins pages walk through running a scenario as a Jenkins build step. The outline is the same as a normal setup, applied to the Jenkins server: Install the runtime on the Jenkins server and set the variables in Jenkins's own configuration screen. Jenkins builds do not see your personal environment, so the home variable and PATH must be set where Jenkins reads them. Register the Jenkins server in the web platform and download its Server Profile into the server's .genrocket folder. No person is logged in on a build server, so it uses a server profile, not a user profile. Create a Freestyle job and add a build step that runs the scenario. First the page has you run the bare genrocket command to prove Jenkins can find it, then replace it with genrocket -d -r SCENARIO_NAME.grs . What you should see: a SUCCESS message in the console output, and your generated files in the output folder. Official screenshot: The vendor's Jenkins example: the build step first runs plain genrocket to check that Jenkins can find the runtime. Later in the same article the command is replaced by one that runs a named scenario file. Source page ↗ The CI/CD page adds two ways to trigger generation from a pipeline: a shell or batch command running the runtime, or a REST request to a GenRocket server component. It also describes Java and REST APIs that let a pipeline create or modify a scenario in real time, for example to change a loop count (how many rows) per test. Not covered here Linux and Mac setup, the multi-user server, G-Repository administration and API method details are separate topics in the help centre. I read only the overview-level material for them, so I do not describe them further.

h: 6.8.1 What a project is, and how many you need
x: 6.8.1 What a project is, and how many you need A Test Data Project contains the data model for one application or database you want data for. It contains aspects of your model (domains, attributes, generators, receivers, scenarios) but no customer data. This is also the unit of licensing: the Test Data Projects page says GenRocket is licensed based on the number of projects a customer needs. Official screenshot: The vendor's simplest rule of thumb: one application with one underlying database is typically one project. Source page ↗ The page gives a way to count. Start with what you are testing, find the applications and their databases, and count them. It then lists factors that may split one thing into several projects: database size, complexity of related tables, whether functions are related, and special message formats. Situation Minimum projects (docs) One application, one database 1 Several unrelated modules, each with its own database 1 each Multi-schema database whose tables are related 1 for all schemas (depending on complexity); unrelated schemas need a project each Next release of the same application The same project, with a new project version A workflow across applications (for example customer, agent, quote, payment, policy) At least 1 per application, database or complex file type, so that referential integrity holds between applications Closed or packaged systems such as SAP or Salesforce 1 per module or group of related functions SWIFT or EDI messages 1 per message type Subsetting or masking a SQL database 1 per related group of tables For ShopSphere's "Customer Orders" app with its single SHOPSPHERE_PROD schema, the docs' rule suggests one project, because the four tables are related.

x: 6.8.4 Project versions A project is born with a version numbered 1.0. A new version is normally created when the release your domains and scenarios test goes to production, and the next release needs testing. Each version has its own domains, receivers, scenarios and configuration. There are two ways to make one, both from the Manage menu in the Project Versions pane. New Version A blank slate. No domains or scenarios from before. Use it when the data model changes so much that starting fresh is easier. The dialog asks for a version number and description, an optional default date format (for the whole version; a more specific format at attribute or generator level wins), and an optional Enforce Type/Limit checkbox. Copy Version Replicates the whole version, or a subset of domains, so the new version matches the next release of your software. The docs state a limit: permitted users can copy a version five times in 24 hours, counted from the first copy. Official screenshot: The Create Project Version dialog: version number, description, optional default date format, and the Enforce Type/Limit checkbox, which keeps generated values within each column's declared type and size (explained in the generators chapter). Source page ↗ Official screenshot: A Project Versions pane with several versions. Each row has a set of icons for tools such as the wizards and reports mentioned earlier. The green Manage button opens the New Version and Copy Version menu. Source page ↗ The Project Dashboard page lists some of those icons: generator search, the Domain Referencing Wizard, a project-version status report (which flags attributes with no generator, id attributes without a range generator, and foreign keys without the proxy reference generator), a global seed assigner and a generator tuning wizard. Terms like proxy reference generator are explained in the generators chapter.

x: 6.8.5 Project categorization A company with hundreds of projects needs a way to find them. Project categorization lets an organisation administrator build a three-level list, then lets users filter projects by it: Business Unit: the top level, such as a department or team (the docs' example is "Bank"). Category: a group of similar projects within a unit (Credit Card, Checking, Savings). No limit on how many. Tag: the lowest level, a keyword for a category (New Accounts, Payments Received). A category can have up to five tags. Official screenshot: The Project Categorization dashboard. Left: business units. Right: the categories of the selected unit (Checking, Credit Card, Savings) with their tags underneath. Opened from the Management menu in the menu bar. Source page ↗ Only an Org Admin creates the units, categories and tags; an Org Admin or the project's creator assigns them to projects; any user can then filter projects by them. The docs recommend using this only when you have many projects, and say a small organisation can find projects by name. A user can find a matching project, copy it, and adapt the copy: reuse, not rebuilding.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.9 Users, roles and licensing basics The licensing facts I found stated are these, and nothing more (prices and contract terms are not in the help centre): Licence is counted in test data projects (see above). Users are named users : a real, registered person whose email address is their unique ID. The number of users per organisation is unlimited. A named user may have a desktop and a laptop, but should run scenarios on only one at a time. When a scenario runs, the runtime checks that the user has a valid, enabled profile. An administrator can disable users. Role What the docs say it can do Organization Admin Creates users, resets passwords, sets password expiry, accesses all projects, domains and scenarios, and can add or delete resources and organisation variables Team Manager Creates teams, adds projects and members to them and sets each member's permissions per project General User The default role; changes only their own account and works with projects, domains, attributes, receivers and scenarios not placed in a team. Inside a team, permissions depend on what the team manager granted Enable Web Service API Lets the user call GenRocket's web API A team is how an organisation restricts who sees which projects: if a project is placed in a team, members get exactly the permissions they were given, and a user without permission to manage, for example, receivers sees them read-only. Further administration topics exist (multi-factor login, restricting log-in by IP address, SCIM user provisioning); the help centre's User Management section covers them and I have not summarised them.

x: 6.11 Common mistakes and gotchas Things that trip up beginners Expecting data to appear in the web platform. The cloud holds designs, not data. Rows are created only when a downloaded scenario runs under the runtime on your machine. The "Preview" you see in the web platform is a sample for checking configuration. Forgetting the profile. Without a valid .grp profile (or offline certificate) in .genrocket , the runtime refuses to run. Download a fresh profile whenever a resource value changes. Environment variables set but not picked up. A terminal opened before you changed variables keeps the old values. Close it and open a new one. Port 443 blocked. The runtime cannot validate the licence. Use the browser or curl test, then ask the network team or use the offline certificate. Treating the number of generators or receivers as fixed. The docs give changing counts ("765+", "120+", "more than 100"). Look the name up in your version rather than relying on a number. Creating a new project for every release. A new version is the documented tool for that, and project count is a licensing unit. Confusing the five components with the four phases. See the warning in the four-steps section .

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.12 Recap Key points GenRocket makes synthetic data from a model: no production rows are copied, and projects contain no customer data. Five components do the work: domain (table or file), attribute (column), generator (value recipe), receiver (output format), scenario (instruction sheet). "Model, Design, Deploy, Manage" is GenRocket's own methodology and the Test Data Automation four-step process. Design happens in the cloud web platform; generation happens on your machine with the GenRocket Runtime, which needs Java, a profile, and usually port 443. Docker and Jenkins are two ways to run the same runtime in automated environments. A project is one data model and a licensing unit; a version is one release of it; categories help find projects. Roles and teams control who may change what; named users run scenarios on one machine at a time. GenRocket: domains, attributes and generators The GenRocket overview chapter gave you the five building blocks and the map of the product. This section works on the first three: domains (the tables), attributes (the columns) and generators (the recipes that decide each value). Together they are the Model and part of the Design phase. By the end you will be able to describe the ShopSphere CUSTOMERS, ORDERS and ORDER_ITEMS tables to GenRocket, link them so every foreign key is valid, and choose a generator for every column. The output side, receivers and scenarios, is in the receivers and scenarios chapter . The patterns you can build with generators (boundary, sequential, random, edge cases, null) get their own treatment in the data patterns chapter . What you will learn What a domain is, the dashboard where you work on it, and four ways to create one (new, scratch pad, DDL import, database schema extract). The three default domain variables ( id , loopCount , seed ) and what they control. Parent, child and sibling relationships, why GenRocket allows one parent only, and how this gives valid foreign keys. How to add attributes, reorder them, reference one from another and copy them. How GenRocket picks a generator automatically, how to replace one, how to assign one to many attributes, and how generator tags override the default. The generator families the docs name: list, string, date, conditional (business logic), query, UUID, name and identification generators. ProxyReferenceGen versus ReferenceGen, Enforce Type/Limit, seeding, linked generators and starting a primary key after the current maximum. A complete generator-per-column design for the ShopSphere tables. What this section is based on Official GenRocket help-centre pages, read in full, with the vendor's screenshots embedded and each one viewed before I described it. The main pages: Domains: " Domains Overview ", " Domain Dashboard ", " How do I create a New Domain? ", " How do I import my data model into GenRocket? ", the single and multiple DDL pages, the XTS file and XTS Import Wizard pages, " Scratch Pad ", the relationship pages, the Domain Referencing Wizard, " What are Domain Variables? ", " How to update Domain loopCounts " and " How do I create a Domain Category? ". ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.13 Words to know first Template domain A domain as defined in a project version. Think of it as the master copy. When you build a scenario, GenRocket makes a copy of it called a scenario domain . Scenario domain The per-scenario copy of a template domain. Changes to the template flow down to it unless it is locked. Domain variable A named setting that belongs to a domain, written global.DomainName.variableName , which generator parameters can refer to. Every domain gets three: id , loopCount and seed . loopCount How many rows (records) a domain generates. Seed A starting number for random generators. The same seed gives the same "random" data on every run. Parent, child, sibling GenRocket's way to express relationships between domains. A child has exactly one parent; "describing" tables are marked as siblings. Primary attribute The attribute marked as the key (shown with a key icon). Children refer to it. Generator parameter A setting on a generator, such as startRange . Required ones carry an asterisk in the web platform. Linked generators Several generators placed in one attribute so that later ones can use the values of earlier ones. Preview A sample of generated values shown in the web platform so you can check a configuration before downloading anything. DDL Data Definition Language: the SQL text that creates tables ( CREATE TABLE ... ). See the data basics chapter .

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.14.1 What a domain is A domain "defines real-world objects", a noun such as a person, place or thing. When you model a database, a domain is a table and its attributes are the columns. The docs' own example has four tables, Company, Department, User and Address, each becoming a domain with its columns as attributes. At least one domain must exist in a project to generate any data. A domain inside a project version is a template : it holds the attributes, generators and relationships. When you create a scenario, GenRocket copies the template into a scenario domain . Changes you make to the template cascade down to every scenario unless the scenario (or the scenario domain) is locked. This is similar to a document template and the letters printed from it, with one difference: you can pin a printed letter so that later edits to the template leave it alone. The docs also state a rule that surprises beginners: a template domain works independently and cannot really reference another domain's attributes. Relationships at the domain level are "just probable". The real references are made at the scenario level, where related domains are put together. You will see this again with ProxyReferenceGen below. Each time a domain is created or imported, it gets three default variables, all initially 1 ( details below ): id , loopCount and seed . Names have a small rule. The "New Domain" page notes that a domain name should contain only letters and numbers (spaces are now also allowed), so for the ShopSphere table ORDER_ITEMS I would name the domain OrderItems and put the real table name ORDER_ITEMS in the Table Name field you can see on the dashboard. The page does not say what happens with an underscore, so I avoid it. x: 6.14.4 Lab-style walk: a new domain by hand Select your project in the Projects pane. The Domains pane only appears once a project is selected. Click New Domain , then choose New Domain . This is the single-domain method. Type a name, for example Customers , and click Save . Use letters and numbers. What you should see: the Domain Dashboard for the new domain, with just one attribute called id and three domain variables ( global.Customers.id , .loopCount and .seed , each 1). Official screenshot: What a freshly created domain looks like: one id attribute, the three default variables set to 1, no receivers or scenarios yet, and a preview that simply counts 1, 2, 3. Source page ↗ You would then add attributes . That is fine for two or three columns; for a whole database use an import.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.14.5 Importing from DDL You can paste one table's DDL, or upload a file with many. The vendor's sample single-table DDL creates a user table with an id primary key and columns such as first_name varchar(25) not null . Choosing the database vendor from a list tells GenRocket how to read the SQL dialect. Multi-table import: Open New Domain and choose Import from DDL , then Import Multiple Domains from DDL . The other choice in that first dialog is single-table import. Pick the vendor (for example mysql ) and choose the DDL file. Optionally tick Enforce Type/Limit , which makes every assigned generator respect each column's declared type and size ( explained below ). Official screenshot: The multi-table DDL dialog: choose the database vendor, choose the file, and decide whether to enforce type and size. Source page ↗ Click Save and wait. The file goes into a queue (you can watch the Queue Status pane). The user who started the import gets an email when it starts and when it ends. What you should see: new domains with their attributes, a primary key marked, and generators assigned automatically. Optionally open the DDL audit from the Project Versions pane. The "GenRocket Table Schema (GTS) Audit Details" option shows what was imported and any errors. What the DDL import does not do The page is explicit: relationships between domains are not created automatically, receivers are not assigned and scenarios are not created. You must do these yourself (relationships with the Domain Referencing Wizard, below). It also lists SQL keywords the importer does not support, such as DEFAULT 'N'::bpchar , WITHOUT TIME ZONE and ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(N) . Remove them from the DDL before importing.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.14.6 Importing a live database schema (XTS) "XTS" stands for Extract Table Schema. This is the documented way to pull a database's structure straight from the database. Two steps: Extract the schema with the runtime. Run the runtime's -xts option with the path to a JDBC properties file and, optionally, the table names ( genrocket -xts /path/config.properties company,department,user ). With no names, every table is extracted. Options exist to exclude tables ( -xt , -xf ), and tables in a specific schema are written schema1:tablename . The properties file holds four required entries: driver , user , password and url . What you should see: an encrypted schema file, tied to your organisation. The page calls it a schema extract; it does not say more about what is read. Import the file with the XTS Import Wizard. Open Self Serve Options then XTS Wizard (or choose Import from XTS in the New Domain menu), choose the file, optionally enable Enforce Type/Limit, click Save and wait. The project is frozen until the import finishes. What you should see: domains, attributes and generators created for every extracted table, and the wizard's step 1 ready to be marked completed. Official screenshot: The XTS wizard hub: six numbered steps (import, referencing, generator tuning, receiver assignment, scenario assignment, domain families) with a completion checklist, plus edit and delete wizards for later changes. Source page ↗ Why use a wizard hub? Because after importing hundreds of tables, the remaining setup is also repetitive. Each step has its own wizard that works on a filtered set of domains at once, and you tick each step as complete so that the next unlocks. ShopSphere: which method? ShopSphere has three tables to generate. If the team gives you CREATE TABLE scripts, a DDL import takes minutes and keeps the primary key and sizes. If the QA lead can reach a dev copy of the database with a read-only account, an XTS extract avoids typing anything. For this section's walk-through, either works. The docs describe DDL and XTS imports as importing a schema, not rows.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.15 Relationships: parent, child and sibling Real tables point at each other: ORDERS.customer_id is a foreign key to CUSTOMERS ( data basics chapter ). If you generate 50 customers and 80 orders with random customer numbers, some orders will point at customers that do not exist, which breaks referential integrity . GenRocket's answer is to generate data in order, from parent to child , so a child can only pick a key a parent has already made. The documentation says GenRocket "generates synthetic data with full referential integrity" because every domain has an id or primary attribute, and children refer to the parent's primary attribute. It also says GenRocket looks at relationships differently from a database. A database table can have several foreign keys. A GenRocket domain may have only one parent but many siblings , because generating sequentially along several parents would produce "a large amount of unnecessary data". Official screenshot: The vendor's picture of the rule: the user table has three foreign keys, but in GenRocket only department is the parent; role and security_level are siblings (the vendor's earlier diagram shows all three as plain parents, the way a database sees it). Source page ↗ Term Meaning Rule of thumb from the docs ShopSphere Parent The domain whose rows are created first and which children point to A real relationship between two tables, such as department and user CUSTOMERS for ORDERS; ORDERS for ORDER_ITEMS Child A domain that refers to its single parent's primary attribute Exactly one parent ORDERS, ORDER_ITEMS Sibling A domain that only "describes" another, used for lookups If the table is an adjective of another (role is an adjective of user), mark it a sibling PRODUCTS describes an item: a sibling of ORDER_ITEMS The scenario page adds a vocabulary pair: the primary domain is the one a scenario is created for, and the root domain is the first parent up the chain. For an ORDER_ITEMS scenario, ORDER_ITEMS is primary and CUSTOMERS is root, so the scenario creates customers, then orders, then items, and every key matches. Why it matters Valid foreign keys are the reason a test can load generated data into a real database and not see constraint errors. The same guarantee is what the generation concepts chapter asked for in principle (parents before children); GenRocket builds it into the domain model.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.15.1 Setting a parent or sibling by hand
x: 6.15.1 Setting a parent or sibling by hand Open the child domain's dashboard and click the Relationship tab. The relationship is stored on the child. Click Add Referential Parent and tick the parent's radio button, then Save . Radio buttons enforce the one-parent rule. Official screenshot: Choosing the parent: the dialog lists the other domains with one radio button each, so only one can be chosen. Source page ↗ For a lookup table, click Add Referential Sibling , tick one or more domains, and add them to the scenarios you want. What you should see: the Relationship tab draws a small diagram of the parent, the child and its siblings. If scenarios already exist, you are asked which scenarios should receive the new relationship.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.15.2 The Domain Referencing Wizard After importing many tables, setting parents one by one is tedious. The wizard shows every domain with radio buttons for parent and checkboxes for siblings, and a diagram that updates as you click. It opens from the Project Versions pane or from step 2 of the XTS wizard. Official screenshot: The Domain Referencing Wizard. Left: domains and a Reviewed checkbox. Middle: for the selected domain (Account), the parent radio buttons and sibling checkboxes, and a progress pie. Right: a relationship diagram that redraws as you choose. Source page ↗ Select a domain on the left. Its possible parents appear in the middle pane. Click a parent's radio button. Siblings are ticked automatically for the other domains, and the domain is marked Reviewed because you changed it. If a domain is already right, click Mark as Reviewed . This is how you track progress when hundreds of tables exist. What you should see: the progress pie fills as domains are reviewed. In the XTS wizard, finish by clicking Mark Completed for step 2.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.16 Domain variables, loopCount and categories A domain variable is an instance variable of a domain, named global.DomainName.variableName . Generator parameters throughout the project can refer to it, and changing the value instantly changes everything that references it. Three exist by default: Variable Controls Default Example from the docs global.X.id The start of the id attribute. The id attribute's RangeGen reads it as startRange 1 Set to 100: ids run 100, 101, 102... global.X.loopCount How many rows the domain generates 1 Set to 10,000: ten thousand rows global.X.seed The seed for random generators 1 Same seed in two domains gives the same random numbers in both You can add your own, such as global.User.startDate . Defaults cannot be deleted.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.16.1 Changing how many rows The docs describe three levels at which the row count can be set, from broad to narrow: the domain (template) level, which applies everywhere; the test data case level, which they recommend as the most flexible because different tests can have different counts; and the scenario level, for special cases. This section changes it at the domain level. Open the domain and find the loopCount variable in Domain Variables. It starts at 1, which is why a first run produces a single row. Click its pencil icon, type the new value and click Save . What you should see: the Value column changes (in the vendor example, from 1 to 25). Official screenshot: Editing loopCount : the name is fixed, the value is the number of rows. The vendor example changes it to 25. Source page ↗ For many domains at once, the Global Editing menu has an "Edit Domains LoopCount" screen with checkboxes. One quirk: if a domain's first generator is a ListGen with setLoop set to true, the list length overrides the loop count and you cannot edit it from the scenario.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.16.2 Domain categories When a version has dozens of domains, group them: open a domain, click Categorize , create a category and save. Then filter the Domains pane by category or use Advanced Search. The same categorising works for scenarios, scenario chains and chain sets.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.17 Attributes: the columns An attribute defines a characteristic of a domain, and a domain needs attributes for any data to exist. Importing creates them from the schema; otherwise you add them by hand. Every new domain starts with an id attribute that produces a unique number per row. Click an attribute to open the Attribute Dashboard . The top half holds the attribute's own parameters; the bottom half holds its generators. Official screenshot: The top half of the Attribute Dashboard: the attribute's own parameters and, on the right, a preview of values it would generate. Source page ↗ Attribute parameter Meaning (docs wording, shortened) Name / Original Name Name is the camel-case name shown in the web platform. Original Name is the real column name as imported, and is what appears in output % Null and Null Value The percentage of rows that get a null (for negative tests) and what "null" looks like Output Condition Whether to leave the attribute out of a receiver's output when it is null, blank or both Visible If false, receivers do not see the attribute (useful for helper attributes) Primary Marks the key that children reference (a key icon appears) Type, Size, Required, Unique, Table Reference Imported from DDL or XTS: the column's declared type, length, null-ability, uniqueness and foreign-key target Date Format Format when the attribute generates a date Name versus original name For ShopSphere's customer_id column the attribute would be named customerId (GenRocket's camel-case convention), while its Original Name stays customer_id . Receivers such as the SQL-insert one use a separate columnName property key to write the real column name in the output.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.17.1 Adding an attribute In the Domain Dashboard, click New Attribute , type a name and Save . The name matters, because GenRocket uses it to guess a generator. Official screenshot: Adding an attribute needs only a domain and a name. Source page ↗ Look at the generator that was assigned, change parameters if needed and click Save Generator . What you should see: for firstName , the NameGen generator with parameters nameType , caseType , sortOrder , seed and waitAmount , and sample names in the preview. To add columns that appeared later in the real database, the docs use Scratch Pad: type the existing domain name exactly as it is in GenRocket (not the table name), list the new column names, and choose Create with Generators .

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.17.2 Referencing one attribute from another, and the ordering rule
x: 6.17.2 Referencing one attribute from another, and the ordering rule Many generators have a reference parameter that takes another attribute's value. EmailGen, for example, can reference the id so each email is unique (user1@example.com, user2@example.com...). Double-click the reference field and pick the attribute with the plus button. Official screenshot: The reference picker: double-click a reference parameter and choose from domain attributes, other generators in the same attribute, global variables, resources and organisation variables. Source page ↗ Official screenshot: The result: the reference parameter now shows #{User.id} . Save the generator, then check the preview. Source page ↗ Only look upward An attribute can only reference attributes above it in the list, because the engine fills attributes from top to bottom. Referencing one below returns an empty value. If you need to, click Rearrange Attributes and drag the attribute lower, then close the dialog to save. Other attribute tasks, in brief: Copy an attribute to another domain or project version (rename it if copying within the same domain); use Group Edit to change one parameter on many attributes, or remove many attributes at once; and use the gear icon (Browse and Manage Attributes) to see which generators are in use.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.18 Generators: the recipe for each value
x: 6.18 Generators: the recipe for each value A generator creates synthetic data (or queries existing data) for one attribute. Every attribute needs one. GenRocket advertises over 765 generators (a growing number), grouped by purpose and, for many countries, by country. Generators produce raw values only; receivers format them ( receivers and scenarios chapter ).

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.18.1 How a generator gets assigned automatically
x: 6.18.1 How a generator gets assigned automatically You rarely pick generators from scratch. For each new or imported attribute GenRocket tries these steps in order, according to the "How are Generators Assigned" page: Is there a matching Project generator tag ? If yes, use it. Otherwise, a matching Organization generator tag ? Otherwise, an intelligent guess from the domain name, attribute name, the project's industry type and usage patterns of other users. If Enforce Type/Limit is on, the column's type is considered too (a date column gets FlexibleDateRangeGen, a uniqueidentifier gets UUIDGen). If nothing fits, SimplePatternGen , which builds a value like name1, name2, name3 from the attribute name and the row's id. Official screenshot: The assignment flowchart: project tags first, then organisation tags, then the intelligent guess, and SimplePatternGen as the last resort. Source page ↗ Treat SimplePatternGen as a to-do marker It generates values like street1 , which are unique but not realistic. When you see it on an attribute, the tool could not guess; pick a better generator. The Project Version status report flags attributes without a generator.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.18.2 Replacing a generator on one attribute
x: 6.18.2 Replacing a generator on one attribute Open the attribute and use the Quick Generator Replacement menu below the generator. Typing part of a name filters the list (typing "town" offers BulgariaTownGen and UKTownGen ). Pick the generator and click Replace , then set its parameters and click Save Generator . What you should see: the new generator's name and parameters, and a fresh preview. Not sure of the name? Use Remove Generator and the Add a Generator dialog, which has categories and a search box. Official screenshot: Quick Generator Replacement: type any part of a generator's name, choose it, then click Replace. Source page ↗

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.18.3 Assigning one generator to many attributes
x: 6.18.3 Assigning one generator to many attributes If first_name and last_name both need NameGen, do it in one go through the gear icon above the attribute list. Click the gear icon (Browse and Manage Attributes) and tick the attributes. Selected rows turn blue. Type the generator name in Select Generator , click Set Generator and confirm with Yes . The dialog warns that existing generators on those attributes will be replaced. Official screenshot: The confirmation: NameGen will be applied to two attributes, replacing what they have. Source page ↗ Click Modify Generator Parameters to set a parameter for several attributes together. Here you can give firstName the value firstName in nameType and lastName the value lastName , each in its own row, or tick rows and set a shared parameter such as sortOrder . Official screenshot: Global Edit of generator parameters: one row per attribute, one column per parameter. Source page ↗ The Generator Tuning Wizard (step 3 of the XTS wizard) does the same across the whole project version, with statistics on how well generators match attributes. Copying a configured generator to other attributes is possible too: Simple Copy to chosen attributes (up to 20 per bucket; it replaces the target's generator) and Pattern Copy to all attributes whose names follow a pattern.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.18.4 Generator tags: steering the automatic choice
x: 6.18.4 Generator tags: steering the automatic choice A generator tag is a rule "if an attribute's name matches this text, assign this generator". Each has a value, a match type (starts with, ends with, contains or matches) and an optional ignore-case flag. Project-level tags apply to all versions of a project; organisation-level tags apply everywhere. The page's example: every attribute named like firstName in a Canadian project should get CanadaNameGen . Tags live in the Generator Tags tab of the Management pane (project) or the Organization menu. Official screenshot: Creating a project tag: when an attribute name matches firstName , assign CanadaNameGen . Source page ↗ To see which generators GenRocket thinks fit an attribute, click the small icon beside it in the attribute list. A ranked list appears (in the vendor's example NameGen 84%, AustraliaNameGen 5%, and so on); the top one is the default, and a tag icon lets you promote another.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.18.5 The families you will use The generator overview pages group generators into families. You need only the ideas below; each generator has a "How do I use..." page with parameters. Family What it does Examples named in the docs Numbers and ranges Counting, random numbers RangeGen (increasing numbers; startRange , endRange , jumpAmount , waitAmount , sortOrder ), RandomGen ( startRange , endRange , uniqueLimit , seed ) Names and identity People data NameGen ( nameType , caseType , sortOrder ), FullNameGen , EmailGen ( prefix , reference , suffix , extension ), PhoneNumberGen ( areaCode , prefix ), SSNGen ( generationType , includeDash ) List Pick from a fixed set, in order or random ListGen (up to 15 values; list , random , unique , setLoop ), ListCSVGen and ListExcelGen (read a file), PermutationGen (all combinations) String Combine and alter text ConcatGen , SubstringGen , PadGen , StringCaseGen , StringRegexGen , RandomStringGen , StringReplacementGen Date and time Dates in ranges and formats FlexibleDateRangeGen ( format , startDate , startRange , endRange , nextBy , randomize ), SystemDateGen , DateFormatGen Conditional (business logic) Output depends on a rule or percentage EvalCaseGen , EvalCaseActionGen , SwitchGen , IfThenElseGen (conditions); CalcGen (formula); WeightGen , MultiWeightGen (percentages); EdgeCaseGen Query Read real data from a database or file and blend it with generated data QueryOnceGen , QueryBeforeLoopV2Gen , QueryEachLoopV2Gen , QueryToMapGen (they need a JDBC connection) UUID 128-bit unique identifiers UUIDGen (random), UUIDSeedGen (patterned), UUIDTimeBasedGen Reference Copy a value generated elsewhere ReferenceGen , ProxyReferenceGen , LoopSetGen (sets the loop count) Conditional generators can express rules such as "if age is under 18, return Child; between 18 and 60, Adult" or "50% Regular, 30% Premium, 20% VIP". The docs contrast them with test data rules (G-Rules), which attach conditions to cases instead of single attributes. The patterns they enable are taken further in the data patterns chapter .

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.18.6 Seeding: repeatable randomness If two runs of a "random" generator give different numbers, test failures cannot be reproduced. A seed fixes this: the docs show a RandomGen for numbers 1 to 25 giving a new set every run when the seed is empty, but the same set whenever the seed is 1; a different seed (2) gives a different, but also repeatable, set. A seed can be set on an attribute's generator or through the domain's seed variable (button Global Seed applies it to the whole domain).

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.18.7 Linked generators One attribute can hold several generators in a row ( gen1 , gen2 ...). They run left to right, a generator may use any generator to its left , and the last one gives the value. The docs' example builds a full name in a single fullName attribute: NameGen, AlphabetGen (middle initial), NameGen (last name), then ConcatGen joining the three. Without linking you would need four attributes and would have to hide three of them with Visible turned off. Official screenshot: Linked generators: one fullName attribute holds four generators; the last one joins the first three. Source page ↗

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.18.8 ReferenceGen and ProxyReferenceGen: how a child finds its parent key
x: 6.18.8 ReferenceGen and ProxyReferenceGen: how a child finds its parent key This pair is the mechanism behind foreign keys, and it confuses everyone once. The docs explain it as follows. ProxyReferenceGen (domain level) A placeholder. Because a template domain cannot see another domain, the foreign-key attribute holds this generator, whose only parameter is startRange (default 1000). It marks "a parent's key goes here". Assigned automatically when you import with DDL or XTS and the column has a foreign key. ReferenceGen (scenario level) The real thing. When a scenario is created and the parent relationship exists, GenRocket swaps the proxy for ReferenceGen. Its one parameter reference points at the parent's primary attribute, such as #{AddressScenario.User.id} . It can also be set up manually, as in the docs' "User and Address" example. Official screenshot: How a manual proxy is set up: the attribute has Type = Reference and Table Reference = User (the parent domain), then the ProxyReferenceGen generator is assigned. Source page ↗ It explains why the project version status report asks for "foreign key attributes that do not have the ProxyReferenceGen". If the proxy is missing, the child will not find its parent when a scenario is made, and the reference value will not be filled in. The referenced attribute is the parent's primary attribute; if another column should be the target, tick its Primary checkbox.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.18.9 Enforcing data type and size A generator does not know that first_name is varchar(5) unless you tell it. The Enforce Type/Limit option makes the generator keep values within the attribute's Type and Size . It is on automatically for generators assigned by a DDL or XTS import, can be enabled for a whole project version when you create it, and can be set manually per generator. The docs list integer limits it applies, for example 127 for tinyint , 32767 for smallint and 2147483647 for int . Open the attribute, set Type (for example varchar ) and Size (for example 5) and save. These tell GenRocket the limits. Tick Enforce Type/Limit in the generator section and save the generator. What you should see: the preview now shows names of at most five characters. Official screenshot: Type and size set on the attribute, and Enforce Type/Limit ticked on the generator. Source page ↗

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.18.10 Primary keys after the current maximum
x: 6.18.10 Primary keys after the current maximum When you insert into a table that already holds rows, new keys must not collide with old ones. The docs' recipe links two generators in the id attribute. gen1 is QueryOnceGen with resourceName pointing at the JDBC resource, query = select max(id) + 1 from <tableName> and a sampleValue (5001 in the example) used for previews. gen2 is RangeGen whose startRange references gen1 . Official screenshot: The finished setup: gen2 (RangeGen) starts at gen1 (QueryOnceGen) and the preview begins at 5001. In a real run the start value comes from the database. Source page ↗ The General FAQ adds a second pattern for the parent side: write the parent's ids to a delimited file as you insert, then read them back with ListCSVGen at scenario level (the FAQ says "in the Parent Domain"), so the keys match.

Domain names avoid underscores; the table name keeps them. "Domain variable" shows the setting that gives a sensible start. variable (1001) Unique, increasing, matches the sample row 1001 firstName (first_name) NameGen nameType firstName, caseType capitalize, sortOrder random, a seed Realistic and repeatable lastName (last_name) NameGen nameType lastName Same generator, different type email EmailGen prefix customer, reference the id, suffix example, extension com Unique (the id is in it) and on a safe domain phone How many orders per customer and items per order is set per scenario, which is covered next. Because total_amount is generated independently, it will not equal the sum of its items. If a test needs that, use the conditional and calculation generators from the table above, or a G-Rule (the docs describe both). Lab: model ShopSphere in a practice project Goal: Build the three domains with relationships and a preview of each. (Needs a GenRocket account; do it in a trainer's sandbox project.) Create the domains by DDL import or by hand. Use the sample DDL of your team, or create Customers , Orders and OrderItems by hand with attributes from the tables above. Run the Domain Referencing Wizard (or Relationship tabs). Set Customers as the parent of Orders and Orders as the parent of OrderItems. Expected: a three-box chain in the relationship diagram. Replace generators where the table says so, set parameters, and save each generator. Expected: previews show names, ids from 1001, emails like customer1001@example.com , and dates in your range. Set the Customers loopCount to 50. Expected: the variable shows 50.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.20 Common mistakes and gotchas Watch for these Expecting a DDL import to set relationships. It does not. Run the Domain Referencing Wizard. Giving a table several parents. Use one parent and mark describing tables as siblings. Referencing an attribute below the current one. The value is empty. Reorder first. Leaving SimplePatternGen in place. It means no better guess was found. Forgetting Enforce Type/Limit. Values may not fit the target column. Forgetting that a new domain's loopCount is 1. A first run gives one row. Using ListGen for large lists. It supports up to 15 values. The docs recommend ListCSVV2Gen or another file-based list generator for more. ListCSVGen loads the whole file into memory. Exhausted unique values. RandomGen with a small range and uniqueLimit 1 stops with "Exhausted attempts to find the next valid random value" when the loop count is too high (the page's own example is a range of 1 to 20, a limit of 1 and 20 rows). Widen the range, raise the limit or lower the row count.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.21 Recap Key points A domain is a table (template), an attribute is a column, and each attribute needs a generator. Create domains by hand, with Scratch Pad, from DDL, or from a database with XTS. Imports do not set relationships or receivers. Each domain has three variables: id , loopCount and seed . One parent, many siblings. Parents generate first, so child foreign keys always find a parent. ProxyReferenceGen is the domain-level placeholder; ReferenceGen is the scenario-level real reference. GenRocket assigns generators by tags, then by guess, then SimplePatternGen. Replace them one at a time or in groups. Seeds make random data repeatable; linked generators build complex values; Enforce Type/Limit keeps values inside column limits. GenRocket: receivers and scenarios You have described the data ( domains, attributes and generators ). Two jobs remain: say what format the rows must arrive in, and say how many of what, in which order . The first job belongs to receivers , the second to scenarios . Once both exist, you download the scenario, run it with the GenRocket Runtime , and files or database rows appear. This section explains receivers (the common ones in detail, the rest by family), then scenarios, scenario chains and related controls, and finishes with an end-to-end ShopSphere build and a troubleshooting table. Patterns and the 50-record hands-on exercise follow in the data patterns chapter and the GenRocket hands-on chapter . What you will learn What a receiver is, the categories and output formats the vendor lists, and how to add a receiver to one domain or many. The receiver dashboard, property keys, file configuration, V2 receivers, resources and bulk-load receivers. The documented parameters of DelimitedFileReceiver, FixedFileReceiver, JSONFileReceiver, XMLFileReceiver, ExcelFileReceiver, SQLFileInsertReceiver and the SQL insert and update receivers. What segment-and-merge receivers (nested data) and masking receivers are, at overview level. What a scenario is, how to create, download and run one, and what the scenario dashboard, variables, state, chains, thread engine and locks do. A full walk: ShopSphere CUSTOMERS to CSV and ORDERS to SQL insert statements. A troubleshooting table built from the vendor's error pages. The category list comes from the vendor's receiver browser page ( app.genrocket.com/browse/receivers ), which I read. Scenarios: Scenarios Overview, How do I create a Scenario?, Scenario Dashboard, How do I run a GenRocket Scenario?, Scenario Variables, Managing Scenario State, the three scenario-chain pages, the Scenario Thread Engine, Scenario Level Locks, scenario-level relationships, the Jenkins page, and the error pages used in the troubleshooting table. The ShopSphere build is my own illustration made from documented parameters. Where a page and its screenshots disagree, I say so.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.22 Words to know first Receiver The component that takes a domain's raw generated values and writes them in a usable format: file, database insert, message and so on. Receiver parameter A setting for the receiver as a whole (where to write, what to name the file). A star in the web platform marks required ones. Attribute property key A setting for one attribute within a receiver, such as columnName (the header or column) or include (leave it in or out). Output format The shape of the result: delimited file, fixed-width file, JSON, XML, Excel, SQL statements and many others. Organization resource A named folder setting that each user fills in with their own path, for example resource.output.directory . Receivers refer to it instead of a hard-coded path. Scenario The saved instruction sheet: a primary domain, its parents, how many rows of each, and which receivers run. Primary domain and root domain The primary domain is the one the scenario is built for. The root is the first parent at the top of the chain. Scenario chain Several scenarios linked so that one command runs them in order. .grs file The downloaded, encrypted scenario file that you run with genrocket -r . Stateful scenario A scenario that remembers generator positions between runs, so a counter continues where it stopped.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.23.1 What a receiver is, and what it supports
x: 6.23.1 What a receiver is, and what it supports A receiver receives unformatted raw data from a generator and "morphs it into a usable output format". The overview says 120+ types exist (the count grows), and groups what they reach: SQL databases, NoSQL databases such as MongoDB, web-service formats (REST, SOAP, XML, JSON), fixed-file formats (CSV, Excel, VSAM, NACHA, BAI2), big-data formats (Parquet, Avro), message formats (Kafka, MQ, SWIFT), packaged applications (Salesforce, SAP, Guidewire, Duck Creek), complex feeds (X12 EDI, FHIR), documents and images (PDF, JPEG, TIFF, PNG), and cloud services. The vendor's receiver browser lists sixteen categories : Category What it holds (examples from the list) Common DelimitedFileReceiver, FixedFileReceiver, JSONFileReceiver, XMLFileReceiver, ExcelFileReceiver, SQLFileInsertReceiver, PDFFileReceiver JDBC and MySQL GenericSQLInsertReceiver, GenericSQLInsertV2Receiver, SQLUpdateReceiver, SQLBatchUpdateReceiver, StoredProcedureCallReceiver, MySQLInsertV2Receiver Data File OracleSQLFileInsertReceiver, SQLFileUpdateReceiver, ExcelFileMultiSheetReceiver, RandomAccessFixedFileReceiver Segment And Merge SegmentDataCreatorReceiver plus the JSON, XML, Avro, Parquet, Delimited, EDI and SWIFT merge receivers (nested data) Masking DelimitedFileMaskReceiver, JSONFileMaskReceiver, XMLFileMaskReceiver and others (replace values in an existing file) Partition Bulk-load receivers such as MySQLPartitionReceiver and DelimitedPartitionReceiver Web Service, Message Broker, Compression REST and SOAP callers, Kafka, zip-style receivers Image, PDF, Template, In Memory, Parquet, Miscellaneous Images, PDFs, template-driven output, memory formats, Parquet files, Groovy and Python script receivers The "Supported Output Formats" page is a large checklist rather than prose. For each format it marks whether GenRocket supports it, whether the vendor validated it, whether a bulk-load receiver exists, and for databases whether a JDBC driver exists. It also notes that a missing format can be requested from the vendor. Use it when a project asks "can you produce X?". Why it matters Receivers are why the same design can feed a CSV for a spreadsheet user, SQL inserts for a database tester and JSON for an API test. You never change the generators for that, only add or swap a receiver. More than one receiver may be attached to a domain: they run in the order listed, which is useful when you need several outputs or several folders.
