h: 6.23.2 Adding a receiver to a domain
x: 6.23.2 Adding a receiver to a domain Open the domain's dashboard and click New Receiver in the Domain Receivers pane. A receiver must be on a domain before its values reach any output. Official screenshot: The Add A Receiver dialog: pick a category on the left or type in the filter, then click the plus on the receiver you want. Source page ↗ Click the plus on the receiver, optionally rename it, and click Save . The name only has to be unique within the domain. If scenarios already exist for the domain, tick the ones that should get the receiver and click Add Receiver . Receivers copied into scenarios are separate from the template. Without this step, old scenarios will not have the new receiver. Official screenshot: Adding the receiver to existing scenarios: tick the scenarios that should receive it. Source page ↗ Fill in the required parameters (marked with a star) and click Save . What you should see: the receiver listed in the Domain Receivers pane of the Domain Dashboard. Many domains at once. In the Domain Dashboard open the Global Editing menu and choose "Add a New Receiver to Multiple Domains". This opens the Receiver Assignment Wizard: take ownership, choose the receiver and its parameters, filter to the domains, and execute. The vendor's example adds a DelimitedFileReceiver to the Department, User and Address domains in one pass.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.23.3 The Receiver Dashboard Click a receiver's name to open its dashboard. Four tabs matter. Tab Use Parameters The receiver's own settings. Starred ones are required to download and run a scenario Attributes Property Keys Per-attribute settings such as column name and include. Drag attributes to reorder output columns, use Sync Receiver Attribute Order , or the name-conversion menus (camel case is the default) File Config When available: when to start a new output file (for example by a count) and how to name files dynamically Directory Config When available: how many files per sub-folder and how to name sub-folders Official screenshot: A receiver's Parameters tab (DelimitedFileReceiver). Note the default path : #{resource.output.directory} , a reference to the organisation resource, not a typed folder. Source page ↗ The column order of an output file normally follows the attribute order in the domain, which is shaped by the rule that attributes only reference attributes above them. If that order is not what the consumer wants, drag the attributes into the desired order in the Attributes Property Keys tab.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.23.4 Output folders: organisation resources Receivers do not hold a user's folder name. They use resource references. A new account has three: resource.home.directory , resource.jdbc.directory and resource.output.directory (the dashboard screenshot in the overview chapter shows them). The resource page recommends the home directory be the real home folder, and the other two be different folders, preferably sub-folders of home, because using the same path for all three can cause errors "or, in some cases, a process that never finishes". After changing any resource value you must download your profile again and replace the old file in .genrocket ; otherwise you get the error "Unable to Download Users Profile" if a resource has no value, or stale paths if you forget.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.23.5 Configuration files, V2 receivers and bulk load
x: 6.23.5 Configuration files, V2 receivers and bulk load Configuration file. A file that tells a merge receiver how to combine data from different domains into one nested output. It defines file name segments, the segment files and the element layout. It is created in the Configuration Management tab and its name goes in the merge receiver's configName . Some imports (JSON, XML) create one for you. V2 receivers. Names contain "V2" just before "Receiver", for example GenericSQLInsertV2Receiver. They add two parameters, resourcePath and resourceSubDir , so a receiver can point to different configuration folders without creating more global resources. The vendor says V1 receivers will eventually be hidden from the picker; scenarios that already use them keep working. Bulk load receivers. Inserting through JDBC averages about 4,000 records per second, according to the page, which is slow for millions of rows. Bulk-load (partition) receivers write the database's native bulk-load file format instead. The page lists receivers for MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, MS SQL, DB2, Sybase, Snowflake, Databricks, Parquet and delimited files.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.24 The common receivers in detail These are the ones a beginner meets first. Parameters below are those the vendor pages list; a star means the page marks it required. Defaults and exact spellings can differ between product versions, so check the Parameters tab in your own project.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.24.1 DelimitedFileReceiver (CSV and other delimited files) Writes attribute values, separated by a delimiter, to a file. This is your CSV maker. Parameter Meaning path *, subDir Folder (and optional sub-folder) for the file fileName * Name of the file delimiter * The separator character. The screenshots show a tab ( \t ) as the default; type a comma for CSV includeHeader * Whether to write a header row of column names. Set to False for no header quoteTextData None, Single or Double quotes around text nullValue *, booleanValue * How null and true/false appear appendToFile * True adds to an existing file; false overwrites it uniqueAttribute An attribute used to stop a value being written twice headerFilePath , headerFileName Optional XML file that defines a multi-row header Property keys per attribute: columnName (the header text) and include . With no header file, each attribute's Original Name becomes the header. Official screenshot: Property keys: one row per attribute with the column name that will appear in the header and an include flag. Source page ↗ Header still showing after setting includeHeader to False? Two vendor reminders: re-download the scenario after any change, because the old file contains the old settings; and if it still shows, your receiver jar may be out of date (the jar-update page explains how to update).

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.24.2 FixedFileReceiver Writes fixed-width columns (every value padded to a set length), the shape of many mainframe and legacy files. Parameters: outputPath *, outputFileName *, subDir , lineSeparator (for example \n ), delimiter , quoteTextData * and includeHeader *. Property keys: columnName , include and length , the width of each attribute. Entering #{BLANK} or #{EMPTY} as a column name blanks a header cell.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.24.3 JSONFileReceiver Writes a flat JSON file ( not nested). Parameters: path *, subDir , fileName *, rootElementName and alwaysArray (true forces a JSON array even for a single record). Property keys: columnName , include , useQuotes (numbers such as SSNs are often quoted on purpose). One discrepancy worth flagging: the parameter list says path , while the page's use case mentions resourcePath . They are probably the same setting in different versions; trust the Parameters tab you see.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.24.4 XMLFileReceiver Writes flat XML. Parameters include path *, fileName *, rootElementName *, rowElementName * and exportStyle *, which chooses how values appear: ATTRIBUTES_ONLY (each value as an XML attribute of the row element), ELEMENTS_ONLY (child elements with text) or ELEMENT_VALUE (child elements with a value attribute). Property keys: name and include .

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.24.5 ExcelFileReceiver Writes an Excel file. The type parameter selects xlsx or xls ; path *, fileName * and type * are required, along with quote, boolean and null formatting settings. The page warns that Excel generation is generally slower than delimited files, and that on Linux a "Permission denied" error can mean the temporary profiles folder under /tmp is not writable.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.24.6 SQLFileInsertReceiver (SQL statements in a file) Creates a file of standard SQL insert statements, ready to run in any SQL client. Nothing touches a database while generating, which makes it a safe first choice for learning. Parameter Meaning path *, subDir , fileName * Where the .sql file goes and what it is called tableName * The real table name in the database batchCount * How many insert statements per batch written statementSeparator *, rowDelimiter * End-of-statement text (for example a semicolon) and line endings (UNIX/Linux/Mac-LF or Windows-CR/LF) quoteTextData *, nullValue *, booleanValue *, escapeCharacter Quoting and special-value formatting appendToFile *, uniqueAttribute Append or overwrite; avoid duplicates Property keys: columnName ( must match the real column name , such as first_name ), include and useQuotes . This is where the attribute name versus original name distinction from the generators chapter pays off. Official screenshot: The SQL-insert receiver's property keys: the attribute firstName is written to the column first_name . Make the columnName values match the database. Source page ↗ Example output from the vendor page: insert into user(id,first_name,last_name,middle_initial,emailAddress) values ('1','Penelope','Spaeth','F','user@email.com'); . If a nullable column should show a real NULL rather than a quoted string, set nullValue to NULL and quoteTextData to Double (or the style your database wants).

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.24.7 Writing straight into a database: the JDBC receivers
x: 6.24.7 Writing straight into a database: the JDBC receivers GenericSQLInsertReceiver inserts generated rows directly into a table through JDBC. Its parameters include resourceName * (the resource that points to the connection information), databaseName *, tableName *, truncate *, statementSeparator *, nullValue * and quoteTextData *. Property keys are columnName , columnType and include . The newer GenericSQLInsertV2Receiver adds resourcePath , resourceSubDir , continueOnError and logErrorDetails . The V2 page says it suits "up to 10,000 rows into a table with 25 columns or fewer", and recommends the GenericSQLInsertThreadReceiver for larger loads. truncate empties the table The V2 page warns that its truncate parameter can truncate or delete all existing rows before inserting, and that this cannot be undone. The default is "notApplicable" (nothing deleted). Never point a truncating receiver at a database you have not backed up. Direct database receivers need a JDBC configuration file ( config.properties ) on the machine running the scenario. It holds driver , user , password , url and, for receivers, batchCount . Its folder comes from resource.jdbc.directory . You can check a connection with the runtime's --test-jdbc option before running a scenario. Update receivers. SQLUpdateReceiver runs batched UPDATE statements whose values come from attributes (up to 20 attributes mapped to variables var1 to var20 ), which is the basis of replacing real values with synthetic ones in a table. SQLBatchUpdateReceiver reads one or more update statements from an XML configuration file that can address several databases, using placeholders such as #{firstName} . The FAQ also names StoredProcedureCallReceiver for calling procedures, while the FAQ says SQLUpdateReceiver can run DDL and DML scripts before or after a load, and another page uses SQLUpdateV2Receiver to create a database table.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.24.8 Nested data: segment-and-merge receivers (overview) JSONFileReceiver and XMLFileReceiver are flat. For nested output (customers containing orders containing items) GenRocket uses two receiver types together: Add SegmentDataCreatorReceiver to each domain except the merge domain. Each domain writes its rows as a small XML "segment" file, tagged with its parent's id so relationships survive. Create a merge domain and add a merge receiver, such as JSONSegmentMergeReceiver or XMLSegmentMergeReceiver . The merge receiver reads the segments and the configuration file, and writes nested files. Others exist for Avro, Parquet, delimited, fixed, EDI, HL7, SWIFT and SOAP. Put the merge scenario last in a scenario chain, create the configuration file, and download both. Merging only works once every segment exists. Imports of JSON, XSD and some other models set most of this up for you. The JSON merge page lists parameters such as outputPath , configName , segmentPath and recordsPerFile . If the root domain's loop count is 50 and recordsPerFile is 8, seven files are made (six with 8 records, one with 2). I do not walk through a full nested build here; the vendor pages do it with many screenshots.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.24.9 Masking receivers (overview) GenRocket also masks: it replaces sensitive values with synthetic ones, a method the file-masking overview calls Synthetic Data Masking (SDM). The file-masking receivers take an existing file and write a new one with the targeted values replaced: DelimitedFileMaskReceiver, ExcelFileMaskReceiver, JSONFileMaskReceiver, XMLFileMaskReceiver, ParquetFileMaskReceiver, ORCFileMaskReceiver, EDIFileMaskReceiver and FileMaskMultiBlockReceiver (fixed files such as VSAM). The same documents describe database masking in place (IPM). The vendor states that production data is never sent to GenRocket, since only metadata is used. How this compares with masking in other tools is in the Informatica masking chapter and the masking concepts chapter .

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.25.1 What a scenario is A scenario contains instructions that tell the GenRocket engine what synthetic data to generate and how much. You select the domains, say how many rows each produces, decide their order, download the scenario to a computer, and run it with the runtime. Domains, attributes, generators and receivers are its building blocks, so all four must exist first. A scenario is for one primary domain . If the primary domain has parents, the scenario pulls them in as helper domains so that foreign keys are valid: a scenario for Address with parents User and Department also creates departments and users. To output data for several related domains, create a scenario per domain and link them in a chain (below). The docs recommend a scenario for every domain, except pure helper domains.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.25.2 Creating a scenario There are three ways: New Scenario (with or without a primary domain), Quick Scenario (named after the domain and built from its relationships) and Batch New Scenarios (a quick scenario for each of several domains). Open the domain's dashboard and click Quick Scenario . Quick is the fastest way when the domain's parent relationships are already right, because it builds the parent domains in for you. Official screenshot: Quick Scenario is in the Domain Scenarios pane of the domain. Source page ↗ Accept the name (it matches the domain), add an optional description and click Save . What you should see: the Scenario Dashboard for the new scenario. Official screenshot: The Quick Scenario dialog states what it does: it builds in parent and sibling relationships so referential integrity holds. Source page ↗ For New Scenario , you enter a name and then choose to create it with or without a primary domain; with one, a wizard asks which domain and whether to add referential integrity automatically. Choose "without" when you want a different parent for this scenario only (see "Scenario domains and relationships" below).

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.25.3 The Scenario Dashboard Open a scenario from the Scenarios pane of the Project Dashboard (or from the domain's Domain Scenarios pane). Official screenshot: The Scenario Dashboard. The Scenario Domains table shows each domain, its loop count and a summary such as "1 User For Each Department". Receivers, generators and variables for the selected scenario domain are underneath. Source page ↗ Area What it does (docs) Top buttons Save name and description, Download the scenario, Copy , Delete , make stateful or stateless, Categorize , Lock and Sync Variable Set drop-down Chooses a project-version variable set for the downloaded scenario Scenario Domains Name, loop count, summary, which domain is primary and which is root. Add a template domain, remove a domain, randomise or change the loop count, choose the primary domain, Optimize , or Disable Non-Primary Receivers Scenario Domain Receivers Enable or disable each receiver for this scenario, and add references to its parameters Scenario Domain Generators All generators in use; click one to see which attributes use it Scenario Variables Create variables that exist only in this scenario Relationship tab The parent, child and sibling diagram of this scenario The loop count of a child domain is counted per parent row . In the vendor's chain example, Department generates 2 rows, User generates 10 per department (20 in total) and Address generates 1 per user (20 in total). So to get 100 orders for 50 customers, you set the Orders loop count to 2. A reminder about where to change the number of rows The domain page recommends test data cases for varying row counts. For this section, edit the loop count in the Scenario Domains table or on the domain. One quirk from the docs: if the first generator of an attribute is ListGen with setLoop true, the list length decides the count and the pencil icon is absent.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.25.4 Scenario domains, relationships and locks A scenario holds copies of template domains (scenario domains). Template changes flow into scenarios unless the scenario, a scenario domain or an attribute is locked . A lock stops changes made higher up from cascading down; while a scenario is locked the Sync button is hidden, and a locked item cannot be deleted. Use Sync to pull in template changes deliberately. You can also change a relationship for one scenario only, leaving the template alone. The vendor's story: for the Student scenario, make Teacher the parent of Student instead of Subject. The steps are to add the Teacher domain to the scenario, remove the Student domain's current parent, and add Teacher as its parent. Changes at scenario level do not flow back up. Relationships cannot be changed at the test data case level, so this is the place to do it.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.25.5 Scenario variables and scenario state Variables. Scenario variables are name-and-value pairs usable only inside the scenario that created them. In the Scenario Variables pane click New Variable , give a name and value and save, then reference it from a parameter (double-click the parameter field and pick it). State. Normally every run of a scenario produces the same data, for example a RangeGen starting at 10000 starts there every time. Sometimes you want the next run to continue (ids 10000 to 10099 first, then 10100 and on). Clicking Make Stateful saves each generator's position at the end of every successful run; Make Stateless turns it off. By default scenarios are stateless. The state is kept in a small H2 database in the .genrocket folder of the machine, and two runtime options list or clear it: --state-list and --state-clear (with an id or all ).

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.25.6 Scenario chains and chain sets A scenario chain links two or more scenarios so that one downloaded file runs them in order. The vendor example has Department, User and Address scenarios that produce three files from one command. A chain set links chains. A chain holds up to 25 scenarios and a chain set up to 25 chains. Optionally set a delay in seconds after a scenario. In the Scenario Chains pane click New Scenario Chain , enter a name and description and click Save . Naming makes the chain findable among many. Official screenshot: Naming the chain. Source page ↗ Click the plus beside each scenario to add it, in the order they should run. Parents must come first so that their output exists before children use it. Set delays with the pencil icon if you want one, then Save and Download . What you should see: a chain file you run just like a scenario.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.25.7 Running a scenario with the runtime
x: 6.25.7 Running a scenario with the runtime The scenario file is run from a command window on a machine that has the runtime and your profile. Download the scenario (or chain). The Download button on the dashboard, or the cloud icon in the Scenarios pane. Several scenarios can be downloaded together as a ZIP with Batch Download (up to 15). Open a command window or terminal in the folder where the file was saved. The command needs to find the file. Official screenshot: Start in the folder that holds the downloaded scenario. Source page ↗ Run genrocket -r <ScenarioName>.grs . The -r option means "run". Chains use the same command. What you should see: lines saying the licence was validated, the runtime versions, "Running Scenario ..." for each scenario, and finally "All done!" with the elapsed time. Official screenshot: A chain run in a terminal. The two green arrows mark the delays between scenarios. Source page ↗ When data is inserted into a database and loading fails, the runtime throws an exception to the command line (or to the testing framework when it runs in an automated pipeline), so no error means success. The vendor's note on stopping a run: press Ctrl+C , and on Windows answer the "Terminate batch job (Y/N)?" prompt with Y to abort. In automated environments the same command is placed in a build step (see the Jenkins section in the overview chapter ). Scenarios can also be run through a repository server or an API, which this guide does not cover.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.25.8 The Scenario Thread Engine (overview) The thread engine speeds up chains and chain sets by running several of their scenarios at the same time: genrocket -r Chain.grs -threaded 10 . The docs caution that threads may run in any order, so use it only where order does not matter, for example many segment files that a merge receiver combines later (the engine waits for every segment before merging). Do not use it where SQL inserts depend on parent rows already being present, because the order matters for referential integrity. Their example generated 10,000 EDI documents in 23 minutes 50 seconds with 20 threads against 53 minutes 20 seconds with one (on the vendor's test machine).

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
h: 6.26 ShopSphere end to end: CUSTOMERS to CSV and ORDERS to SQL inserts
x: 6.26 ShopSphere end to end: CUSTOMERS to CSV and ORDERS to SQL inserts Everything below uses the design from the domains, attributes and generators chapter . It is a practice build, not copied from a vendor page, so each step says which documented feature it uses. I chose SQLFileInsertReceiver for orders because it needs no database connection. Lab: one chain, two outputs Goal: produce Customers.csv with 50 customers and Orders.sql with 100 insert statements whose customer_id values all exist in the CSV. Check your resources. In the Resources pane the home and output directories must point to real folders on the machine that will run the scenario, and your profile must be in .genrocket . If you change one, download the profile again. Expected: three resource rows with paths (JDBC may be N/A). Add a DelimitedFileReceiver to the Customers domain. Set fileName to Customers.csv , delimiter to a comma, includeHeader True, quoteTextData None, appendToFile false. Leave path as the output resource. Expected: the receiver appears in Domain Receivers. In its Attributes Property Keys tab, set columnName to the table's column names. Set the id, names and other columns to customer_id , first_name and so on, so the CSV header matches the source database. Set include false for anything the consumer does not want. Add a SQLFileInsertReceiver to the Orders domain. Set tableName to ORDERS , fileName to Orders.sql , batchCount 100, statementSeparator a semicolon, quoteTextData Single, nullValue NULL, appendToFile false. Set the column names to order_id , customer_id , order_date and total_amount . Setting useQuotes false on the numeric columns is a reasonable choice, but the vendor page only says "sometimes a numeric value should be quoted". Expected: the property-key tab shows the real column names. Create the scenarios. Use Quick Scenario on Customers and on Orders. The Orders scenario brings Customers in as its parent. Both will normally have their receivers, so in the Orders scenario open the Scenario Domain Receivers pane and disable the Customers receiver (or use Disable Non-Primary Receivers ), so the CSV is written once, by the Customers scenario. Expected: the Orders Scenario Dashboard lists Customers and Orders, with Orders as primary and Customers as root. Set the row counts in the Scenario Domains table. Customers: 50. Orders: 2, meaning two orders for each customer, so 100 in total. Expected: the summary for Orders reads like "2 Orders For Each Customer" (the product's wording). Create a chain called ShopSphereChain with CustomersScenario first and OrdersScenario second, then download it. Order matters: parents first. Run genrocket -r ShopSphereChain.grs from the download folder. Expected: "Running Scenario CustomersScenario", then "Running Scenario OrdersScenario", then "All done". Output folder holds Customers.csv and Orders.sql . Show how to check the result Open the CSV: it should have a header and 50 rows with customer ids from 1001 to 1050 (if the id variable was set to 1001). Open the SQL file: it should contain 100 insert into ORDERS(order_id,customer_id,order_date,total_amount) values (...) lines whose customer_id values lie between 1001 and 1050, and every customer should appear twice. If you load both into a test database, load customers first so the foreign key is satisfied. (Load order is general database practice, not a documented GenRocket feature.) A header row in the CSV needs includeHeader true; if the Excel viewer shows a single column, the delimiter is wrong. Variation: insert straight into a database Replace the SQLFileInsertReceiver with GenericSQLInsertV2Receiver. Create a config.properties file with driver , user , password , url and batchCount , place it in the JDBC resource folder, set resourceName , databaseName and tableName , leave truncate on "notApplicable", and put the JDBC driver jar in the runtime's lib folder. Test the connection with --test-jdbc , then run the chain. This needs a database and credentials from the trainer or DBA, so it is optional here.

x: 6.27 Troubleshooting The vendor publishes several pages titled "ERROR: ..." plus related receiver and runtime notes. They are condensed here. Message or symptom Cause (docs) What the docs advise "Could not find the required profile: GRXXXXXXXProfile.grp" (may add "Unable to validate license. Reason: INVALID ACCESS KEY") The user profile is missing or outdated in .genrocket Download your profile again and place it in the .genrocket folder (replace any old one), then re-run "Unable to find domain <Domain> from <Domain.Attribute>" An attribute refers to another domain's attribute at test-data-case level while no relationship exists between the domains Define the relationship at the template domain level; add the parent to the scenario java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded Not enough heap: unique limits on generators, huge files read into memory, or large database queries Set JAVA_OPTS (for example -Xms1024m -Xmx2048m ), relax unique limits, use a batch-reading generator (CSVToMapGen instead of ListCSVGen), or raise the heap further "Communication link failure" when connecting to a database Network, firewall, server down, wrong host, port or credentials in the JDBC file, or an incompatible driver Check connectivity, that the server runs, firewall and VPN, the config.properties values and the driver (the page lists a dozen fixes, including MySQL settings) PostgreSQL: "column ... does not exist" PostgreSQL folds unquoted names to lower case Quote the identifier or change the receiver's column names to lower case "'genrocket' is not recognized" or "command not found" Runtime folder, home variable or PATH is wrong Check that the folder is named genrocket , the variables are set, and open a new terminal UnsupportedClassVersionError , "JAVA_HOME is set to invalid directory" Java too old, or the variable points to the wrong place Check java -version , set JAVA_OPTS for Java above 1.8, correct JAVA_HOME or install the JDK "Could not find or load main class ..." The dependent jars did not download Run genrocket -a , or download the jars manually into lib "Unable to Download Users Profile" A resource has no value Give every resource a valid path, then download again Excel generation: "Permission denied" The temporary profiles folder under /tmp is not accessible Fix folder permissions "Exhausted attempts to find the next valid random value" RandomGen unique limit cannot supply that many rows Widen the range, raise the limit or lower the row count

x: 6.28 Common mistakes and gotchas Watch for these Changing a receiver or loop count and re-running the old file. The scenario file is a snapshot. Download it again after every change. Wrong chain order. Children before parents means keys do not exist when you load the data. Column names that do not match the database. In SQL receivers, columnName must be the real column. Parent data written twice. A child scenario brings its parents in; disable the non-primary receivers if you only want the child's file. Using the thread engine with SQL inserts. Order matters there. Truncating a table by accident. Leave truncate on "notApplicable". Expecting the profile to refresh itself. After resource changes, download it again.

ct: GenRocket (1): the building blocks
x: 6.29 Recap Key points A receiver turns generator output into a format. Sixteen categories, 120+ receivers; more than one can sit on a domain. Receivers use organisation resources for folders. Download your profile again whenever a resource changes. Delimited, fixed, JSON, XML, Excel and SQL-file receivers cover most beginner needs; segment-and-merge receivers make nested output; masking receivers replace values in existing files. JDBC receivers insert directly and need a JDBC config file; V2 adds resource path settings; bulk-load receivers are for very large volumes. A scenario is built for a primary domain and pulls in its parents. A child's loop count is per parent row. Download, then run with genrocket -r . Chains run several scenarios in order. Locks, state and variables control behaviour between runs. When something fails, the commonest causes are a missing profile, wrong paths or variables, relationship or ordering mistakes, and Java memory settings.

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
h: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: GenRocket: data patterns for realistic and tricky test data So far in this part you have met the building blocks of GenRocket ( the overview , domains, attributes and generators , receivers and scenarios ). This section asks a sharper question: which values should a generator produce so that your tests find bugs? The bugs live at the edges: an order total of exactly 0.00 or 999999.99, a customer exactly 18 years old, an empty email, a phone number with a digit too few. Testers call these deliberate shapes data patterns . This section covers the Day 47 patterns: sequential, random, boundary and edge cases, and null. For each one you get a plain-words explanation with a ShopSphere example, then how GenRocket does it using only documented generators and parameters, then a pattern coverage table and a boundary-value lab. The next chapter uses several of these patterns in a full hands-on lab.

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: 7.1 Words to know first Positive test A test that feeds the app data it should accept, to check it works. Example: a valid order of 49.99. Negative test A test that feeds the app data it should reject or handle gracefully, to check it fails safely. Example: an order total of -5.00. Sequential data Values that follow a fixed order, such as 1, 2, 3, 4. The usual choice for ids and numbered records. Random data Values picked unpredictably from a set or range. Good for realistic variety. Seed A starting number for the random picker. Same seed in, same "random" values out, every run. This is how random data becomes repeatable. Boundary value A value at, just below or just above the limit of what is allowed. The limit is the "boundary". Edge case A rare or unusual situation outside the typical pattern, such as a name longer than the column allows. GenRocket's own definition is "a rare or unexpected scenario outside the typical usage pattern". Null "No value at all" in a database column. Different from an empty string, which is a value that happens to contain zero characters.

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: 7.2 Why test data needs patterns A vending machine tested only with the exact price always passes. Bugs appear with one coin too few, one too many, or none. Software is the same: defects hide where rules change, at a limit, an empty field or a rare combination. So testing needs typical data (positive tests: looks real, proves the main flows) and tricky data (negative and edge tests: sits on the rules, proves the app rejects bad input safely). A production copy is poor at the second kind: it may contain no order of exactly 0.00 and no 17-year-old customer. Synthetic data fixes that, because you decide what exists. GenRocket's CI/CD page says its web platform can design "any form of test data (positive, negative, patterns, permutations, boundary values, dynamic, load, etc.)" for a data model ( Automating Data Generation using CI/CD Pipeline ).

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
h: 7.2.2 How GenRocket thinks about a pattern
x: 7.2.2 How GenRocket thinks about a pattern In GenRocket a pattern is a generator choice plus its parameters on an attribute; there is no separate "pattern" switch. You pick a generator (see the chapter on domains, attributes and generators ), set its parameters and read the Preview pane. Generators only create raw values; receivers format them. Three mechanisms cover this section: one generator with parameters (RangeGen, RandomGen, ListGen), several generators linked in one attribute, and attribute settings such as % Null that sit outside the generator. The help centre says GenRocket has over 765 generators, so we stay with the ones that map to the syllabus.

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: 7.3.1 In plain words Sequential data follows a fixed, predictable order: 1, 2, 3, 4, like numbered tickets at a bakery counter. Testers want sequential data in three places: Primary keys. A primary key must be unique, so counting up is the simplest safe pattern. ShopSphere's customer_id values 1001, 1002, 1003 are sequential. Numbered records. Order numbers such as ORD-1001, ORD-1002, where you want to look at row 5 and know exactly what should be there. Predictable walks. A list of statuses walked in order (Pending, Shipped, Delivered) so a test can assume which row has which status. Sequential data is easy to read when a test fails, but looks nothing like real life, so mix it with random data for other columns.

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: 7.3.2 RangeGen: counting up (and down) The generator for counting is RangeGen . The help page says it "produces an increasing value from startRange to endRange", or to long.MAX_VALUE when no end range is given, and that "once the endRange has been reached, the value is reset to the startRange" ( RangeGen help page ). The page also notes it can be set to start at a number other than 1, for example to continue a database's primary keys. RangeGen parameters as documented (asterisk means required) Parameter What it does ShopSphere use startRange* The first value. 1001 for customer_id . endRange The largest value before the count restarts at startRange . If empty, it is long.MAX_VALUE . Leave empty for a primary key so it never wraps. jumpAmount* How much to add each time. 5 to leave gaps between ids. waitAmount* How many rows to wait before adding jumpAmount . 3 to give each customer three rows (for example three order items). iterate A true/false that decides when to move to the next value. Can reference another generator that produces true/false. Advance only when a linked generator says true. sortOrder* ascending or descending . Descending for negative ranges. The help page shows five worked examples. Here are the four that matter most, each with the official screenshots of the parameters and the preview. Start at a chosen value. Setting startRange to 500 makes the first row 500, then 501, 502 and so on. Official screenshot: The RangeGen parameter form with startRange set to 500, jumpAmount and waitAmount both 1, and sortOrder ascending. Source page ↗ Official screenshot: The Preview pane for that setting: 500, 501, 502, 503 and onward, one value per row. This is exactly the "start at a specific value" pattern. Source page ↗ Jump and wait. With startRange 0, endRange 100 and jumpAmount 5 the values are 0, 5, 10, 15 and so on. Raising waitAmount to 3 makes each value repeat three times (0, 0, 0, 5, 5, 5) before the jump, the pattern for one parent value repeated across several child rows. Count down through negatives. Set startRange -1, endRange -100 and sortOrder descending. Official screenshot: The preview for that setting: -1, -2, -3 down to -10. Negative numbers like these are the raw material for negative tests, such as a negative quantity. Source page ↗ Direction and range must agree If you give a descending order a positive end range, GenRocket stops you. The help page names the error "startRange cannot be less than or equal to endRange" and gives two fixes: change endRange to a negative value, or change sortOrder to ascending. The official screenshot below is the red error box the form shows. Official screenshot: The "Generator Parameter Errors" message shown when the start and end values contradict the sort order. It names the attribute and both values, so you can see which one to change. Source page ↗

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
h: 7.3.3 Other ways to get sequential values
x: 7.3.3 Other ways to get sequential values RangeGen is the main tool, but the documentation shows several more sequential patterns. The domain id. When a domain is created or imported it automatically gets an id attribute that "generates a unique ID for each test data record" ( Attributes Overview ). For many tests that is the primary key and you need do nothing. RangeConstantGen. The string-generators list describes it as an increasing value "similar to the RangeGen" with an optional prefix and suffix. With range 1 to 5 and prefix test the output is test1 to test5. The StringRemoveGen page confirms the parameter names startRange and prefix for it. For ShopSphere, a prefix of ORD- and start 1001 gives ORD-1001, ORD-1002 and so on (this adaptation is mine, the mechanism is documented). ListGen in order. ListGen "generates items in a provided list in sequential or random order". Its random parameter defaults to False, so the list is walked in order. Its example sets waitAmount to 5 so each of Pending, Shipped and Delivered repeats for five rows before moving on ( ListGen ). PhoneNumberGen. The page says it "generates phone numbers in a sequence (100-1000, 100-1001, ..., 999-9999)", with two optional parameters: areaCode (the three-digit area code placed in front) and prefix (the starting prefix, from which the number increases). It points to RandomPhoneNumberGen for random numbers. Official screenshot: The PhoneNumberGen preview: (800) 600-1000, (800) 600-1001, (800) 600-1002 and so on. Each row is the previous number plus one, the sequential pattern applied to phone numbers. The numbers are fake. Source page ↗

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: 7.3.4 Continuing after existing data Sometimes the target database already has rows, and new primary keys must start after the largest existing one. The help centre shows a linked-generator recipe ( primary key values after the max value ): Add QueryOnceGen to the id attribute. It runs one query before generating. Set resourceName to the JDBC resource, query to select max(id) + 1 from <tableName> and give sampleValue (the page uses 5001) so the Preview pane has something to show. gen1 holds "the next free id". Add RangeGen after it. For startRange , double-click the field and choose the Attribute Generator tab, then pick gen1 (it is written #{self.gen1} ). New ids begin after the largest existing id, so inserts will not collide with existing rows. RangeGen can reference QueryOnceGen only because QueryOnceGen sits to its left, a rule covered in section 7.6 . Gotcha: a sequence that wraps is not unique RangeGen goes back to startRange when it reaches endRange . If you set a small endRange on a primary key and generate more rows than the range holds, you create duplicate keys. Leave endRange empty for ids, or make sure the loop count is no larger than the range.

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: 7.4 Random data and repeatable randomness

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: 7.4.1 In plain words Random data is data picked without a visible order. Random data is what makes a generated customer list look real: different names, ages and cities. Random data has one practical problem. If a test fails today with a random customer, and tomorrow's run creates different customers, you cannot reproduce the failure. The fix is the seed : a starting number for the random picker. The same seed gives the same "random" sequence every time. Random but repeatable is the best of both.

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
h: 7.4.2 RandomGen: a random number in a range
x: 7.4.2 RandomGen: a random number in a range RandomGen "randomly generates a number within a range"; the page's own example is random ages between 18 and 65 ( RandomGen ). RandomGen parameters as documented Parameter Meaning startRange* The smallest value that can be produced. endRange* The largest value that can be produced. uniqueLimit How many times a given value may be produced. Empty means no limit. 1 means each value appears at most once; 10 means each value can appear ten times. It does not apply to dynamic start and end ranges that change per row. seed Makes the same random data come out every run. The page's second example limits repeats: numbers 1 to 10, uniqueLimit 2, and a domain loop count of 15 so the possible values are not used up. Each number appears at most twice. Official screenshot: RandomGen set to startRange 1, endRange 10 and uniqueLimit 2, so no number may appear more than twice. Source page ↗ Official screenshot: The delimited output for that setting: 15 rows, numbers between 1 and 10, none more than twice. This is how you generate "random but not too repetitive" values. Source page ↗ The error you get when uniqueness runs out With uniqueLimit 1, range 1 to 20 and a loop count of 20, the page reports "Exhausted attempts to find the next valid random value from range of 1 to 20" . The fixes it lists: raise the loop count, widen endRange or raise uniqueLimit . The rule of thumb is that rows asked for must be no more than (range size times uniqueLimit ). The same Java memory exhaustion can appear for very large unique sets: the troubleshooting page for "GC overhead limit exceeded" lists "generator parameters that limit the amount of data, such as a unique limit" as a cause ( that error page ).

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: 7.4.3 Random names, lists and strings NameGen. Generates first, last, male or female names ( nameType ), cased as capitalize , upperCase or lowerCase ( caseType ), in random , ascending or descending order ( sortOrder ), with an optional seed and a waitAmount . Its pool (1,000 male, 3,000 female and 10,000 last names) gives 40,000,000 combinations. ListGen. Set random to True to pick from a fixed list in random order (the page example picks one of five colours). Add unique True to use each list value only once; then the loop count must not exceed the number of values, or GenRocket throws an exception. ListGen supports up to 15 list items; for bigger lists the page recommends ListCSVV2Gen. RandomStringGen. Random text of a given length and stringType (letters, numbers, lettersAndNumbers, specialCharacters, ASCIICharacters or allCharacters), with caseType , seed , unique , include and exclude . The help page lists "test boundary conditions or invalid characters" and "filling a notes field with random strings to test character limits" among its uses. Its promo-code example links ConstantGen (PROMO), RandomStringGen (6 unique digits) and ConcatGen. Official screenshot: NameGen with nameType firstName, caseType capitalize, sortOrder random, an empty seed and waitAmount 1. This is the setting you will use for first names in the next chapter's lab. Source page ↗

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
h: 7.4.4 Seeding: random, but the same every time
x: 7.4.4 Seeding: random, but the same every time The help page "What is Seeding?" defines seeding as generating "the same set of random data for the same value of a seed". It says a seed can be entered in several places in GenRocket, including the domain's Global Seed variable and the generator's own seed parameter ( What is Seeding? ). The page's example uses two attributes, number1 and number2 , both RandomGen from 1 to 25: No seed on number1 : a different set of numbers every time the data is generated. Seed 1 on number1 : one fixed set, the same every run. Seed 1 on number2 too, same configuration: number2 gets the same set as number1 , so use different seeds for columns that should look independent. Seed 2 on number2 : a different fixed set. Official screenshot: The preview without a seed (11, 3, 6, 20, 2, 3, 3, 21, 20 and so on). Refreshing or regenerating would give a different list. Source page ↗ Official screenshot: The preview with seed 1: 10, 22, 2, 17, 15, 20, 8, 19, 6. With this seed these are the values you would get on every run. Source page ↗ Official screenshot: The preview with seed 2: 19, 8, 19, 8, 4, 14, 11, 25, 1. It differs from the seed 1 list, and it will be the same on every run of seed 2. Source page ↗ Why seeding matters for a TDM engineer Without a seed, "random" test data differs each run, so a failing test is a ghost. With a fixed seed, a regression suite sees identical data every night, and a failure can be replayed on a developer's laptop. Seed attributes you want repeatable. Leave the seed empty on attributes where you want fresh variety each run, such as a load test.

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: 7.5.1 In plain words Real data is lumpy. In a real shop, most orders are Delivered, a few are Pending and a handful are Cancelled. If your generator gives each status the same share, your test data is unrealistic, and reports built on it (percentage cancelled, say) look wrong. A weighted pattern says "give value A to 70 percent of the rows and value B to 30 percent". There are two related ideas. A list is the set of allowed values (Pending, Shipped, Delivered). A weight says how often each list value should appear. Lists come first, weights shape them. A ShopSphere order-status mix we might want (illustrative) Status Share of orders Why that share Delivered 70 percent Most historical orders are finished. Shipped 15 percent In transit. Pending 10 percent Just placed. Cancelled 5 percent Rare, but the app must handle it.

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: 7.5.2 ListGen: the allowed values ListGen "generates items in a provided list in sequential or random order" and is "a great choice when generating data from a fixed set of values (e.g., lookup table or categorical data)". Its documented parameters are list (one item per line), random (False by default), unique , waitAmount , iterate , seed , resetIndex and setLoop . It supports up to 15 items. One parameter deserves attention because the boundary lab at the end of this section uses it. setLoop "gives users the ability to OVERRIDE the loop count at the Scenario Level and ONLY produce the number of rows defined in this list". If the first generator of an attribute is a ListGen with setLoop True, the scenario's loop count is locked to the list length and shows as "N" with no edit pencil. The help page "Why can't I update the Loop Count Value from the Scenario?" explains that this lock is the reason ( link ).

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: 7.5.3 WeightGen: a two-way split WeightGen "defines a percentage between 1 and 100 to determine how often values generated from variable1 will be selected over values generated from variable2". The parameters are percentage* , variable1* , variable2* and an optional seed . Variables can be constants or references to other generators or attributes ( WeightGen ). The page's example: percentage 70, variable1 Pass, variable2 Fail gave 7 Pass and 3 Fail in ten rows. WeightGen splits between exactly two things; for more use MultiWeightGen.

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
h: 7.5.4 MultiWeightGen: any number of weighted values
x: 7.5.4 MultiWeightGen: any number of weighted values MultiWeightGen "allows multiple values to be weighted to determine how often each value is generated". The page's own example is rental vehicle types: economy 50 percent, midsize 35 percent, luxury 15 percent ( MultiWeightGen ). MultiWeightGen parameters as documented Parameter Meaning valueList The values. Press Enter after each. Each value is paired with the percentage in the same position. percentList The percentages (whole numbers) or references to values holding them. The page says to make them add up to 100 and notes the generator tolerates more than 100 in rare cases. seed Same random data every run. exactPercentage* When True, the distribution matches the percentages exactly. When False it is decided as rows are generated and may be off, with larger row counts converging on the percentages. totalLoopCount Total rows across a scenario, used when the loop count is dynamic. With 100 records and exactPercentage True, the page says you get exactly 50 economy, 35 midsize and 15 luxury (one screenshot on that page shows exactPercentage False, so set it deliberately). Official screenshot: The loan-type example: valueList Personal, Mortgage, Auto with percentList 50, 30, 20. Source page ↗ Official screenshot: The output of the page's second example: a loanType column chosen by weight, and an interestRate column that depends on it (Personal rows show 5%, 10% or 15%; Mortgage rows 3% to 5%; Auto rows 6% to 8%). One column driving another is the linked pattern in the next section. Source page ↗ The overview also names MultiWeightCSVGen (weights loaded from a file) and MultiWeightChildGen (spreads values across the children of each parent), and notes that MultiWeightGen "works in the totality of all rows and does not consider parent/child relations". For ShopSphere's status mix (Delivered 70, Shipped 15, Pending 10, Cancelled 5) use the same recipe with exactPercentage True and a seed ; with 1,000 orders expect exactly 700, 150, 100 and 50. How to give each parent a different number of children by weight is covered by the help page "How to generate Children based on Weights (Percentages)", and you will build it in the parent and child lab .

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: 7.6.1 In plain words Sometimes a value depends on another value. A voting-age check depends on age. A "refund reason" only makes sense if the order is cancelled. In a spreadsheet you would write an IF formula. GenRocket has the same idea in two parts: linked generators (several generators chained in one attribute) and conditional logic generators (generators that choose one result by testing a condition).

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: 7.6.2 Linked generators: the left-to-right rule The "Linked Generators Overview" page gives the rules that every conditional recipe relies on ( Linked Generators Overview ): Linked generators run left to right (top to bottom in the table): the first generates first, the second next, and so on. A linked generator may only reference sibling generators to its left . Referencing one to the right "will yield null values" because it has not generated yet. The rightmost generator holds the value returned for the attribute. The earlier ones are workings that do not appear in the output. Each one gets a default name ( gen1 , gen2 and so on) and you can add an alias. In a parameter, a reference to a sibling looks like #{self.gen1} , as in the ConcatGen design-pattern page. The same ordering applies between attributes: "Attributes can only reference other Attributes that are above them in the Attribute pane of a Domain." An attribute that references one below it "will return an empty value". The page "When can an Attribute not reference another Attribute?" shows the fix: click Rearrange Attributes and drag the attribute ( link ). Official screenshot: The attribute list of a User domain (id, version, emailAddress, firstName, lastName and so on) with an arrow pointing at the Rearrange Attributes button. Source page ↗ Official screenshot: The Rearrange Attributes dialog: a numbered list with a drag handle beside each attribute and a Close button, which saves the new order. Source page ↗

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: 7.6.3 The conditional logic generators The page "Conditional Logic Generators" groups them into calculation, condition-based and percentage-based generators ( link ). The table below keeps the descriptions short; check the generator's own page for parameters. Conditional logic generators and a ShopSphere use for each Generator What the docs say it does ShopSphere use EvalCaseGen Evaluates one equation using up to 5 variables; returns caseTrue or caseFalse . Recommended. If age >= 18 then "Yes" else "No". EvalCaseActionGen Several if-then-else cases; returns the first true. Recommended. Loyalty tier by points. SwitchGen Like a Java switch: returns the value of the matched case. Recommended. Shipping fee by country code. EdgeCaseGen Generates edge-case data for negative testing. A negative age every few rows. WeightGen / MultiWeightGen Percentage-based choice. Order status mix. The overview adds that G-Rules can hold the same logic with conditions and actions, which suits complex multi-condition data.

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
h: 7.6.4 EvalCaseGen: if age is 18 or more
x: 7.6.4 EvalCaseGen: if age is 18 or more EvalCaseGen takes an equation that uses var1 to var5 , plus caseTrue and caseFalse . Allowed operators include && , || , ! , >= , <= , == , != , < , > , % and / . Two cautions from the page: put string comparisons in double quotes (for example var1 == "Male" ), and for numbers of type long append a lower-case L ( var1l ) ( EvalCaseGen ). Its voting example is a perfect small boundary test. A domain Voting has an age attribute (RandomGen from 10 to 65) and an allowedToVote attribute using EvalCaseGen with equation var1 >= 18 , var1 referencing the age attribute, caseTrue Yes and caseFalse No. Notice that the attribute order matters: age sits above allowedToVote . = 18, var1 referencing the age attribute, caseTrue Yes, caseFalse No" loading="lazy"> Official screenshot: The EvalCaseGen form: equation var1 >= 18 , var1 referencing the Voting age attribute, caseTrue Yes and caseFalse No. Source page ↗ Official screenshot: The output: ages such as 29, 22, 46, 45 show Yes, while 14 and 11 show No. Ages 18 and above are accepted, below are rejected. Source page ↗

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
h: 7.6.5 EdgeCaseGen: sneak in the tricky value
x: 7.6.5 EdgeCaseGen: sneak in the tricky value EdgeCaseGen mixes a normal value with an edge-case value. It "generates edge case data useful for negative testing and testing edge cases". The page lists example edge cases: rounding issues in currency conversion, mismatched time zones, special characters in passwords, names longer than the character limit, names with invalid characters, uncommon file formats and validating a user's age ( EdgeCaseGen ). EdgeCaseGen parameters as documented Parameter Meaning source* The value (or reference) returned normally, when the edge-case condition is false. edgeCase* The value (or reference) returned when the edge case applies. condition A reference to a generator that returns true or false. True returns the edge case, false returns the source. cycle How many cycles the source value is returned before the edge-case value is returned. percentage The percentage of time the edge-case value is returned. seed Seed for the internal random picker used with percentage . So there are three ways to decide when the edge case appears: a true/false condition, a fixed cycle, or a percentage. Example 1 from the page: a negative age every few rows. Three linked generators: RandomGen age (1 to 120), RangeGen negative (-120 up to -1) and EdgeCaseGen case with source the age, edgeCase the negative value and cycle 5. Official screenshot: The three linked generators: age (RandomGen), negative (RangeGen) and case (EdgeCaseGen). Source page ↗ Official screenshot: The preview with three columns. The case column repeats the age value for five rows (88, 76, 112, 51, 59) and then shows the negative value -115 on the sixth row, so the edge value arrives after five source values. Read the screenshot rather than assuming "every fifth row". Source page ↗ Example 2: a first name longer than 10 characters, 25 percent of the time. Two ListGens hold short and long names, and EdgeCaseGen has percentage 25. Official screenshot: The output: twenty first names. Five of them are long (for example Maximiliano, Peleloperose, Anavictoria, Oliviagrace, Marcoantonio), which is the 25 percent edge share. A name field that holds only 10 characters should reject or truncate those rows. Source page ↗ The documentation disagrees with itself here The condition parameter is documented as "True returns the edge case". In the page's third example (RandomGen source, RandomStringGen edge case, RandomTrueFalseGen condition) the screenshot shows the opposite: rows with True carry the source value, rows with False the edge value. Do not guess: build it, read the Preview pane, and flip the condition if the result is reversed. G-Cases and permutations A G-Case "modifies the components within a Scenario", so one scenario can produce typical data in one case and edge-heavy data in another, with categories such as Beta, Unit, Load and Negative ( G-Cases Overview ). PermutationGen "can generate all possible combinations of data for a given set of values" from a list parameter: my arithmetic, not the page's: drop-downs with 3, 4 and 2 choices give 24 combinations. Use boundary values for single fields and permutations for combinations of fields.

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: 7.7.1 In plain words Imagine a paper form with a "middle name" box. There are three different situations. The person wrote a name (a value). The person wrote nothing and left the box empty (blank). Or the box was crossed out because the question did not apply (not applicable). Databases make the same distinction. Four things an email column can hold (illustrative) What is stored Name Typical bug it exposes asha.menon@example.com A value None, this is the normal case. (nothing, the cell is "unknown") NULL Code that calls a method on the email crashes with a null error. (zero characters) Empty string Validation lets "" through because it is not null. (only spaces) Blank text Trim logic missing, so the app thinks a value exists. Applications treat these four differently, so test data needs all of them. GenRocket gives you three places to produce null and blank data.

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
h: 7.7.2 Place 1: the attribute's own null settings
x: 7.7.2 Place 1: the attribute's own null settings Every attribute has parameters on the Attribute Dashboard, above the generator. Four of them control nulls and visibility ( Attribute Dashboard ): Attribute parameters that affect nulls and output, as documented Parameter What the docs say Use % Null "Defines the percentage of time the null value is used for negative testing." Make about 10 percent of emails null with one number. Null Value "Define the null value or click * for an empty string." Choose what a null looks like. The asterisk means an empty string. Output Condition Whether to exclude the attribute from a receiver's output when its value is null, blank, or both. Drop empty keys from JSON. Visible Visible to receivers when true, invisible when false. Hide helper attributes from the output. Official screenshot: The Attribute Dashboard for a firstName attribute. The top-left block holds the fields from the table: % Null (0 here), Null Value (blank, with a star button for "empty string"), Output Condition (None) and the Visible and Primary checkboxes. The generator form (NameGen) is underneath and a Preview pane sits on the right. Source page ↗ I found no worked example of % Null in the pages I had, so set it, save, and watch the Preview pane. The DelimitedFileReceiver documents a required parameter nullValue ("Represents a Null value") and a booleanValue format ( DelimitedFileReceiver ). The screenshot of its form shows nullValue pre-filled with (null) . If a downstream loader expects the literal text NULL or an empty cell, change this parameter before you generate. A mismatch here is a classic source of "the data looks right in GenRocket but my load fails". Official screenshot: The DelimitedFileReceiver form. Look at nullValue , pre-filled with (null) , together with delimiter , quoteTextData , booleanValue , includeHeader and appendToFile . Source page ↗ Common null-testing mistakes Only testing NULL. NULL, empty string and spaces are three different inputs. Cover all three. Nulls in a primary key. Never use % Null on an id or a foreign key unless you are deliberately testing that the database rejects it. Forgetting the receiver. A null written as (null) may load as the five-character text "(null)". Check nullValue . Referencing a generator to the right. h: 7.8.1 Boundary value analysis, explained from zero
x: 7.8.1 Boundary value analysis, explained from zero Suppose a form accepts an age from 18 to 65. You cannot test every possible number. Boundary value analysis (BVA) is a way to pick a handful of values that find most bugs. The idea comes from experience: programmers make "off by one" mistakes. They write age > 18 when they meant age >= 18 . Such a bug is invisible when you test age 40 and obvious when you test age 18. Here is the method in four steps. Find the rule. Write down the allowed range. ShopSphere example: an order total is valid from 0.00 up to 999999.99. Split the world into groups ("partitions"). Everything below the range is invalid, everything inside is valid, everything above is invalid. Testing one value from inside each group covers "the typical case" of each. Pick the values at each edge. For each boundary test the value just below it, on it and just above it. Write the expected result for each value. Decide accept or reject for every value before generating anything, so the data file doubles as a test oracle. For an inclusive range from a minimum to a maximum, the classic set is seven values: just below the minimum, the minimum, just above the minimum, one typical value, just below the maximum, the maximum, and just above the maximum. Boundary values for a ShopSphere order total valid from 0.00 to 999999.99 (illustrative rule, written for this guide) Case Value Expected result Bug it would catch Just below minimum -0.01 Reject App accepts negative totals. Minimum 0.00 Accept Code says total > 0 and rejects a free order. Just above minimum 0.01 Accept Rounding drops one cent to zero. Typical 500.00 Accept The normal flow itself is broken. Just below maximum 999999.98 Accept Off-by-one at the high end. Maximum 999999.99 Accept Column too small for the largest legal value. Just above maximum 1000000.00 Reject Overflow: the column or code cannot hold it. An age rule works the same way. Say a ShopSphere customer must be 18 or older on a reference date of 2026-01-01. Boundary values for the 18-or-older rule, reference date 2026-01-01 (illustrative rule) Date of birth Age on 2026-01-01 Expected result Note 2008-01-02 17 (turns 18 the next day) Reject The classic 17-versus-18 boundary. 2008-01-01 18 (birthday is the reference date) Accept Tests the "on the day" case. 2007-12-31 18 (birthday was one day earlier) Accept Just inside the valid group. 1990-04-12 35 Accept Typical adult (Asha Menon's fake date of birth).

Recipes for boundary and edge data, all built from documented generators Need Recipe Source page A small fixed set of exact values, each exactly once ListGen with setLoop True and the values in list . The loop count becomes the list length (up to 15 items). ListGen Mostly typical data, with the edge value every few rows EdgeCaseGen with source the typical generator, edgeCase the edge value and cycle N. EdgeCaseGen Mostly typical data, with an edge value a set share of the time EdgeCaseGen with percentage , or WeightGen/MultiWeightGen. EdgeCaseGen; WeightGen Too-long text for a column EdgeCaseGen with a list of short names and a list of long names, or RandomStringGen with a large length . x: 7.9.1 In plain words Every database column has a type and a size. A first_name VARCHAR(5) column holds at most five characters. An INT column holds whole numbers up to about two billion. If your generator produces "Maximiliano" for that first-name column, the insert fails, and a hundred rows of perfectly good data are lost because one name was too long. There are two opposite needs. For positive data, the generated values must always fit the column, so loads never fail. For negative data (the long-name edge case in 20.6.5 ) you deliberately break the size. GenRocket handles the first need with a switch called Enforce Type/Limit.

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: 7.9.2 Enforce Type/Limit The page "How to Enforce Data Type and Size in Generated Data" explains the option ( link ): Value limits are enforced automatically when you import a DDL (database table definition) or an XTS file (GenRocket's extracted table schema). The option is switched on for every generator assigned during such an import. It is available on every generator and can be set on any individual generator in a domain. Use it "whenever you want the generated data to be within a defined data type and size". When on, it limits output to the Type and Size parameters of the attribute. The page's example: NameGen with Enforce Type/Limit on, Type varchar and Size 5. First names in the Preview pane are limited to 5 characters. Integer limits the page lists for Enforce Type/Limit Data type Largest value enforced tinyint 127 smallint 32767 mediumint 8388607 int or integer 2147483647 bit or vbit 1 Those numbers are useful boundary values in their own right. If a column is smallint , then 32767 is its maximum, 32768 is "just above maximum", and a good negative test sends exactly that.

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: 7.9.3 Setting it by hand For a manually built domain: open the attribute, type a data type ( varchar , int , float , decimal ) in Type and the limit in Size , click Save, then tick Enforce Type/Limit in the generator form and save the generator. The Preview pane then shows values within the size. Official screenshot: The NameGen form with the Enforce Type/Limit checkbox ticked (arrow), nameType firstName, caseType capitalize and sortOrder random. Source page ↗ The imported Required flag matters too: if it is ticked, do not put % Null on that attribute unless you are testing the rejection. Turning it off for edge cases Because it is on by default for imported models, a generator will not produce the too-long name a negative test wants. Switch it off on that generator, or use a separate generator for the edge value, and check Preview.

x: 7.9.4 Decimal places and number formatting Money needs a fixed number of decimal places: 49.9 and 49.90 are different text, and a DECIMAL(8,2) column expects two places. NumberFormatGen formats a referenced number: pad with leading zeros, fix the number of decimal places, fix the number of digits, add commas, include a sign. Parameters ( NumberFormatGen ): reference* : the attribute (or linked generator) to format. It should produce a floating-point number. decimalFormat* : a pattern. The page's samples: 123456.789 with ###,###.### gives 123,456.789; with ###.## gives 123456.79; 124.78 with 000000.000 gives 000123.780; 9.95 with 000.### gives 009.95. includeSign* : NEVER, ALWAYS, POSITIVE_ONLY or NEGATIVE_ONLY. includeDecimal* : whether the decimal point appears. padLength* : how many zeros to pad on the left (a value of 10 turns 120024 into 0000120024). The page links NumberFormatGen to RangeDecimalGen and RandomDecimalGen , which supply the decimal number. I did not have separate pages for those two. From the page's screenshots, RangeDecimalGen shows parameters startRange , endRange , decimalFormat , jumpAmount , waitAmount and sortOrder , and RandomDecimalGen shows startRange , endRange , decimalFormat and seed . Official screenshot: The output of the page's first example: gen1 is a decimal sequence from -10.00 in steps of 0.75, and gen2 is the same number padded to five digits with the sign kept (-00010.00, -00009.25 and so on). Source page ↗ Official screenshot: The result of formatting those numbers to two places: gen1 shows 53.8970 and gen2 shows 53.90, 49.6710 and 49.67, and so on. This is the pattern for money columns. Source page ↗ For the typical partition of total_amount use RandomDecimalGen from 1 to 5000 with a seed ; by analogy with the screenshot's #0.0000 , two decimals would be #0.00 (check in Preview). Boundary rows come from the boundary lab .

x: 7.10.1 In plain words Dates are a rich source of bugs. A birth date that makes someone 17 versus 18, an order dated 29 February, a timestamp at midnight, a date written month-first in one system and day-first in another. Date test data needs three things: a format (how the date is written), a range (earliest and latest) and a pattern (sequential, random, or specific edge dates).

ct: GenRocket (2): data patterns and a hands-on build
x: 7.10.2 FlexibleDateRangeGen GenRocket automatically picks FlexibleDateRangeGen for attributes whose imported data type is "date" or "time" ( How are Generators Assigned ). It generates dates from a start date, moving by a range and a jump ( FlexibleDateRangeGen ). FlexibleDateRangeGen parameters as documented Parameter Meaning format* The date format for the start date and the output. Default yyyy-MM-dd . Others: MM/dd/yy , MM-dd-yy , yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss . startDate The anchor date. Empty means the current date. startRange* , endRange* Integers: how far forward (positive) or backward (negative) to move from the start date. Zero means no change. An error occurs if startRange is more than endRange . initialJump* How much to jump before the first value (Year, Month, Week, Day or Hour). jumpAmount* How much to jump by for each value. nextBy* Which part of the date moves: Year, Month, Day, Hour, Minute, Second or Millisecond. waitAmount* Rows to repeat a date before moving on. randomize* Sequential (false) or random (true) within the range. randomizeMonthDay* Whether month and day are random when neither is the nextBy part (None, MonthAndDay, MonthOnly or DayOnly). seed Repeatable random dates. exclude Values to skip, as comma-separated integers within the range of the nextBy part (1 to 31 for days, 1 to 12 for months). Official screenshot: The complete FlexibleDateRangeGen form on one screen: format , startDate , startRange , endRange , initialJump , jumpAmount , nextBy , waitAmount , randomize , randomizeMonthDay , seed and exclude . Source page ↗ The page's first example: startDate 01-01-1970, startRange 0, endRange 4, initialJump 0, jumpAmount 10, nextBy Year, randomize false and randomizeMonthDay None. The first record is 01-01-1970 and the year grows by 10 each record: 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, then the pattern restarts at 1970 on the fifth record. Official screenshot: The preview of that example: 01-01-1970, 01-01-1980, 01-01-1990, 01-01-2000, then 01-01-1970 again. The four-record cycle comes from endRange minus startRange . Source page ↗ Check the direction yourself Example 2 contradicts itself: its jumpBy line says the year increases, but the title, records and screenshot go 1965 down to 1961. In the examples a cycle holds endRange minus startRange values (0 to 4 gives four dates). Change one parameter at a time and read the Preview pane. Official screenshot: The preview for the negative-range example: 01-01-1965, 01-01-1964, 01-01-1963, 01-01-1962, 01-01-1961, then back to 01-01-1965. The decreasing order is what the screenshot shows. Source page ↗

x: 7.10.4 DateDeltaGen: the gap between two dates DateDeltaGen "computes the delta between two dates", in days, months, years or hours. Parameters: conversion* , formatOne* , formatTwo* , dateRefOne* , dateRefTwo* . The page's example links two FlexibleDateRangeGen generators and subtracts their dates ( DateDeltaGen ). The pages do not say how partial years are rounded, so verify the 17 versus 18 rows by eye before trusting the computed age column. Worked example: the 17 versus 18 rows For the boundary rows, a ListGen with setLoop True holds 2008-01-02 , 2008-01-01 , 2007-12-31 and 1990-04-12 , the four rows of the age table in 20.8.1 . x: 7.13 Recap Recap Test data needs patterns: typical data for positive tests, tricky data (boundary, edge, null) for negative tests. Sequential: RangeGen ( startRange , jumpAmount , waitAmount ), the domain id , ListGen in order, PhoneNumberGen. A range that wraps is not unique. Random: RandomGen, NameGen, ListGen and RandomStringGen; a seed makes random data repeatable, and two attributes with the same seed and settings repeat each other. Weights: WeightGen for two-way splits, MultiWeightGen with exactPercentage True for exact shares. Linked and conditional generators run left to right and may only reference what is to their left (and attributes above them). EvalCaseGen handles if/else; EdgeCaseGen mixes in edge values by cycle, percentage or condition. Null and blank: attribute % Null and Null Value , NullGen, ConstantGen with #{BLANK} or #{EMPTY} , Output Condition, and the receiver's nullValue . Boundary value analysis: test just below, on and just above each limit, plus one typical value. In GenRocket use exact lists (ListGen with setLoop True) for boundaries. Enforce Type/Limit keeps values inside the column; NumberFormatGen fixes decimals; FlexibleDateRangeGen and DateDeltaGen cover dates. Verify uncertain behaviour in Preview. Hands-on: generate 50 customer records with GenRocket The previous chapters gave you the vocabulary ( the GenRocket overview , domains, attributes and generators , receivers and scenarios ) and the patterns ( the data patterns chapter ). Now you do the work. The syllabus for Days 49 and 50 asks for one concrete deliverable: generate 50 records with the columns FirstName, LastName, Full Name (FirstName MiddleName LastName) and Phone Number . This section builds exactly that, click by click, explains why each click is needed, and shows what you should see. Before the lab there is a short planning section for Day 48, "end-to-end data generation plan development". Real work never starts at the keyboard. Someone decides what data is needed, tries a small proof first, checks the environment, and plans how the data generation will run every week. The 50-record lab is, in miniature, the proof-of-concept step of that plan.

x: 7.14 Words to know first TDG (test data generation) Creating test data from scratch with a tool instead of copying production. The syllabus uses the abbreviation. In this section it means doing it with GenRocket. POC (proof of concept) A small, quick trial that shows an approach can work before you commit to the full effort. Loop count How many rows a domain generates. The documentation variable is global.<DomainName>.loopCount and it starts at 1. Reference A parameter value that points at another attribute or generator, written like #{self.gen1} or #{Domain.attribute} , so one value is built from others. Visible An attribute setting. Visible means it is written to the output; not visible means it is used only as a helper. Delimited file A text file where each row is one record and columns are separated by a character such as a comma or tab. CSV is the comma version. Output directory The folder where files are written. GenRocket stores it as an organization resource named resource.output.directory , set per user. User profile A small file downloaded from GenRocket Cloud that links your computer to your licence. It goes in a .genrocket folder and is needed to run a scenario.

A good POC: Uses one domain , a few attributes and a small row count (the 50-record lab fits). Covers the whole path : model, design, deliver, run, check the file. A half-built POC proves nothing. States success criteria in advance, for example "50 rows, no empty values, phone numbers all the same length, runs in a command line without manual edits". Records what was hard : licence, runtime install, access to the output folder. The documentation frames GenRocket's own method as Model, Design, Deploy, Manage ( The GenRocket Methodology , whose text is a title and a video that I could not watch, and the CI/CD page above that spells the four steps out). The POC exercises the first three: you model a Customer domain, design its attributes and scenario, and deploy by running the scenario. "Manage" is stage 4.

x: 7.15.3 Stage 3: assess the application and data environment Before you scale up, look at what is around the data. The table gives the questions and the documented facts that help you answer them. Environment assessment checklist Question Why it matters Documented anchor Where is the data model defined? If a DDL, XSD, CSV, JSON or YAML exists, import it instead of typing attributes. The project-creation page lists import options: XTS, XSD, CSV, DDL, JSON, JSON Schema, Avro JSON Schema, Spark Schema, YAML, Salesforce and Presets; or create domains manually ( link ). What formats must the data arrive in? Decides the receiver. "120+ types of Receivers" (receivers overview). We use DelimitedFileReceiver. How are tables related?
