h: 7.16 What we are building, and the design decisions
x: 7.16 What we are building, and the design decisions The syllabus deliverable is four columns and 50 rows. Here is the target, with each column's source. Target file layout and how each column is produced Column header Attribute Generator Notes (not in output) id automatic Every domain gets an id attribute. We exclude it from the file with the receiver's include setting. FirstName firstName NameGen, nameType firstName GenRocket assigns NameGen automatically to attributes with "name" in the name. (not in output) middleName NameGen Helper only. Visible is switched off. LastName lastName NameGen, nameType lastName Full Name fullName ConcatGen First name, a space, middle name, a space, last name. Phone Number phoneNumber PhoneNumberGen Sequential numbers, one per row. Four choices deserve a reason. Why a separate middleName attribute? The syllabus defines Full Name as "FirstName MiddleName LastName". For the Full Name to contain the same first and last name as the other columns, it must refer to those columns, not generate new names. So the middle name needs its own attribute too. Which generator for the middle name? NameGen's documented nameType choices are firstName, lastName, maleName and femaleName. There is no "middleName" type, so I use firstName , because middle names are usually given names. That is my choice, not a documented rule. The help centre also has a FullNameGen , which generates "a full name consisting of a first, middle, and last name with an optional title and suffix" ( FullNameGen ). It is a valid alternative, but it creates its own first and last names inside one value, so they would not match the FirstName and LastName columns. Its title and suffix percentages also default to 100, so you would have to set them to 0. Why reference attributes instead of linked generators? The documentation shows both. The linked way builds the full name inside one attribute with three generators and no helper attributes ( Linked Generators Overview , "Generate a Person's Full Name"). Our task needs separate FirstName and LastName columns as well, so we build the pieces as real attributes and reference them. The overview notes the cost of this approach: the helper attributes "would then need to have the visibility Parameter set to false"; otherwise they appear in the output. Why PhoneNumberGen and not a random phone generator? PhoneNumberGen is documented, with parameters. A random alternative, RandomPhoneNumberGen, is named on its page and appears in an API example with the parameters useAreaCode and uniqueNumbers , but I had no page of its own for it, so I do not use it in the main lab. What the docs do not say about phone format The PhoneNumberGen page describes a sequence "100-1000, 100-1001, ..., 999-9999" and its preview screenshot shows numbers like (800) 600-1000 . It does not list a format option. If your project needs 10 plain digits like ShopSphere's sample phone 9876543210 , the documented route is a second linked generator such as StringRemoveGen (parameters reference , valueToRemove , removalType ) or StringReplacementGen ( value , fromText , toText ) to strip punctuation. See the extension ideas in 21.9 .

x: 7.20 Verification checks A file that "looks fine" in the first few rows can still be wrong in row 37. Check it deliberately. The commands below are general shell commands (macOS, Linux or Git Bash on Windows), not from the GenRocket documentation; a spreadsheet can do the same with COUNTA, LEN and conditional formatting. Checks, how to run them and what you expect Check Command Expected Row count wc -l Customers.csv 51 (header plus 50). It shows 50 if the file has no final newline, so also check the last row number. Header names head -1 Customers.csv FirstName,LastName,Full Name,Phone Number Four columns per row awk -F, 'NR>1 && NF!=4' Customers.csv No output. No empty values awk -F, 'NR>1{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) if($i=="") bad++} END{print bad+0}' Customers.csv 0 Full Name consistent awk -F, 'NR>1{n=split($3,p," "); if(n!=3||p[1]!=$1||p[3]!=$2) print NR}' Customers.csv No output. Phone length awk -F, 'NR>1{print length($4)}' Customers.csv | sort | uniq -c One line: 50 rows with the same length (14 characters for the (800) 600-1000 format). Phones unique cut -d, -f4 Customers.csv | tail -n +2 | sort | uniq -d No output (no duplicates). Full checklist before you call the lab finished: The file is where resource.output.directory says, and is named Customers.csv . Exactly 50 data rows; the header is present once. Only the four wanted columns: no id , no middle name. No empty or "null" cells in any column. Full Name equals FirstName, a middle name and LastName for every row. All phone numbers have the same length and are unique. Running the scenario a second time still gives 50 rows, not 100 ( appendToFile false). If you set a seed , the names are the same as before. Why verify at all? Test data is an input to other tests. If the data silently has 49 rows or an empty phone, every test that uses it can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the application. A five-minute check protects hours of debugging.

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: Delphix masking: what it is and how it is organised You have now seen two other families of tools. Informatica TDM is a large suite that discovers, subsets, masks and generates data. GenRocket builds synthetic data from scratch. This part of the guide is about the third tool, Delphix , and more precisely its masking product, called Delphix Continuous Compliance . Its engine finds sensitive values in a database or a file and replaces them with realistic but fictitious ones, so that a copy of production can safely go to testers. This opening chapter is a map. You will not create anything yet. You will learn what the product is for, what its screens look like, which objects the engine keeps (an environment, a connector, a rule set, an inventory and so on), and in what order a masking project touches them. Every later Delphix chapter assumes this map. When a button or a field name confuses you later, the cause is nearly always "I forgot which object lives inside which". The chapters after this one go deeper on one slice at a time. Connecting to data and to a VDB covers environments and connectors. Rule sets, primary keys and data integrity covers the next layer. Profiling , algorithms and masking jobs and file masking finish the engine, and the hands-on labs put it together.

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.1 Words to know first These are the words you meet in the first five minutes. Each one gets a fuller treatment later in the chapter. Continuous Compliance engine The Delphix product that discovers sensitive data and replaces it with realistic fictitious data. It runs as a virtual appliance (a pre-built machine image), and people also call it the masking engine or the Compliance Engine. Profiling Scanning column names and, optionally, the data itself to decide which columns hold sensitive values such as names or Social Security numbers. Delphix documentation also calls this sensitive data discovery . Masking Replacing sensitive values with fictitious ones so the original cannot be recovered. It is one-way. Tokenization A reversible alternative: values are swapped for meaningless tokens, and the engine can later turn the tokens back into the originals (re-identification). Application and environment An application is a label for the system whose data you protect. An environment is the folder-like container, inside one application, that holds your connectors, rule sets and jobs. Connector The saved connection details (host, port, user and so on) that tell the engine how to reach one database or one set of files. Rule set The list of tables (or files) of one connector that you want to profile and mask. Inventory The detailed list of every column or field in a rule set, with its data classification and the masking algorithm chosen for it. Domain A named kind of sensitive data (for example "first name") paired with the default algorithm that should protect it. Algorithm The recipe that turns one real value into a masked one. A single recipe can be reused on many columns. Job A saved, runnable task: a profiling job, a masking job, a tokenization job or a re-identification job. VDB A virtual database: a lightweight, writable copy of a database that Delphix's virtualization product creates in minutes. The next chapter explains it from zero.

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.2.1 The problem it answers You already know the story from the chapter on sensitive data and regulations and the chapter on masking concepts . Production holds real customers. Testers and developers need data that behaves like production but must not leak real people. The Delphix introduction frames the same problem: breaches, pressure from regulators and the fact that teams also want to move faster. It says that encryption suits data in motion or at rest on disks, but is a poor fit for protecting non-production copies used for development, testing and reporting. Its answer is masking: replace confidential values (the page names Social Security numbers, patient records and credit card numbers) with fictitious yet realistic data. It adds that masking, unlike encryption, protects data irreversibly in downstream environments, and that masking should stay consistent across different data sources while keeping referential integrity . Referential integrity means that a value which points to another table's row (a foreign key) still points to the right row after masking. That idea drives the rule set and keys chapter . Why this matters for ShopSphere ShopSphere's testers need CUSTOMERS, ORDERS and ORDER_ITEMS that join correctly (every order belongs to a customer). If the tool blanked the names but broke the joins, test cases such as "show a customer's last five orders" would return nothing. Realistic and consistent is the whole point.

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.2.2 The platform around it The masking capability is one part of the Delphix DevOps Data Platform. The introduction page describes four services: virtualize (compressed, lightweight, writable virtual copies), identify and secure (find sensitive values and mask them), manage (provision and audit copies from one point of control) and self-service (let developers and testers refresh, rewind, bookmark, branch and share their copies). Official screenshot: The vendor's platform picture. Read it left to right: sources (applications, files, databases, on-premises or cloud) are connected, virtualized (sync, compress, provision), secured (compliance policy, masking), managed (distribute, audit and report) and then handed to people such as a developer, QA and an analyst. The masking engine of this section is the "Secure" box. Source page ↗ Delphix sells more than one product, and the terminology page separates them. Delphix Continuous Data (the Data Engine) delivers data on demand and creates VDBs ( next chapter ). Delphix Continuous Compliance (the Compliance or masking engine) discovers sensitive data and replaces it, and is the subject of this whole part. Data Control Tower unifies governance across applications and clouds; I did not read its pages. The words "engine" and "Delphix" alone are ambiguous, so say which one you mean. Two numbers that disagree inside the docs The introduction page says "eighteen algorithm frameworks" in one place and "seven out-of-the-box algorithm frameworks" in another. Both appear in the same page. I cannot tell which is current, so this guide does not quote a count. The algorithms chapter lists the frameworks that the algorithm pages actually describe.

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
h: 8.3 What the engine does for you
x: 8.3 What the engine does for you Think of the engine as a three-step assembly line that you configure once and re-run on every refresh: find the sensitive columns, decide what replaces them, apply the replacement. 1. Connect tell the engine where the data lives → 2. Profile find the sensitive columns → 3. Assign pick an algorithm per column → 4. Mask or tokenize run a job

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.3.1 Finding sensitive data: profiling The introduction names two methods. Column-level profiling uses regular expressions to scan the names of columns (metadata) against dozens of pre-configured classifiers, for example a pattern that recognises a column called ssn or last_name . Data-level profiling also uses regular expressions but scans the values . You can write or import your own classifiers. When something is judged sensitive, the engine recommends and assigns a masking algorithm. A regular expression (regex) is a compact pattern language for text. The pattern [0-9]{3}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{4} describes the shape of a US Social Security number, so a data-level classifier can ask "do the values in this column match that shape?". The profiling chapter covers profile sets, domains and classifiers in practice. The object model section shows where they fit. For background on why discovery comes first, see discovery and subsetting concepts .

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
h: 8.3.2 Replacing the values: masking and tokenization
x: 8.3.2 Replacing the values: masking and tokenization The docs list two ways to secure data. Masking (also called anonymization on that page) replaces values with realistic, fictitious ones. Tokenization (also called pseudonymization) uses reversible algorithms so the data can be returned to its original state later. The page describes a token as something that conveys no meaning in appearance or format. Official screenshot: The masking idea in one picture: one person's name goes in, a different but still name-shaped value comes out. The documentation chose famous names for the example; in ShopSphere you would see Asha Menon replaced by another believable name. Source page ↗ Official screenshot: The tokenization idea: a number-shaped value is replaced by a meaningless string. Unlike masking, the engine keeps what it needs to reverse this on request. Source page ↗ ShopSphere example Row 1001 of CUSTOMERS holds Asha | Menon | asha.menon@example.com | 123-45-6789 . After masking, the test copy might hold Divya | Pillai | email9482@example.com | 481-92-3057 (values invented by me): same shape, different person, and nobody can work back to Asha. Tokenization would instead be chosen only if an outside vendor must analyse accounts and ShopSphere must later reverse the result. Masking is not tokenization Tokenization is the only reversible method: the engine stores both token and original. Do not use it on a test copy just to "be safe", because the originals stay recoverable by design.

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.3.3 In-place versus on-the-fly A masking job has a Masking Method : In-Place or On-The-Fly . The job-creation page defines them in one sentence each. In-Place The job updates the data in the source environment with masked values. It reads rows, masks them, and writes the masked values back over the originals in the same database. Consequence: run it on a copy of production, never on production itself. The unmasked originals are gone after the run. This is why the Delphix pages keep recommending a VDB or other copy as the thing you mask (see the VDB chapter ). On-The-Fly The job reads unmasked data from a source and writes the masked result to a different target. You choose a source environment and source connector when you define the job. Consequence: the source stays untouched. The supported pairings are limited: same-type to same-type (Oracle to Oracle, delimited file to delimited file), and database to delimited file. It needs a second environment and connector for the source side. In-Place Copy of the database (real values inside) Masking engine reads, masks, updates Same database (masked values now) After the run the originals are gone. Each row is found again by its key to be updated. On-The-Fly Source database or files (untouched) Masking engine reads, masks, writes Different target (masked values only) Needs a second environment and connector for the source side. Source stays as it was. Original diagram: the two masking methods. The one-sentence definitions come from the job-creation page; the "found again by its key" note comes from the database preparation pages and is explained in the keys chapter. One more difference shows up in the keys discussion of the rule set chapter : because an in-place job has to find each row again in order to update it, it needs a key per table. The database preparation pages for SQL Server, Db2 and Sybase offer on-the-fly masking as the alternative when a table has no usable key.

x: 8.4.1 The grid: the control you use everywhere Domains, classifiers, profile sets, roles, inventories and rule sets all use one table component, which the GUI page calls the Grid UI. x: 8.4.3 A rule you will trip over: object names The naming requirements page lists the objects you may name yourself: algorithm, application, connector, domain, environment, file format, job, profiling group, record type, role and rule set. For all of them, leading and trailing spaces are not allowed, and a long list of special characters is rejected, including brackets, braces, parentheses, ~ ! @ # $ % ^ * " ? : ; , / \ ` + = < > ' | . An attempt to create or rename an object with one of them fails with an error. The maximum name length varies by object; the page says to look it up in the engine's API client. h: 8.4.4 Monitor, Admin and Audit in brief
x: 8.4.4 Monitor, Admin and Audit in brief Long actions (saving a database rule set, exporting an environment) return an Async Task ID in a message at the bottom of the screen. Open Monitor > Async Tasks , search that ID, and download an export file or the log of a failed import from the row's Actions menu. Monitor > Job Executions is the history of job runs. Cancelling a RUNNING job leaves semi-masked data, and any indexes, constraints or triggers it dropped are not re-created, so cancel only in an emergency and expect to restore your copy. Under Admin you find Roles, Users (later in this section), Application Settings (administrators only; engine-wide defaults such as the default update threads, streams and non-conformant data handling, grouped by area), Logs, Utilization (PDF reports of job executions and of database sizes) and About. The Audit tab, open to administrators only, records who did what (create, edit, delete, run, test, import, export, login and more) and can be exported to PDF. For a compliance officer it is the evidence that a masking job ran, and who ran it.

x: 8.5 The object model in plain words This is the most important picture in the chapter. The engine stores a handful of kinds of objects, and almost every confusion is "where does X live?". The short answer is that work objects live inside an environment , and shared objects live in Settings . Application: "ShopSphere Customer Orders" (a label) Environment: SHOPSPHERE_DEV (a folder for work) Connector how to reach one database Rule set which tables of that connector to mask Inventory column, domain, algorithm, keys Jobs profile job masking job tokenize job re-identify job each job points at one rule set Deleting the environment deletes everything in this box (connections, inventory, rule sets, and so on), but not Settings. h: 8.5.1 The objects, one at a time
x: 8.5.1 The objects, one at a time Here is each object, with the documentation's own definition in my words, and what it is in ShopSphere terms. Object What the docs say ShopSphere Application A tag assigned to one or more environments. The docs recommend naming it after the real application. An application must exist before you can create an environment. "ShopSphere Customer Orders". (Illustrative name; avoid special characters.) Environment A construct describing a collection of masking jobs associated with a group of data sources. In practice a folder for connectors, rule sets and jobs. Its Purpose is either Mask or Tokenize/Re-Identify and cannot be changed after creation. SHOPSPHERE_DEV: one place for everything needed to mask a development copy. Connector The connection to one data source: a database, a set of files or a mainframe data set. Grouped by "Meta Data Source" on screen. A connector to the VDB that holds the unmasked copy of SHOPSPHERE_PROD. Rule set A group of tables or flat files in one data source on which you may run profile, masking or tokenization jobs. The four tables CUSTOMERS, ORDERS, ORDER_ITEMS, PRODUCTS. Inventory All the data in a rule set plus the method chosen to secure each piece: table or file name, column or field name, data classification and algorithm. For CUSTOMERS: first_name assigned a first-name algorithm, ssn an SSN algorithm, customer_id a key-safe algorithm. Domain A correlation between a category of sensitive data (such as Social Security numbers) and the way it should be secured. Each domain has one default masking algorithm (and optionally a tokenization algorithm). A "Social Security Number" domain whose default algorithm is the SSN algorithm. Algorithm An algorithm framework is a family (Secure Lookup, Segment Mapping and so on). An algorithm instance is a named framework-plus-settings that you assign to a column. Example from the docs: "FIRST NAME SL" is an instance of the Secure Lookup framework. One instance reused on both CUSTOMERS.customer_id and ORDERS.customer_id (see the keys chapter). Profile set A named set of classifiers that decides what a profiling job can detect. Several built-in sets ship by default. (The terminology page describes it, in the profile job concepts, as a subset of expressions such as financial expressions.) A standard profile set run over the four tables. Classifier One piece of recognition logic, tied to a domain. Frameworks are PATH, TYPE, REGEX and LIST; PATH and TYPE work on column names and types, REGEX and LIST on the data itself. The pattern that decides the column called ssn is an SSN column. Job A saved task you run: profiling and masking in a Mask environment; profiling, tokenization and re-identification in a Tokenize environment. "Mask SHOPSPHERE DEV rule set (in-place)". The classifier frameworks and the claim that a domain has exactly one default algorithm come from the Discovering your sensitive data and Managing domains pages. One consequence the domains page spells out: because a domain has a single default algorithm, you need a distinct domain (with recognition logic) for each distinct algorithm if you want the profiler to assign that algorithm. "Connector" means two different things in Delphix The terminology page defines Connector as the data-source connection mechanism and, separately, a Delphix Connector as a service that runs on Windows staging and target hosts to let them talk to the Continuous Data engine. It warns that the two should not be confused. In this guide, "connector" always means the first one, the data-source connection you create inside a masking environment. A related word with a licence flavour is also defined: Standard, Select and Premium connectors differ by who builds them and whether you need a separate licence (see the connectors chapter ). Official screenshot: Inside an environment: three tabs (Jobs, Rule Sets, Connectors). The Jobs tab shows buttons to create a Profiling Job or a Masking Job and to export the environment, and a grid of existing jobs with Job ID, Name, Rule Set, Type, Status, Completed Time, Run Time and Data Processed. Note the line under the name: Application, Purpose and Approval. This is the "folder" in action. Source page ↗ Official screenshot: The same tab in an environment whose purpose is Tokenize. The buttons change: Profiling Job, Tokenization Job and Re-Identification Job appear instead of Masking Job. This is why the Purpose of an environment is fixed at creation. Source page ↗

x: 8.6 How a masking project flows With the objects named, the order of work follows from the nesting: you cannot create a rule set before a connector, and you cannot create a connector before an environment. The documentation's own table of contents for "Connecting data" (environments, connectors, extended connectors, file formats, rule sets, inventories) follows exactly this order, and the Continuous Compliance home page groups the rest as "Identify sensitive data", "Preparing data" and "Connecting data". 1 Engine install, first setup, users 2 Database masking user, prepare copy 3 Container application + environment 4 Connector test the connection 5 Rule set tables, keys, checklist 6 Profile find sensitive columns 7 Inventory review, assign algorithms 8 Mask run job, monitor Steps 3 to 5 are the "Connecting data" part. Steps 6 and 7 are "Identify sensitive data". Step 8 is "Securing sensitive data". Optional after step 8: if the masked copy is a VDB, the Virtualization Engine can run the masking job while provisioning it. Steps 6 and 7 can loop: profile, review, adjust, run the profile again. Original diagram: a typical order of work. The sequence is my summary of how the documentation's sections depend on each other; the documentation does not publish a single numbered "project plan". Section titles in the last notes are the documentation's own. Where each step is taught: step 1 and the roles are in this section; steps 2 to 4 in the connectors and VDB chapter ; step 5 in the rule sets and keys chapter ; steps 6 and 7 in the profiling chapter ; step 8 in the algorithms and jobs chapter and, for files, the file masking chapter . Profiling only proposes domains and algorithms; a human, usually the data steward, confirms them. How a TDM team splits this The "best practices for defining masking roles" page gives a sample RACI (who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed). It makes IT Security accountable for deciding which data types are sensitive, the application owner accountable for inventory management, data masking and masked-data validation, and the data masking admin team responsible for masking administration (domains, classifiers, roles, users). In ShopSphere terms: the compliance officer decides that SSN, email and phone are sensitive, the data steward reviews the inventory, and the TDM engineer builds and runs the jobs. This is a sample from the vendor, not a rule.

h: 8.7 The terminology page, term by term
x: 8.7 The terminology page, term by term The terminology page is a one-page glossary and worth reading yourself. Here is the part you need for masking, with a ShopSphere picture for each idea. The objects (application, environment, rule set, domain, connector) were covered above, so I move to the algorithm and job vocabulary.

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.7.1 Algorithm words Algorithm framework A type of masking algorithm. You can create one or more usable instances from it. "FIRST NAME SL" is an instance of the Secure Lookup framework. Algorithm instance A named combination of a framework and its settings. This is what you actually assign to a column in the inventory. Built-in algorithm An algorithm instance or framework shipped with the engine. Some built-ins have behaviour that matches no built-in framework. Non-conformant data A value that does not fit the format an algorithm expects (for example a 10-digit rule fed a 7-digit number). By default such values are not masked and a warning is recorded, shown as a yellow triangle beside the job execution. You can choose per job, or globally under Admin > Application Settings > Default Non-Conformant Data Handling, whether the job fails, leaves the value unmasked, or sets it to null. Collision Two different real values masked to the same fake value. "Amy" and "Jane" both becoming "Beth" is the docs' example. Non-conformant data means "silently left real" by default This default surprises beginners. If ShopSphere's phone column contains n/a in some rows, an algorithm expecting ten digits does not fail the job. It leaves n/a unmasked and logs a warning. That is harmless for n/a , but a real SSN typed with spaces might slip through the same way. Always read the warning count after a job.

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
h: 8.7.2 The algorithm families in one table
x: 8.7.2 The algorithm families in one table The terminology page describes eight families. The algorithms chapter shows how to build them. Here is only the idea, so the names are not strange later. Family How it works (docs, in short) Typical ShopSphere use Secure Lookup Replaces each value by one picked from an input file using a cryptographic hash of the original, so the same input always gets the same output. Most common. Collisions are possible. first_name, last_name: a name list. Segment Mapping Permutes short numeric or alphanumeric values to others of the same format; guaranteed collision-free if the allowed output range is at least as large as the input set. Maximum 36 digits or characters in the masked value (as the terminology page states). ssn, tax_id, and key columns that need unique values. Mapping You supply the replacement values. The engine records all input-to-output pairs in encrypted form so no two inputs share an output. You must know how many values you will mask. On engines before 6.0.10.0 you cannot mask more than one table at a time with it. A small fixed list of codes, such as product_code, if you want to hand-pick substitutes. Tokenization The only reversible family. Creates a unique token per input and stores both token and original. Only if an outside vendor must analyse accounts and ShopSphere must later reverse the result. Binary Lookup, Min Max, Data Cleaning, Free Text Redaction Replace images with a supplied image; move extreme values toward the middle; standardise spellings without masking; remove sensitive material from free-text columns. Not needed for the core ShopSphere columns. Two documented warnings you should hold onto now, because the keys chapter relies on them. First, Secure Lookup is deterministic on its input (same hash, same output), and Segment Mapping and Mapping are the collision-free choices, so these are the ones used on unique and key columns. Second, the terminology page's wording for Segment Mapping explicitly lists "Social Security Numbers, primary key columns, or foreign key columns" as its use.

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.7.3 Job options, in one look The terminology page lists the options of both job types, and you will meet them on real screens in the profiling chapter and the algorithms and jobs chapter . A profiling job has a unique Job Name, a Rule Set, No. of Streams (tables processed in parallel), optional memory limits, Feedback Size, Profile Sets and Email. A masking job adds the Masking Method (In-Place or On-The-Fly), Update Threads (too many can deadlock T-SQL databases), Commit Size, Disable Trigger and Drop Index (both clear by default, so the job leaves indexes and triggers alone unless you turn them on), and Prescript and Postscript SQL files. Both have a Multi-Tenant option that lets one rule set serve identical schemas through different connectors chosen at run time.

h: 8.8 Where the engine runs: deployment options at overview level
x: 8.8 Where the engine runs: deployment options at overview level As a TDM engineer you will rarely install the engine yourself, but you should know what shape it takes, because that decides who you ask when something is down. The documentation offers two families. Virtual machine image A virtual appliance : a ready-made machine image imported into a hypervisor or cloud. The Installation page lists VMware, AWS EC2, Azure, Google Cloud Platform, IBM Cloud, Hyper-V and OCI. You set the network from a console, then finish in the browser-based Setup Wizard . Containerized The same engine as a pod of three containers on Kubernetes (tested on OpenShift, MicroK8s, AWS EKS and AWS ECS with Fargate), deployed directly or with Helm. FTP and FTPS file connectors are disabled in this form.

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.8.1 What the Setup Wizard asks The wizard walks through Welcome (pick Continuous Compliance as the engine type), passwords and the three administrator accounts, time, network, certificates, storage, outbound connectivity (support proxy, usage analytics and the SMTP server used for job email), authentication (LDAP, SAML/SSO, OAuth2), Kerberos and password vaults, registration and a summary. Facts worth keeping: the documented first logins use default accounts that you must change; the engine type cannot be changed once chosen; three failed logins lock the account; the engine works only in UTC , so read job times in Monitor accordingly; and in non-containerized engines LDAP is configured in the setup application, not in the masking UI, a change from earlier releases.

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.8.2 Sizing, in one line The best-practices page gives a dedicated Compliance Engine 8 vCPUs, at least 64 GB of RAM (128 GB or more recommended), a 127 GB system disk and at least 50 GB of data storage, plus rules of thumb of about one vCPU and 1 GB of memory per concurrent masking job. It also says cloning an engine through hypervisor features is not supported as a backup.

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.8.3 What the engine must reach The network requirements page lists the traffic. Outbound, the engine needs SMTP (25), DNS (53), NTP (123, VM engine), HTTPS to Delphix Support and to an S3 endpoint if you use one (443), LDAPS (636) and, most important for you, "various" ports to your own databases (JDBC) and file servers (FTP, SFTP, NFS, CIFS) . Inbound, users reach the web interface on 443 (use HTTPS, not 80) and administrators use SSH on 22. The engine cannot be deployed behind a reverse proxy. Supported browsers are the latest and previous versions of Edge, Firefox and Chrome. When a connector test hangs, suspect a firewall on the database port before you suspect the password. The containerized product is meant for ephemeral engines (spun up for a need, then discarded) and differs from the VM engine: no FTP file masking, no Kerberos, no SSO/OAuth, no upgrade validation and no Db2 z/OS or iSeries connector. Two engines, never one machine Both the masked-provisioning pages and the configuration page say that Delphix Masking and Delphix Virtualization must never run inside the same virtual machine. Use separate, dedicated engines. The best-practices page also says that Continuous Data and Continuous Compliance are delivered in one OVA, and you pick which one at first setup. So an engine image can become either product, but one running engine is only one of them.

x: 8.9 Users and roles overview The masking engine uses role-based access control: a role is a set of allowed actions on certain kinds of objects, and a user is a person who has one role and access to certain environments. This is how ShopSphere keeps the data steward from editing connection passwords and keeps testers away from masking jobs. Official screenshot: Admin > Roles. The left-hand list shows About, Application Settings, Logs, Roles, Users and Utilization. Built-in roles have type DEFAULT; one role created by a user has type CUSTOM. The + Role button adds a new one. Source page ↗ Official screenshot: Adding a role. The matrix lists objects (Environment, Connection, Rule Set, Inventory, then Jobs such as Profile Job and Masking Job, then Settings, Report, Approval Workflow) against actions. In this picture the role gets View on Environment and View, Add, Update, Delete and Run on Masking Job. Some objects depend on others: the page notes that Masking Job actions depend on Environment - View. Source page ↗

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.9.1 Roles, actions, objects Actions you can grant: View, Add, Update, Delete, Copy, Export and Import (not every action exists for every object). Objects you can grant them on include Environment, Connection, Ruleset, Inventory, Profile Job, Masking Job, Tokenize Job, Re-identify Job, Domains, Algorithms, Classifier, Profiler Set, File Format, JDBC Drivers, Plugins, Password Vault, User, Report, Approve Inventories and Diagnostic. Role type : DEFAULT roles come with the product and can be viewed and duplicated but not edited or deleted. CUSTOM roles can be added, edited, deleted and duplicated. Five default roles exist: IT Security Analyst, DBA, SME, Operator and Environment Owner, plus a default All Privileges role if one exists. Each user has one role and a list of environments. Access to an environment does not grant unlimited access: the role still limits what the user can do there. The Administrator setting on a user gives unrestricted access to everything, plus some admin-only powers (sync, audit page, user API-access settings, deleting any object, and others). With it enabled, the role and environment fields disappear. Role (docs) One-line meaning Administrator Unrestricted. Manages the engine, domains, algorithms, roles, users. IT Security Analyst All settings functions and almost all application functions except creating, deleting or updating environments. All Privileges Everything inside the environments a user is given, but may delete only objects they created. DBA Manages connections, scripting and scheduling; no settings. SME / Analyst / Developer Manages inventories, creates and views jobs. Operator All job privileges. Environment Owner Approves workflow and inventories; view access to settings and environment. A role that is also a security risk The Users and roles page warns that a user allowed to add or update JDBC drivers can upload code that runs inside the engine's JVM, which is effectively running code on the engine host. The built-in DBA role includes that permission by default; the page suggests a custom role or fewer DBA assignments if you separate database work from driver installation. Treat JDBC-driver permission as administrative. Creating a user needs a user name, an email (job completion mail goes there), a password, a role and the environments the user may open, or the Administrator checkbox. An account locks after three invalid login attempts.

h: 8.10 Moving work between engines: export, import and sync
x: 8.10 Moving work between engines: export, import and sync Real organisations often run several engines: one per stage of the software life cycle (development, QA, production), or several production engines to share a large workload. Objects must then be copied between them. Export Settings / Import Settings (on the Environments page) moves shared settings such as domains, algorithms and file formats. Export / Import Environment moves everything inside one environment (connectors, rule sets, inventory, jobs). An API-based sync does the same at scale; the docs advise moving objects in one direction only. Sync does not currently support the Application object or certain algorithms, and bundles from a newer engine may not import into an older one. Official screenshot: The dialog you use to bring settings from another engine. The blue note matters: passwords are not carried across, so every imported connector needs its password set again before it can connect. Source page ↗

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.11 ShopSphere in object terms For ShopSphere the objects will be: application SHOPSPHERE_APP; environment SHOPSPHERE_DEV (purpose Mask); a connector to the VDB that holds an unmasked copy of SHOPSPHERE_PROD; a rule set with CUSTOMERS, ORDERS, ORDER_ITEMS and PRODUCTS; a profile job and an in-place masking job; and roles for the TDM engineer (All Privileges), data steward (SME) and DBA. Notice that CUSTOMERS.customer_id and ORDERS.customer_id must get the same algorithm so every order still points to the right customer; the keys chapter is about exactly that. Lab: find your way around an engine Goal: confirm you can locate every object type in this section on a real engine (or on the screenshots, if you have no engine yet). This lab uses documented screens only, with ShopSphere names as illustration. Do not click Delete anywhere. Sign in and note the version. Open the engine's address in a browser and sign in with the account your administrator gave you. The Environments page appears, with menus Environments, Monitor, Settings, Admin and Audit. A version number sits next to the logo in the top bar. Add an application. Click + Application, enter SHOPSPHERE_APP and Save. This needs a role that allows it. You return to the Environments list. Choose the application, name it SHOPSPHERE_DEV , leave Purpose as Masking and leave the approval checkbox clear. Click Save And View. The environment opens with tabs Jobs, Rule Sets and Connectors, all empty. The line under the name shows Application, Purpose and Approval. Visit each tab. Open Connectors, then Rule Sets, then Jobs. Each shows an empty grid. Connectors offers a connection button, Rule Sets an add button, Jobs the profiling and masking job buttons. Visit the shared Settings. Open Settings and click Algorithms, then Domains. A long list of built-in algorithms (Owner: System) and domains. Note the framework name column, for example Secure Lookup. Try the grid. x: 8.14 Common mistakes and gotchas Things that trip beginners Looking for algorithms inside the environment. They live in Settings and survive an environment delete. Assuming profiling masks anything. It only proposes; data changes when a masking job runs. Running an in-place job on production. It overwrites the source values. Mask a copy. Expecting to change an environment's Purpose. It is fixed; create a new environment. Ignoring warnings. Non-conformant data is left unmasked by default and only shows a yellow warning.

x: 8.15 Recap Recap Delphix Continuous Compliance is the masking engine: it profiles to find sensitive data, masks irreversibly, or tokenizes reversibly. Masking is in-place (overwrite the source, so use a copy) or on-the-fly (read one place, write another). The interface has five menus: Environments, Monitor, Settings, Admin, Audit. The same grid control (sort, filter, pin, actions) appears everywhere. Work objects (connector, rule set, inventory, jobs) live inside an environment inside an application. Shared objects (domains, algorithms, profile sets, classifiers, file formats, JDBC drivers) live in Settings. A project flows: engine, prepare the database, environment, connector, rule set, profile, review the inventory, mask. The engine is a VM image or a Kubernetes deployment, never in the same machine as the Virtualization Engine. It works in UTC. Roles are sets of actions on objects; each user has one role plus environments. The product changes often. Check your version and trust your screen over this text. Delphix: connecting to data and to a VDB A masking engine that cannot reach your data cannot mask it. This section is about the connection layer of Delphix Continuous Compliance: the application and environment that hold your work, the connector that tells the engine how to log in to a database or a file store, and the database-side preparation that has to happen before the first job. It also answers a question the syllabus asks on Day 51 in the hands-on list as TDM_Handson4 : what does it mean to "create a connector to a VDB from the Delphix masking engine"? To answer that we start from zero on VDBs. You met the vocabulary in the Delphix overview chapter ; here you will see why a VDB is the recommended thing to mask, and what the Delphix pages do and do not tell you about connecting to one. The chapter then hands over to the rule sets and keys chapter , which builds the next object on top of the connector, and to the profiling chapter and the hands-on labs , which use it.

x: 8.16 Words to know first Application A tag, assigned to one or more environments, naming the system whose data you manage. You must create one before you can create an environment. Environment The folder-like container that holds the connectors, rule sets and jobs for one group of data sources. Connector A saved definition of how the engine reaches one data source: type, host, port, credentials and options. Meta Data Source The grouping label on the connector screen: Database, File or Mainframe. JDBC Java Database Connectivity: the standard way a Java program talks to a database. The engine uses a JDBC driver (a library) for each kind of database and a JDBC URL (a connection string such as jdbc:vendor://host:port/name ) to say where to connect. Extended connector A connector built on a JDBC driver that you upload, for databases the engine does not support natively. Masking user A dedicated database account that the connector logs in as, with just the permissions masking needs. dSource In Delphix virtualization, the engine's compressed copy of a source database's data, from which VDBs are made. VDB (virtual database) A full read-and-write copy of source data, provisioned from a dSource or from another VDB and managed by the Continuous Data engine. Masked VDB A VDB whose data was masked by a masking job during provisioning. SDD (Selective Data Distribution) A way to replicate a masked VDB to another Delphix Engine in non-production without sending the original unmasked data.

h: 8.17.1 What they are and why they exist
x: 8.17.1 What they are and why they exist Think of a shared drive at work. You do not dump every project's files in one folder; you create a folder per project and put sub-folders inside. An environment is that project folder. The environments page describes it as a place where "a specified user can create and manage connectors, rule sets, and jobs". The application is a label above it that groups related environments: for ShopSphere, one application "SHOPSPHERE_APP" and environments such as SHOPSPHERE_DEV and SHOPSPHERE_QA. Analogy limit: unlike a shared-drive folder, an environment also carries rules (its Purpose and whether approvals are required). The main Environment screen is the first page every user sees after signing in. It lists only the environments that user may access. Its columns are ID (the number used to refer to it from the Masking API), Application, Environment, Purpose, and Actions (Edit, Export, Duplicate, Delete). The screenshots below show it. Sorting a column also sorts the Environment column ascending. Official screenshot: The Environments list. The three buttons at the top right are the three places you will start: + Application, + Environment, and an Actions menu (which holds Export Settings, Import Settings and Import Environment). The environment name is a link that opens the environment. Source page ↗

x: 8.17.3 Creating an environment Click + Environment. It opens the Add Environment dialog. A dialog with Select Application, Environment Name, Purpose and an approval checkbox. Choose the application. The dropdown shows existing applications. It is "for informative purposes", the page says: it labels the environment and does not change behaviour. Type an Environment Name. For example SHOPSPHERE_DEV . Choose the Purpose. Mask or Tokenize/Re-Identify . This decides which job types the environment offers. The screenshot shows the default as "Masking". Purpose becomes read-only after creation, so choose carefully. Decide on "Enable Approval Workflow (Database rulesets only)". If ticked, inventories must be approved before masking jobs can run in this environment. It applies only to database rule sets. For a first lab leave it clear. Click Save, or Save And View. Save returns to the list; Save And View opens the environment's Jobs screen. The new environment is in the grid. Opening it shows tabs Jobs, Rule Sets and Connectors. x: 8.17.4 Editing, copying, exporting and deleting All of these are in the Actions (...) menu beside each environment. Edit. You may change the application and the name and the approval workflow setting. Purpose is read-only. Duplicate. Makes an exact copy (the page calls this "a very powerful feature" when you want several similar environments). You give a new name; the copy has the same purpose. Choose Duplicate or Duplicate And View. Export. Writes everything in the environment (connectors, rule sets, inventory, jobs and so on) to a file, with an optional passphrase. The engine returns an Async Task ID; follow it under Monitor, and when it succeeds, use Download File in that task's Actions menu. The main reason to export is moving environments between masking engines. Delete. After a confirmation, deletes everything for that environment: connections, inventory, rule sets and so on. It does not delete universal settings such as algorithms and domains. Two more actions live in the page-level Actions menu: Export Settings / Import Settings (Domain, Algorithm, File Format and similar; the import has a Force Overwrite checkbox and must use the same passphrase as the export) and Import Environment (with options to import settings too, to overwrite, to choose the target application and environment, and an OTF Environment checkbox for importing on-the-fly connectors). Details are in the overview chapter's section on moving work between engines . Official screenshot: Export Settings. Notice the text: settings such as Domain, Algorithm and File Format go into the file. A passphrase is optional, but if you set one you need the same passphrase to import. Source page ↗ Delete is bigger than it looks Deleting a connector also deletes its rule sets and inventory data (the connector page says so). Deleting an environment deletes all its connectors, rule sets, inventories and jobs. Neither can be undone from the screen. Export the environment first if you might want it back.

x: 8.18 Connectors: what they are A connector is a saved answer to the question "how does the engine log in to this data?". Without it, the engine has nowhere to read tables from. Connectors are grouped within an environment: open the environment and click its Connectors tab. There are three families, shown as groups on the Connectors screen (the page calls the grouping field "Meta Data Source"). Meta Data Source What it points at Examples of Type (from the docs and screenshots) Database A relational database reached over JDBC. Oracle, MS SQL, Sybase, Mysql, Postgres, Db2 and Extended (see below). File Files in a directory or storage location. Delimited, Fixed Width, XML, JSON, Parquet. Mainframe Mainframe data sets, usually encoded in EBCDIC (the mainframe character encoding). Dataset. Official screenshot: The Connectors tab. Rows are grouped by Meta Data Source. Some names have an orange warning triangle: the page says that icon means authentication is missing, and hovering it tells you whether the password, SSH key, credential path or access keys are absent. The button at top right reads "+ Connection" in this release (other screenshots in the docs read "+ Connector"). Source page ↗ The columns are: Connector ID (used by the API), Name , Type and Actions (Edit, Test Connection, Delete). You can filter and sort by ID, Name and (filter only) Type inside each group. Encryption is not on by default The connectors page states that connections are not encrypted by default, but you can enable TLS/SSL. The per-database pages (for example Oracle and SQL Server) explain how, typically by importing the database's certificate into the engine's truststore through the setup application, restarting the engine, and using a JDBC URL that asks for TLS. For Oracle the page adds that SSL with the BASIC Oracle connector is not supported, so you must use an advanced (JDBC URL) connector for TLS. For SQL Server the page says the needed JDBC properties depend on your instance and your DBA must supply them.

h: 8.19.2 Step 2: Credentials for a database connector
x: 8.19.2 Step 2: Credentials for a database connector The fields that appear depend on the source type, and the docs say to ask your DBA if you are unsure of a value. This is the full documented list of database fields. Field Meaning (from the docs) Watch out for Schema Name The schema containing the tables this connector will access. A schema is a named group of tables inside a database. The rule set can only list tables in this schema. Database Name The database you connect to. Case-sensitive. It must match exactly the name as the instance knows it. The 2026.5 release notes even fix a case where leading or trailing spaces here passed the connection test but made jobs fail. Host Name/IP Network name or address of the database server. The engine itself must be able to resolve and reach it. Port TCP port of the server. For MS SQL Server optional: defaults to 1433 and need not be specified if the server uses it. SID (Oracle only) the Oracle System ID. Instance Name (MS SQL Server only, optional) the instance name. If given, the connector ignores Port and contacts the SQL Server Browser Service on port 1434 to learn the instance's port. So the firewall must allow 1434 and the instance's port. JDBC URL (Advanced mode for Oracle, MS SQL Server and Sybase) the custom URL, typically with host and port. Also used by Generic and Extended connectors. Authentication type, Username, Password The login the connector uses. The password is stored encrypted. Options below. Official screenshot: Step 2, Credentials, for the same Sybase example. Fields in this release: Schema Name, Database Name, Host, Port, an authentication-type dropdown, Username and Password. The values are the documentation's sample values, not anything to copy. Source page ↗ The authentication type dropdown is offered according to the source type. The authentication-types page describes three kinds. Username/Password. The simplest. The password is stored encrypted. Kerberos. The engine authenticates to the Kerberos server first, then uses its Kerberos credentials instead of a password. The Login ID is then treated as the Kerberos user principal name, and extra fields (Principal Name, and for Sybase a Service Principal) appear. The appliance must be configured for Kerberos beforehand, and Kerberos is disabled in containerized masking. Password Vault. The engine asks an external vault for the credentials using a Credential Path you enter. The vault must be configured first.

x: 8.19.3 Step 3: Custom Properties Optional. Use it to upload a connection properties file , normally a Java properties file (lines of key=value ), that adds settings to the JDBC connection. The rules, all from the managing-connectors page: the file must have the extension .properties and follow Java properties syntax; it is read as ISO 8859-1 text; any property you list is passed to the driver even if the driver does not officially support it, and every property loaded is logged. Official screenshot: Step 3, Custom Properties. The table stays empty until you upload a file. After upload, or when editing an existing connector, it lists each property with its Value and whether it was Modified from the driver default. Source page ↗ When the same property can be set in several places, the engine applies a fixed order. This matters when a connector "ignores" something you typed. Property Winner, then runner-up Username, Password, Schema The form field always wins. Everything else (database name, host, port, SID, instance name, other driver properties) 1. The properties file, 2. the form fields, 3. the JDBC URL. The page adds that the JDBC driver itself decides what happens with duplicates, and that a connector form shows either the Basic fields or the Advanced URL, never both, so those two cannot clash. It also notes a driver quirk: for Caché DB the schema cannot be set through the URL, so it has to come from the form field or a properties file. Customising the JDBC URL is limited to Advanced, Generic and Extended connectors, while a properties file works for every database connector. Secrets in properties files are visible Anything in a properties file, including a password, is shown in plain text to every user who has the View Connector privilege. The page recommends putting sensitive values in the form fields (obfuscated everywhere) or, second best, in the JDBC URL (plain text on screen but redacted in support bundles).

x: 8.21.1 Testing Test a connector as soon as you create it. You can do it in two places: with the Test Connection button inside the wizard at any step, and with Test Connection in the connector's Actions (...) menu on the grid. The engine takes the information on the screen, tries to open a database connection, and shows a success or failure message. Official screenshot: Test from the grid: open the "..." menu on a connector row and choose Test Connection. Source page ↗ Official screenshot: Test from inside the wizard: the Test Connection button is in the footer of every step. Source page ↗ Why a failed test is useful information A failure tells you which layer to blame. Wrong password, wrong schema or wrong database name usually return a login or "not found" message. h: 8.22 Which data sources are supported, and extended connectors
x: 8.22 Which data sources are supported, and extended connectors The supported-connectors page splits what the engine can profile, mask and tokenize into two kinds. Delphix connectors are built in and come in three licensing flavours: Standard (built and supported by Delphix, included with the licence), Select (built and supported by Delphix but needing a separate licence) and Premium (built by a third party, often with a separate licence). FEML (File Extract, Mask and Load) is a technique for sources with no dedicated connector: extract data to files through the source's APIs, mask the files, load the masked data back. Kind Sources named on the page Standard, databases Db2 LUW, Oracle, MS SQL, MySQL, SAP ASE (Sybase), PostgreSQL, MariaDB Standard, files Fixed Width, Delimited, XML, JSON, Parquet Select and Premium Salesforce, CockroachDB, SAP HANA 2.0; mainframe and midrange: Db2 z/OS, Db2 iSeries, mainframe data sets Two rules from that page matter for ShopSphere. Database masking applies only to physical tables : views, materialized views, federated systems and proxy objects are not supported. And JSON or XML stored inside database columns can be masked with a separate "Document Store Type" feature. Pricing is usage-based, per terabyte managed. The per-database pages give versions and feature tables (for example Oracle: TLS, password vault, Kerberos, in-place and on-the-fly options and "identity column support" all available), but the version matrix page was missing from my copy, so check your version there.

h: 8.22.1 Extended connectors: bring your own JDBC driver
x: 8.22.1 Extended connectors: bring your own JDBC driver If your database is not natively supported, an extended connector lets you upload a JDBC driver and use it. The rules, from the extended-connectors page: the driver must be a type 4 (pure Java) .jar , packaged inside a .zip even if it is a single file; anything needing compilation or an install script on the engine is not supported; drivers needing a Java version above 8 are listed as unsupported (a line that looks out of date, since release 2026.5 runs on Java 17); and extended connectors lack some native features, though driver support plugins can add Disable Constraints, Disable Triggers and Drop Indexes. Delphix supports them under its support policy. Get the driver from the database vendor's official site and, where a checksum is published, verify it. The page warns that uploaded drivers run inside the engine's JVM, so a tampered driver could run arbitrary code on the engine host. Zip the driver files together and open Settings > JDBC Drivers , then click + JDBC Driver . The Add JDBC Driver dialog: Name, optional Description, Class Name (the class that implements java.sql.Driver ) and a file chooser. Create a connector with Source Type Database - Extended . The Credentials step asks for the JDBC driver, a Schema Name, a JDBC URL (avoid putting the username and password in it, because URLs may be logged), an Enable Logger checkbox (slows things down; for debugging only), Username and Password. Official screenshot: Settings > JDBC Drivers. Each native database already has a default driver listed here with its version, and your uploaded drivers appear in the same list. Source page ↗ Official screenshot: The upload dialog. The grey hint under Class Name says it is the class that implements java.sql.Driver. Source page ↗ Official screenshot: Credentials for an extended connector. The extra field compared with a native connector is Select JDBC Driver. Source page ↗

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.23.1 A dedicated masking user The permissions page recommends creating a separate database user for the engine, in non-production, rather than reusing a person's account. Reasons given: it is easy to replicate with its privileges, it can be a central directory user used in many places, and access audits on the database host become simpler. For masking jobs that user needs to read, write and update table data; create, drop, disable and enable indexes, triggers and constraints; and add or delete columns (the engine may add a temporary column, as you will see in the keys chapter ). For profiling jobs it needs only to see object definitions (the schema) and read table data.

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.23.2 Preparing each database The "Preparing data" pages say, first of all, that using a VDB is recommended: it is also the best security practice because the database runs in a sandbox, and the page adds that Selective Data Distribution is advised for further security. The per-database pages share one logic. In-place masking changes every row of every masked table , which creates huge amounts of log and undo data, so the database should be tuned for a heavy write load, and log files can hold unmasked copies of the data and must be cleared afterwards. Database What the page asks for (overview) Oracle Switch off archive logging for the copy ( NOARCHIVELOG ), enough memory (automatic SGA management), larger undo space and retention for big in-place updates (about 2 to 3 times the largest table) to avoid "snapshot too old" (ORA-01555), well-sized redo logs, PCTFREE 40 to 50, and use ROWID as the logical key. Grant SELECT on several V$ views, and SELECT_CATALOG_ROLE if jobs drop or disable indexes, constraints or triggers. SQL Server Use the SIMPLE recovery model (transaction logs may contain unmasked data), tune memory, prefer a clustered primary key, and turn on the drop indexes, constraints and triggers options. Add the masking user to db_datareader , db_datawriter and db_ddladmin . Identity columns cannot be masked without special steps. When provisioning a masked VDB, this user must exist on the source the VDB is made from. Db2 For z/OS, DESCSTAT must be YES or rule set creation fails. Size the journal (about 3 times table size for in-place, 1.5 times for on-the-fly) and purge it after masking, because it holds unmasked data. Sybase (SAP ASE) Size memory and the transaction log (larger than all masked tables combined; a full log makes the job appear to hang). Create a masking user with grants such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and ALTER on the tables. All four pages also explain how the engine finds a row to update: with a primary key, logical key or identity column. That topic is the heart of the next chapter . Never prepare production like this Switching off archive logging, dropping constraints or giving a user schema-altering rights are fine on a disposable copy and unacceptable on production. That is one more reason the docs steer you to a VDB or another non-production copy.

h: 8.24 What a VDB is, from zero
x: 8.24 What a VDB is, from zero Suppose ShopSphere's production database is 500 GB. Testers need a copy, and so do developers, and the compliance team will not allow the unmasked copy anywhere near them. Making four physical 500 GB copies takes hours and terabytes, and refreshing them is a chore. Delphix's virtualization product solves the copying half of the problem. Its pages describe it this way. The Continuous Data engine compresses the data it gathers, often to a third of the original size or better, and from that creates lightweight virtual copies that are fully readable and writable, independent of one another and created or removed in minutes. The introduction claims ten virtual copies fit in the space of one physical copy. A dSource is the engine's copy of a source database's persistent data layer, from which VDBs are made and refreshed. A snapshot is the state of a dataset at one moment, and a TimeFlow is the timeline of those states. A VDB (virtual database) is a full read-and-write copy of the source data, provisioned from a dSource or from another VDB, and managed by the Continuous Data engine. You can refresh it (pull newer data), rewind it (go back in time), disable it and enable it. Analogy, with its limit: think of a VDB as your own editable version of a shared master file. Everyone edits their own version, and the big file is stored once. The documentation does not explain the storage mechanism, so do not push the analogy further than "cheap, fast, independent copies". To the application a VDB looks like an ordinary database with a host, a port and a name, which is what makes the connector idea below work. SHOPSPHERE_PROD real customers dSource copy in the engine VDB (unmasked) then masked by the job Masked VDB safe parent copy Child VDB: QA Child VDB: Dev Masking Engine runs the masking job Non-production Virtualization Engine receives the masked VDB (SDD), never the originals Original diagram of the masked-VDB flow as described on the provision-masked-VDBs page. Box labels such as "unmasked" are my wording for the moment before the job runs; the docs say masking happens during provisioning. Why masking a VDB beats masking a copy by hand An in-place job overwrites its source (see the overview chapter ). On a VDB that is safe: production is untouched, the VDB can be thrown away, and a refresh brings fresh data and re-runs the masking job. Child VDBs of a masked VDB contain only masked data, so you can hand out many independent masked copies cheaply.

h: 8.24.2 Rules and restrictions you must know
x: 8.24.2 Rules and restrictions you must know Provisioning or refreshing masked VDBs is supported only for Oracle, MS SQL Server and Sybase ; Db2, for example, is not supported. One job per VDB. A masking job cannot be assigned to several VDBs at once; if you reuse a rule set on many VDBs, create a unique job for each. Only in-place jobs can be selected. Masking happens during provisioning . A VDB that was provisioned without a masking job can never be masked later, and a masked VDB cannot be unmasked, changed to another job, or given extra masking jobs. You cannot make an unmasked snapshot of it. The connector used for masked provisioning must be a "basic" connector (host and port), unless you mask an Oracle pluggable database, which needs an "advanced" connector. Masking and Virtualization must never run in one virtual machine , and engine versions must be compatible (a compatibility matrix is on the page: for example 5.3.0.0 and later pairs with 5.3.0.0 and later, and minor versions need not match). Refreshing a masked VDB (Refresh VDB, choose a snapshot or point in time) re-runs the masking job. To let the Virtualization Engine reach the masking engine, an administrator can change the host, port and credentials it uses through the engine's CLI ( maskingjob , then serviceconfig , then update , set values and commit). It lists jobs automatically at each login, and maskingjob fetch refreshes the list on demand. The page notes that Delphix does not check network availability between the two engines.

Delphix: rule sets, primary keys and data integrity You now have an environment and a connector ( the connectors and VDB chapter ). The next object in the chain is the rule set : the list of tables, or files, that the engine will profile and mask. Building one is mostly point and click. The part that needs real understanding is keys . Delphix, like most masking engines, wants to know for every table which column or columns identify one row, and it expects masked values in related tables to stay matched. This section covers both, and it covers the syllabus's Day 51 topics: primary key basics and discovery, and data integrity in primary and foreign key columns. You will build a rule set for the ShopSphere tables, run the engine's checklist on it, and add a logical key. If you skipped the basics of keys, the data basics chapter is a good first stop; here they are explained again briefly, with the masking twist.

x: 8.28 Words to know first Rule set A group of tables or flat files, within one data source, on which you may run profile, masking or tokenization jobs. Inventory The detailed list of every column or field in a rule set with its domain and algorithm. You open it by clicking the rule set's name. Primary key (PK) A column (or columns) that uniquely identifies each row of a table and is never empty. Foreign key (FK) A column in one table that holds the primary key value of a row in another table, linking them. Referential integrity The promise that every foreign key value matches a real row in the table it points to. Logical key A unique, non-null column (or comma-separated columns) you tell Delphix to treat as the key . It changes nothing in the database; it is only information for Delphix. Identity column A database column that numbers rows automatically. Delphix can use an existing one as the key, or create a temporary one when a table has no key. ROWID In Oracle, a built-in pseudocolumn holding each row's address. The Oracle preparation page recommends it as the logical key for speed. Deterministic (consistent) algorithm One that always turns the same input into the same output (for a given algorithm key). This is what keeps matching values matching. Checklist An action on a rule set (and on a job) that checks every table has a primary key, an indexed identity column or a logical key.

h: 8.29 Primary and foreign keys from zero, with ShopSphere
x: 8.29 Primary and foreign keys from zero, with ShopSphere A database table is like a spreadsheet, but databases promise things a spreadsheet does not. One promise is that each row can be found unambiguously. Two customers may share a name, so the name cannot find a row. A primary key is the column designed to do it. In ShopSphere, CUSTOMERS.customer_id is the primary key: 1001 is Asha Menon, 1002 is Ravi Kumar, 1003 is Meera Nair, and there will never be two 1001s or an empty one. Tables connect through foreign keys . ORDERS has a column customer_id that stores which customer placed the order. Each value there must exist in CUSTOMERS.customer_id . Original data (fake). CUSTOMERS.customer_id is the primary key; ORDERS.customer_id is a foreign key to it. CUSTOMERS.customer_id first_name last_name ssn 1001 Asha Menon 123-45-6789 1002 Ravi Kumar 234-56-7890 1003 Meera Nair 345-67-8901 ORDERS (fake). Which customer made each order? order_id (PK) customer_id (FK) order_date total_amount 5001 1001 2026-03-02 1499.00 5002 1001 2026-03-19 299.00 5003 1003 2026-04-07 849.50 The query "show every order with its customer's name" joins the two tables on customer_id . That join is what the application does all day. It is also what a careless masking job can break, as the integrity section below shows. "Primary key discovery" in Delphix The syllabus lists "primary key discovery using Delphix". The documentation has no separate feature of that name. What it does show: the database inventory marks each column that is a Primary Key, Foreign Key or Index (written beneath the column name, as in the screenshot later in this section), and the Checklist reports tables that lack a usable key. So "discovery" here means reading the key information from the database and checking it . This is my reading of the pages; ask your trainer if the course expects something more.

h: 8.30 Why a masking engine needs a key on every table
x: 8.30 Why a masking engine needs a key on every table In-place masking works in three moves: read a row, compute the masked values, write them back to that same row . To write to the right row, the engine must be able to name it. The preparation pages for SQL Server, Db2 and Sybase say so plainly: a key is a unique, non-null value that identifies a row, and for in-place masking "this key looks up the row to update the masked record". For speed the key should be indexed (a clustered index is best, the pages say). Analogy: a librarian who must correct the address on 100,000 library cards. If each card has a printed number, she can pull card 48213 directly. If cards have no numbers she must compare every card to find the right one, and with duplicate names she might correct the wrong person. The key is the card number. The analogy stops at speed: the engine updates in batches, not card by card. The pages then list what the engine does with a table, in this order of preference. Situation What the engine uses You defined a logical key That key. It "can override the key used". One or several columns, but always unique and never null. The table has a primary key The primary key. No primary key, but an identity column The identity column. If it is not indexed, the engine adds an index (named with i_MASKING_GENERATED_IDENTITY_TMP on SQL Server). No key at all The engine adds a temporary identity column called MASKING_GENERATED_IDENTITY_TMP and removes it when the job ends. This needs a database user allowed to alter the table, and slows the job. If identity support is unavailable the job may fail. A detail the pages disagree on: the SQL Server page lists the order as logical key, primary key, identity column, none. The Db2 and Sybase pages list primary key, identity, logical key, none, but still describe the logical key as the override. The practical rule is the same: define a logical key when you want to control the choice . The documentation recommends on-the-fly masking as the alternative when a table has no key, since that method writes new rows rather than updating old ones. Why the temporary column is not a free pass The 2025.5 and 2025.6 release notes list known issues: failed jobs on heap tables (tables without a clustered index) may leave the generated temporary identity column and index behind. So "the engine will add one for me" is a fallback with a cost. Give the table a real key.

h: 8.34.1 What a logical key is, and when you must add one
x: 8.34.1 What a logical key is, and when you must add one A logical key tells Delphix "treat these columns as the row identifier for this table". The page defines it as a unique, non-null value that identifies a row. It does not change the target database ; it is information for Delphix only. The rule from the page: if a table has no primary key defined in the database and you use in-place masking, you must name an existing column or columns as a logical key. For several columns, separate them with commas. If you do not, and there is no primary key, the engine creates an identity column, which needs a database user allowed to modify the schema, otherwise the job may fail. Limits worth knowing, all from the pages: a logical key cannot exceed 1,024 characters; the column must exist (the dialog warns that masking jobs fail if the key column does not exist); a fixed-issues entry says null values in logical key columns are now rejected at create or update; and if some tables get an invalid key, the other changes are still saved, the old key stays, and the failures are listed in the Async Tasks page under "Exception Detail". Which ShopSphere tables need one? All four core ShopSphere tables have a declared primary key (customer_id, order_id, item_id, product_code), so none needs a logical key. A staging table with no declared key is the typical case. In the lab you will add one on an illustrative table. A composite key is also possible: ORDER_ITEMS could use the logical key order_id,product_code if that pair is unique, though its own primary key is the better choice.

A filter is a WHERE condition that restricts which rows the job loads (the dialog's hint: prefix the column with the table name, as in customer.cust_id < 1000 ). Custom SQL replaces the engine's own SELECT. A table can have a filter or custom SQL, never both; adding one removes the other. The page's rules for custom SQL: it must include the primary key column(s) and every column you will mask; it must include the ROWID column (the engine uses it to identify and update each row, and omitting it may fail the job or leave masking incomplete); and you can edit only one table at a time. The "Generate Custom SQL" link suggests a statement for you. Filters are covered with subsetting ideas in the discovery and subsetting chapter . x: 8.35 The Checklist: does every table have a usable key? The engine can check your keys for you. It confirms that every table in the rule set has a primary key, an indexed identity column or a logical key. If tables lack a key, it lists their names and explains that, for connectors that support identity columns, the engine will add a temporary column before the job starts, which may lengthen the run, and that where identity support is not available the job may fail. You can either update the rule set or go ahead with the job. If everything has a key, the dialog says the check passed . Official screenshot: A failing checklist for a rule set. h: 8.36.1 What breaks if you mask the two sides differently
x: 8.36.1 What breaks if you mask the two sides differently Suppose ShopSphere's profiling flagged only the sensitive columns, and a well-meaning engineer also masked customer_id , but gave CUSTOMERS and ORDERS different algorithms, or a random one on each side. Each value is replaced independently. After masking customer_id differently on each side (invented values). The join no longer works. CUSTOMERS.customer_id first_name (masked) ORDERS.order_id ORDERS.customer_id 7342 Divya 5001 2199 9051 Karthik 5002 2199 3318 Lakshmi 5003 6670 No order's customer_id (2199, 6670) exists in CUSTOMERS (7342, 9051, 3318). The orders are orphans . Worse, the two orders that belonged to one customer (5001, 5002) happen to match each other here only because the same input gave the same output in ORDERS. Test cases such as "show the last five orders of customer Divya" now return nothing, and a database that enforces its foreign key will refuse the change outright (a constraint violation). The fix is to give both columns the same algorithm , one that is deterministic (same input gives same output) and that produces unique outputs. After masking both customer_id columns with the same deterministic, unique algorithm (invented values). The join works. CUSTOMERS.customer_id first_name (masked) ORDERS.order_id ORDERS.customer_id 7342 Divya 5001 7342 9051 Karthik 5002 7342 3318 Lakshmi 5003 3318 1001 became 7342 in both tables, and 1003 became 3318 in both. Every order still points at its customer. The IDs no longer reveal the real ones. The same logic applies to ORDER_ITEMS.order_id against ORDERS.order_id. Often the best choice is not to mask the key A profiler marks customer_id as non-sensitive, because it is a meaningless number. If nobody can identify Asha from 1001, leaving key columns unmasked is the simplest and safest way to keep integrity. Mask a key only when the key itself is sensitive (an SSN used as a key, for example). This advice is my general engineering judgement, not a statement from the documentation.
