h: 8.36.2 How Delphix keeps matching values matching
x: 8.36.2 How Delphix keeps matching values matching The documentation's promise appears in the introduction: Delphix masks consistently, so data is masked the same way across tables and databases. The pages that explain how give four ingredients. Use the same deterministic algorithm on columns that reference each other. The Oracle, PostgreSQL and Db2 driver pages all say this almost word for word: use the same deterministic algorithms on primary key fields that reference each other so referential integrity is kept when constraints are re-enabled. The PostgreSQL and Db2 pages add that if a foreign key column and the key it references do not share one deterministic algorithm, the job fails with an integrity constraint violation. The SQL Server page says it too, with a stronger warning: the failure is near certain. Use an algorithm whose output is unique. Secure Lookup picks a value from a list by hashing the input, so it is consistent, but different inputs can collide on the same output, which is fine for names and wrong for keys. The Segment Mapping page says to use it for columns with unique values such as SSNs, primary keys and foreign keys, and that for keys you must use the same Segment Mapping algorithm on each side. The Character Mapping page says the same input always gives the same output (until you rekey it) and no two different text inputs share an output, "useful for masking primary and foreign key columns". The SQL Server page's examples of unique algorithms are Dlpx-Core CM Alpha-Numeric, and the CM Numeric page describes a numeric one that keeps the number of significant digits. The algorithms chapter covers them. Do not use algorithms that are random or unsuitable. The Secure Lookup page says its RANDOMIZE hash method picks a random value every time and "should never be used where referential integrity is required". The Gender SL page says the same of itself. The Date Shift Discrete page says it is not suitable for columns with unique constraints, unique indexes, primary keys or foreign keys. The terminology page notes the Mapping algorithm can mask only one table at a time (the Mapping page says this limit ended with engine 6.0.10.0), so on older engines tables must be masked one after another. Let the database allow the update. A primary key referenced by foreign keys cannot normally be changed. So a job that masks a key must enable Disable Constraints and also Drop Indexes . The known-issues page records a job failure when primary keys are masked without Drop Indexes together with Disable Constraints, and the Oracle plugin page says the same. The constraints are re-enabled after masking, which is when mismatched values would be caught. Where the domain helps The discovery page says the domain mechanism "helps to ensure that the same masking algorithm is applied consistently across rule sets whenever a particular type of sensitive data is discovered". If ShopSphere defines one domain for customer identifiers and gives it one algorithm, every profiling run that finds such a column assigns the same algorithm. That is a good way to keep both sides of a key aligned, though I did not find the documentation claiming it handles key relationships by itself.

h: 8.36.3 Algorithm syncability: the same output on two engines
x: 8.36.3 Algorithm syncability: the same output on two engines Many teams run a masking engine for each stage (see the overview chapter's note on multiple engines). If the dev engine and the QA engine mask 1001 differently, test data from the two will not join. The Algorithm syncability page is about this. It says algorithms can be synced between engines through an API, and that syncing out-of-the-box instances updates their individual keys . An algorithm key is the secret value that decides the output; two engines produce the same masked value only if they have the same algorithm and the same key. The page also separates two kinds. Non-deterministic algorithms cannot guarantee the same output for the same input across jobs, so they "cannot be used for syncable masking": it lists DATE SHIFT(VARIABLE), the Gender SL and SexualOrientation SL instances and SECURE SHUFFLE, and says all Secure Lookup (Random) algorithms are non-deterministic by design. Fixed algorithms, such as DATE SHIFT(FIXED) and ZIP+4, always give the same result and need no syncing. Everything else is deterministic and depends on its key. The page does not mention primary or foreign keys at all: its subject is consistency between engines . Within one engine, consistency comes from using the same algorithm on both columns.

x: 8.37 Hands-on lab: a rule set for the SHOPSPHERE tables Lab: create a rule set, run the checklist, add a logical key Goal: a rule set SHOPSPHERE_RS over the ShopSphere tables, a passing Identity Column Check, and a logical key on a table that has no primary key. Prerequisite: the environment and tested connector from the connectors and VDB chapter . The steps and screens are . The table CUSTOMER_STAGING is my illustrative addition , because the four core tables all have primary keys and you need a keyless table to practise the logical key. Ask your DBA to create it in the lab database, or read steps 6 and 7 without running them: CREATE TABLE CUSTOMER_STAGING ( staging_row_id INTEGER NOT NULL, email VARCHAR(100), first_name VARCHAR(50), last_name VARCHAR(50), ssn VARCHAR(11) ); -- no PRIMARY KEY declared (illustrative) Start the wizard. Open SHOPSPHERE_DEV , click the Rule Sets tab, then + Rule Set , choose Database and click Continue. The "Add a Rule Set for a Database" wizard opens on the Details step. Details. Name it SHOPSPHERE_RS and select the connector SHOPSPHERE_VDB_CONN . Check the connector details shown below the dropdown, then Next. Confirming the database name and host now saves a confusing failure later. Add the tables. Click Add Tables and tick CUSTOMERS, ORDERS, ORDER_ITEMS, PRODUCTS (and CUSTOMER_STAGING if it exists). Save the dialog. All related tables go in together so parent and child keys can be masked consistently. Five (or four) rows in the grid with empty Logical Key, Filter and Custom SQL. Save the rule set. Next, check the Summary, click Save, and note the Async Task ID. Watch Monitor > Async Tasks. The task completes and SHOPSPHERE_RS appears in the Rule Sets grid with a green Refresh/Save tick. Run the Checklist. In the rule set's Actions menu choose Checklist . It tests every table for a primary key, indexed identity column or logical key before any job exists. With the staging table present: a dialog titled Identity Column Check listing CUSTOMER_STAGING as missing a key. Without it: a passing result. Add the logical key. Actions > Edit, Next to Data Tables, tick CUSTOMER_STAGING, click Edit Logical Key , type staging_row_id , Save the dialog. staging_row_id is unique and never empty, which is what a logical key requires. It changes nothing in the database. The Logical Key column of that row shows staging_row_id . Save the wizard. Click Next, then Save in the wizard, and wait for the Async Task. The dialog Save only staged the change. Check again. Run Checklist again. The check passes (the job version of the dialog reads "Identity Column Check PASSED"). Read the keys in the inventory. Click the rule set name to open the inventory and look under the key columns. Key columns carry the words "Primary Key" (and "Index" if indexed); a foreign key column such as ORDERS.customer_id is marked "Foreign Key" if the database declares it; the staging table is labelled "Logical Key". Show a worked answer: the integrity plan for the next chapters Keys are not masked in this lab, but plan them now. In the later algorithm and job chapters you will assign algorithms in this inventory. Write this plan down first. Key columns and what to do (illustrative plan) Parent column Child column Plan CUSTOMERS.customer_id ORDERS.customer_id Leave unmasked, or give both the same deterministic, unique algorithm (for example a Character Mapping based numeric one). ORDERS.order_id ORDER_ITEMS.order_id Same rule. Include both tables in the rule set. PRODUCTS.product_code ORDER_ITEMS.product_code Not sensitive; leave unmasked. CUSTOMER_STAGING.staging_row_id (none) It is only the logical key, so do not mask it. If you do mask a key, the job must enable Disable Constraints and Drop Indexes. The two table-level steps (Checklist and logical key) are documented; the plan is my application of the integrity rules in the section above.

x: 8.38 Common mistakes and gotchas Key and rule set pitfalls Believing a passing Checklist means integrity is safe. It only proves each table has a key. Masking the primary key with a non-unique algorithm. Duplicates break the key. Use a unique, deterministic algorithm, and the same one on the foreign key side. Masking a key without Disable Constraints and Drop Indexes. The job fails on the key constraint. Using a random algorithm on a key. RANDOMIZE and the Gender SL type never preserve integrity. Forgetting the wizard's Save. The logical key, filter or table list is lost. Typing a logical key column that does not exist. The job fails, or the table is listed under Exception Detail in Async Tasks. Leaving out a child table. A foreign key table linked to a masked key must be in the rule set. Assuming refresh wipes your masking choices. It keeps existing algorithm assignments and updates the table list and columns.

x: 8.39 Recap Recap A rule set is the list of tables or files of one connector that jobs run on. There are four types: Database, Semi-Structured Files, Flat Files and Copybook. Creating one takes three steps (Details, Data Tables, Summary); the wizard's Save stores everything and starts an Async Task. Edit, Refresh, Duplicate, Delete and Checklist are in the Actions menu. In-place masking finds each row by a key: a logical key if you set one, otherwise the primary key, otherwise an identity column, otherwise a temporary one the engine creates. A logical key is a unique, non-null column (or comma-separated columns) given to Delphix only; it changes nothing in the database. On Oracle, ROWID is the recommended one. The Checklist's Identity Column Check reports tables that have no usable key; it does not test integrity. If you mask a primary key, mask the foreign key with the same deterministic, unique algorithm, and enable Disable Constraints and Drop Indexes on the job. Algorithm syncability concerns producing the same output on several engines; non-deterministic algorithms cannot be synced. Delphix: profiling to find sensitive data You cannot protect data you have not found. A real application database has hundreds of tables and thousands of columns, and nobody remembers which of them hold a customer's phone number, a tax id, or a note typed in by a support agent. Profiling is Delphix's answer: a job that scans your data source, decides which columns look sensitive, and writes its decisions into a list that you review before any masking happens. This section explains that scan from zero. It covers what a profile set, a classifier, a domain and an inventory are, how they fit together, how to create and run a profiling job, how to read the results, and how to correct them by hand. It ends with the Day 52 lab (TDM_Handson5) on the ShopSphere sample database. The connections and rule sets the lab needs are set up in the Delphix connectors chapter and the rule sets and keys chapter ; the algorithms that profiling assigns are explained in the algorithms and masking jobs chapter . If you want the Informatica view of the same idea, see the Informatica discovery and profiling chapter .

x: 8.40 Words to know first Sensitive data discovery / profiling The process of scanning a data source to find columns or file fields that hold sensitive information. The docs use both names for the same thing. Profiling job A saved set of instructions that says "scan this rule set using this profile set". You create it once and can run it many times. Rule set The list of tables (or files) that a job is allowed to look at. A profiling job covers only what is in the rule set; new tables are not discovered until you add them. Profile set A bundle of recognition rules (classifiers). Choosing a profile set decides which kinds of sensitive data the job can detect. Classifier One recognition rule, tied to one domain. Example: "a column whose name looks like ssn " or "a value that looks like an email address". Domain A named kind of sensitive data, such as FIRST_NAME, SSN or EMAIL, together with the default masking algorithm for it. Algorithm The recipe that actually replaces a real value with a safe one. Profiling only chooses an algorithm; the masking job runs it. Inventory The table of every column or field in a rule set with its domain and algorithm. It is the profiler's output and the masking job's input. Confidence The number (shown 0 to 100 in the UI) that says how sure the profiler is about a match. Assignment threshold The minimum confidence needed before the profiler writes a domain and algorithm into the inventory. ASDD profiler Automated Sensitive Data Discovery, the current profiler. It uses classifiers. The older "legacy" profiler uses search and type expressions.

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.41 Why profile at all? Picture the ShopSphere developers asking for a copy of SHOPSPHERE_PROD to test the Customer Orders app. A TDM engineer must hide every real name, phone number and tax id before handing it over. With four tables and nine customer columns you could do that by reading the table definitions. With a real database of 3,000 columns you cannot, and one forgotten column is a privacy incident. A profiling job automates the first pass. The documentation describes it as examining metadata (column names and types) and potentially the data itself, then assigning the matching domain and its algorithm to each column it judges sensitive . A person then reviews the result. That last step matters: the profiler is a fast assistant, not an auditor. Why it matters Profiling is where masking projects are won or lost. Masking jobs only protect what is in the inventory. A column the profiler missed, and nobody caught, goes to the test environment untouched.

h: 8.41.1 The whole pipeline on one line
x: 8.41.1 The whole pipeline on one line Rule set which tables to scan → Profile set which rules to use → Profiling job scan and score → Inventory column, domain, algorithm → You review fix and approve → Masking job applies algorithms Analogy: an airport scanner flags bags using a rulebook (the profile set). A security officer (you) opens the flagged bags, waves through the harmless ones, and sometimes stops a bag the scanner missed. The analogy stops being accurate in one place: the scanner has no memory of the officer's decisions unless you tell it, which is what the "automatic updates" checkbox, described in the inventory review part of this section, is for.

h: 8.42 Profile, domain, algorithm assignment and inventory: how they differ
x: 8.42 Profile, domain, algorithm assignment and inventory: how they differ Beginners often use these four words as if they meant one thing. They are four different layers, and each answers one question. Layer Question it answers Where you manage it ShopSphere example Profile set (made of classifiers) How do we recognise sensitive data? Settings, Profile Sets and Classifiers "ASDD Standard" Domain What kind of sensitive data is this, and what is its default algorithm? Settings, Domains FIRST_NAME, SSN, TELEPHONE_NO Algorithm assignment Which recipe masks this particular column? Inventory screen of a rule set CUSTOMERS.first_name gets dlpx-core:FirstName Inventory For this rule set, what is every column's domain and algorithm? Click a rule set name The whole list for SHOPSPHERE_PROD Two consequences follow, both stated in the docs : Because the profiler assigns an algorithm through the domain, the same kind of data is masked the same way everywhere. Every FIRST_NAME column in every rule set gets the same default algorithm, which keeps results consistent. Each domain has exactly one default algorithm, so if you want the profiler to pick a different algorithm for some data, a separate domain (with its own recognition logic) has to exist for it. Changing a domain later Editing a domain's default algorithm affects only future profiling runs. It does not change assignments already sitting in existing inventories . If you change a default and expect old inventories to follow, they will not.

h: 8.43 How the profiler decides: classifiers, strengths and thresholds
x: 8.43 How the profiler decides: classifiers, strengths and thresholds The profiler looks at each column and asks a panel of four judges. Each judge looks at a different kind of evidence and answers with a score. The scores are combined into one confidence per domain. If the best confidence reaches the assignment threshold, that domain (and its algorithm) is written into the inventory.

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.43.1 The four classifier frameworks A classifier framework is a kind of judge; a classifier instance is one configured judge for one domain. The docs list four frameworks and say you cannot install more . Framework Looks at Level Plain-English job PATH The name (for databases: table name and column name) Column "The column is called first_name , so it is probably a first name." TYPE Data type and length Column Rejects impossible matches, e.g. a yes/no flag cannot be an SSN. REGEX The actual values, using patterns Data "The values look like 123-45-6789 ." LIST The actual values, checked against a list Data "The values are all on the list of known first names." PATH and TYPE are cheap, because they only need the table definition. REGEX and LIST must read sample rows, so they are what lets the profiler find a sensitive column even when its name is meaningless, such as COL_17 . The built-in value lists carry English values, so data-level detection is limited to English .

h: 8.43.2 Match strength, reject strength and how scores combine
x: 8.43.2 Match strength, reject strength and how scores combine Inside the engine every classifier reports a number from -1.0 to 1.0. The UI shows the same idea as -100 to 100, and in practice you only see 0 to 100 because non-matches are not displayed . Match strength : how sure the classifier is that this data belongs only to its domain. 0.01 means "maybe, but it could be many things". 1.0 means "certainly this and nothing else". Reject strength : how strongly a non-match counts against the domain. -1.0 eliminates the domain at once. Combining : if results disagree in sign, the larger absolute value wins; if they agree, the match gets stronger. Only the strongest column-level result and the strongest data-level result are combined, and the docs warn that the exact formula may change. Two worked examples from the docs Rejection. A column named ssn_present matches the SSN PATH classifier (0.67). But it is boolean, the SSN TYPE classifier returns -1.0, and the verdict is -1.0, so SSN is not assigned. Competition. A column named passport_no holds 9-digit numbers. Both the SSN and the PASSPORT_NO REGEX classifiers give 0.5. Only the PASSPORT_NO PATH classifier also matches (0.67). Final confidence: PASSPORT_NO 0.84, SSN 0.5, so PASSPORT_NO wins. Column passport_no (9 digits): how the scores add up SSN REGEX 0.5 PATH: no match (0) ⇒ final 0.5 PASSPORT_NO REGEX 0.5 PATH 0.67 ⇒ final 0.84 (wins) 0 0.5 1.0 The block widths are drawn to scale from the docs' example. The engine's exact combining formula is not published and may change. Original diagram: the "passport_no" example from the classifier documentation. Both domains get the same data-level score, and only PASSPORT_NO also matches by column name. The built-in PATH classifiers usually carry 0.67. A REGEX or LIST classifier has to beat that to override a name match, which is why the docs advise a low match strength (0.1 to 0.5) for patterns that are not unique. A nine-digit pattern could be an SSN, an account number or a row id, so it gets a small score. A dashed pattern like 001-23-4567 is distinctive, so it gets a high one.

h: 8.43.3 What the SSN classifiers actually look like
x: 8.43.3 What the SSN classifiers actually look like The ASDD Standard profile set is published as JSON. For the SSN domain it holds three classifiers (listing as of the 21.0.0.0 release). I summarise rather than copy: Classifier Framework What it checks Strength Social Security Number - Path PATH Name ends in ssn or contains social security plus number, code or id match 0.67 Social Security Number - Regex REGEX Dashed or spaced pattern, plain nine digits dashed forms 0.7, plain nine digits 0.1, reject 0.1 Social Security Number - Type TYPE Number or String, at least 9 long no match strength, rejects other types Notice the design: the name gives a good clue, the value pattern confirms it, and the type check rules out nonsense. The same three-part shape repeats for most domains.

h: 8.43.4 Which domains can be found by value, and which only by name?
x: 8.43.4 Which domains can be found by value, and which only by name? Not every domain has all three kinds of evidence. Reading the ASDD Standard listing (21.0.0.0) shows the pattern, and it matters when column names are cryptic. I grouped the domains by the classifier frameworks that the listing gives them: Evidence available Domains (examples from the listing) What it means for you Name, type and value list FIRST_NAME, LAST_NAME, FULL_NAME, CITY, COUNTRY, COMPANY_NAME, GENDER, JOB_TITLE, US_STATE Can be found even in a column called COL_17 , as long as values are in the English lists Name, type and value pattern SSN, EMAIL, TELEPHONE_NO, ZIP, CREDIT CARD, IBAN, IP ADDRESS, US_PASSPORT, PAYMENT_AMOUNT, ADDRESS Value patterns can rescue a badly named column, if the values fit the pattern (US-shaped for ZIP and phone) Name and type only DOB, TAX_ID, ACCOUNT_NO, CUSTOMER_NO, USER_ID, TEXT, PASSWORD, SERIAL_NO No value check: if the column is not named sensibly, the profiler will not find it Two ShopSphere consequences follow. date_of_birth and tax_id are found only because their names are clear, so a legacy table with a column called DT1 would slip through. And all grouping here comes from my reading of the JSON, so check the live Classifiers screen of your engine for the exact picture.

x: 8.43.5 Assignment threshold The default minimum confidence for ASDD is 1, so "any positive match, no matter how weak, triggers an assignment" . That is very permissive, and the docs contrast it with the legacy profiler, which by default wanted an 80% match for data-level expressions. You can raise the threshold per profile set (integer 1 to 100) or globally with the application setting ASDD/DefaultAssignmentThreshold . A higher threshold means fewer false alarms and more missed columns. Because a missed column is worse than a false alarm, many teams keep the threshold low and review the inventory.

h: 8.43.6 How much data the profiler reads
x: 8.43.6 How much data the profiler reads For data-level classifiers the ASDD profiler samples rows instead of reading whole tables. These documented settings steer it; the values are the defaults in the 2026.5 Masking API client page . Application setting (ASDD group) Default What it controls DefaultTableSampleRows 1000 Rows sampled per table DefaultAssignmentThreshold 1 Minimum confidence to assign DefaultNullFilterThreshold 75 Percent of null or empty values that triggers an extra query for more values DefaultMultipleProfilerExpressionAlgorithm NullValueLookup Algorithm used when the "multiple profiler expression" option finds a tie Statistical sampling (so the sample reflects the whole table) is supported for Oracle, SQL Server and SAP ASE. When sampling is used, the sample percentage is always 1%, and if that yields too few rows the query is repeated without sampling . The page does not say what happens on other databases beyond this; check your version.

x: 8.43.7 The legacy profiler, briefly Before ASDD, profiling used search expressions (patterns on column names or data) and type expressions (data type and minimum length). The legacy profile sets are kept so that old jobs keep giving the same results, and they contain no type classifiers to restrict matches by column type . The legacy classifier tables list patterns such as ssn(?!\w*ID) for SSN and (?>((tele?)?phone)|...) for telephone. The legacy version of the Add Profile Set dialog (not the ASDD one pictured below) carries a banner saying legacy profile sets are deprecated and will be removed in a future release. Use ASDD for new work; the profileTypeExpressions page only shows API scripts for legacy type expressions. ASDD currently supports databases, delimited files, fixed-width files, JSON files, XML files and mainframe data . Its stated limits: XML or JSON documents stored inside database columns are not profiled, and the Informix database is a known problem for discovery because of the column-truncation SQL.

x: 8.44.1 Create your own profile set (ASDD) You would build a custom set when, for example, a project wants only a handful of domains scanned, or a different threshold. The steps below are for the ASDD profiler . Click + Profile Set above the grid. This opens the Add Profile Set dialog. Type a unique Set Name; add a Description if you like. Names must be unique across all profile sets. Leave ASDD Support ticked (the default). This tells the engine the set will hold classifiers rather than legacy expressions. You cannot flip this later on an existing set; you would have to create a new one. Optionally enter an Assignment Threshold, 1 to 100. If you leave it empty, the application setting DefaultAssignmentThreshold applies. Tick the classifiers you want. Each classifier is tied to a domain, so the ticked list decides which domains this set can ever detect. Click Save . The new set appears in the grid and in the profile set drop-down of the profiling job wizard. Official screenshot: The Add Profile Set dialog with ASDD Support ticked. On screen: it shows Set Name, Description, an optional Assignment Threshold field, a single "Classifiers" tab, and a checklist such as "Account Number - Path" and "Address Line 1 - Regex"; a few boxes are ticked. Source page ↗ Other actions in the row menu are View (everything read-only), Edit (tick or untick classifiers), Duplicate (copy with a new name) and Delete . You cannot delete a profile set that is assigned to any job . Profile sets can also be created through the API with two calls (see the ASDD profile set import and export page, which I did not read in full).

h: 8.46 Creating and managing a profiling job
x: 8.46 Creating and managing a profiling job Profiling jobs live inside an environment , next to masking jobs. Click an environment and you land on its Jobs tab. The documentation says profiling jobs can be created for relational databases (examples: Oracle, PostgreSQL) and for XML, JSON, mainframe, delimited and fixed-width rule sets. It is not supported for XML or JSON documents stored inside database columns, or for NoSQL databases . Which jobs an environment offers depends on its purpose. A masking environment supports Profiling and Masking jobs. A tokenize environment supports Profiling, Tokenization and Re-Identification jobs . In both, the Jobs tab can be sorted and filtered by Job ID, Name, Rule Set, Type, Status and Completed Time, and Export Environment packs the environment's connectors, rule sets and jobs into a file (with an optional passphrase). Tokenization is explained in the algorithms and masking jobs chapter . A documentation disagreement to be aware of The profiling jobs page lists JSON rule sets as supported, while the inventory page says "Profiling is not supported on the JSON file rule sets". I could not settle this from the text. For delimited, fixed-width and database rule sets, which this course uses, there is no conflict. If you must profile JSON, test it on your engine version. x: 8.46.1 Create a profiling job, step by step In the environment, open the Jobs tab and click + Profiling Job . The Create Profile Job wizard opens with three steps: Details, Configuration, Summary. Details: enter a unique Job Name and pick the Rule Set. The rule set is the scope of the scan. Tables not in it are never examined. Details: choose the Profile Set. The UI pre-selects the profile set named in DefaultProfileSetName , which is ASDD Standard in the screenshot below. Details: decide on the two checkboxes. Multiple Profiler Expression Check assigns a fallback algorithm when classifiers in different domains tie at the same confidence; the report will mention the multiple matches. Clear previous auto domain assignments wipes domains assigned by earlier runs for columns whose automatic updates are on, so the run starts fresh. A third box, Multi Tenant , lets one rule set be reused for identical schemas through different connectors, with the connector picked at run time. Click Next. Configuration: set streams, memory and notes. See the table after the screenshots. Click Next to reach Summary, check it, and click Save . The job appears in the Jobs list with no status until you run it. Official screenshot: Step 1, Details. On screen: Job Name, a "Target" environment label, Multi Tenant, Select Rule Set, Multiple Profiler Expression Check, a Select Profile Set drop-down showing ASDD Standard, and Clear previous auto domain assignments. Before it starts, the engine checks two resources: total memory allowed for all running jobs, and the number of jobs allowed to run at once (the application setting NumSimulJobsAllowed , default 7). If either limit would be exceeded, the job waits in a queue . You cannot edit or delete a job while it is running. To stop it, use Cancel and confirm. The docs' warning about semi-masked data is about cancelling a running masking job (see the algorithms and masking jobs chapter ); a profiling job does not mask anything. x: 8.48 From findings to a reviewed inventory The profiler writes its decisions into the rule set's inventory . Reaching it takes one click: Environment > Rule Sets tab > click the rule set's name . The "Inventory" tab that older versions had was removed, and the banner in the screenshots says so . Official screenshot: The Rule Sets tab (engine 22.0.0.0). h: 8.48.1 Correcting one column: the Edit dialog
x: 8.48.1 Correcting one column: the Edit dialog Click the pencil (Edit) icon in the Actions column of the column's row. The Edit Column (or Edit Field) dialog opens. From the inventory screen only the Masking section is editable. Decide about Enable Automatic Updates . When ticked (the default), a profiling job may change this column's masking decision. When unticked, your choice wins over the profiler. If you are about to override the profiler, untick it first, otherwise the next profiling run may undo your work. Pick the Domain and the Algorithm . The Domain drop-down fills in that domain's default algorithm; you may replace it with any other algorithm. If you chose a DATESHIFT algorithm on a column that is not a native date or datetime, fill in the Date Format. The default is yyyy-MM-dd . The letters are case sensitive: D means day of the year, d day of the month, MM month, yyyy four-digit year. Add a note if useful, then click Save . Nothing takes effect until you save. Official screenshot: Edit Field with automatic updates ON. On screen: field FIRSTNAME_00, Record Type "All Records", Position 3, "Enable Automatic Updates" ticked, Data Model Plain, domain FIRST_NAME, algorithm dlpx-core:FirstName. The instruction line reads "Uncheck 'Enable Automatic Updates' to make Masking assignments editable". Source page ↗ Official screenshot: The same dialog with automatic updates OFF. On screen: the checkbox is clear and the Select Domain and Select Algorithm boxes now show clear (x) and drop-down controls, i.e. they can be edited. Source page ↗ Three more inventory tools worth knowing : Clear Masking Assignment (the circular-arrow icon in a row's Actions column, enabled only when that column or field has an assignment) removes the applied masking assignment and, in the same click, switches automatic updates off for it. A confirmation bar appears for a few seconds; if you do nothing, the clearing goes ahead, and Cancel keeps your assignment. Nulling algorithms. If you pick an algorithm that can return null (such as Null SL) for a column that has a NOT NULL constraint, the UI shows an error. Inventory Approval Workflow (database rule sets only, enabled per environment). Every edit sets the status to NEW; the editor clicks Submit; an Admin or a user with the Inventory Approval privilege clicks Approve or Reject. A masking job for that rule set will not run unless the status is Approved. This gives a data steward a formal sign-off point. Official screenshot: A database inventory under the approval workflow. On screen: the header shows "Status: Rejected" in red, buttons "All Logical Keys", "All Filters" and "Actions", and column rows with domain ZIP and algorithm RepeatFirstDigit on the ID column. The key, filter and code icons on the table row are for logical key, filter condition and custom SQL. Source page ↗ Review every row in this order: is the domain right, is the algorithm right for the application (see the algorithms chapter ), is confidence low (worth a second look, not necessarily wrong), and what is missing. Rows with no domain, such as UNMASKED_00 in the database screenshot, matter as much as flagged ones. Put the reason for each manual change in the Notes field for the audit trail. Everything above is also available through the Masking API. The documentation's createInventory example assigns an algorithm and a domain to a column with PUT /column-metadata/{id} and a body such as {"algorithmName": "AddrLine2Lookup", "domainName": "ADDRESS_LINE2"} . The script needs helper files that are not shown, so it cannot be run as printed. Why the checkbox matters in teams A TDM engineer who fixes ten columns by hand, and a colleague who re-runs profiling the next day, are a common cause of "my changes disappeared". Untick automatic updates on every column you corrected deliberately, and let the profiler keep updating the rest.

h: 8.49 ShopSphere: what should the profiler flag?
x: 8.49 ShopSphere: what should the profiler flag? Before running the Day 52 lab, practise the skill a TDM engineer needs most: predicting the profiler's answer from the classifier definitions, so that you can spot a wrong result. Our ShopSphere tables are in the data basics chapter . I checked each column name against the published ASDD Standard PATH regexes (the 21.0.0.0 listing) using an ordinary regular-expression engine. The real engine also applies type checks, data sampling and its own matching options, so read the table as a prediction , not as engine output. Predicted ASDD Standard result for ShopSphere (illustrative prediction by the author, not engine output) Table.column Expected domain Why (evidence) Human check CUSTOMERS.customer_id none The Customer Number PATH rule wants "number", "num", "nbr" or "no" after "customer"; customer_id has none of them Primary key. Usually left alone or masked consistently as a key, see the rule sets and keys chapter CUSTOMERS.first_name FIRST_NAME PATH f(irst)?_?-? ?(na?me?) matches; a first-name list also checks values Confirm algorithm is dlpx-core:FirstName CUSTOMERS.last_name LAST_NAME PATH for "last name" matches; last-name list checks values Confirm dlpx-core:LastName CUSTOMERS.email EMAIL PATH "email"; value pattern with strength 0.9 Check column length is not tiny; the EMAIL type rule lists a minimum length of 20 CUSTOMERS.phone TELEPHONE_NO PATH "phone". Plain 10-digit values like 9876543210 only reach the weakest value pattern (0.05), so this is mostly a name match Check the algorithm suits 10-digit numbers CUSTOMERS.ssn SSN PATH ends with "ssn"; dashed values like 123-45-6789 fit the 0.7 pattern Algorithm choice is in the algorithms chapter CUSTOMERS.date_of_birth DOB PATH matches "date of birth"; type must be Date or a string of 6+ characters Check which date algorithm and date format CUSTOMERS.zip_code ZIP PATH "zip code" matches. The value patterns are US shaped (5 digits, or 5+4); ShopSphere's 6-digit PINs such as 560001 do not fit them Confirm the ZIP assignment survived, and that the ZIP algorithm accepts 6 digits CUSTOMERS.tax_id TAX_ID PATH "tax id"; type String or Number, 6+ long Check how it handles letters and digits ORDERS.total_amount PAYMENT_AMOUNT (false alarm) The Payment Amount PATH rule matches names ending in amount, amnt, amt, balance or price Business decision: an order total is not personal data. Clear it ORDER_ITEMS.unit_price, PRODUCTS.price PAYMENT_AMOUNT (false alarm) Name ends in "price" Catalogue prices are public. Clear them ORDERS.order_date, ORDERS.customer_id, ORDER_ITEMS.*_id and quantity, PRODUCTS.product_code and product_name none No rule matches these names Keep as is. Foreign keys must follow the key policy Uncertain claim The listing gives each TYPE classifier a minimumLength (for example 20 for email, 10 for first name). The documentation excerpt I had does not define it exactly; I read it as the declared length of the column. If that is right, a very short first_name column might be rejected. Do not take this as fact: run the job and look. If the prediction holds, 8 of the 9 CUSTOMERS columns and 3 price or amount columns (11 in total) will carry a domain after the first run. Three of those are false alarms and one real column ( customer_id ) is deliberately left alone. Learning to see that pattern is the point of the lab.

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.50 Lab: profile ShopSphere Lab: Create a profiling job for ShopSphere, run it, and correct the inventory Goal: scan the four ShopSphere tables with the ASDD Standard profile set, compare the result with the prediction table above, and fix what is wrong. This lab assumes you already created the environment, the connector and the rule set (all four tables) in the connectors chapter and the rule sets chapter . The data is fake; the screens follow the official documentation, but your engine version may differ slightly. The names I give ( ShopSphere_Profile_01 ) are my own choices, not Delphix defaults. Open your ShopSphere environment, Jobs tab, and click + Profiling Job . Profiling jobs are grouped with masking jobs inside the environment. The Create Profile Job wizard opens at Details. Name it ShopSphere_Profile_01 , pick the ShopSphere rule set, keep profile set ASDD Standard , and leave both checkboxes clear. The rule set limits the scan to your four tables. Leaving "Clear previous auto domain assignments" clear means nothing from older runs is wiped. On Configuration, keep 1 stream and set Max Memory to at least 1024 MB. The docs require 1024 MB per stream for ASDD profile sets. Add your own email address if SMTP is configured. Summary shows ASDD Standard and your memory values. Save, then ... > Run . The engine may queue the job if too many are running. Status goes Queued or Running, then Succeeded. Warning means it finished with caveats; open the logs. Click the job name and read Profile Results . Write down every table, column, domain and algorithm. Count the rows. Compare with the prediction table. Mark each column as: as predicted, extra (profiler flagged more), or missing (profiler flagged less). Explain any difference using classifier evidence, for example "column name matched PATH but the type was rejected". Open the rule set (Rule Sets tab, click its name) and fix the inventory. For the three price or amount columns: click the Clear Masking Assignment icon on each row (it removes the assignment and switches automatic updates off), and confirm the bar. For each real finding, confirm the algorithm. For customer_id and the foreign keys, apply the key policy from the rule sets and keys chapter . For any column the profiler missed that you know is sensitive, assign domain and algorithm by hand and untick automatic updates. Only truly sensitive columns carry an algorithm. Export the rule set to CSV ( Actions > Export Rule Set ). This is your evidence file. Open it in a spreadsheet and check that the Is Masked, Algorithm and Domains values match your intent. Re-run the profiling job and check the inventory again. The columns you corrected with automatic updates off should keep your choices. If they changed, the checkbox was still ticked. Download the PDF ( Report and Logs > Job Report ) and keep it with the CSV. These two files are what you would hand to a data steward. Show a worked answer Likely corrections (prediction-based): Clear PAYMENT_AMOUNT from ORDERS.total_amount , ORDER_ITEMS.unit_price and PRODUCTS.price with the Clear Masking Assignment icon, which also switches automatic updates off so a re-run does not bring them back. Keep FIRST_NAME, LAST_NAME, EMAIL, TELEPHONE_NO, SSN, DOB, ZIP and TAX_ID on CUSTOMERS . Check the algorithm shown for each against the algorithms chapter , especially SSN, TAX_ID and ZIP, whose default algorithms the documentation excerpt I had does not state. If the profiler skipped zip_code or phone because of length or type rules, assign ZIP or TELEPHONE_NO by hand and untick automatic updates. Leave customer_id unassigned unless your key policy says otherwise. What profiling cannot fully tell you: imagine a free-text column that support agents fill with phone numbers and names. The TEXT domain's PATH rule recognises names such as note or comment, but no rule can know what was typed into it. ShopSphere has no such column, yet real systems do, so always ask the application team about free-text columns and look at their data.

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.51 Common mistakes and gotchas Watch out for these Treating profiling as the finish line. The output is a draft. Review every flagged and every unflagged column, especially free-text and oddly named ones. Forgetting that only the rule set is scanned. A table added to the database after the rule set was built is invisible to profiling. Editing assignments and leaving automatic updates ticked. The next profiling run can replace your edits. Untick it on columns you decided by hand. Changing a domain's default algorithm and expecting old inventories to change. They do not; only future profiling runs are affected. Max Memory below 1024 MB per stream with an ASDD profile set. The docs say the job needs at least that. Four streams need 4096 MB or more. Trusting name matching alone. A column called ssn_present is a flag, not an SSN; TYPE classifiers exist to reject these, but they only help when the data type is right. Using legacy profile sets for new work. They are deprecated and give less coverage. Expecting value-level detection in languages other than English. The built-in lists are English only. Sharing the PDF report or CSV without thinking. They list table and column names with their domains, which tells a reader exactly where your sensitive data lives, so store them with care.

ct: Delphix (1): connecting, keys and profiling
x: 8.52 Recap Key points Profiling scans a rule set with a profile set and writes domain and algorithm assignments into the inventory. Classifiers come in four frameworks: PATH and TYPE look at columns; REGEX and LIST look at values. Scores combine into a confidence compared with the assignment threshold (default 1). A domain is a kind of sensitive data with one default algorithm. Changing it affects only future runs. Create the job in an environment: rule set, profile set (ASDD Standard by default), streams, memory (at least 1024 MB per stream for ASDD). Read results on the job page, in the PDF, in the rule set inventory or in an exported CSV. Correct findings in the Edit dialog and untick Enable Automatic Updates so that the profiler does not overwrite you. For ShopSphere, expect the customer columns to be flagged and price or amount columns to be false alarms.

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
h: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: Delphix: masking algorithms and masking jobs Profiling told you which columns are sensitive. Masking is the step that actually changes them. In Delphix the work is split in two: an algorithm decides how one value becomes another, and a masking job applies the assigned algorithms to every row of a rule set. This section covers both halves. First the idea of algorithms (frameworks, instances, keys, lookup files, uniqueness), then a catalogue of every algorithm framework the documentation lists, then a close look at the algorithms you need for the syllabus: first name, SSN, alphanumeric text and telephone number. The second half explains how to build, run, monitor and tune a masking job. It ends with two labs: TDM_Handson7 (mask FirstName, Day 55) and TDM_Handson8 (mask alphanumeric text, SSN and telephone number, Day 56), using the ShopSphere tables. Before this section you should know how rule sets and inventories work ( the rule sets and keys chapter , the profiling chapter ). For the generic ideas behind masking see the masking concepts chapter , and for the Informatica equivalent see the Informatica data masking chapter . Masking files is the topic of the file masking chapter , and the full lab walkthrough set is in the Delphix hands-on labs chapter .

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: 9.1 Words to know first Algorithm (instance) A named, ready-to-use masking recipe with its configuration, such as dlpx-core:FirstName . You assign instances to columns. Algorithm framework A kind of algorithm that you can configure to create new instances, such as Secure Lookup or Segment Mapping. "FIRST NAME SL" is an instance of the Secure Lookup framework. Out-of-the-box instance An instance that ships with the engine. These cannot be edited or deleted; you create your own from a framework instead. Algorithm key A secret value inside most algorithms. Changing it changes the output, so the same input masks to something different. Deterministic Same input, same algorithm, same key, same configuration gives the same output every time. This keeps joins working across tables and across runs. Lookup file A plain text file with one replacement value per line (no header). The algorithm picks a line based on the input, so the output is always something from your file. Collision Two different inputs masked to the same output. Fine for names, harmful in a unique column. Non-conformant data A value that does not fit the format an algorithm expects, such as letters in a numeric-only algorithm. By default it is left unmasked and a warning is recorded. Masking job A saved set of options saying "apply the inventory of this rule set", with a method (in-place or on-the-fly), threads, memory and scripts. In-place / on-the-fly In-place changes the data where it sits. On-the-fly reads from a source and writes masked data to a different target. Stream One parallel lane of work. More streams let the engine mask several tables at once.

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
h: 9.2 The big picture: from domain to masked row
x: 9.2 The big picture: from domain to masked row The previous chapter ended with an inventory: every sensitive column carries a domain and an algorithm. The masking job reads that inventory, takes each row from the source, runs each assigned algorithm on the matching value, and writes the result. Inventory column → algorithm → Masking job method, threads, memory → Algorithms value in, masked value out → Target data safe copy → Verify counts, joins, formats Where do the algorithms live? Open Settings > Algorithms . The grid shows Algorithm Name, Framework Name, Mask Type and Owner; sortable by name, framework and mask type, filterable by name, framework, mask type and owner . The "+ Algorithm" button creates new instances. Official screenshot: The Settings > Algorithms screen (engine 23.0.0.0, 138 algorithms on that test engine). On screen: rows such as "ACCOUNT SL" (framework Secure Lookup, mask type STRING, owner System) next to user-made ones like "ACCOUNT_TK" (Tokenization, owner admin) and "ALG_JRTIYFXL" (Dependent Date Shift, mask type GENERIC_DATA_ROW). A "+ Algorithm" button and an "Extension Support Policy" link are top right. Source page ↗ The Owner column tells you which instances are yours: System rows ship with the engine. The docs say system-defined instances and those from algorithm plugins can only be viewed, never edited or deleted. Administrators and users with the EDIT Algorithm permission can edit any user-defined one, but the name and framework cannot change after creation .

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: 9.3.1 Idea 1: framework versus instance Think of a framework as a recipe template ("replace each value with one chosen from a list") and an instance as a filled-in recipe ("...using this list of first names, ignoring case"). The documentation's own example: "FIRST NAME SL" is an instance of the Secure Lookup framework . The analogy stops being accurate in one place: a framework is not something you assign to a column. Only instances are assigned.

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
h: 9.3.2 Idea 2: the key makes output repeatable but secret
x: 9.3.2 Idea 2: the key makes output repeatable but secret Most algorithms include a key. If FirstNameLookup masks "Michelle" to "Rachael", changing the key might make it "Ben" instead . The key can be randomised through an API call ( PUT /algorithms/{algorithmName}/randomize-key ). Two consequences: Within one key, repeatable output means the same customer name masks the same way in every table and every run, so test data stays internally consistent. Whoever knows the key and the algorithm might be able to rebuild mappings, so treat the key like a password and do not casually re-key production algorithms, because every later run would produce different test data.

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: 9.3.3 Idea 3: unique versus non-unique Some algorithms may give two inputs the same output (collisions). Others guarantee that different inputs give different outputs. The docs are consistent about which is which: Property Frameworks Use it for Collisions possible (non-unique) Secure Lookup, Name, Full Name, Date Shift Discrete or Variable, Free Text Redaction, Min Max Names, cities, comments: values that repeat naturally in real data No collisions (unique) Character Mapping, Segment Mapping, Mapping, Tokenization Keys and identifiers: primary keys, foreign keys, SSN, account numbers Caveat from the docs: even Character Mapping can collide for numeric data types, because "001" and "1" are the same number once stored in a numeric column .

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
h: 9.3.4 Idea 4: a lookup file is just a list
x: 9.3.4 Idea 4: a lookup file is just a list Lookup-based algorithms (Secure Lookup, Name and their out-of-the-box instances such as FirstNameLookup, LastNameLookup and FullNMLookup) hold a list of fake values. The engine hashes the input, uses the hash to choose a line, and returns that line. The file has one value per line, no header, in ASCII or UTF-8 . For example, a tiny file for cities could be: Smallville Clarkville Farmville Townville With a hash method of SHA256 (the default) the same input always chooses the same line. The framework also offers LEGACY (to mimic old behaviour) and RANDOMIZE, which picks a random line each time and therefore does not keep referential integrity. RANDOMIZE suits things like gender, where you want a statistical spread rather than consistency .

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: 9.3.5 Idea 5: masking versus tokenization Almost all masking is one-way. Tokenization is the one family that can be reversed, which is why it exists: mask data, send it to an outside vendor, and later re-identify the vendor's findings . It is covered in the framework catalogue below. Generic technique names and their Delphix counterparts Your syllabus (Day 44) names substitution, shuffle, key masking and encryption. This mapping is my own reading, marked : Substitution : Secure Lookup, Name, Mapping (replace a value with another real-looking value). Shuffle : SecureShuffle (moves existing values between rows). Key masking : Character Mapping and Segment Mapping (keyed permutation that keeps uniqueness). Encryption : Tokenization (AES-128 in the framework description, reversible).

x: 9.5 Deep dive: masking a first name The default tool is dlpx-core:FirstName , an instance of the Name framework. It needs String input. If the value is null, empty or only spaces, it comes back unchanged. Words joined by a hyphen count as one word, a single letter is treated as an initial and masks to a single letter, and by default at most two names are masked and extra ones dropped. It raises no non-conformant data errors, and it can occasionally mask a name to itself . dlpx-core:FirstName behaviour (documented examples) Input Output Lesson (null) / "" / " " unchanged Nothing to mask M S Initials stay initials M. h: 9.6 Deep dive: alphanumeric text with Character Mapping
x: 9.6 Deep dive: alphanumeric text with Character Mapping Character Mapping swaps each maskable character for another one from the same group , using a key. You define groups such as [0-9] and [a-zA-Z] ; a digit becomes a digit and a letter a letter; anything not in a group (dashes, spaces) is left alone. Every maskable position affects every other, no two text inputs share an output, and a masked value never equals the original if at least one character is masked. That makes it suitable for keys and identifiers . Three ready instances cover most needs: Instance Masks Use on Documented example dlpx-core:CM Alpha-Numeric Digits, lower and upper case letters, some Latin and Cyrillic Text columns only "ABCxyz123" to "HANwhp391" dlpx-core:CM Digits Only ASCII digits; letters and symbols stay Text columns holding numbers (codes, ids) "ABCxyz123" to "ABCxyz391" dlpx-core:CM Numeric Digits, keeps digit count; first digit never 0 Numeric database columns "99" to "75" If no character at all is masked (say, CM Digits on "ABC"), the engine records non-conformant data. CM Numeric also ignores database numeric limits, so on DB2 INTEGER or SQL Server INT columns a masked value can exceed the range and cause a conversion error. Official screenshot: The character group editor for a custom Character Mapping algorithm. On screen: two groups, "[a-zA-Z]" and "[0-9]", each with + and delete icons. Because they are separate groups, letters only become letters and digits only digits. Source page ↗ ShopSphere CUSTOMERS.tax_id with CM Alpha-Numeric (illustrative; the values are invented by the author) customer_id Before After What to notice 1001 ABCDE1234F KMQTR6021Z Same shape: 5 letters, 4 digits, 1 letter 1002 PQRST5678K HWBNL3947C Different input, different output

h: 9.7 Deep dive: SSN with Segment Mapping (or Character Mapping)
x: 9.7 Deep dive: SSN with Segment Mapping (or Character Mapping) An SSN has structure (3 digits, dash, 2 digits, dash, 4 digits) and often serves as a lookup key, so you want unique, format-preserving output. The Segment Mapping page names Social Security Numbers as a typical use and describes exactly the controls you need : Up to 10 segments, each up to 6 characters, each treated as Mask alpha-numeric , Mask numeric , Preserve or Mask with a constant value . Ignore characters (such as the dash) are removed before masking and put back afterwards, so "123-45-6789" and "123456789" mask alike. Numeric segments are masked as whole numbers, alpha-numeric ones character by character. Values must match the segment pattern; data longer than the pattern passes through unmasked, and short numeric segments are reported as non-conformant unless you choose "Mask partial segments". Setting for the ShopSphere SSN algorithm (my design) Value Segment 1 Length 3, Mask numeric Segment 2 Length 2, Mask numeric Segment 3 Length 4, Mask numeric Ignore Characters Ignore specific characters: - Short Numeric Segment Handling Report nonconforming data (default) Official screenshot: The Segment Mapping configuration. On screen: a "Segments" list (empty here, with a pencil to edit), Short Numeric Segment Handling "Report nonconforming data", Ignore Characters "Ignore specific characters", a Specific Characters box, Ignore Commas, a CTRL button and "Process Preserve Segments Before Ignore Characters". The right panel describes the framework. Source page ↗ Two alternatives exist. CM Digits (or CM Alpha-Numeric) masks every digit and keeps the dashes automatically, with no setup: the docs' examples turn "999-12-3456" into "453-71-6283" (Character Mapping framework, group [0-9]) and "999-12-3456." into "668-23-1138." (CM Alpha-Numeric). Redact Digits-Zero turns every digit into 0 ("999-12-3456." to "000-00-0000."), which is not unique: many different SSNs become the same value. Accuracy flags for SSN The documentation excerpt I had does not say which algorithm the SSN domain uses by default; look at Settings > Domains on your engine. It also does not promise that a masked SSN follows real issuing rules (the profiler's patterns exclude area numbers 000 and 666, for example). If your application validates SSNs, test the output, and consider restricting a numeric segment's mask value range. h: 9.9 More algorithms you will meet: dates, email, mapping, tokenization
x: 9.9 More algorithms you will meet: dates, email, mapping, tokenization The labs use four algorithms, but the rest of ShopSphere (and any real project) needs a few more. Each paragraph below is a short orientation from the framework pages .

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: 9.9.1 Dates (date_of_birth, order_date) Three out-of-the-box instances differ in how much they preserve. Date Shift Fixed moves every date five days forward and rolls within the month, so the same input always gives the same output and no two dates collide ("2001-02-27" becomes "2001-02-04"). Date Shift Variable picks a random day within the same month and year and can collide. Date Shift Discrete sends every date of one year-month to one fixed day (about one in thirty dates may collide), so it is unsuitable for columns with unique, primary or foreign key constraints. When you build your own Date Shift instance you choose a minimum and maximum shift and a unit; equal values give a fixed shift, 0 inside the range is never used (a date never masks to itself), and Roll keeps all larger and smaller units unchanged. For a column that is not a native date type, set the Date Format in the inventory (default yyyy-MM-dd , case sensitive). Pairs such as admission and discharge need Dependent Date Shift so the order and the interval survive.

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: 9.9.2 Email The Email framework splits at the "@". The default dlpx-core:Email Unique hashes the whole input into a 52-character Base32 name and replaces the domain with example.com , so every input gets its own output (64 characters in total, which matters for short columns). dlpx-core:Email SL instead picks a readable name such as "E.Duboise" from a 20,000-value lookup, so collisions are possible but the data looks more human. The Email Unique output is what the profiling screenshots showed for the EMAIL domain, so ShopSphere's email column is covered by default; check that the column is wide enough for 64 characters.

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: 9.9.3 Mapping: you decide the replacements A Mapping algorithm replaces each distinct input with a value you supplied, and it never reuses an output, so there are no collisions. You must provide at least as many replacement values as there are distinct inputs, or the job reports "No free mappings are available". Mappings can be imported as a plain list of outputs or as a CSV with input,output columns, and exported (encrypted with a passphrase), reset or deleted. All mappings load into memory during a job, so give the job enough memory. Mappings can live on the engine or in your own PostgreSQL database shared by several engines. Before engine 6.0.10.0, only one table could be masked at a time with a mapping algorithm; later versions allow concurrent jobs.

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: 9.9.4 Tokenization: masking you can reverse The Tokenization framework encrypts values with AES-128 and Base64 so a vendor can analyse data they cannot read, and you can later re-identify their findings. The output is longer than the input; if it would not fit the column, the framework either fails the job or falls back to a reversible Character Mapping. Segment Mapping, Character Mapping and Mapping can also be used for tokenization under conditions the framework pages list. You create a domain with both a masking and a tokenization algorithm, then a Tokenization environment, and use + Tokenization Job and + Re-Identification Job ; the form has the same fields as a masking job. Official screenshot: The Create Tokenization Job form: the same layout as a masking job, with a "Select Tokenization Method" drop-down in place of the masking method. Source page ↗

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
h: 9.10.2 Choosing between Character Mapping and Segment Mapping
x: 9.10.2 Choosing between Character Mapping and Segment Mapping The docs say Character Mapping is intended to replace Segment Mapping in many cases, but not all . Prefer Character Mapping when Data is dirty or inconsistently formatted: it keeps non-masked characters automatically You need Unicode (first plane) rather than just a-z and 0-9 Inputs differ in length and you want to preserve the last characters (reverse preserve ranges) You want every position to influence every other Prefer Segment Mapping when Parts of the value must be masked differently by position You need to map input ranges to different output ranges (A-D to W-Z) You need numeric segments limited to a value range (up to 6 digits)

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: 9.10.3 Multi-column algorithms A multi-column algorithm (for example Dependent Date Shift or Multi Column Address) is assigned once but spans several columns, each filling a logical field . It is meant for coordinated masking, such as two dates that must keep their interval. Each non-optional logical field must be assigned for every Algorithm Group number, and incomplete assignments may only be noticed when the job runs. They only work where whole rows are processed together, and cannot be called by other algorithms through chaining .

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: 9.10.4 Usage and syncability (engine administration) Usage. GET algorithm/{algorithmName}/usage lists every column, file field, domain and other algorithm that uses it. PUT on the same path with replacementAlgorithmName swaps it everywhere, with optional environment and rule set filters. The docs warn that this can change many inventories and is hard to undo, so first GET usage for both algorithms and export global settings and affected environments . Syncability. Algorithms are fully syncable between engines ( GET /syncable-objects?object_type=USER_ALGORITHM ). Non-deterministic ones (all Secure Lookup Random algorithms, DateShiftVariable, Gender SL, SexualOrientation SL, SecureShuffle) cannot give the same output twice, so they cannot be used for syncable masking. DateShiftFixed and RepeatFirstDigit are listed as fixed. Syncing an out-of-the-box instance updates its key but does not replace its files . Why this matters to a TDM engineer: if two engines mask the same source, identical output on both needs the same keys, which is what syncing delivers. The consistency argument is my reasoning, not a quote.

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: 9.11 Masking jobs: in-place or on-the-fly A masking job lives in an environment next to the profiling jobs of the profiling chapter . A masking environment supports Profiling and Masking jobs; a tokenize environment supports Profiling, Tokenization and Re-Identification jobs, created with the same flow . Start with the one choice that shapes everything else, the masking method. In-Place Updates the source environment with masked values. Typical use: you already copied production into a test database (for example a virtual database) and mask that copy where it sits. Risk: if the job fails midway, that database may be partly masked. On-The-Fly Reads unmasked data from a source environment and connector, and writes masked data to the target. Typical use: production stays untouched and the masked copy goes elsewhere. Supported pairs: same connector type (Oracle to Oracle, delimited file to delimited file) and database source to delimited-file target. For a database-to-file job, tick Database to File Job so that the source connector list shows database connectors. Target files need not exist in advance if the file name pattern matches the source, but in a database-to-delimited-file job the target files must be created first, with names matching the source tables. You need the View Connector role to create or run on-the-fly jobs .

h: 9.11.1 Create a masking job, step by step
x: 9.11.1 Create a masking job, step by step In the environment's Jobs tab click + Masking Job . The Create Masking Job wizard opens: Details, then Database Options (database rule sets only), Configuration, Summary. Details: unique Job Name, Masking Method, Rule Set. The name must be unique across the entire application. For On-The-Fly you also choose Source Environment and Source Connector. Details: decide the optional boxes. Multi-Tenant reuses a rule set for identical schemas through different connectors, chosen at run time. Selective Data Distribution must be on if the job will be used in masked VDB provisioning. Stop job on first occurrence aborts on the first non-conformant value, but only where the algorithm or global setting says non-conformant data is a failure. Database Options: commit size, update threads and friends. See the table below. This step only appears for database rule sets. Configuration: streams, row limit, feedback size, memory, comments, email. These control speed and memory, not what is masked. Summary, then Save. The job appears in the Jobs list with status CREATED until you run it. Official screenshot: Step 1 of the wizard (engine 22.0.0.0): Job Name, Target, Multi Tenant, Select Masking Method, Select Rule Set and the Non-conforming Data checkbox "Stop job on first occurrence". Source page ↗ Official screenshot: On-The-Fly with a delimited rule set: Source Environment, the "Database to File job" checkbox (red arrow), and Source Connector, which only fills in after you choose. Source page ↗ Official screenshot: Database Options step: Commit Size (empty), Update Threads 1, Batch Update ticked by default, three clear checkboxes and two script pickers. Source page ↗ Field What it does (from the docs) Commit Size Rows processed before a commit. The related application setting DatabaseCommitSize has default 10000; the docs excerpt does not spell out how it interacts with an empty field. Update Threads Parallel threads writing to the target database; default from DefaultUpdateThreads (1). Do not use several threads if any table lacks an index, and reduce them if a deadlock appears, especially on T-SQL databases. Batch Update Loads masked rows in batches of Commit Size. Recommended because it usually speeds the job. Truncate On-The-Fly only: empty the target tables before loading. Drop Indexes / Disable Triggers / Disable Constraints Switch off and automatically restore indexes, triggers or constraints so that keys and foreign keys can be updated. Not supported for every database. With driver-support plugins they appear under Enable Tasks . Pre SQL / Post SQL Script A file of plain SQL statements separated by semicolons (maximum 10 MB) run before or after the job. No PL/SQL or T-SQL extensions, no dynamic SQL, and schema-changing SQL cannot run as a pre-script. The engine always opens a connection, even if no script is loaded. Number of Streams How many tables are masked in parallel; default from DefaultStreams (1). Even one stream has separate input, masking and output threads. Expect some streams to finish before others. Row Limit Rows in flight per stream (lines, records or XML elements for files). 0 means unlimited; -1 or blank picks a default by rule set type. Defaults assume rows of about 2000 bytes with 100 masked columns; for bigger rows, add memory or lower the limit. Feedback Size Rows between log messages. Min / Max Memory (MB) Memory for the job; the docs recommend at least 1024. Official screenshot: Configuration step: Number of Streams (1), Row Limit, Feedback Size, Min and Max Memory, Comments and Email (a placeholder address). Source page ↗ Edit, view, delete. Use the ... menu on the job row; the name cannot be edited, and delete asks for confirmation. A job cannot be edited or deleted while running. The row menu also offers a Checklist for database jobs that runs an Identity Column Check: the rule set's tables must have a primary key, an indexed identity column or a logical key. The check looks only at the rule set, so it still passes if a primary key constraint is disabled by the job .

x: 9.11.2 Run, stop and monitor Run. Click ... then Run . The engine checks the memory allowed for all running jobs (by default 75% of system memory minus 6 GB reserved for the web application, overridable with MaximumMemoryForJobs ) and the number of simultaneous jobs ( NumSimulJobsAllowed , default 7). If either limit would be exceeded the job queues . Stop. Cancel a running masking job and the data can be left semi-masked ; indexes, constraints or triggers that were dropped are not recreated. Cancelling a queued job has no effect on your data . Plan to restore from a copy rather than trust a half-masked database. Monitor. Open Monitor > Job Executions or click the job name. The execution page shows a summary (tables masked, rows masked and remaining, tables and columns with non-conformant data, streams), the sequence of events (Initializing, Collecting Configurations, Preparing, Running Pre-execution Custom Driver Tasks, Starting, Creating Identity Column, Running PreSQL and PostSQL Scripts, Dropping Created Identity Column, Running Post-execution Custom Driver Tasks, Collecting Information, Job Completed) and a grid of Execution Components, one row per table or file. h: 9.11.3 Non-conformant data: when a value does not fit the algorithm
x: 9.11.3 Non-conformant data: when a value does not fit the algorithm If a value does not match what an algorithm expects (letters going into a numeric-only algorithm, an 11-digit string into a 10-digit segment pattern), the job, depending on settings, fails, skips the value, or nulls it. The global default is the application setting DefaultNonConformantDataHandling ; an algorithm's own setting overrides it, and a job can override both with Job-level Non-Conforming Data Handling : Use global setting, Fail on encounter (FAIL), Don't mask value (DONT_MASK) or Set value to null (NULLIFY). The job-level override applies only to Hop-based jobs. By default non-conformant data is not masked and the job ends with a warning . Unmasked data in a test database is a leak, so never ignore a yellow warning. Open the execution component's logs. The Error Report lists the event type (UNMASKED_DATA, or JOB_ABORTED if the job stopped), the cause (PATTERN_MATCH_FAILURE), the row count and the column, plus a sample of the pattern of the bad value, never the value itself. Each character is shown as a class: N digit, L letter, M mark, P punctuation, S symbol, Z separator, O other, U unknown. Official screenshot: The Error Report for one table: Event UNMASKED_DATA, Cause PATTERN_MATCH_FAILURE, Event Count 1, and a sample pattern made only of the letter L, followed by the masking log text. Source page ↗ To find the offending rows, translate the pattern into a database query. For the pattern LLLLL on an Oracle column, the docs use SELECT EXCEPTION_00 FROM testdata_EXCEPTION WHERE regexp_like(EXCEPTION_00, '[[:alpha:]]{5}'); . For a multi-column algorithm the pattern is shown for every masked column of that algorithm, so you must read the message to find the real culprit.

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: 9.11.4 Speed: PerfLogger and best practices From version 2026.3 the throughput log is called PerfLogger . It logs at job start (every 10,000 rows), then every 30 seconds after 100,000 rows, and once at the end with totals. The main number is RPM , rows per minute; MB/sec is only informational, and BPR is the average bytes per row. Rows of about 1 KB or more lower RPM. A sharp RPM drop to zero with an unchanged BPR points at the target side (transaction log pressure, auto-growth, many indexes). If RPM falls below earlier runs, check for concurrent jobs, new indexes, constraints or triggers, and bigger rows . The best practices page recommends, for a dedicated compliance engine, 8 vCPUs and 64 GB RAM minimum (128 GB or more preferred), about one vCPU per concurrent job, at least 1 GB of memory per job and per stream (more for particularly wide rows or big lookup files such as 500,000 values), the engine near the database server on a slow network, and tuning the masked VDB first (for Oracle, no-archivelog mode; for SQL Server, SIMPLE recovery) . Mapping algorithms are the other big memory user: all mappings load into memory, so a 2 GB mapping needs much more job memory than a 2 MB one.

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: 9.12 Labs on ShopSphere Both labs mask a test copy of ShopSphere, never SHOPSPHERE_PROD . They assume the environment, connector and rule set from the connectors chapter and the rule sets chapter , and an inventory from the profiling chapter . The SQL is generic; adjust it for your database (Oracle, PostgreSQL and SQL Server differ in small ways, noted where it matters). The Delphix hands-on chapter repeats these labs in a wider flow: the Delphix hands-on labs chapter . Take a "before" snapshot first An in-place job overwrites the data, so create a copy of the original rows to compare against. In PostgreSQL or Oracle: CREATE TABLE customers_before AS SELECT * FROM customers; (SQL Server: SELECT * INTO customers_before FROM customers; ). This snapshot table is my lab convention, not a Delphix feature. Drop it when you finish: it holds the real-looking data. Lab A (Day 55, TDM_Handson7): mask FirstName Goal: mask CUSTOMERS.first_name with dlpx-core:FirstName , run an in-place job and prove the result with SQL. Take the snapshot (above) and note the row counts of CUSTOMERS and ORDERS. You need the "before" numbers to judge "after". Open the rule set inventory and make sure only first_name carries an assignment: domain FIRST_NAME, algorithm dlpx-core:FirstName . One column keeps the lab clear. Use the Clear Masking Assignment icon on other columns, as described in the profiling chapter. The inventory shows one assigned column in CUSTOMERS. Create the job: + Masking Job , name ShopSphere_Mask_FirstName , Masking Method In-Place, your rule set. In-place is right here because the target is already a disposable copy. Database Options: leave Commit Size at the default, Update Threads 1, Batch Update ticked. Configuration: 1 stream, Min and Max Memory 1024. Tiny tables need no tuning; one update thread avoids deadlock risk. Save, run the job from its "..." menu and watch Monitor > Job Executions. Status Queued or Running, then Succeeded. Open the job: Tables Masked 1, Rows Masked equals your CUSTOMERS row count, Tables with Nonconforming Data 0. Verify with SQL. Run the queries below and compare to the expected results. -- 1. row count unchanged SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers_before) AS before_rows, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers) AS after_rows; -- 2. side by side SELECT b.customer_id, b.first_name AS before_name, a.first_name AS after_name FROM customers_before b JOIN customers a ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id ORDER BY b.customer_id; -- 3. how many names were left unchanged SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers_before b JOIN customers a ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id WHERE a.first_name = b.first_name; -- 4. distinct counts before and after SELECT (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT first_name) FROM customers_before) AS d_before, (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT first_name) FROM customers) AS d_after; -- 5. determinism: any original name mapped to more than one output? SELECT b.first_name, COUNT(DISTINCT a.first_name) AS outputs FROM customers_before b JOIN customers a ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id GROUP BY b.first_name HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT a.first_name) > 1; -- 6. other columns untouched, joins intact SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers_before b JOIN customers a ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id WHERE a.last_name <> b.last_name; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id; Show a worked answer Expected results. Query 1: both counts equal. Query 2: every row shows a new name; compare with the illustrative table in the first name section. Query 3: a small number. The documentation says dlpx-core:FirstName can mask a name to itself, so do not demand zero. With three rows, zero or one is normal. Query 4: d_after is at most d_before , because Name algorithms are not unique. Query 5: no rows. The same input must give the same output (deterministic). Rows here would mean the algorithm was re-keyed during the run or case settings differ. Query 6: zero mismatches, and the orders-to-customers join count equals the total number of orders, because customer_id was not touched. If it fails: status Warning means open the Error Report (see the non-conformant data part above); status Failed means read the Execution Log. An unchanged column means the algorithm was never saved in the inventory. Lab B (Day 56, TDM_Handson8): mask alphanumeric text, SSN and telephone number Goal: mask tax_id (alphanumeric), ssn and phone with format-preserving algorithms and prove uniqueness, format and consistency. Start from a fresh test copy (restore the original rows and take a new customers_before snapshot). Create the SSN algorithm: Settings > Algorithms > + Algorithm , name SHOPSPHERE_SSN , framework Segment Mapping. Built-in instances exist, but building one shows how Segment Mapping works and guarantees uniqueness. Add three segments: length 3 Mask numeric, length 2 Mask numeric, length 4 Mask numeric. Set Ignore Characters to specific characters and enter - . Leave Short Numeric Segment Handling on "Report nonconforming data".
