x: 9.13 Common mistakes and gotchas Watch out for these Using a non-unique algorithm on a key or unique column. Secure Lookup, Name and Date Shift Discrete can collide. Use Character Mapping, Segment Mapping or Mapping for keys, and the same algorithm on every column that must still match, including foreign keys. Ignoring the yellow Warning status. Non-conformant values are left unmasked by default, so real data can reach the test database. Read the Error Report after every run. Testing for "zero unchanged values" with name algorithms. The documentation says a masked name can equal the input; test for "a small number", and use Character Mapping when a changed value is mandatory. Running an in-place job on the only copy of the data. Cancelling or failing midway can leave data semi-masked, and dropped indexes or triggers are not recreated. Several update threads on tables without indexes. The docs warn of deadlocks, especially on T-SQL databases. Re-keying an algorithm casually. It changes every masked value, so test data from before and after no longer matches. Letting the profiler overwrite your algorithm choice. Untick Enable Automatic Updates when you assign by hand (see the profiling chapter ). Assuming a masked SSN or phone number is a valid real-world number. The frameworks keep shape and uniqueness, not issuing rules. Giving a job too little memory. Below the recommended 1024 MB, and with large lookup files or mappings, performance suffers or jobs fail.

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: 9.14 Recap Key points A framework is a configurable kind of algorithm; an instance is a ready recipe you assign to a column. Output is repeatable for the same input, key and configuration. Lookup frameworks (Secure Lookup, Name) pick a line from a list file and may collide. Character Mapping and Segment Mapping are keyed and collision free, which suits keys and identifiers. Syllabus algorithms: dlpx-core:FirstName for first names, Segment Mapping or CM Digits for SSN, dlpx-core:CM Alpha-Numeric for alphanumeric text, dlpx-core:Phone Unique for telephone numbers. A masking job is in-place (changes the data where it sits) or on-the-fly (reads a source, writes a target). Key settings: commit size, update threads, batch update, streams, row limit, memory, pre and post SQL. Run the job, then monitor status, components, logs and the Error Report; non-conformant data is left unmasked by default. Always verify with SQL: row counts, side by side, distinct counts, uniqueness, format and join checks. Delphix: masking files (txt and dat) Not all sensitive data sits in a database. Customers export spreadsheets, partners drop .dat feeds on an SFTP server, and batch jobs write flat text files that testers later load. A masking project has to cover those files too. The good news is that Delphix masks files with the same algorithms and the same ideas you have already met: a connector, a rule set, an inventory and a masking job. The new piece is the file format : because a text file has no built-in column names, you must tell the engine where the fields are. This section teaches that from zero and ends with the Day 53 lab (TDM_Handson6): masking a ShopSphere customers.dat file end to end. Connectors and rule sets are introduced in the connectors chapter and the rule sets chapter ; profiling and the inventory are in the profiling chapter ; the algorithms and job options come from the algorithms and masking jobs chapter . Flat-file basics are also in the data basics chapter .

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: 9.15 Words to know first Flat file A plain text file where each line is a record and each record holds fields in a fixed order, such as a .txt , .csv or .dat file. The extension is only a habit; the engine cares about the layout. Record / field A record is one line (one customer). A field is one value in it (the phone number). Delimited file Fields are separated by a character such as , or | . Fixed-width file Every field has a set length, so field two starts at a known position, with no separator. File format (definition) A small description file you upload that lists a file's field names (and, for fixed width, lengths). It is metadata only. Many data files can share one format. End-of-record The character or characters that end a line: LF on Linux, CR+LF on Windows. Text enclosure A character, often a double quote, that wraps a value so the value may contain the delimiter. "Menon, Asha" is one field. Escape How a literal enclosure character inside an enclosed value is written, by default by doubling it. Record type and qualifier When one file mixes record layouts, a record type names each layout and up to three qualifiers say how to recognise it. Header and footer Lines at the start or end that should be copied through unmasked. File connector / rule set The connector says where the files are. The file rule set lists which files (or name patterns) to process and which format each uses. Encoding How characters become bytes. ASCII and UTF-8 are supported for the main file types; mainframe data must be EBCDIC.

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
h: 9.16 How a text file becomes fields the engine can mask
x: 9.16 How a text file becomes fields the engine can mask A database table knows its own columns. A text file does not. Here is the ShopSphere sample used throughout this section, as a pipe-delimited file. All data is fake. customer_id|first_name|last_name|email|phone|ssn|date_of_birth|zip_code|tax_id 1001|Asha|Menon|asha.menon@example.com|9876543210|123-45-6789|1990-04-12|560001|ABCDE1234F 1002|Ravi|Kumar|ravi.k@example.com|9123456780|234-56-7890|1985-11-02|600017|PQRST5678K 1003|Meera|Nair|meera.n@example.com|9988776655|345-67-8901|1999-07-23|682001|LMNOP9012Q To the engine this is just characters. For it to apply "first name algorithm to field 2", it needs a map: field 1 is customer_id , field 2 is first_name , and so on. That map is the file format. The rest of the chain mirrors databases: File format names the fields → Connector where the files live → Rule set which files, which format → Inventory field → algorithm → Masking job reads, masks, writes The docs state the reason directly: unlike databases, files typically carry no built-in metadata describing their fields, so you supply it in Settings > Data Formats .

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
h: 9.16.1 Look at the file before you describe it
x: 9.16.1 Look at the file before you describe it The extension ( .txt , .dat , .csv ) tells the engine nothing; only the layout matters. Before you write a format, answer four questions about the actual file. These commands are ordinary Linux tools, not Delphix features, and are my suggestion: head -3 customers.dat # what separates the fields? cat -A customers.dat | head -2 # $ marks LF; ^M$ means CR+LF (Windows) awk -F'|' '{print NF}' customers.dat | sort | uniq -c # same field count on every line? file customers.dat # ASCII or UTF-8 text? If cat -A shows ^M$ at line ends, the end-of-record is CR+LF. If the field counts vary, the file has several record layouts or stray delimiters, which points to record types or enclosures. The same ShopSphere record as fixed width, with lengths 6, 12, 12 and 30, looks like this (dots stand for padding spaces): 1001..Asha........Menon.......asha.menon@example.com...... ^1-6 ^7-18 ^19-30 ^31-60 Field 2 starts at position 7 because field 1 is six characters long. The engine computes every start from the lengths you list, which is why one wrong length shifts everything after it.

h: 9.18 Delimited versus fixed-width, and the characters that matter
x: 9.18 Delimited versus fixed-width, and the characters that matter Delimited Fields separated by a delimiter. Needs: the delimiter, optionally a text enclosure, an end-of-record. Fields can have any length. The format file lists field names, one per line, and no header. Sample: 1001|Asha|Menon Fixed-width Fields occupy fixed positions. Needs: an end-of-record and exact field lengths. The format file lists name,length per line. Length is counted in characters, not bytes, so multi-byte characters count once. Sample: 1001Asha Menon

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: 9.18.1 End-of-record Choose LF for Linux-style files and CR+LF for Windows-style ones in the rule set's file properties. The docs do not describe the failure mode; my expectation is that a wrong choice glues lines together or leaves a stray carriage return in the last field. The rule set page also lets you use a control character as delimiter or end-of-record: click the CTRL button for a virtual keyboard, or type it as $[hex value] , for example $[01] for ^A. The docs say to avoid typing ^t or \t .

ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: 9.18.2 Enclosures and escaping Take the line 1004|"Rao, Kiran"|... with a pipe delimiter and a double quote enclosure. The comma inside the quotes belongs to the value. If a value itself contains a quote, it must be escaped. The rule set offers an Enclosure Escaping Strategy : Double Enclosure (the default): the escape character is the enclosure character, so "" means one literal quote. Custom : any single character except escape sequences and control characters. Escape "Enclosure Escape Character" (checkbox): the escape character can also escape itself, so with * as escape, ** is one literal * . For a large number of rule sets the docs provide an API script that updates these settings through PUT /file-metadata , for all delimited rule sets with an enclosure or for one rule set ID. A custom escape character or the "escape the escape" flag is not supported for delimited fields holding structured (JSON or XML) data; only double enclosure is.

x: 9.19.1 Build a format file You create the definition as a small text file, then import it. File type What the definition file contains Delimited Field names, one per line, no header Fixed-width Field name, a comma and the length, one per line, no header XML, JSON An example document with the structure only Parquet A schema-only file, or a .txt or .fmt file listing the schema Mainframe The COBOL copybook itself (duplicate field names are not supported) Official screenshot: A delimited format file as shown in the docs: field names only, one per line (First_Name, Last_Name, DOB, SSN, Address, City, State, Zip_Code). Source page ↗ Official screenshot: The fixed-width equivalent: each line is a name, a comma and a length, such as First_Name,20 and Zip_Code,10. Source page ↗ If your data does not match the format, the docs describe two behaviours for delimited files. Fewer fields than the format: delimiters are added after masking to reach the full count ( Data1,Data2 becomes Masked1,Masked2, ). More fields than the format: the extras are lost ( Data1,...,Data4 becomes three masked fields). In both cases the output no longer matches the input shape, so keep formats accurate. For fixed-width files a wrong length shifts every later field, so you mask the wrong characters. On Windows, save format files with LF line endings, since CRLF can pass your eye but fail the engine's parser .

h: 9.20 Record types, qualifiers, header and footer
x: 9.20 Record types, qualifiers, header and footer Real feeds often mix layouts in one file. The docs' example has lines like address, account1234, 9A Lexington Street, ... and email, account1234, bar@example.com : the first field says what kind of record follows. A record type describes one layout; up to three qualifiers (a field plus a regular expression) tell the engine which lines belong to it. A line gets exactly one record type, and if several qualifiers match, the engine cannot guarantee which wins. Record types and header/footer apply only to delimited and fixed-width formats, and can be managed only on the Formats page, not on the inventory page . Official screenshot: A delimited format (engine 24.0.0.0): buttons "+ Field", "+ Record Type", "+ Qualifiers", "+ Header & Footer" and "Actions"; the grid is grouped by record type, "All Records (6)" and "new_record (2)", with Domain and Algorithm columns and Automatic Updates enabled or disabled. Source page ↗ Add a record type: + Record Type , enter a Record Name, Choose File (a definition file for that layout), Save. Each layout needs its own field list. Add qualifiers: + Qualifiers , pick the record type, choose 1 to 3 qualifiers, and for each give a Field Name and a Regular Expression. The record type applies when its expressions match the chosen fields. For the example, field type with expression address . Header and footer: + Header & Footer , enter how many records at the start and the end to leave unmasked, Save. Those lines reappear unchanged in the masked output. Without this, a header such as customer_id|first_name|... would be treated as data. Official screenshot: The Record Type Qualifiers dialog: Select Record Type, No. of Qualifiers (3), and for Qualifier 1 a Regular Expression box (here ([A-Z])\w+ ) and a Field Name drop-down set to "id". Source page ↗ Editing a record type's name and deleting a record type are in its row's Actions column. To reach the format from a rule set inventory, use the Edit File Format button.

x: 9.22 Connectors that reach files A file connector tells the engine where files live. In Environments > your environment > Connectors > + Connection , choose a Source Type that starts with "File" (Delimited, Fixed Width, XML, JSON, Parquet) and then a Connection Mode . Official screenshot: Create Connector, Details step: Connector Name, Select Source Type "File - Delimited", and the Connection Mode list (AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, File System Mount Point, FTP, Other S3 Compatible Storage, SFTP). A banner warns that the legacy generic database connector type is deprecated. Source page ↗ Connection mode You provide Notes from the docs Filesystem Mount Point A mount defined through the Mount Filesystem API (NFS or CIFS server address and path), then path Mounts sync with the connector; a CIFS password does not sync SFTP Path, server name, port, user name, password or public key "User Directory as root" makes the path relative to the user's home FTP Same fields as SFTP FTP and FTPS are disabled in containerized deployments FTPS Same fields Mainframe data sets only AWS S3 Bucket, region, prefix, delimiter, auth type Auth by access and secret key, or by role (role only works for engines hosted on AWS EC2) Other S3 Compatible Storage Bucket and endpoint details For vendors that speak the S3 protocol, for example GCP Azure Blob Storage Account, container, prefix, delimiter, auth type Auth by access key, managed identity or service principal; prefix and delimiter are not checked by Test Connection Official screenshot: Credentials step for an SFTP file connector: Port 22, Server Name, Path, "User Directory as root", authentication type "Username/Password", Username and a masked Password. Click Test Connection before saving. Source page ↗ Mounts in plain words. A mount makes a folder on a file server (shared over NFS or CIFS) appear as a folder on the engine, so the engine can read and write files there as if they were local. You register the mount first (a name, the server address and the shared path) and then pick it in the connector. Use SFTP when the files sit on a normal server you can log in to, and a mount when the share already exists. Cloud storage. "Prefix" and "delimiter" work as in the cloud vendor's list-objects calls: the prefix (for example json/ ) limits which objects the engine sees. On-the-fly note. For on-the-fly file masking you need a second connector (and environment) for the target. One page says the target rule set's file path must already point to a file with the same name in the target directory, which the masked file then replaces. The masking job page says target files need not exist in advance if the file name pattern matches the source. I could not reconcile these two statements; test on your engine version.

x: 9.25 File masking jobs A file job uses the same + Masking Job wizard as in the algorithms and masking jobs chapter , with differences you will notice at once: there is no Database Options step (no commit size, update threads, triggers or constraints), and for files the Row Limit counts delimited or fixed-width lines, mainframe records or XML elements in process per stream . The choice that matters is the method. In-Place The engine reads the original file, masks each field, writes the result to a hidden temporary file ending .msk in the connector's location, and only after success writes it over the original. If anything fails, the original stays intact, and the user and group permissions stay the same. On-The-Fly Reads the source file and writes masked data straight to the target file, with no temporary file. The docs say it is significantly faster than in-place. Source and target use different connectors, so you create a separate environment and connector for the source. Official screenshot: The Details step with Masking Method "On-The-Fly": Select Rule Set, Select Source Environment and Select Source Connector appear. For In-Place they do not. Source page ↗ For file-to-file jobs the target does not need to be a database. If your source is a database and the target a delimited file, tick Database to File Job as described earlier, make the target files in advance with the source table names, and expect binary data to be written as hex strings (the default hex prefix is \x ) . If a file pattern matches nothing on the source, the job still reports success although no file was masked, so check the Execution Components for the file names. Monitoring and logs work as for databases; file jobs report Bytes Masked as well as Rows Masked, and the execution summary calls them Files rather than Tables.

h: 9.25.1 A ShopSphere variant: database table to masked delimited file
x: 9.25.1 A ShopSphere variant: database table to masked delimited file Suppose the test team wants a masked extract of CUSTOMERS as a file, without ever writing unmasked data to disk. That is the database-to-delimited-file on-the-fly case: Create the target connector and an empty target file named like the source table (for example CUSTOMERS ) in the target directory. The docs require the target file to exist and match the table name for this case. Create a delimited file rule set for the target file, with a format whose field names are the table's column names, and assign algorithms to those fields. The Create Masking Job screenshot with the "Database to File job" checkbox (in the algorithms and masking jobs chapter) shows a delimited rule set chosen for such a job. The documentation excerpt I had does not spell out how fields are matched to table columns, so confirm this on your engine version. Create the masking job: On-The-Fly, tick Database to File Job, choose that rule set and the source environment and database connector. Without the tick, only file connectors appear in the source list. Run it and open the output file. Masked rows appear as delimited lines; binary columns, if any, appear as hex strings.

x: 9.26 JSON, XML, Parquet and whole-file masking (brief) These are covered by the same connector, format, rule set and job chain, with a path language instead of positions. Type How fields are named What the format file shows JSON JSON Path: $[*]['First_Name'] for a list of objects, $['First_Name'] for one object Only fields you want to mask need to appear (values may be null placeholders); one record per structure is enough XML XPath: /Person/First_Name ; attributes use "@" (for example /employee/@name ) A document with empty tags or dummy values; the root element is required Parquet Column path: First_Name ; nested Location/Address ; lists Emails/list/element A schema-only file or a .txt or .fmt schema listing; binary columnar format Whole-file masking. Sometimes a file should go to one algorithm in one piece (a free-text document, say). Create a fixed-width connector and a format with exactly one field of length 0, tick Mask whole file in Edit Selected for the data file (End of Record then disappears), and assign an extended algorithm to the one field. The default limit is 200 MB per file, adjustable with the application setting Whole File Masking Max File Size In MB ; Add Record Types, Add Fields and Delete are disabled for such formats .

h: 9.27 Lab: mask a ShopSphere customers.dat file
x: 9.27 Lab: mask a ShopSphere customers.dat file Lab: from a text file to a masked file Goal: mask customers.dat in place on a file server, using a delimited format, a connector, a file rule set, algorithm assignments and a masking job, then verify the output with shell commands. All data is fake. Use a work copy on a disposable path, never a real feed. The names ( customers_delimited.fmt , /data/shopsphere/work ) are my own choices. The algorithms were introduced in the algorithms and masking jobs chapter . Create the sample file on the file server and keep an untouched backup elsewhere. Use the four lines shown earlier, saved with LF line endings. Put customers.dat in /data/shopsphere/work/ and a copy named customers.dat.orig somewhere the connector cannot see, such as your home directory. You need the original to prove the change. The work directory holds exactly one file. Create the format definition customers_delimited.fmt : nine lines, one field name per line, in file order, no header. customer_id , first_name , last_name , email , phone , ssn , date_of_birth , zip_code , tax_id . The first line of data is a header, but the definition lists names only. Import it: Settings > Data Formats > + File Format > Delimited, choose the file, set 1 header record and 0 footer records, Save. The header line customer_id|first_name|... is then copied through unmasked instead of being treated as a customer. A format named customers_delimited.fmt of type Delimited appears in the File tab. Create the connector: Connectors > + Connection, Source Type File - Delimited, mode SFTP (or Filesystem Mount Point), server, port, path /data/shopsphere/work , credentials. Click Test Connection, then Save. The connector's path is where the engine looks for files. Test Connection reports success. Create the rule set: Rule Sets > Add Rule Set > Flat Files, name ShopSphere_Files , choose the connector, then in Data Files click Add File Name , tick customers.dat , and set Format File to customers_delimited.fmt , End of Record LF, Delimiter | , Text Enclosure blank. Save, Next, Save. Delimiter and end-of-record are properties of the data file, not of the format. The rule set shows Source Type Delimited with one file. Optional: run a profiling job on the rule set (see the profiling chapter) to see which fields the ASDD profiler flags. Field names such as first_name, ssn and email are recognisable, so most fields should be flagged. Compare with your plan below. Open the inventory and assign algorithms, one Edit per field, unticking Enable Automatic Updates first. Plan: first_name FIRST_NAME with dlpx-core:FirstName ; last_name LAST_NAME with dlpx-core:LastName ; email EMAIL with dlpx-core:Email Unique ; phone TELEPHONE_NO with dlpx-core:Phone Unique ; ssn SSN with your SHOPSPHERE_SSN or dlpx-core:CM Digits ; date_of_birth DOB with a Date Shift algorithm and Date Format yyyy-MM-dd ; zip_code ZIP with dlpx-core:CM Digits ; tax_id TAX_ID with dlpx-core:CM Alpha-Numeric . Leave customer_id unassigned. Eight fields carry an algorithm; customer_id has none. Create the job: + Masking Job, name ShopSphere_Mask_File , In-Place, rule set ShopSphere_Files . Configuration: 1 stream, memory 1024, Save. Run it from the "..." menu. There is no database step for file rule sets. Status Queued, Running, Succeeded. Execution Components lists customers.dat with 100% progress. Verify with the commands below. Run them in the work directory and compare to the expected results. # 1. line count and header wc -l customers.dat customers.dat.orig head -1 customers.dat # 2. every line still has 9 fields awk -F'|' '{print NF}' customers.dat | sort | uniq -c # 3. no original value survives in the columns that use unique-style algorithms for c in 4 5 6 9; do cut -d'|' -f$c customers.dat.orig | tail -n +2 > /tmp/orig_$c.txt echo "column $c exact matches:" $(cut -d'|' -f$c customers.dat | tail -n +2 | grep -c -x -F -f /tmp/orig_$c.txt) done # 4. SSN shape (expect 0) and duplicates (expect 0) cut -d'|' -f6 customers.dat | tail -n +2 | grep -c -v -E '^[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{4}$' cut -d'|' -f6 customers.dat | tail -n +2 | sort | uniq -d | wc -l # 5. customer_id untouched diff <(cut -d'|' -f1 customers.dat.orig) <(cut -d'|' -f1 customers.dat) && echo ids identical # 6. no leftover temporary file, same owner and permissions ls -la Show a worked answer Expected results. Command 1: both files have 4 lines; the first line of the masked file is still the header. Command 2: 4 9 , meaning four lines with nine fields each. A different number means the delimiter or format is wrong, or a masked value contained the delimiter. Command 3: all zeros. The algorithms for email, phone, SSN and tax id are designed to change every value. Do not run this check for names: the docs allow a masked name to equal the original. Command 4: 0 and 0. x: 9.28 Common mistakes and gotchas Watch out for these Uploading real data as a "format". Format files are schema only. A copy of last week's feed in the format dialog puts real values in the engine. Forgetting that a format is shared. Editing fields or algorithm assignments for one file changes every file and rule set that uses the same format. Wrong delimiter or end-of-record. The job may succeed while masking the wrong text. Open the output and look. Header not declared. The header row is masked as if it were a customer. Field count mismatch. Extra fields are silently dropped and missing ones are padded with delimiters. Wrong fixed-width lengths. Every later field shifts. Count characters, not bytes. File name pattern that matches nothing. The job can still end in success, so read the Execution Components. Windows line endings in the format file. Use LF to avoid parsing failures. Assuming UTF-16 or other encodings work. The docs list ASCII and UTF-8 (UTF-8 for Parquet, EBCDIC for mainframe). Treating a masked file as safe without checking it. Run the verification commands and grep for known real values.

x: 9.29 Recap Key points Files have no built-in column names, so a file format definition (schema only) maps positions or names to fields. Formats are global and shared. Delimited files need a delimiter and end-of-record (and optionally an enclosure and escape strategy); fixed-width files need exact lengths. Record types with up to three qualifiers handle mixed layouts; header and footer counts protect unmasked lines. Connectors reach files by filesystem mount, SFTP, FTP or FTPS, S3, S3-compatible storage and Azure Blob; mainframe data needs EBCDIC and a copybook. A file rule set lists files or patterns and gives each its format, end-of-record and delimiter; the inventory assigns algorithms to fields. In-place file masking writes a hidden .msk file and replaces the original on success; on-the-fly writes to a separate target and is faster. Always verify the output file: line counts, field counts, original values gone, unique fields still unique. Delphix hands-on labs The earlier Delphix chapters taught the parts one at a time: the engine, connectors, rule sets and inventories, profiling, algorithms and files. Here you put them together in five labs, run in order on one small data set (ShopSphere), so that each lab leaves behind what the next one needs. The labs are the syllabus hands-ons for Days 51 to 56: TDM_Handson4 (connector to a VDB), 5 (connections and profiling), 6 (masking files), 7 (masking FirstName) and 8 (masking alphanumeric text, SSN and telephone number). Concepts are not re-taught; each lab links to the chapter that owns them. What you will learn How to prepare the same fake ShopSphere data in a database and in two file formats. Lab 4: create an environment and a connector that points at a VDB, and prove it works. Lab 5: build a rule set, run a profiling job, and correct the results in the inventory. Lab 6: mask a delimited and a fixed-width file. Labs 7 and 8: assign and verify algorithms for FirstName, alphanumeric text, SSN and phone with before/after queries. How to keep a checklist and an evidence pack that a reviewer can sign off. What this section is based on UI steps come from the Delphix Continuous Compliance 2026.5 documentation (last published October 16, 2026); the sources list names each page. The ShopSphere data, lab order, expected results and verification queries are my own illustrative design . marks a documented fact; "design" or marks my choices. The official screenshots come from different releases: the corner label in the images I opened reads 21.0.0.0, 22.0.0.0, 24.0.0.0, 26.0.0.0 and, in one, a development build number. Your engine will differ in labels, button order and extra fields, so read each screenshot as "what to look for". Your trainer's lab may also differ in database type, file access method or login method; where I do not know, I say so.

x: 9.30 Words to know first Masking engine The Delphix Continuous Compliance engine, where you define connectors, rule sets, profiling jobs and masking jobs. VDB (virtual database) A full read-and-write copy of source data that Delphix Continuous Data provisions from a dSource or another VDB. To the masking engine it is another database. See the Delphix overview and terminology chapter . Application and environment An application is a tag for the real system (here ShopSphere). An environment groups connectors, rule sets and jobs; its purpose is Mask or Tokenize/Re-Identify. Connector Saved details the engine uses to reach one database or file location ( connectors and VDB ). Rule set and inventory A rule set lists the tables or files to profile or mask. Its inventory records, per column or field, the domain and algorithm ( rule sets and keys ). Profiling job, domain A profiling job assigns a domain (a kind of sensitive data such as FIRST_NAME, with one default algorithm) to columns that look sensitive ( Delphix profiling ). In-place and on-the-fly In-place masking updates data where it sits; on-the-fly reads a source and writes masked values to a target ( algorithms and masking jobs ). Non-conformant data A value that does not fit what an algorithm expects. By default it is left unmasked and the job records a warning, so a "successful" job can still leave data exposed.

x: 9.32.1 The database Ask your trainer which database holds the lab copy. It must be one the engine may change: a VDB or other disposable copy, never SHOPSPHERE_PROD . The docs recommend a VDB as the masking target and call it the best security practice because it runs in a sandbox ( Preparing data ). Load the four ShopSphere tables with three customers (plus two or three orders each and a few items and products): CUSTOMERS in the lab VDB (fake data; tax_id values invented for this lab) customer_id first_name last_name phone ssn zip_code tax_id 1001 Asha Menon 9876543210 123-45-6789 560001 ABCDE1234F 1002 Ravi Kumar 9123456780 234-56-7890 600017 PQRST5678K 1003 Meera Nair 9988776655 345-67-8901 682001 LMNOP9012Q The table omits email and date_of_birth for width; the other columns are as in the running example. Take the "before" snapshot now and save the output: SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name, phone, ssn, zip_code, tax_id FROM customers ORDER BY customer_id; SELECT COUNT(*) AS orphans FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL; The orphan query counts orders whose customer is missing. It must return 0 before and after masking; if it is not 0 now, the "keys survived" check later means nothing. A masking job can report success while a column was never masked, so only a comparison of the data proves the work: the snapshot is the left-hand side of that proof.

x: 9.33.1 Goal and prerequisites Create an application, an environment and a database connector so that the engine can reach the ShopSphere VDB, and prove the connection works. Every later lab depends on it. You need the setup data and "before" snapshot, plus from your trainer or DBA: database type, host, port, database name, schema, and a masking user and password. A wrong guess here is the most common reason Test Connection fails. What "a connector to a VDB" means. The documentation pages I read describe database connectors and describe a VDB as a database that Delphix Continuous Data provisions ( Delphix masking terminology ); they describe no special "VDB connector". My reading, to confirm with your trainer, is that you create an ordinary database connector and point it at the VDB's host, port and database name. In-place masking rewrites data, so doing it on a disposable VDB keeps production untouched. (Masking as part of VDB provisioning is a separate setup with restrictions, described on Provision masked VDBs ; this lab does not use it.)

x: 9.35.3 Steps Create two file connectors. In the new environment open Connectors, click + Connection, and choose a File source type: Delimited for SS_Delim_Conn and Fixed Width for SS_Fixed_Conn . The type matters because it decides what the rule set will ask for later. For SFTP the credential step asks for Path (the directory that holds the files), Server Name, Port and User Name, plus Password or a public key. The docs add that, from version 6.0.9.0, an "User Directory as root" option exists when the path is relative to the SFTP user's home directory. Test the connection if the wizard offers it. Both connectors appear under the FILE group in the Connectors grid, with types Delimited and Fixed Width. Write the two format files. The docs say the engine needs a description of the fields and that a format file contains only the structure, never production data or personal information. For a delimited file the format file lists the field names, one per line, with no header. For a fixed-width file each line is a field name, a comma and the field length. The two official sketches below show the shape. My versions for ShopSphere, saved as ss_delim.fmt and ss_fixed.fmt : customer_id first_name last_name ssn phone customer_id,4 first_name,10 last_name,10 ssn,11 phone,10 Give the fields meaningful names. The profiler uses names (and, with ASDD, values) to decide what is sensitive, so first_name is findable and FIELD_03 is not. On Windows, save with LF line endings, because the docs warn that CRLF files can fail the engine's validation. Official screenshot: the contents of an example delimited file format: only field names, one per line, no header. Source page ↗ Official screenshot: an example fixed-width format file: field name, comma, length. Note SSN has length 11, which is exactly the width of 123-45-6789 with its dashes. Source page ↗ Import the formats. Go to Settings, Data Formats, tab Files, click + File Format. The wizard asks for the Format Type, then the file to import (a custom name is optional), then, for delimited and fixed-width formats only, the number of header and footer records (leave them empty: the lab files have none), and ends with a Summary. Save. Do this twice, once per file type. Both formats appear in the Data Formats grid with their Type (Delimited or Fixed Width). Official screenshot: Settings, Data Formats. Each row has export, duplicate and delete icons. Remember what the docs say: a file inventory belongs to its format, so editing a format changes every file that uses it. Source page ↗ Create a flat-file rule set for each file. In the environment's Rule Sets tab click + Rule Set, choose Flat Files, and pick the matching connector. In the Data Files step click Add File Name, tick customers.dat (or customers_fixed.txt ), and set its properties: Format File (ss_delim.fmt or ss_fixed.fmt), End of Record (Linux LF unless the file came from Windows), and, for the delimited file, the Delimiter | . Text Enclosure stays empty because the sample has no quotes. Save as SS_Delim_RS and SS_Fixed_RS . Each rule set lists one file with its format and delimiter. Official screenshot: the Data Files step of a flat-file rule set. The columns are the properties you set per file. The sample rows are test data from the docs team, not a pattern to copy. Source page ↗ Profile both rule sets. Create one profiling job per rule set exactly as in Lab 5 (+ Profiling Job, rule set, ASDD Standard) and run them. ASDD supports delimited and fixed-width files. The results grid lists File Name, Field Name, Algorithm and Domain. Fields first_name, last_name, ssn and phone get domains. If the field names in your format were meaningless, only a data-level match could find them. Official screenshot: a completed profiling job on a fixed-width file. DATA_00 and DATA_01 have uninformative names yet were still classified as TELEPHONE_NO (dlpx-core:Phone Unique) and EMAIL (dlpx-core:Email Unique): the engine inspected the values. Open each rule set's inventory, choose the file format in the drop-down if asked, and edit the fields: first_name gets dlpx-core:FirstName , last_name gets dlpx-core:LastName , ssn gets dlpx-core:CM Digits (the reason is in Lab 8). x: 9.35.4 Verification checks Run these in a shell on the folder that holds both the masked and the original files: diff original/customers.dat customers.dat awk -F'|' '{print NF}' customers.dat | sort | uniq -c awk '{print length($0)}' customers_fixed.txt | sort | uniq -c diff <(cut -c1-4,36-45 original/customers_fixed.txt) <(cut -c1-4,36-45 customers_fixed.txt) The last command compares only the customer_id (characters 1 to 4) and phone (characters 36 to 45) columns of the fixed-width file. It should print nothing. It needs a shell that supports process substitution, such as bash. Names and SSN differ between original and masked, and the SSN still looks like ddd-dd-dddd . customer_id and phone are identical to the original (they were out of scope). Every line of the delimited file has 5 fields, and every line of the fixed-width file is still 45 characters. A different count means the masked value did not fit the field or the format did not match the data. Row count is unchanged: 3 lines in each file. Consistency: save the masked files as run1 , copy the originals back into the working folder, run both jobs again, and run diff against the run1 copies. It should print nothing, because the docs describe the Name and Character Mapping frameworks as deterministic for the same configuration and key.

CREATE TABLE customers_before AS SELECT * FROM customers; INSERT INTO customers (customer_id, first_name, last_name, email, phone, ssn, date_of_birth, zip_code, tax_id) VALUES (1004, 'Asha', 'Iyer', 'asha.i@example.com', 'CALL-ME-NOW', 'N/A', '1992-01-15', '560002', NULL); INSERT INTO customers_before SELECT * FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 1004; Customer 1004 has the same first name as 1001. x: 9.36.3 Steps Make a rule set that contains only today's masking. A masking job masks every column that has an algorithm in the inventory. After Lab 5 your inventory has eight columns assigned. To mask only first_name, duplicate the rule set (the row's actions menu, Duplicate), name the copy SS_DB_RS_FN , and open its inventory. The docs say a copy includes the inventory and any filters. Use the "Clear Masking Assignment" icon on each assigned row (it works per column, as in the profiling chapter): the docs say it removes that assignment and disables automatic updates, after a short confirmation bar. Then edit first_name only. The inventory shows an algorithm for first_name and blank algorithm cells for every other column. Assign the algorithm. Edit CUSTOMERS.first_name: untick Enable Automatic Updates, Domain FIRST_NAME, Algorithm dlpx-core:FirstName , Save. This is the algorithm the profiler proposed in the official profiling screenshot, so you are confirming, not inventing. What the FirstName algorithm does (from its docs page) It is an instance of the Name framework and needs string input. Null, empty and whitespace-only values are returned unmasked, and it raises no non-conformant-data errors. A single character is treated as an abbreviation and masked to a single character. By default at most two names are masked and returned, and leading and trailing white space is not preserved. It is deterministic for the same configuration and key and it is not unique: collisions are possible, and a masked value can even equal the input ( FirstName , Name framework ). The Name framework page adds that its default comparison is case-insensitive, so "Peter" and "peter" mask to the same value. Create the masking job. Jobs tab, + Masking Job. Job Name SS_Mask_FirstName . Masking Method: In-Place. Rule Set: SS_DB_RS_FN. Leave "Stop job on first occurrence" off and Multi Tenant off. Next, the database options: Commit Size and Update Threads can stay default; the docs warn that several update threads can cause deadlocks, especially on tables without an index. Do not tick Disable Constraints, Drop Indexes or Disable Triggers: first_name is not a key. Number of Streams: 1. Save. Official screenshot: the Details step of Create Masking Job. The three choices that matter today are Job Name, Masking Method and Rule Set. The small print under "Stop job on first occurrence" says it works only when non-conforming data is set to fail the job. Open the job name from Monitor, Job Executions. The Execution Summary counts tables and rows masked and, importantly, tables and columns with non-conforming data. The Events list shows the stages in order, from initialising and collecting configuration to job completed. Execution Components lists each table with progress and rows per minute. Masking Completed, one table masked (CUSTOMERS), rows masked equal to the row count (4), nonconforming data 0. Official screenshot: a finished masking job. Left: Execution Summary (tables masked, rows masked, tables and columns with nonconforming data). Top right: the event sequence. SELECT COUNT(*) AS unchanged FROM customers c JOIN customers_before b ON b.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE c.first_name = b.first_name; -- 3. same input, same output (1001 and 1004 are both Asha) SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT first_name) AS distinct_masked FROM customers WHERE customer_id IN (1001, 1004); -- 4. nothing else changed SELECT COUNT(*) AS other_changes FROM customers c JOIN customers_before b ON b.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE c.last_name <> b.last_name OR c.phone <> b.phone OR c.ssn <> b.ssn; Query 1 shows a different name on every row. Query 2 should return 0, but it is not guaranteed to: the docs say the masked value can equal the input. If one row matches, record it and move on; it is a property of the algorithm, not a failure. Query 3 returns 1: both Asha rows got the same masked name. Query 4 returns 0 and the "orphans" query from the setup still returns 0. ct: Delphix (2): algorithms, file masking and hands-on labs
x: 9.37.3 Choosing the algorithms The choice column below separates what the docs state from what I decided. The default algorithm for the SSN domain is not stated in the pages I read, so confirm it in Settings, Domains instead of relying on my memory of any product. Column Algorithm Basis in the docs Design choice or caution membership_code (alphanumeric text) dlpx-core:CM Alpha-Numeric Masks ASCII digits, lower and upper case letters, keeps other characters; for non-numeric data types. Example: "ABCxyz123" becomes "HANwhp391" The "SS-" prefix will be masked too. To keep it, a custom Character Mapping instance with a preserve range is the documented route ssn (text, ddd-dd-dddd) dlpx-core:CM Digits Masks every digit and keeps letters and punctuation; Character Mapping gives one-to-one output for text inputs and is deterministic until the key changes My choice. Segment Mapping with dashes ignored is the other documented option for SSNs. The docs I read do not say outputs follow US SSN validity rules phone (10 digits) dlpx-core:Phone US Keeps the first digits, replaces the three digits before the last four with 555, and masks the last four with a hash of the digits; other characters are preserved; input up to 30 symbols and at least one digit My choice for a clearly fake number. Phone Unique (last 7 digits hashed) was the profiler's own pick in the official screenshot; the page does not promise uniqueness Pages: CM Alpha-Numeric , CM Digits , Phone US , Character Mapping and Segment Mapping .

For each of the three columns, Edit, untick Enable Automatic Updates, set Domain (membership_code has no built-in domain: pick one that fits or leave the domain empty as your engine allows) and Algorithm, Save. Three assigned rows, every other column blank. Create and run the job SS_Mask_Sensitive . In-place, rule set SS_DB_RS_Sens, defaults elsewhere. Take the snapshot first. Run it. The status is WARNING (non-conformant) rather than SUCCEEDED, because customer 1004's SSN and phone do not fit. This is the expected outcome in this lab. Read the warning. Open the job, then View Logs on the CUSTOMERS row in Execution Components. The docs say each event shows Event type UNMASKED_DATA (or JOB_ABORTED), Cause PATTERN_MATCH_FAILURE, a row count and the column name, and that only a pattern of the bad value is shown (L for letters, N for digits, P for punctuation), never the value itself. x: 9.39 Common mistakes and gotchas Mistakes that cost the most time Masking a database you cannot restore. Cancelling a running in-place job leaves semi-masked data, the docs warn. Snapshot first. Believing SUCCEEDED means "all masked". Non-conformant values are skipped by default; read the non-conforming-data line of the summary every time. Running a rule set with leftover assignments. A job masks every assigned column in its rule set. Letting the profiler overwrite your choice. Untick Enable Automatic Updates before assigning by hand. Trusting a file format without checking the data. A wrong field count or length silently drops or shifts data, and editing a shared format changes every file that uses it. Using a non-unique algorithm where uniqueness matters. Name and lookup-style algorithms can collide; Character Mapping is the documented unique-output family.

x: 9.40 Recap Recap The labs form a chain: connector, rule set and profile, files, FirstName, then text, SSN and phone. A "connector to a VDB" is an ordinary database connector pointed at a VDB, a safe place to mask. Profiling proposes; the inventory is where you decide. Turn off automatic updates before overriding. Files need a format file: field names for delimited, names and lengths for fixed-width. Verify with before/after queries, not job status alone. Explain every warning before sign-off. CM Digits and CM Alpha-Numeric keep format with unique text output; Phone US gives fake but plausible numbers; FirstName is realistic but not unique. Evidence is what you hand a reviewer, with each choice marked "docs" or "mine". ct: Putting it together: real engagements, the capstone and the glossary
h: Putting it together: real engagements, the capstone and the glossary
x: Planning a real TDM engagement: use cases, POC, assessment and sign-off Knowing how to run a masking job is one skill. Getting a company to trust you with its data, agreeing what "done" means, and leaving behind something the audit team accepts is another, and it is the one that decides whether a TDM project survives. This section is about that second skill. It turns the syllabus items on end-to-end plan development into templates you can fill in: a use-case questionnaire, a data inventory, a sensitivity assessment, a tool-selection matrix, a proof-of-concept (POC) plan, an assessment report, a risk register, a deployment plan, a sign-off checklist, a RACI table, KPIs, and a final-presentation outline. Everything is worked through with ShopSphere, the fictional online retailer. The numbers and names are invented to show the shape of each document. Where a statement is about what a tool can do, it comes from the sources I read and is marked. Everything else is common project practice and is labelled . What you will learn How the Day 43, 48, 54 and 57 syllabus items fit one life cycle: discover, assess, choose a tool, prove it, plan, deploy, sign off, present. How to ask the right questions to find TDM use cases, and how to record the answers. How to inventory a data landscape and rate the sensitivity of each column. How Informatica TDM, GenRocket and Delphix differ on what each is best at, using the three sources. How to write a POC plan with success criteria that can be measured. What goes into an assessment report, a risk register, a deployment plan and a sign-off checklist. Who does what (RACI), what to measure (KPIs), how projects fail, and how to present the result. What this section is based on statements about the tools come from the Informatica TDM 10.5.10 User Guide (PDF, February 2026, 455 pages), cited as (User Guide 10.5.10, p.NN); the Delphix Continuous Compliance 2026.5 documentation (last published October 16, 2026); and the GenRocket help centre pages named in the sources list. The templates, scoring examples, KPIs, RACI and ShopSphere figures are or my own illustration, not from any vendor. Real organisations use their own formats. x: 10.1 Words to know first Engagement One piece of TDM work for one client or business unit, from first conversation to hand-over. ShopSphere's "protect QA data" project is an engagement. Use case A specific situation where test data causes a problem, written in terms of who needs what data and why. "QA needs 90 days of orders without real customer identities" is a use case. TDG Test data generation: creating synthetic data instead of copying real data. The syllabus abbreviates it that way on Day 48. LOB Line of business: one business area with its own applications and data, such as ShopSphere's order management. Technology landscape The list of systems, databases, files and interfaces that hold or move the data in scope. The "map" you draw before you choose tools. POC (proof of concept) A small, time-boxed trial of the chosen approach on a slice of real systems, to show it works before a full rollout. Assessment A structured review of an application and its data environment, ending in a written report with findings and recommendations. Sign-off Formal written approval by named people that agreed criteria have been met. Success criteria Measurable statements that decide pass or fail, agreed before the POC starts. Risk register A living table of things that could go wrong, with likelihood, impact, owner and mitigation. RACI A table that marks, for each task, who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted or Informed. KPI Key performance indicator: a number you track to show whether TDM is helping. BU SME Business-unit subject-matter expert. The syllabus says the BU SME evaluates the final project deliverables.

h: 10.2 The life cycle in one picture
x: 10.2 The life cycle in one picture A real engagement moves through the same stages every time, whether the goal is masking or generation. The stages differ in depth, not in order. 1. Use cases what hurts, for whom → 2. Landscape systems and data → 3. Sensitivity what needs protecting → 4. Tool choice matrix and scoring 5. POC prove it on a slice → 6. Assessment report on the LOB → 7. Plan and deploy phases, runbook → 8. Sign-off evidence and approval Why plan before touching a tool The costly mistakes in TDM are decided early: masking a column that is never used, missing a file that carries the same SSN, picking a tool that cannot read the main database, or promising "all sensitive data masked" without agreeing how to measure it. Each of those is cheap to fix on paper and very expensive after the first refresh has reached 200 testers.

ct: Putting it together: real engagements, the capstone and the glossary
x: 10.2.1 Two plans: generation (Day 48) and masking Masking plan Starts from existing data. The central question: which real data can we safely make available, and how do we prove it is protected? Heavy on: landscape, sensitivity rating, algorithm choice, referential integrity, evidence. Generation (TDG) plan Starts from a model of the data. The central question: what shape of data do the tests need, and how much? Heavy on: data model, rules and patterns, volumes, edge cases, repeatability. The tools themselves draw the same line. In Informatica TDM a data generation operation needs a separate plan: the guide says generation cannot be combined with masking or subsetting in the same plan (User Guide 10.5.10, p.33). GenRocket describes its own method as Model, Design, Deploy, Manage ( The GenRocket Methodology ; the page itself carries only a video). Many engagements need both: mask the customer data, generate the data that never existed.

x: 10.3 Finding the use cases A tool can only solve a problem someone has named. The questionnaire below is how you collect the problems. Ask it in short interviews with QA, development, DBA, security and compliance people, not by email. Write the answers down in the same table every time. # Question Why you ask Ask U1 Which test environments exist (dev, QA, UAT, performance, training), and what data does each hold today? Shows where real data may already be sitting QA lead, DBA U2 How does data reach each environment (full copy, backup restore, extract, manual script)? How long does it take and how often? Gives the baseline for provisioning and refresh time DBA, TDM engineer U3 Who can see each environment's data (employees, contractors, vendors, offshore teams)? Decides the severity of exposure Security, compliance U4 Which fields are personal, financial, health or secret? Which regulations apply (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI, others)? Sets what must be protected (see the sensitive data chapter ) Compliance officer U5 What test cases fail or are skipped today because the right data is missing? Finds generation use cases QA engineers U6 Which tests need volume (performance, load) or rare conditions (edge cases, negative cases)? Shows where synthetic data beats a copy Performance tester, QA U7 Which data must stay realistic and linked (same customer across systems, valid-looking IDs)? Defines the integrity requirements for masking Developers, data steward U8 How many defects in the last year were caused by wrong, stale or missing test data? Gives the business case and a KPI baseline QA lead U9 What else will need the data: demos, training, third-party sandboxes, analytics? Widens the scope early Product owner U10 What already exists: scripts, masking tools, virtualization, licences? Avoids duplicating or fighting an existing tool IT manager U11 What would "success" look like in six months, in numbers? Seeds the success criteria Sponsor

x: 10.4 Mapping the technology landscape Day 54 asks you to analyse the technology landscape. In practice that is a table: every place where in-scope data lives or moves, who owns it, and which environments it feeds. Draw it before choosing tools, because a tool that cannot reach one of the rows leaves a hole in the protection. ShopSphere landscape inventory (illustrative) ID System or store Type Holds Feeds Refresh Owner L1 SHOPSPHERE_PROD Relational database (engine to confirm) CUSTOMERS, ORDERS, ORDER_ITEMS, PRODUCTS QA, UAT, PERF copies Monthly full copy, about 3 days DBA team L2 QA and UAT databases Relational database Copies of L1 Testers, contractors On refresh QA lead L3 customers.dat Delimited file Customer id, names, SSN, phone Marketing partner's test system Nightly Marketing IT L4 billing_fixed.txt Fixed-width file Customer id, name, tax id Finance test system Monthly Finance IT Then check each row against what the tools can read. The sources say: Informatica TDM builds subsets from relational, flat file or XSD sources (User Guide 10.5.10, p.112). Delphix lists Fixed Width, Delimited, XML, JSON and Parquet files as supported ( Files connector ) and databases through its connectors. GenRocket's G-Subset subsets and masks MySQL, MSSQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, DB2, Sybase and Databricks, but only between databases of the same type ( G-Subset overview ). A row that no candidate tool reads goes straight into the risk register. The same SSN appears in L1, L3 and L4. That is the central integrity requirement: whatever masks it must give the same result everywhere, or the partner's test data no longer joins to ShopSphere's. The masking concepts are in the masking concepts chapter .

x: 10.5 Sensitivity assessment For each column in scope, decide whether it is sensitive, how badly, and what to do. Do not trust column names alone: both Informatica and Delphix profile the data itself as well as the names. Informatica discovers data domains by patterns in data or metadata (User Guide 10.5.10, p.31). Delphix's ASDD profiler adds data-level classifiers, which found fields called DATA_00 and DATA_01 as phone and email in an official screenshot (see the Delphix labs chapter ). A simple, defensible rating is impact if leaked (1 to 3) times exposure in test (1 to 3). Sensitivity assessment for CUSTOMERS (illustrative ratings) Column Category Impact Exposure Score Decision Integrity need customer_id Key 1 3 3 Keep (do not mask) Primary key; foreign key in ORDERS first_name, last_name Personal 2 3 6 Mask Realistic; same input, same output email Personal 2 3 6 Mask Valid shape; unique if used as a login phone Personal 2 3 6 Mask Same digit count ssn National ID 3 3 9 Mask Format ddd-dd-dddd; same value everywhere tax_id Tax identifier 3 3 9 Mask Format kept; consistent across L1 and L4 date_of_birth Personal 2 3 6 Mask (shift) Still a valid date and plausible age zip_code Location 1 3 3 Mask or coarsen 6 digits; region may need to stay for tax tests total_amount Business 1 3 3 Keep Sums must still reconcile The decision rule (my illustration): score 6 or more gets masked; below that is a business discussion. The compliance officer, not the TDM engineer, owns the final "keep" decisions. Record each decision with a reason, because it will be questioned in the sign-off.

h: 10.6.1 Turning the matrix into a decision

List criteria, give each a weight, score each tool 1 to 5 from POC evidence, and multiply. The weights below are a template. Criterion Weight Informatica GenRocket Delphix Reaches every row of the landscape 5 score after POC score after POC score after POC Masking quality and integrity (format, consistency) 5 Generation of volume and edge cases 3 Delivery speed to testers 4 Team skills, licences and cost 3 Automation and audit evidence 3 For ShopSphere, UC1, UC2 and UC6 are masking and subset use cases, so the masking tool is chosen by the score, with existing licences and the VDB question (U10) usually deciding close results. x: 10.7 The proof of concept A POC answers one question: will this approach work here, on our data, with our people? It is small on purpose. It uses a copy, never production, and it ends with a pass or fail against criteria written before it started. A POC without agreed criteria turns into a demo that everyone declares a success.

ID Criterion Measured by Threshold Gate S1 Every sensitive column found and masked Inventory export plus before/after query 8 of 8 columns changed Must S2 Keys survive Orphan query on ORDERS 0 orphans; row counts unchanged Must S3 Formats preserved Pattern queries (SSN, tax id, phone, zip) 100% match the original pattern Must S4 Same value, same masked value everywhere Compare the SSN in the database and in the file 0 mismatches Must S5 No unexplained warnings Job summary: tables or columns with non-conforming data 0, or each explained in writing Must S6 No real value left behind Search the masked output for five known real test values 0 found Must S7 Evidence accepted Compliance officer reviews the evidence pack Signed Must S8 Time to a usable masked copy Stopwatch from start of run to verified copy Report against the 3-day baseline Reported S5 exists because of how the tools behave. x: 10.10 The deployment plan A deployment plan turns a successful POC into a repeatable service. It names phases, the condition for entering and leaving each one, and who owns it. Phase Main activities Exit condition P0 Mobilise Approve scope and success criteria; accounts and approvals; baseline KPIs measured Signed charter and baseline P1 Prepare Size and install the tool; network routes; masking database users with only needed rights; backup and restore tested Smoke test: connect, profile one table P2 Configure Connectors, rule sets, profiling, inventory review, algorithms, keys or seeds, roles; for Informatica, policies, projects and plans Inventory approved by the data steward P3 Pilot the LOB Run the full LOB in one environment; verify with the POC criteria Evidence pack accepted P4 Roll out Remaining environments and files; schedule jobs; connect to the refresh process; train users Sign-off checklist complete P5 Operate Monitor jobs, re-profile on releases, report KPIs, review risks Quarterly review Some tool features support promotion. Delphix lets you export an environment, with its connectors, rule sets and jobs, and import it into another masking engine; the docs say moving environments between engines is the main reason ( Managing environments ). It also offers an inventory approval workflow that makes an approver sign off a database inventory before any masking job can run. Informatica generates a workflow from a plan and runs it (User Guide 10.5.10, p.32). Use these to move work from the pilot to production setups without re-typing it.

x: 10.10.1 The refresh runbook The safest ordering is: copy into a closed area, mask, verify, and only then open the copy to testers. Nobody sees unmasked data at any point. Delphix's masked provisioning enforces a version of this for supported databases by masking during VDB provisioning (see Provision masked VDBs ). Request tester asks for a refresh → Copy into a closed area → Mask run the approved job → Verify queries and warnings → Release open to testers

x: 10.10.2 The generation (TDG) deployment plan For Day 48 the same phases apply with different content. GenRocket describes a hybrid design: modelling and design happen in the cloud component, and the data itself is generated locally in the on-premises component ( GenRocket architecture ). Its five components are domain, attribute, generator, receiver and scenario ( five key components ). Step For ShopSphere Model Domains for CUSTOMERS, ORDERS, ORDER_ITEMS, PRODUCTS; attributes per column; parent-child links Design A generator per attribute, scenarios for UC3 to UC5, volumes (5 million orders), boundary and null cases (see the data patterns chapter ) Deploy Runtime on the generation machine, a receiver that loads the QA database or writes files, access to the target Manage Version the scenarios, rerun on schema change, track generation time and test coverage gained

x: 10.16 Recap Recap Every engagement follows one life cycle: use cases, landscape, sensitivity, tool choice, POC, assessment, deployment, sign-off. Generation (Day 48) and masking (Day 54) differ in emphasis, not order. Find use cases by interviewing; record them in a register with a type and priority. Inventory the landscape and rate each column; check every row against what the tools can read. The three tools have different centres of gravity: Informatica TDM is one console for discover, subset, mask and generate; GenRocket is synthetic generation, with G-Subset for subsetting and masking; Delphix pairs masking with virtual copies. Gaps in the sources mean "not covered", not "not possible". A POC needs measurable criteria, a copy, and a pass or fail decision made in advance. The assessment, risk register, deployment plan and sign-off checklist turn the POC into a service. Keep keys and seeds under change control, keep audit logs, define RACI and KPIs. Partnership and Cog IPs are organisation-specific: ask your trainer. Next: the capstone project applies these plans to three concrete activities. Capstone: the project case study The programme ends with a project, evaluated by the business-unit subject-matter expert (BU SME) in the final project evaluation and the final technical evaluation on Days 58 to 60. The syllabus lists three activities: data profiling and masking of FirstName and LastName; data profiling and a data subset; and data profiling and masking of SSN, alphanumeric values, TaxID and ZipCode. Daily progress tracking is good practice, so this section gives you a day-by-day plan, a brief for each activity, acceptance criteria you can test with queries, and the evidence to collect. Nothing new is taught here. Each step links to the chapter or lab that teaches it. What is new is the set of design decisions, mainly how to mask SSN, TaxID and ZipCode while keeping format and integrity. Every such decision is labelled as taken from the documentation or as my own design. What you will learn How to plan and track the project daily, from set-up to the final presentation. Which tool to use for each activity and why. For each activity: inputs, steps, acceptance criteria, test queries and evidence. Both are instances of the Name framework; they are deterministic, require string input, return null, empty and whitespace-only values unmasked, and are not unique, so a masked value may equal the input ( FirstName , LastName ). x: 10.20.2 Steps with Informatica TDM (primary) Create a project and import the metadata. The process (User Guide 10.5.10, pp.30 to 32) starts with a project and imported source metadata. See the Informatica tour . Profile keys and relationships. Run primary key and entity profiles where keys are not declared, and apply the results (p.31; the Informatica profiling chapter ). A subset follows relationships, so missing or undeclared ones (for example ORDER_ITEMS to PRODUCTS through product_code) give a broken subset. Create an entity with CUSTOMERS as the driving table. The guide says an entity is a driving table plus related tables, found by physical and logical constraints; you add filter criteria on a column, which can be a value or a parameter changed at run time (pp.113 to 114). Put the criterion on zip_code and check the Entity Map: confirm ORDERS, ORDER_ITEMS and PRODUCTS are present and the relationships are enabled. See the Informatica subset chapter . Create a subset plan, generate the workflow and run it. Add the entity to a plan with a target connection ( plans and workflows ). The guide notes a masking and a subset operation can share one plan (p.32), which is what a real project would do so the subset is never exposed unmasked. Run the Row Count Report on the plan: it lists the tables and rows each plan affects (p.324). Keep it as evidence. Alternatives, to name but not use as primary. Delphix rule sets accept a per-table filter ( customers.zip_code LIKE '560%' , with the table prefix on the column, as the docs show) or custom SQL that must include the key columns; the pages I read do not describe following related tables automatically, so related-table filters would be yours to write ( Managing rule sets ). GenRocket's G-Subset subsets by a where clause, percentage or row count, supports no composite keys, and migrates only between databases of the same type ( G-Subset overview ).

x: 10.21.1 Brief Goal. Mask four kinds of identifying value so the data stays useful: formats are kept, the same real value always becomes the same masked value, and keys and joins still work. Inputs. CUSTOMERS with ssn, membership_code, tax_id and zip_code; the customer extract customers.dat (which carries the SSN); the "before" copy; and the edge row 1004 with SSN N/A . Tool. Delphix primary; Informatica as a cross-check. Output. Four verified columns, an algorithm sheet where every line says "docs" or "design", and the evidence. The word "integrity" has two meanings here, and you must show both. Referential integrity : foreign keys still match. None of these four columns is a key, so the safest decision is not to mask any key at all. Consistency : the same SSN or TaxID appears in several places (the database and the extract file) and must mask to the same value everywhere, or joins between systems fail. Deterministic algorithms, with the same algorithm instance and key used everywhere, give consistency.

x: 10.21.2 Algorithm design, column by column The table separates what the sources say from what I chose. The default algorithm for the SSN, ZIP and TAX_ID domains is not stated in the Delphix pages I read; look at Settings, Domains on your engine and decide whether to keep or replace each default. Column Delphix choice What the docs state Design choice and cautions ssn 123-45-6789 dlpx-core:CM Digits Masks every ASCII digit anywhere in the string and keeps letters and punctuation; it is an instance of Character Mapping, which is deterministic until rekeyed, and gives no two text inputs the same output ( CM Digits , Character Mapping ) Chosen for format keeping and uniqueness. Caution: on a numeric column leading zeros are not significant, so collisions can occur ("7" and "007"); the docs advise CM Numeric for numeric types. Nothing I read says the output obeys US SSN validity rules ssn, alternative Segment Mapping instance, dashes ignored The docs name SSNs as a use for Segment Mapping, say it produces no repeats if the allowed output range is at least as large as the input range, and allow ignoring dashes and preserving segments such as the last four digits ( Segment Mapping ) Use if you need position-specific rules. Configuration sketch below membership_code SS-A7K29X dlpx-core:CM Alpha-Numeric Masks ASCII digits and upper and lower case letters, preserves other characters; for non-numeric types; at least one maskable character per value, else a warning; "ABCxyz123" becomes "HANwhp391" ( CM Alpha-Numeric ) Digits stay digits and letters stay letters, but the "SS-" prefix is masked too. To keep it, a Character Mapping instance with a preserve range of length 2 (see zip below) tax_id 98-7654321 A Character Mapping instance with group [0-9] (or CM Digits) Digits are mapped within the group and the hyphen, being outside it, is kept A separate instance gives TaxID its own key, so that SSN and TaxID values with equal digits do not mask alike. Use the same instance for the database and any file that carries TaxID zip_code 560001 A Character Mapping instance: group [0-9] , preserve range start 0 length 3, forward The preserve-range parameter exists: positions count only maskable characters, start at 0, and cannot be combined with preserve-leading-zeros Keeping the first three digits keeps the region, which is a privacy trade-off: postal codes are partly identifying, so the compliance officer must approve it. Store as text. For US ZIP+4 values, RepeatFirstDigit masks only the "+4" part ( RepeatFirstDigit ) To create the custom instances in the UI (Settings, Algorithms, + Algorithm): enter a unique name, choose the Character Mapping framework, add the character group, tick Case Sensitive if relevant, set Minimum Masked Positions, and add the preserve range. Through the API the shape is as below. The framework ids differ between engines, so look them up first with GET /algorithm/frameworks ; the field names are from the documentation examples. { "algorithmName": "SS_ZipKeepRegion", "algorithmType": "COMPONENT", "frameworkId": <Character Mapping id>, "algorithmExtension": { "caseSensitive": true, "characterGroups": ["0123456789"], "minMaskedPositions": 1, "preserveLeadingZeros": false, "preserveRanges": [ { "start": 0, "length": 3, "direction": "FORWARD" } ] } } { "algorithmName": "SS_SSN_Seg", "algorithmType": "COMPONENT", "frameworkId": <Segment Mapping id>, "algorithmExtension": { "autoIgnoreCharacters": true, "allowShortSegments": false, "segments": [ { "length": 3, "segmentType": "MASK_NUMERIC" }, { "length": 2, "segmentType": "MASK_NUMERIC" }, { "length": 4, "segmentType": "MASK_NUMERIC" } ] } } The Segment Mapping sketch masks the three groups of digits separately and ignores the dashes. Left at its default ranges it may produce area numbers such as 000, which real SSNs never use. Restricting ranges is possible (the docs describe input and mask value ranges), but if input and mask ranges differ, values outside the input range are left unmasked and the mapping is no longer reversible for tokenization, so test it before relying on it.

x: 10.22 Common mistakes and gotchas Where capstones lose marks Masking a key to "be safe". It breaks joins. Leave keys alone unless the same deterministic algorithm is applied on both sides. Different algorithms for the same value. An SSN masked differently in the database and the file ruins consistency; reuse one instance. Numeric columns and leading zeros. Digit masking on a numeric zip or tax id can collide; keep such values as text or use the numeric algorithm. Trusting profiling for six-digit postal codes. The documented ZIP data patterns target US formats; the column name does the work. A subset left unmasked. It is real data; say how it will be masked. Presenting design choices as product facts. "CM Digits is the SSN algorithm" is false; "I chose CM Digits for SSN because..." is right.

x: 10.23 Recap Recap The project has three activities: names, subset, and SSN, alphanumeric values, TaxID and ZipCode. Plan them over daily steps and log progress every day. Use Delphix for the masking activities and Informatica for the subset, with the other tool as a cross-check and GenRocket for fake source rows; follow your trainer if the assignment differs. Every activity has acceptance criteria that a query or report can prove. Format-preserving, deterministic algorithms (CM Digits, CM Alpha-Numeric, a Character Mapping instance with a preserve range, or Informatica key masking with a mask format and seed) keep shape and consistency. Segment Mapping and Informatica SSN masking are documented alternatives with their own limits. Integrity means both intact foreign keys and the same value masked the same way in every system. A subset is real data until it is masked. Label every decision as documented or designed, and explain every warning. Glossary This glossary collects the terms used in the guide, in plain words, with a pointer to the section that explains each one. Use it when a word in a tool chapter feels unfamiliar: find the group that matches where you met it, scan the alphabetical list, then follow the link for the full explanation and the examples. Terms are alphabetical within each group. General ideas come first, then privacy, then ETL, then one group per tool. Tool-specific terms carry the tool name in brackets, for example "(Delphix)". The same word often means different things in different tools, so each tool gets its own entry. Same word, different tool A domain is a named kind of data found by patterns in Informatica, a kind of sensitive data with one default algorithm in Delphix, and a table-like thing you generate rows for in GenRocket. A rule changes data in Informatica, but a Delphix rule set only lists tables or files. Check the bracketed tool name before you trust a definition.

Section 10.17 Assessment A structured review of an application and its data environment, ending in a written report of findings and recommendations. Section 10.8 Audit trail A record of who ran what, when and with which settings, kept so compliance questions can be answered later. Section 2.16 Data subset A smaller copy of a database that still hangs together: fewer rows, same structure, referential integrity intact. Section 2.32 Discovery (data discovery) Finding out what a data source holds: which tables and columns exist, which are sensitive and how tables relate. x: 10.25 Privacy and regulation Anonymisation A goal: data that identifies no one, even in combination. Legal tests are strict, so masking alone does not guarantee it. Section 2.30 Business associate Under HIPAA, a vendor that handles PHI for a covered entity, such as a firm testing a hospital's billing system. Section 2.5 CCPA California Consumer Privacy Act: gives California residents rights over personal information businesses hold. Section 2.5 Compliance officer The person responsible for making sure the organisation follows laws and internal data rules. Section 2.9 Consent / lawful purpose Ideas shared by privacy laws: data needs a lawful reason, and testing is a different purpose from running the shop. Section 2.5 Covered entity Under HIPAA, a health plan, healthcare provider or healthcare clearinghouse. Section 2.5 Data classification Labelling data by how much damage a leak could do (for example public, internal, confidential, restricted) so protection fits. Section 2.6 Data minimisation Collecting and keeping no more data than needed. It is the legal argument for subsetting. Section 2.5 Data steward The person who knows a data set's meaning and quality and says what a column holds and who may see it. Section 2.9 De-identification Making data no longer point to a person. HIPAA names two ways: remove 18 listed identifier kinds, or get an expert to certify tiny risk. Section 2.5 Detection signals The clues tools use to find sensitive columns: column name, data pattern, list of values, plus type and length. Section 2.7 Direct identifier Data that points to one person on its own, such as an SSN. Section 2.4 DPDP Act India's 2023 consent-centred law on digital personal data. Rules are phased in, so check current status. Section 2.5 Especially sensitive data Data many laws treat as extra delicate, such as ethnic origin, religion, health or biometrics. Blanking it can beat faking it. Section 2.6 GDPR General Data Protection Regulation: EU law, applying since May 2018, covering personal data of people in the EU wherever the company sits. Section 2.5 HIPAA US law from 1996 whose Privacy and Security Rules protect health information that identifies a person. Section 2.5 Identifier A piece of data that points to one person, alone (direct) or in combination (indirect). Section 2.1 Indirect identifier (quasi-identifier) Data that identifies only in combination, such as zip code plus birth date plus gender. Section 2.4 Minimum necessary HIPAA idea: people and systems get only the least PHI their job needs. Testers rarely need the real thing. Section 2.5 PCI data Payment card details such as card number and expiry date. Section 2.3 PCI DSS Data Security Standard from the card brands for anyone handling card data. A contractual standard, not a law. Section 2.3 PHI (Protected Health Information) Health data that can be tied to a person. The link to an individual, not the diagnosis alone, makes it PHI. Section 2.3 PII (Personally Identifiable Information) Data that identifies a person alone or combined with other data, such as name, email, phone or government ID. Section 2.3 Pseudonymisation Replacing identifiers with pseudonyms while a way back exists elsewhere; still personal data under GDPR. Section 2.30 Regular expression (regex) A compact text recipe for a pattern, for example three digits, a hyphen, two digits, a hyphen, four digits. Section 2.7 Re-identification Working out who a "nameless" record belongs to by combining it with other information. Section 2.4 Sensitive data Data that could hurt a person or company if leaked or misused. "Sensitive" is a business and legal judgement. Section 2.2

Section 3.27 Batch processing Collecting data for a period and processing it as one group; easy to re-run. Nearly all test data provisioning is batch. Section 3.19 Cleaning Making values consistent so equal things look equal, such as "MENON" and "Menon ".
